subject: life-sciences
description: Life Sciences FET (Grades 10-12) consolidated bank. Topics keyed by atomic skill id (from data/life-sciences-skill-tree.json). Each pool = 20 items spread across CAPS Aims 1.1 Recall, 1.2 Understand, 1.3 Apply, 1.4/2.6 Analyse-data, and 3 IK/Applications. Input types: choice, true-false, cloze, match, sequence, scenario, diagram-label, data-interpret. FET rule: no timer, 60% pass mark.

LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A1.title: Inorganic compounds, food tests and nutritional analysis
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A1.description: Water, minerals, deficiency diseases, fertilisers/eutrophication, food tests (iodine, Benedict's, Biuret), RDA analysis.
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A1.recovery_strategy: Each mineral = one role + one deficiency. Water = solvent + transport + temperature. Eutrophication = run-off → bloom → O2 drop → fish die. Food tests: iodine→starch (blue-black), Benedict's+HEAT→sugars (orange), Biuret→protein (purple), translucent→lipids.

questions.question: Which of these is the MAIN inorganic compound in a living cell?
questions.expected: Water
questions.memo: About 70% of a cell is water. Glucose, protein and DNA are organic (they all contain carbon).

questions.question: Water in living cells is mostly used as a:
questions.expected: Solvent for chemical reactions
questions.memo: Nearly all biological reactions happen dissolved in water. Energy comes from glucose/lipids; genes from DNA; fats from glycerol + fatty acids.

questions.question: Which mineral is needed to make haemoglobin?
questions.expected: Iron (Fe)
questions.memo: Iron sits at the centre of each haem group, which carries oxygen in red blood cells. Deficiency causes anaemia.

questions.question: Which mineral deficiency causes goitre?
questions.expected: Iodine (I)
questions.memo: The thyroid uses iodine to make thyroid hormone. Too little iodine → the gland enlarges (goitre). This is why SA table salt is iodised.

questions.question: Calcium is needed mainly for:
options: Strong bones and teeth, and muscle contraction
questions.expected: Strong bones and teeth, and muscle contraction
questions.memo: 99% of body calcium is in bone and teeth. The rest is essential for muscle contraction and nerve signals.

questions.question: True or false: All mineral elements are needed in large amounts (macro elements).
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Macro elements (Ca, P, K, Na, Mg, S) are needed in larger amounts. Micro elements (Fe, I, Cu, Zn) are needed in tiny amounts but are still essential.

questions.question: Plants take in nitrogen from the soil mainly as _________ ions.
questions.expected: nitrate
questions.memo: Plant roots absorb soluble nitrate (NO3⁻) and ammonium (NH4⁺) ions. They cannot use N2 gas directly — nitrogen-fixing bacteria do that conversion.

questions.question: Eutrophication of a river is most likely caused by:
questions.expected: Run-off of fertilisers from farmland
questions.memo: Nitrate and phosphate fertilisers wash into rivers → algae multiply rapidly → bloom dies → bacteria use oxygen decomposing them → fish suffocate.

questions.question: Explain in one sentence why fish die after an algal bloom dies.
questions.expected: Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen, so the fish suffocate.
questions.memo: Photosynthesis adds O2 while algae are alive, but the bloom blocks light below the surface and the decomposition phase strips dissolved O2.
options: Bacteria decomposing the dead algae use up the dissolved oxygen, so the fish suffocate.
The dead algae release toxic poisons that directly kill the fish.
The fish are starved because the dead algae were their only food source.
The dead algae make the water too acidic for the fish to survive.

questions.question: Which food test gives a BLUE-BLACK colour with iodine solution?
questions.expected: Starch
questions.memo: Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch. This is the classic potato test.

questions.question: Benedict's solution is HEATED with a sample and turns from blue to orange-red. What does this show?
questions.expected: Reducing sugar present
questions.memo: Benedict's needs HEAT (water bath). Blue → green → yellow → orange-red, deeper = more reducing sugar (glucose, fructose, maltose). Sucrose does not react.

questions.question: Biuret reagent added to a sample turns purple. What is present?
questions.expected: Protein
questions.memo: Biuret detects peptide bonds (links between amino acids). Purple/violet = protein. No heating needed.

questions.question:
Match each food test to its positive result:
1. Iodine
2. Benedict's
3. Biuret

A. Purple
B. Orange-red after heating
C. Blue-black
questions.memo: Iodine → starch (blue-black). Benedict's + HEAT → reducing sugar (orange-red). Biuret → protein (purple).

questions.question: A pupil rubs a chip on filter paper. The paper shows a translucent (see-through) spot when held up to light. What is in the chip?
questions.expected: Lipid (fat)
questions.memo: Fats leave a translucent grease spot on paper that doesn't dry — this is the emulsion/grease-spot test for lipids.

questions.question:
The table shows mineral content (mg per 100 g). Which food is the BEST source of iron?

| Food   | Fe | Ca | K  |
|--------|----|----|----|
| Spinach| 2.7| 99 | 558|
| Milk   | 0.1|113 | 150|
| Banana | 0.3| 5  | 358|
options: All three give the same iron
questions.expected: Spinach
questions.memo: Read down the Fe column: 2.7 > 0.3 > 0.1. Spinach has roughly 9× the iron of banana per 100 g.

questions.question: A learner has a diet very low in fruits and vegetables. Which problem is MOST likely?
questions.expected: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy risk)
questions.memo: Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits and many vegetables. A low fruit-and-veg diet is a textbook scurvy/Vit C risk.

questions.question: The 'iodine' added to table salt in South Africa is there to prevent:
questions.expected: Goitre
questions.memo: SA law requires iodised salt because some inland soils are iodine-poor. Goitre used to be common before iodisation.

questions.question: Why are fertilisers used on land farmed for many seasons?
questions.expected: Harvesting removes minerals like N, P and K from the soil, so fertilisers replace them.
questions.memo: Natural ecosystems recycle minerals when plants die in place. Farming breaks the cycle — external mineral inputs are needed.
options: Fertilisers kill the pests and weeds that would otherwise damage the crops each season.
Fertilisers make the soil hold more water so crops do not dry out over many seasons.
Harvesting removes minerals like N, P and K from the soil, so fertilisers replace them.
Fertilisers add new genes that make the crops grow faster each season.

questions.question: Phosphorus is needed by living cells to make:
questions.expected: ATP, DNA and cell membranes
questions.memo: Phosphate groups sit inside ATP (energy currency), nucleic acids (DNA, RNA), and phospholipid bilayers (cell membranes).

questions.question: Explain in 1–2 sentences how natural compost can reduce both fertiliser use and eutrophication risk.
questions.expected: Compost releases minerals slowly, so less washes into rivers, reducing algal blooms.
questions.memo: Slow release matches plant uptake → less run-off. Many SA farming communities have long used kraal manure + crop-residue composting for the same effect.
options: Compost contains no minerals, so it cannot run off and cause algal blooms at all.
Compost kills the algae directly, so blooms cannot form in nearby rivers.
Compost dissolves faster than chemical fertiliser, so plants absorb it before it runs off.
Compost releases minerals slowly, so less washes into rivers, reducing algal blooms.

LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A2.title: Organic compounds — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids, vitamins
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A2.description: Classify organic molecules; SA-relevant food examples; saturated vs unsaturated; cholesterol.
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A2.recovery_strategy: Mono = glucose, fructose; di = sucrose, maltose; poly = starch, cellulose, glycogen. Unsaturated = liquid + healthier; saturated + cholesterol = artery risk.

questions.question: Which elements are found in ALL organic compounds?
questions.expected: Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
questions.memo: All organic compounds are built around C, H and O. Proteins add nitrogen; nucleic acids add N and P.

questions.question: Glucose is an example of a:
questions.expected: Monosaccharide
questions.memo: Glucose and fructose are single sugars (mono). Sucrose and maltose are double sugars (di). Starch, glycogen, cellulose are many-sugar (poly).

questions.question: Sucrose, the sugar in your tea, is a:
questions.expected: Disaccharide (glucose + fructose)
questions.memo: Sucrose is two monosaccharides joined: glucose + fructose. SA cane sugar (KwaZulu-Natal) is pure sucrose.

questions.question: Which polysaccharide is the main energy STORE in plants?
questions.expected: Starch
questions.memo: Starch = energy store in plants. Cellulose = structural cell walls. Glycogen = energy store in animals.

questions.question: Which polysaccharide gives plant cell walls their strength?
questions.expected: Cellulose
questions.memo: Cellulose fibres form a mesh in the cell wall. Humans can't digest it — it passes through as dietary fibre.

questions.question: Lipids (fats and oils) are made of:
questions.expected: 1 glycerol + 3 fatty acids
questions.memo: A triglyceride = one glycerol with three fatty-acid tails. Proteins = amino acids. Carbs = sugars. Nucleic acids = nucleotides.

questions.question: Which is a typical UNSATURATED fat at room temperature?
questions.expected: Olive oil
questions.memo: Unsaturated = usually LIQUID (oils). Saturated = usually SOLID (butter, beef fat, lard).

questions.question: True or false: All cholesterol is bad for your health.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Cholesterol is needed to make cell membranes and some hormones. The problem is high LDL ('bad') relative to HDL ('good').

questions.question: Proteins are polymers (chains) of:
questions.expected: Amino acids
questions.memo: There are about 20 amino acids. Their order in the chain determines the protein's identity and function.

questions.question: Which elements are found in proteins but NOT in carbohydrates or lipids?
questions.expected: Nitrogen and sometimes sulfur
questions.memo: Every amino acid contains an amino group (–NH2), so all proteins contain nitrogen. Some amino acids (cysteine, methionine) contain sulfur.

questions.question:
Match the molecule to its monomer:
1. Starch  2. Protein  3. Triglyceride

A. Amino acid  B. Glucose  C. Glycerol + fatty acids
questions.memo: Starch = chains of glucose. Protein = chains of amino acids. Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids.

questions.question: Vitamin C deficiency causes:
questions.expected: Scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing)
questions.memo: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen. Without it, connective tissue weakens. Citrus fruit is the classic source.

questions.question: Which vitamin is made in the skin when sunlight falls on it?
questions.expected: Vitamin D
questions.memo: UV light converts a cholesterol-like molecule into Vitamin D, which is needed for calcium absorption. Deficiency → rickets in children.

questions.question: DNA and RNA are both ____________ acids.
questions.expected: nucleic
questions.memo: DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid. RNA = ribonucleic acid. Monomer = nucleotide.

questions.question: A diet high in saturated fat and LDL cholesterol raises the risk of:
questions.expected: Atherosclerosis (clogged arteries) and heart disease
questions.memo: Saturated fat + high LDL build up as plaques in artery walls, narrowing them and raising heart-attack and stroke risk.

questions.question: True or false: Humans can digest cellulose for energy.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Humans don't make cellulase. Cellulose passes through as dietary fibre. Cows and termites host microbes that break it down.

questions.question: Why might a doctor recommend swapping butter for olive oil?
options: Olive oil is unsaturated, lowering risk of high LDL cholesterol
questions.expected: Olive oil is unsaturated, lowering risk of high LDL cholesterol
questions.memo: Swapping saturated fats for unsaturated fats shifts the LDL/HDL ratio favourably.

questions.question: Maize meal (pap), eaten widely in SA, is mainly a source of:
questions.expected: Carbohydrate (starch)
questions.memo: Maize endosperm is largely starch. Pap is an energy food — adding beans, meat or milk gives the protein and fat the diet needs.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why proteins are 'sensitive to temperature and pH'.
questions.expected: Heat or extreme pH changes a protein's 3D shape (denaturation), so it stops working.
questions.memo: Function depends on shape. Denatured proteins lose function — that is why a fried egg's clear albumin turns solid white.
options: Heat or extreme pH changes a protein's 3D shape (denaturation), so it stops working.
Heat and acid use up the protein like a fuel, so it is killed and gone.
Proteins are alive, so high temperature or pH kills them like any living cell.
Heat melts the protein into a liquid, which simply reforms when it cools again.

questions.question: A learner says 'all fats should be cut out of the diet'. Explain briefly why this is wrong.
questions.expected: Some fats are essential for cell membranes, hormones and absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K.
questions.memo: Aim is to limit saturated/trans fats and include unsaturated fats — not zero fat.
options: All fats are harmful, but the body cannot survive without at least a little of any poison.
Some fats are essential for cell membranes, hormones and absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K.
Fats are only needed for energy, so cutting them out just makes you slightly tired.
Cutting out all fat is fine because the body makes every fat it needs from sugar.

LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A3.title: Enzymes — properties and the Lock and Key Model
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A3.description: Enzyme as biological catalyst; Lock and Key Model; effect of temperature and pH; everyday examples.
LSC.G10.S1.CHEM.A3.recovery_strategy: Activity rises with temperature UNTIL the optimum, then falls (denaturation). Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Enzymes lower activation energy — they don't change the reaction itself.

questions.question: An enzyme is a:
options: Biological catalyst (a protein) that speeds up reactions
questions.expected: Biological catalyst (a protein) that speeds up reactions
questions.memo: Enzymes are proteins that lower the activation energy of a reaction, speeding it up without being used up.

questions.question: In the Lock and Key Model, the 'lock' is the:
questions.expected: Active site of the enzyme
questions.memo: The enzyme's active site (lock) only fits a specific substrate (key). One enzyme = one type of reaction.

questions.question: Most human enzymes work BEST at about:
questions.memo: 37°C = normal body temperature, the optimum for human enzymes. Below = too slow; far above = denaturation.

questions.question: What happens to an enzyme above its optimum temperature?
questions.expected: It denatures and stops working
questions.memo: High temperature breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's 3D shape. Active site loses its shape → substrate no longer fits.

questions.question: True or false: Denatured enzymes can usually be 'unfolded' back to normal by cooling.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Denaturation is usually permanent — the bonds holding the shape are broken and re-form randomly. A fried egg cannot be un-fried.

questions.question: Pepsin in the stomach works BEST at a pH of about:
questions.expected: 2 (very acidic)
questions.memo: The stomach is acidic (HCl). Pepsin's optimum pH ~ 2 matches its workplace. In the small intestine (pH ~ 8), pepsin would denature.

questions.question: The graph shows enzyme activity vs temperature. Activity rises from 10°C, peaks at 40°C, drops sharply by 60°C. At which temperature is the enzyme MOST active?
questions.memo: Peak (highest activity) = optimum. Above the optimum, the rapid drop is denaturation. Read the peak value off the curve.

questions.question: A washing powder is labelled 'biological — works at 40°C'. Why won't it work in 90°C water?
options: The enzymes denature at high temperature
questions.expected: The enzymes denature at high temperature
questions.memo: Biological washing powders contain enzymes (often proteases and lipases) tuned for ~40°C — hot wash destroys them.

questions.question: What is the substrate of the enzyme amylase?
questions.expected: Starch
questions.memo: Amylase (in saliva and pancreas) breaks starch into maltose. Easy to remember: amylase → amylum (starch in Latin).

questions.question: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) into:
questions.expected: Water and oxygen
questions.memo: Catalase (in liver and many tissues) protects cells from harmful H2O2: 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2 (the bubbles you see on a cut).

questions.question: Why does chicken liver bubble when hydrogen peroxide is added?
options: Catalase in the liver breaks H2O2 into water and oxygen gas
questions.expected: Catalase in the liver breaks H2O2 into water and oxygen gas
questions.memo: The bubbles are O2 gas being released. Boiled liver gives no bubbles — the catalase is denatured.

questions.question: In the Lock and Key Model, when the substrate binds, a temporary structure forms called the:
questions.expected: Enzyme-substrate complex
questions.memo: Substrate fits the active site → enzyme-substrate complex forms → reaction happens → products leave → enzyme is free to bind again.

questions.question: True or false: An enzyme is changed permanently after one reaction.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Enzymes are catalysts — they're released unchanged and can react again and again. One enzyme catalyses thousands of reactions per second.

questions.question: Fresh pineapple juice contains bromelain. Why does jelly NOT set if you add fresh pineapple?
options: Bromelain digests the protein (gelatin) in the jelly
questions.expected: Bromelain digests the protein (gelatin) in the jelly
questions.memo: Gelatin is a protein. Bromelain (a protease) breaks gelatin into amino acids, so the jelly can't gel. Tinned pineapple is heated — its enzymes are denatured — so jelly sets.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a single enzyme cannot work on many different substrates.
questions.expected: The active site has a specific shape, so only a matching substrate can fit and bind.
questions.memo: This 'specificity' is the heart of the Lock and Key Model — like a key only fitting one lock.
options: Enzymes are too small to hold more than one type of substrate at a time.
Each enzyme only has enough energy to break down one kind of substrate.
The active site has a specific shape, so only a matching substrate can fit and bind.
An enzyme is used up after one reaction, so it cannot move on to other substrates.

questions.question: Increasing substrate concentration with plenty of enzyme available will:
options: Increase the rate of reaction up to a maximum, then level off
questions.expected: Increase the rate of reaction up to a maximum, then level off
questions.memo: Rate rises with more substrate UNTIL all active sites are busy (saturation). Then adding more substrate doesn't help.

questions.question: Which is the BEST description of how enzymes speed up a reaction?
options: They lower the activation energy needed for the reaction
They become part of the product
questions.expected: They lower the activation energy needed for the reaction
questions.memo: Activation energy = the energy 'hill' a reaction must climb. Enzymes lower the hill so the reaction proceeds at body temperature.

questions.question: A pupil tested an enzyme at three pH values. The same volume of bubbles formed in 5s at pH 7, in 2 minutes at pH 5, and not at all at pH 12. Which pH is the optimum?
questions.expected: pH 7
questions.memo: Fastest reaction = optimum. pH 5 is suboptimal but the enzyme still works; pH 12 likely denatured.

questions.question: Why does the body have many DIFFERENT enzymes rather than one big one?
questions.expected: Each enzyme is specific to one substrate, so different reactions need different enzymes.
questions.memo: Specificity → the body controls reactions one at a time, switching them on or off as needed (e.g. only digesting in the gut).
options: Each enzyme is specific to one substrate, so different reactions need different enzymes.
One big enzyme would be too heavy for cells to make and move around.
Different enzymes are just spares in case the main enzyme gets used up.
Enzymes wear out quickly, so the body keeps many different ones as replacements.

questions.question: An athlete's body temperature rises to 41°C during a long race. Which is MOST likely?
options: Some enzymes start to denature, slowing metabolism and performance
Enzymes work twice as fast and improve performance
questions.expected: Some enzymes start to denature, slowing metabolism and performance
questions.memo: Body enzymes are tuned for 37°C. A 4°C rise is dangerous because heat sensitive enzymes start to denature — heatstroke is a medical emergency.

LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A1.title: Cell structure — organelles and their functions
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A1.description: Name and locate major organelles; functions; plant vs animal.
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A1.caps_topic: Cells: the basic units of life
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A1.recovery_strategy: Mito = energy. Chloroplast = energy capture (plants only). Cell wall = plants only. Vacuole = large in plants, small in animals.

questions.question: Which organelle releases energy through cellular respiration?
questions.expected: Mitochondrion
questions.memo: Mitochondria break down glucose to release energy as ATP. Nucleus stores DNA. Golgi packages secretions. Ribosomes build proteins.

questions.question: Where in the cell is protein synthesised?
questions.expected: Ribosomes
questions.memo: Ribosomes (free in cytoplasm or attached to rough ER) link amino acids into proteins.

questions.question: Which organelle is found in PLANT cells but NOT animal cells?
questions.expected: Chloroplast
questions.memo: Chloroplasts (a plastid) do photosynthesis — only plants and some protists. Animals eat for energy, so no chloroplasts.

questions.question: Which structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
questions.expected: Cell (plasma) membrane
questions.memo: The cell membrane is partially permeable. The nucleus controls heredity and protein-making instructions, not transport.

questions.question:
Look at the labelled plant cell diagram. Which label points to the chloroplast?
[Diagram: plant cell with A=cell wall, B=cell membrane, C=large central vacuole, D=oval green organelle, E=nucleus]
questions.expected: D
questions.memo: Chloroplasts are oval and green (chlorophyll). A is the rigid wall, B the thin membrane just inside, C the large fluid vacuole, E the nucleus.

questions.question:
On the animal-cell diagram, which structure has a sausage shape with folded inner membranes and releases energy?
[Diagram: animal cell with W=nucleus, X=mitochondrion, Y=Golgi body, Z=ribosomes]
questions.expected: X
questions.memo: Mitochondria have smooth outer + folded inner membrane (cristae) — bigger surface area for respiration enzymes.

questions.question: Which is the function of the Golgi body?
options: Modifying and packaging proteins for secretion
questions.expected: Modifying and packaging proteins for secretion
questions.memo: Think Golgi = the cell's post office: receives proteins from rough ER, modifies them, sends them out in vesicles.

questions.question: Which organelle digests worn-out cell parts and engulfed material?
questions.expected: Lysosome
questions.memo: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes — recycle damaged organelles and destroy engulfed invaders.

questions.question: The _________ contains the chromatin material that codes for proteins.
questions.expected: nucleus
questions.memo: Chromatin = DNA + proteins, packed in the nucleus. The nucleolus (inside the nucleus) makes ribosomes.

questions.question: True or false: Animal cells have a rigid cellulose wall.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Only plant cells (and fungi/bacteria with their own wall types) have cell walls. Animal cells have only a flexible membrane.

questions.question:
Match each organelle to its function:
1. Mitochondrion  2. Ribosome  3. Chloroplast  4. Lysosome

A. Photosynthesis
B. Cellular respiration
C. Protein synthesis
D. Digestion of waste
questions.memo: Mito → respiration. Ribosome → protein. Chloroplast → photosynthesis. Lysosome → digestion.

questions.question: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is studded with which organelle?
questions.expected: Ribosomes
questions.memo: The 'rough' look comes from ribosomes attached to its outer surface, where proteins for secretion are made.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the vacuole of a plant cell from that of an animal cell?
options: Plant vacuoles are large and central, animal vacuoles are small and many
Only plant cells have any vacuole
Vacuoles do not exist in plant cells
questions.expected: Plant vacuoles are large and central, animal vacuoles are small and many
questions.memo: Large plant vacuole holds cell sap → maintains turgor pressure and cell shape.

questions.question: A pupil sees a green cell with a rigid box-like outline and a large empty-looking space in the middle. Which cell is it?
questions.expected: A plant cell
questions.memo: Green (chloroplasts) + rigid box (cell wall) + large central space (vacuole) = plant cell.

questions.question: Predict: A cell that secretes a lot of digestive enzymes (e.g. pancreas) will have especially many of which organelles?
questions.expected: Ribosomes and rough ER
questions.memo: Enzymes ARE proteins → cells exporting enzymes have lots of ribosomes on rough ER + Golgi for packaging.

questions.question: Why is the inner membrane of a mitochondrion folded?
questions.expected: The folds (cristae) increase surface area for respiration enzymes, so more ATP is made.
questions.memo: More surface area = more enzymes = more reactions/sec. Same principle as villi in the small intestine, root hairs.
options: The folds store extra DNA so the mitochondrion can copy itself faster.
The folds (cristae) increase surface area for respiration enzymes, so more ATP is made.
The folds trap sunlight to help the mitochondrion make food for the cell.
The folds make the mitochondrion bigger so it can hold more glucose.

questions.question: Cell theory states that:
options: All living things are made of cells, and cells come from pre-existing cells
Cells form spontaneously from non-living matter
All cells are exactly the same
questions.expected: All living things are made of cells, and cells come from pre-existing cells
questions.memo: Three pillars: all life is made of cells, the cell is life's basic unit, all cells come from pre-existing cells.

questions.question: True or false: A virus is a type of cell.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: A virus is NOT a cell — no cytoplasm, no organelles, can't reproduce on its own. It's genetic material in a protein coat.

questions.question: Which organelle is the jelly-like fluid filling most of an animal cell, where many reactions take place?
questions.expected: Cytoplasm
questions.memo: Cytoplasm holds dissolved sugars, salts and enzymes for many cell reactions, and the organelles are suspended in it.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a leaf cell has many chloroplasts but a leg-muscle cell has many mitochondria.
questions.expected: Leaf cells capture light to photosynthesise, while muscle cells need mitochondria for ATP.
questions.memo: Structure follows function. Cells specialise by having more of the organelles they need.
options: Leaf cells make their own mitochondria, while muscle cells have to borrow chloroplasts.
Leaf cells are bigger, so they fit chloroplasts, while small muscle cells only fit mitochondria.
Leaf cells capture light to photosynthesise, while muscle cells need mitochondria for ATP.
Chloroplasts and mitochondria do the same job, so the choice is simply random.

LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A2.title: Cell membrane and transport — diffusion, osmosis, active transport
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A2.description: Fluid mosaic model; diffusion, osmosis, active transport; hypertonic/hypotonic/isotonic predictions.
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A2.caps_topic: Cells: the basic units of life
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A2.recovery_strategy: Diffusion = particles spread (high→low). Osmosis = WATER moves toward higher solute (lower water) concentration. Active transport = against gradient, needs ATP.

questions.question: Diffusion is the movement of particles from:
questions.expected: High concentration to low concentration
questions.memo: Diffusion happens down a concentration gradient. No energy needed.

questions.question: Osmosis is the diffusion of:
options: Water across a partially permeable membrane
questions.expected: Water across a partially permeable membrane
questions.memo: Osmosis is specifically water, across a partially permeable membrane, toward the side with more solute.

questions.question: Active transport differs from diffusion because it:
options: Moves substances against the concentration gradient and uses ATP
questions.expected: Moves substances against the concentration gradient and uses ATP
questions.memo: Active = uphill, energy-requiring, via carrier proteins. Example: root cells pumping in minerals.

questions.question: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as:
options: A flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it
questions.expected: A flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins floating in it
questions.memo: Phospholipids = two tails (water-hating) point inward, heads (water-loving) point outward. Proteins sit in this layer like icebergs in water.

questions.question: True or false: Osmosis can happen without a partially permeable membrane.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: By definition, osmosis needs a partially permeable membrane (one that lets water through but not most solutes).

questions.question: A plant cell placed in pure water will:
options: Take in water by osmosis and become turgid
Lose water by osmosis and shrink
questions.expected: Take in water by osmosis and become turgid
questions.memo: Water moves into the cell (higher solute concentration inside). Plant cell wall prevents bursting → cell becomes firm (turgid).

questions.question: A red blood cell placed in pure water will:
questions.expected: Take in water and burst (haemolysis)
questions.memo: No cell wall to resist water intake → membrane stretches until it ruptures. Why drips use isotonic saline, not pure water.

questions.question: A plant cell in a strong salt solution will:
options: Lose water; cytoplasm pulls away from cell wall (plasmolysis)
Take in water and become turgid
questions.expected: Lose water; cytoplasm pulls away from cell wall (plasmolysis)
questions.memo: Strong salt outside = lower water concentration outside → water leaves cell → vacuole shrinks → membrane peels off the wall (plasmolysis).

questions.question: The diagram shows a U-tube with a partially permeable membrane in the middle. Side A is 10% sugar solution; Side B is 30% sugar solution. After 1 hour:

data.description: U-tube: side A = 10% sugar, side B = 30% sugar, separated by partially permeable membrane

options: Water level rises on side B (water moved from A to B)
Water level rises on side A
questions.expected: Water level rises on side B (water moved from A to B)
questions.memo: Water moves to the side with MORE solute (and so LESS water). Side B is more concentrated, so water flows in there.

questions.question: Which is an example of ACTIVE transport?
options: Root cells absorbing minerals against a gradient
Water entering through a root by osmosis
questions.expected: Root cells absorbing minerals against a gradient
questions.memo: Soil minerals are often more concentrated INSIDE the root cells than outside — so absorbing them is uphill work = active transport (needs ATP).

questions.question: Which type of molecule passes EASILY through the lipid bilayer?
options: Small uncharged molecules like oxygen and CO2
questions.expected: Small uncharged molecules like oxygen and CO2
questions.memo: Small, fat-soluble molecules slip through. Charged ions and big molecules need protein channels.

questions.question: Why do potato cubes in salt water lose mass after an hour?
options: Water leaves the potato cells by osmosis into the salty solution
Salt enters the potato by active transport
questions.expected: Water leaves the potato cells by osmosis into the salty solution
questions.memo: Salty water is more concentrated → water moves out of the potato cells → mass drops. Classic osmosis practical.

questions.question: True or false: Active transport stops if the cell runs out of oxygen.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Active transport needs ATP. ATP comes mostly from aerobic respiration (needs O2). No O2 → less ATP → active transport slows or stops.

questions.question: Which is the BEST example of diffusion in a living cell?
options: Oxygen moving from the lungs into the blood
questions.expected: Oxygen moving from the lungs into the blood
questions.memo: Higher O2 in alveoli → lower O2 in blood: diffusion down the gradient across the thin alveolar wall.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a wilted plant becomes firm again after watering.
questions.expected: Water enters the cells by osmosis, swelling the vacuoles and restoring turgor pressure.
questions.memo: Turgor = the rigid 'water pressure' state of a plant cell. Loss of turgor = wilting.
options: The water dissolves the wilted cells and rebuilds new firm ones in their place.
Water enters the cells by osmosis, swelling the vacuoles and restoring turgor pressure.
The water pushes air out of the cells, and it is the vacuum that makes the plant firm.
Water reacts with the cell walls to make new lignin that stiffens the plant.

questions.question: Why does putting salt on a slug kill it?
options: Salt draws water out of the slug by osmosis, dehydrating it
questions.expected: Salt draws water out of the slug by osmosis, dehydrating it
questions.memo: Salt outside the slug skin = very high solute. Water rushes OUT of the slug by osmosis → fatal dehydration.

questions.question: Which feature of an alveolus speeds up the diffusion of oxygen into the blood?
options: Wall only one cell thick + huge total surface area
questions.expected: Wall only one cell thick + huge total surface area
questions.memo: Diffusion is faster across a short distance + large surface area. Alveoli have both. Same principle: root hairs, villi.

questions.question: A drop of dye placed in cold water spreads more slowly than in hot water because:
options: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they diffuse faster
questions.expected: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they diffuse faster
questions.memo: More heat = faster random motion of particles = faster diffusion. This is why food smells spread fast in a warm room.

questions.question: An isotonic solution is one where:
options: The solute concentration outside equals that inside the cell
There is no solute at all
questions.expected: The solute concentration outside equals that inside the cell
questions.memo: Iso = same. No net water movement → cells stay the same. This is why drips are isotonic saline.

questions.question: Explain why a cell can absorb minerals from the soil even when there is more of those minerals inside the cell than outside.
questions.expected: Active transport uses carrier proteins and ATP to pump minerals in against the gradient.
questions.memo: This is the textbook case for active transport: against the gradient, needs ATP, uses carrier proteins. Inhibit respiration → uptake stops.
options: The minerals simply diffuse in by themselves, since diffusion always moves both ways.
Osmosis pulls the minerals in along with the water entering the cell.
The cell membrane has holes that let any mineral pass through freely.
Active transport uses carrier proteins and ATP to pump minerals in against the gradient.

LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A3.title: Microscopy and measuring cell size
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A3.description: History of microscopy; magnification; field of view; resolution vs magnification.
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A3.caps_topic: Cells: the basic units of life
LSC.G10.S1.CELL.A3.recovery_strategy: Magnification = drawing size ÷ real size (same units). Resolution = detail (electron > light). High magnification + poor resolution = bigger but blurry.

questions.question: Which person is credited with first naming what he saw under a microscope 'cells'?
questions.expected: Robert Hooke
questions.memo: In 1665 Hooke looked at cork under a microscope and called the small spaces 'cells' because they looked like monks' rooms.

questions.question: Which type of microscope has the HIGHEST resolution?
questions.expected: Electron microscope
questions.memo: Electron microscopes use electrons (shorter wavelength than light) → much finer detail. Can show ribosomes, viruses, cristae.

questions.question: Magnification is calculated as:
questions.expected: Drawing size ÷ real size
questions.memo: Same units on both! If your drawing is 10 mm and the real cell is 0.1 mm, magnification = 10 ÷ 0.1 = 100×.

questions.question: If a drawn cell is 50 mm long and the real cell is 0.05 mm long, the magnification is:
questions.memo: 50 ÷ 0.05 = 1000. Always convert to the same units before dividing.

questions.question: True or false: A magnification of 1000× always gives a sharper image than 400×.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Magnification ≠ resolution. Past the lens's limit, the image just gets bigger and blurrier ('empty magnification').

questions.question: Resolution is the ability of a microscope to:
options: Distinguish two points that are close together as separate
questions.expected: Distinguish two points that are close together as separate
questions.memo: Resolution = clarity of detail. The closer two points can be while still being seen as two, the better the resolution.

questions.question: When using a light microscope, which objective lens gives the highest magnification (typical school scope)?
questions.expected: ×40 (oil immersion ×100 in some)
questions.memo: Standard school light microscopes: ×4 (scan), ×10 (low power), ×40 (high power), some go to ×100 with oil. Multiply by ×10 eyepiece for total.

questions.question: Total magnification of a light microscope is calculated as:
questions.expected: Eyepiece × objective
questions.memo: Eyepiece ×10 with objective ×40 → total magnification = 10 × 40 = 400×.

questions.question: Why are biological specimens usually STAINED before viewing under a light microscope?
options: To make structures visible by contrasting them
questions.expected: To make structures visible by contrasting them
questions.memo: Most cell structures are transparent. Stains (methylene blue, iodine, Sudan III) bind to specific parts → contrast.

questions.question: A specimen on a slide is covered with a thin glass cover slip. The MAIN reason is:
options: To keep the specimen flat, protect the lens, and prevent drying
questions.expected: To keep the specimen flat, protect the lens, and prevent drying
questions.memo: Cover slip → flat plane (so all parts in focus), stops the lens from touching the specimen, slows evaporation.

questions.question: A pupil draws a cell magnified ×400. The drawn cell is 80 mm long. The real cell is:
questions.memo: Real size = drawing size ÷ magnification = 80 ÷ 400 = 0.2 mm = 200 µm. Reasonable size for a plant cell.

questions.question: Why is a light microscope NOT able to clearly see a ribosome?
options: Light's wavelength is too long — ribosomes are below the resolution limit
questions.expected: Light's wavelength is too long — ribosomes are below the resolution limit
questions.memo: Light microscope resolution limit ≈ 200 nm. Ribosomes are ~20 nm — only an electron microscope (resolution down to ~0.1 nm) can see them clearly.

questions.question: The field of view at ×100 is 1.5 mm. Switching to ×400, the field of view will be:
questions.expected: About 0.375 mm (smaller)
questions.memo: Field of view shrinks as magnification increases. ×400 is 4× the magnification of ×100, so field of view is 1/4 the size: 1.5 ÷ 4 = 0.375 mm.

questions.question: Which prepared slide is BEST for showing typical animal-cell structure to a Grade 10 class?
options: Cheek-cell smear stained with methylene blue
questions.expected: Cheek-cell smear stained with methylene blue
questions.memo: Cheek cells = easy to obtain, clearly show nucleus + cytoplasm + thin membrane. Methylene blue stains the nucleus dark.

questions.question: True or false: Electron microscopes can be used on living cells.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Electron microscopes need a vacuum and the specimen has to be fixed and dehydrated → cells are dead. Light microscopes can be used on live cells.

questions.question: A micrograph has a scale bar marked '10 µm' and the scale bar is 20 mm long on the page. The magnification is:
questions.memo: Convert to same units: 20 mm = 20,000 µm. Magnification = drawn ÷ real = 20,000 µm ÷ 10 µm = 2000×.

questions.question: Why was the discovery of the cell DELAYED for so long in history?
questions.expected: Cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so microscopes had to be invented first.
questions.memo: Technology drives science. The Dutch microscopists (Leeuwenhoek) and Hooke's lenses opened a new world that had been there all along.
options: Cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so microscopes had to be invented first.
Cells only began to exist once scientists started looking for them.
Early scientists were forbidden by law from studying living tissue.
Cells were hidden because no one had yet cut open a plant or animal.

questions.question: 1 millimetre (mm) is equal to how many micrometres (µm)?
questions.memo: Each step down is ×1000: 1 m = 1000 mm = 1,000,000 µm = 1,000,000,000 nm. Memorise these.

questions.question: Why is the coarse-focus knob NOT used on high power (×40)?
options: It moves the stage too much and may crack the slide or break the lens
It doesn't work on high power
questions.expected: It moves the stage too much and may crack the slide or break the lens
questions.memo: High-power lens sits very close to the slide. Coarse focus = big movement → risk of contact. Always use the fine-focus knob on high power.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the development of the electron microscope was so important for cell biology.
questions.expected: Its greater resolution revealed organelles and viruses, advancing cell biology.
questions.memo: Resolution from ~200 nm (light) → ~0.1 nm (electron). New world of detail = whole new branches of biology (molecular cell biology, virology).
options: It simply magnified cells much larger, even though the level of detail stayed the same.
It made microscopes cheaper so far more scientists could own one.
Its greater resolution revealed organelles and viruses, advancing cell biology.
It used light more brightly, so colours of cells could finally be seen.

LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A1.title: The cell cycle and mitosis
LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A1.description: Cell cycle phases; PMAT; outcome of two identical daughter cells; role; plant vs animal cytokinesis.
LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A1.recovery_strategy: PMAT: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase. Mitosis = identical copies (2n→2n). Plants build a cell plate; animals pinch in.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of mitosis phases?
questions.expected: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase
questions.memo: PMAT. Prophase → chromosomes condense. Metaphase → line up. Anaphase → chromatids separate. Telophase → two new nuclei.

questions.question: How many daughter cells are produced by one cycle of mitosis?
questions.memo: Mitosis = ONE parent → TWO identical daughters. (Meiosis gives 4 non-identical cells.)

questions.question: The two daughter cells from mitosis are:
options: Genetically identical to the parent cell
questions.expected: Genetically identical to the parent cell
questions.memo: DNA was copied exactly during interphase, then divided equally — same chromosome number, same genes.

questions.question: In which phase do chromosomes line up along the centre of the cell?
questions.expected: Metaphase
questions.memo: 'Meta' = middle. Chromosomes attached to spindle fibres are pulled to the equator.

questions.question: In which phase do sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles?
questions.expected: Anaphase
questions.memo: 'Ana' = apart. Spindle fibres contract, pulling sister chromatids to opposite ends.

questions.question: Cytokinesis differs between plant and animal cells because:
options: Plant cells build a cell plate; animal cells pinch inward
questions.expected: Plant cells build a cell plate; animal cells pinch inward
questions.memo: Rigid plant wall can't pinch → builds a new cell plate. Animal membrane is flexible → cleavage furrow pinches inward.

questions.question: During which phase is DNA copied (replicated)?
questions.expected: Interphase (S phase)
questions.memo: DNA replicates BEFORE mitosis starts, in the S phase of interphase. By prophase each chromosome is already two sister chromatids.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a role of mitosis?
questions.expected: Producing gametes (sex cells)
questions.memo: Gametes are made by MEIOSIS. Mitosis is for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.

questions.question:
Look at the diagram. The chromosomes are at opposite ends of the cell, and two new nuclear membranes are forming. Which phase is this?
[Diagram: cell with two clusters of chromosomes at opposite poles, faint membranes forming around each]
questions.expected: Telophase
questions.memo: Two nuclear membranes reforming + chromosomes at the poles = telophase, the last mitosis phase. Cytokinesis follows.

questions.question: True or false: At the end of mitosis the chromosome number is halved.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Mitosis keeps chromosome number CONSTANT (2n parent → two 2n daughters). Halving happens in meiosis.

questions.question: Which tissue divides by mitosis most frequently in your body?
questions.expected: Skin and bone-marrow cells
questions.memo: Skin and bone marrow constantly make new cells. Mature neurons and heart muscle hardly divide. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus.

questions.question: What is a chromatid?
options: One of two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere
A single DNA molecule before replication
A type of protein in the cell membrane
questions.expected: One of two identical copies of a replicated chromosome, joined at the centromere
questions.memo: After DNA replication, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids held at the centromere. They separate in anaphase.

questions.question:
Order these events from FIRST to LAST in a cell cycle:
(a) DNA replicates
(b) Chromatids separate
(c) Cytokinesis
(d) Nuclear membrane reforms
questions.expected: a → b → d → c
questions.memo: DNA replicates during interphase → chromatids pulled apart in anaphase → nuclear membrane reforms in telophase → cytokinesis splits the cell.

questions.question: Which structure pulls chromatids apart during anaphase?
questions.expected: Spindle fibres
questions.memo: Spindle fibres (microtubules) attach to centromeres and shorten, dragging chromatids to opposite poles.

questions.question: Why is exact DNA replication BEFORE mitosis important?
questions.expected: So that each daughter cell receives a full and identical copy of the genetic information.
questions.memo: Without prior replication, daughters get only half the DNA each. Faulty replication → damaged DNA → cancer risk.
options: So that each daughter cell receives a full and identical copy of the genetic information.
So the cell has spare DNA to throw away if some gets damaged during division.
So that each daughter cell gets exactly half of the parent cell's DNA.
So the DNA has time to change slightly, giving the daughter cells variety.

questions.question: Which does an animal cell form in cytokinesis?
options: A cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two
A new cell wall in the middle
questions.expected: A cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two
questions.memo: Animal cell membranes contract like a tightening drawstring until the cell splits.

questions.question: Which phase takes the MOST time in the cell cycle?
questions.expected: Interphase
questions.memo: Interphase = G1 + S + G2. The cell spends most of its life here. Mitosis itself is brief.

questions.question: A skin wound heals over a week. Which process is mainly responsible?
options: Mitosis of skin cells around the wound
questions.expected: Mitosis of skin cells around the wound
questions.memo: Healthy cells around the wound divide by mitosis to replace damaged ones. Meiosis only happens in the testes/ovaries.

questions.question: True or false: Cells must pass internal 'checkpoints' before being allowed to divide.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Checkpoints test DNA integrity. Damaged cells are either repaired or destroyed (apoptosis). Failure → cancer risk.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why uncontrolled mitosis is dangerous to the body.
questions.expected: Cells dividing without control form a tumour that damages tissue and can spread (cancer).
questions.memo: Healthy cells stop dividing when they touch neighbours and respect checkpoints; cancer cells ignore both.
options: Uncontrolled mitosis uses up all the body's DNA, leaving none for normal cells.
Cells dividing without control form a tumour that damages tissue and can spread (cancer).
Too much mitosis makes the body grow taller and heavier than is healthy.
Uncontrolled mitosis makes cells too small to do their jobs properly.

LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A2.title: Cancer and cell-division biotechnology
LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A2.description: Cancer causes/treatments/attitudes; cloning, stem-cell research, ethics, SA legislation.
LSC.G10.S1.MITO.A2.recovery_strategy: Cancer = cells ignore the stop-dividing signal. Not contagious. Cloning = genetic copy. Embryonic stem cells = pluripotent; adult stem cells = limited.

questions.question: Cancer is BEST described as:
options: Uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour
questions.expected: Uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour
questions.memo: Cancer cells ignore stop-dividing signals and checkpoint controls. They keep dividing → mass of cells (tumour).

questions.question: Which is a known lifestyle risk factor for cancer?
questions.expected: Smoking tobacco
questions.memo: Tobacco smoke contains many carcinogens linked to lung, throat, mouth and bladder cancer.

questions.question: Excess exposure to UV light from the sun is most strongly linked to:
questions.expected: Skin cancer
questions.memo: UV damages DNA in skin cells. SA has high UV levels — sunscreen and hats matter.

questions.question: True or false: Cancer is contagious — you can catch it from someone.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Cancer is NOT contagious. It is a problem with one's own cells. Some VIRUSES that can be passed (HPV → cervical cancer) raise cancer risk, but the cancer itself isn't transmitted.

questions.question: Chemotherapy treats cancer by:
options: Using drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells
questions.expected: Using drugs that kill rapidly dividing cells
questions.memo: Chemo drugs target dividing cells. Side effects (hair loss, gut issues) happen because some healthy cells (hair, gut lining) also divide quickly.

questions.question: Radiotherapy uses:
options: High-energy radiation to damage cancer-cell DNA
questions.expected: High-energy radiation to damage cancer-cell DNA
questions.memo: Targeted radiation breaks the DNA of cancer cells so they cannot divide. Carefully aimed to spare healthy tissue.

questions.question: True or false: A benign tumour is just as dangerous as a malignant tumour.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Benign = stays put, usually less harmful. Malignant = invades surrounding tissue and can spread (metastasise). Some benign tumours can still be dangerous if they press on organs.

questions.question: Metastasis is when:
options: Cancer cells break off and spread to other parts of the body
questions.expected: Cancer cells break off and spread to other parts of the body
questions.memo: Metastasis is what makes cancer dangerous — it can reach the liver, lungs, brain, bone via blood and lymph.

questions.question: A pupil claims that 'cancer happens because cells get bored'. What is the BEST scientific reply?
options: Cancer happens because mutations in DNA disable checkpoints that normally stop division
Cancer is caused only by stress
All cells get cancer at the same age
questions.expected: Cancer happens because mutations in DNA disable checkpoints that normally stop division
questions.memo: Cancer is a DNA-level problem. Mutations stack up over time — that's why cancer rates rise with age.

questions.question: Cloning produces:
options: A genetically identical copy of an organism
questions.expected: A genetically identical copy of an organism
questions.memo: Clone = same DNA. Famous example: Dolly the sheep (1996), cloned from an adult sheep cell.

questions.question: Which type of stem cell can become ANY cell type in the body?
questions.expected: Embryonic stem cells (pluripotent)
questions.memo: Embryonic = pluripotent (can become anything). Adult = multipotent (limited range, e.g. bone-marrow stem cells make blood cells only).

questions.question: Stem-cell research is ethically controversial mainly because:
options: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos, which some people consider human life
questions.expected: Embryonic stem cells come from early embryos, which some people consider human life
questions.memo: The ethical debate is about the embryo's moral status. Adult stem-cell and iPS-cell research avoids that issue.

questions.question: True or false: South African law allows stem-cell research with strict ethical controls.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The National Health Act and SAMRC guidelines regulate stem-cell research in SA — it's allowed under specific ethical oversight.

questions.question: Which is a real medical use of stem cells already in practice?
options: Curing all cancers in a day
questions.expected: Bone-marrow transplants for leukaemia
questions.memo: Bone-marrow transplants use blood-forming (haematopoietic) stem cells to replace cancerous marrow. A long-established treatment.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how chemotherapy can have side effects like hair loss and gut problems.
questions.expected: Chemo targets rapidly dividing cells, and hair and gut-lining cells also divide quickly.
questions.memo: Side effects are usually temporary — these healthy fast-dividing tissues recover after treatment ends.
options: Chemotherapy weakens the immune system, which lets hair and gut cells fall out.
Chemotherapy is poisonous to all cells equally, so every part of the body is harmed.
Chemo targets rapidly dividing cells, and hair and gut-lining cells also divide quickly.
Chemotherapy drugs build up in the hair and gut because those tissues store fat.

questions.question: Plant cloning is done commercially by:
options: Tissue culture — growing many identical plants from a few cells
questions.expected: Tissue culture — growing many identical plants from a few cells
questions.memo: Tissue culture lets nurseries mass-produce disease-free identical seedlings (e.g. bananas, orchids, some indigenous SA plants).

questions.question:
The table compares survival rates after early vs late diagnosis. What does this suggest about screening (early detection)?

| Stage at diagnosis | 5-year survival |
|--------------------|-----------------|
| Early              | 90%             |
| Late               | 20%             |
options: Early detection greatly increases survival, so screening is valuable
questions.expected: Early detection greatly increases survival, so screening is valuable
questions.memo: 90% vs 20% is a huge difference. Why pap smears, mammograms and prostate checks save lives.

questions.question: True or false: Eating processed meat increases the risk of certain cancers.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The WHO classifies processed meat (sausages, bacon) as a Group 1 carcinogen — there is enough evidence it raises bowel-cancer risk.

questions.question: Some indigenous SA plants like Sutherlandia frutescens ('cancer bush') have been used by traditional healers. What is the BEST scientific approach?
options: Test active compounds in clinical trials to see if they really help
Sell them as a cure immediately
questions.expected: Test active compounds in clinical trials to see if they really help
questions.memo: Indigenous knowledge has often pointed scientists to useful compounds. The next step is rigorous trials — for safety, dose, and effectiveness.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a cancer screening programme is more useful at a population level than waiting for symptoms.
questions.expected: Screening catches cancer early, when treatment is far more effective than after symptoms.
questions.memo: Better outcomes + lower cost. SA's national cervical-cancer screening programme is built on this idea.
options: Screening catches cancer early, when treatment is far more effective than after symptoms.
Screening prevents people from ever developing cancer in the first place.
Waiting for symptoms is just as effective but costs the patient more money.
Screening is only useful because it reassures healthy people that they are fine.

LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A1.title: Plant and animal tissues
LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A1.description: Plant tissues (xylem, phloem, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, epidermis, meristematic); four animal tissues (epithelial, connective, muscle, nerve).
LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A1.recovery_strategy: Plant: Xylem=water (one-way, up); Phloem=sugar (both directions); Meristem=dividing. Animal: Epithelial covers; Connective supports (bone/blood); Muscle contracts; Nerve signals.

questions.question: A tissue is BEST defined as:
options: A group of similar cells working together for a function
questions.expected: A group of similar cells working together for a function
questions.memo: Hierarchy: cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organism.

questions.question: Which plant tissue transports WATER from the roots to the leaves?
questions.expected: Xylem
questions.memo: Xylem = water transport (one-way, root → leaf). Phloem = sugar transport (both directions).

questions.question: Which plant tissue transports SUGARS from the leaves to other parts?
questions.expected: Phloem
questions.memo: Phloem carries dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) from photosynthesising leaves to roots, fruits and growing tips.

questions.question: Where in a plant is meristematic tissue mainly found?
questions.expected: Tips of roots and shoots
questions.memo: Meristem = cells that divide. Apical meristems at root/shoot tips drive length growth.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma and collenchyma both function as:
questions.expected: Support tissues
questions.memo: Collenchyma = flexible support (often in growing stems). Sclerenchyma = rigid support (often in mature/woody tissue, with lignin).

questions.question: Parenchyma cells are mainly used for:
questions.expected: Storage and general packing
questions.memo: Parenchyma = the most common plant tissue: thin walls, large vacuole, storage of starch/water/oils. Found everywhere in plants.

questions.question: The epidermis of a leaf is one cell thick and often covered in a waxy layer (cuticle). Why?
options: To protect the leaf and reduce water loss while letting light through
questions.expected: To protect the leaf and reduce water loss while letting light through
questions.memo: Thin + transparent → light reaches photosynthetic cells. Waxy cuticle = water-proof coat.

questions.question: Which is the function of EPITHELIAL tissue in animals?
questions.expected: Covers and lines body surfaces
questions.memo: Skin epidermis, gut lining, lung lining, blood-vessel lining = all epithelial. Protective + absorbing + secreting.

questions.question: Which is an example of CONNECTIVE tissue?
questions.expected: Bone
questions.memo: Connective tissue = bone, cartilage, blood, tendons, ligaments, adipose (fat). They all join, support or transport.

questions.question: Which type of muscle is found in the wall of the heart?
questions.expected: Cardiac muscle
questions.memo: Three muscle types: Skeletal (voluntary, moves bones), Smooth (involuntary, gut wall, blood vessels), Cardiac (heart only, involuntary, striated).

questions.question: Nerve tissue is specialised for:
questions.expected: Sending electrical signals quickly
questions.memo: Neurons have long projections (axons) that conduct electrical impulses to communicate between body parts.

questions.question:
Match each tissue to its function:
1. Xylem  2. Phloem  3. Epithelial  4. Nerve

A. Send signals
B. Cover/line surfaces
C. Transport water
D. Transport sugar
questions.memo: Xylem→water. Phloem→sugar. Epithelial→cover. Nerve→signals.

questions.question: True or false: Blood is a type of connective tissue.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: red and white cells suspended in plasma, transporting substances around the body.

questions.question: The vascular bundle of a stem typically arranges xylem and phloem like this:
options: Xylem toward the centre, phloem toward the outside
Phloem in the centre, xylem outside
questions.expected: Xylem toward the centre, phloem toward the outside
questions.memo: In a typical dicot stem: xylem on the inside of the bundle, phloem on the outside. Cambium (dividing tissue) sits between them.

questions.question: Why must xylem cells be DEAD when they function?
options: Empty hollow tubes let water flow with less resistance
It saves the plant energy only
questions.expected: Empty hollow tubes let water flow with less resistance
questions.memo: Mature xylem vessels = thick-walled, hollow tubes. No cytoplasm = no obstacle for the long water column.

questions.question: Phloem sieve tubes have companion cells next to them because:
options: Sieve tubes have no nucleus and need companion cells to keep them functioning
questions.expected: Sieve tubes have no nucleus and need companion cells to keep them functioning
questions.memo: Sieve tubes are alive but lose their nucleus. Companion cells (with a nucleus) manage their metabolism — the two work as a pair.

questions.question: Smooth muscle is found in the walls of:
questions.expected: The gut and blood vessels
questions.memo: Smooth muscle = involuntary, no stripes, slow + sustained contraction — squeezes gut contents (peristalsis), narrows blood vessels.

questions.question: Why does the trachea (windpipe) have C-shaped rings of cartilage (a connective tissue)?
options: To hold the trachea open while still allowing food to pass behind it
questions.expected: To hold the trachea open while still allowing food to pass behind it
questions.memo: Full rings would press on the oesophagus during swallowing. C-shape keeps the airway open + leaves room behind for food.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the structure of meristematic tissue suits its function.
questions.expected: Meristem cells are small, thin-walled and full of cytoplasm, so they divide quickly.
questions.memo: Function (rapid division) → structure (small cells, thin walls, lots of cytoplasm). Located at root and shoot tips where growth happens.
options: Meristem cells are large with thick walls and big vacuoles to store food for growth.
Meristem cells are dead and hollow, so water can flow through them to growing tips.
Meristem cells are tough and waxy so they protect the growing tip from damage.
Meristem cells are small, thin-walled and full of cytoplasm, so they divide quickly.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why animal cells form many different tissue types instead of all being the same.
questions.expected: Different jobs need different cell structures, so specialisation lets each tissue work efficiently.
questions.memo: Division of labour. One generic cell can't be good at everything; specialisation = better performance overall.
options: Different jobs need different cell structures, so specialisation lets each tissue work efficiently.
Identical cells would be too crowded, so the body changes their shapes to fit them in.
Cells become different only by accident as the animal ages and gets damaged.
Having many tissue types is just to make the body look more complex than it is.

LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A2.title: Tissue biotechnology and indigenous knowledge
LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A2.description: Vaccines, antibiotics, blood transfusions, IVF, tissue cloning; indigenous SA plant remedies; links between IK and modern medicine.
LSC.G10.S1.TISS.A2.recovery_strategy: Vaccine = teaches immune system (viruses + bacteria). Antibiotic = kills bacteria (not viruses). Many SA traditional remedies (Hoodia, Pelargonium, Sutherlandia) now scientifically studied.

questions.question: A vaccine works by:
options: Teaching the immune system to recognise a pathogen in advance
questions.expected: Teaching the immune system to recognise a pathogen in advance
questions.memo: Vaccines expose the body to a harmless version (dead/weakened pathogen, or protein fragment). The immune system makes antibodies + memory cells = ready for real infection.

questions.question: Antibiotics work against:
questions.expected: Bacteria, not viruses
questions.memo: Antibiotics target bacterial structures (cell wall, ribosomes) that humans don't have. Viruses have neither — antibiotics do nothing for a cold.

questions.question: True or false: Antibiotics can cure a common cold (caused by a virus).
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Cold = virus → antibiotics don't help. Misusing antibiotics drives antibiotic RESISTANCE in bacteria.

questions.question: What does 'antibiotic resistance' mean?
options: Bacteria evolve so the antibiotic no longer kills them
questions.expected: Bacteria evolve so the antibiotic no longer kills them
questions.memo: Overuse selects for resistant bacteria (natural selection). Result: 'super-bugs' like MDR-TB, which SA struggles with.

questions.question: Before a blood transfusion, the donor's and recipient's blood groups are matched. The MAIN risk if not matched is:
options: The recipient's immune system attacks the donor blood cells (transfusion reaction)
questions.expected: The recipient's immune system attacks the donor blood cells (transfusion reaction)
questions.memo: ABO and Rh markers must match. Mismatched cells clump (agglutinate) and burst → kidney damage, sometimes fatal.

questions.question: In vitro fertilisation (IVF) involves:
options: Fertilising an egg outside the body, then implanting the embryo
questions.expected: Fertilising an egg outside the body, then implanting the embryo
questions.memo: Sperm + egg combined in the lab → early embryo placed back in the womb. Helps couples struggling with infertility.

questions.question: True or false: A clone of a plant is genetically identical to the parent plant.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Yes — tissue culture (or simpler methods like cuttings) produces genetic copies of the parent. Useful for replicating desirable traits.

questions.question: The South African plant Hoodia gordonii has been used by Khoisan people for hunting trips. Scientists studied it because:
options: Indigenous knowledge said it suppresses appetite
questions.expected: Indigenous knowledge said it suppresses appetite
questions.memo: Khoisan hunters chewed Hoodia to suppress hunger and thirst during long trips. Researchers identified the active compound (P57); legal benefit-sharing arrangements followed.

questions.question: Pelargonium sidoides ('umckaloabo') extract is used commercially for:
questions.expected: Treating respiratory infections
questions.memo: Long-used by Zulu and Sotho healers for coughs and bronchitis. Now sold worldwide as an over-the-counter cough/cold preparation.

questions.question: Sutherlandia frutescens, the 'cancer bush', is being researched mainly because:
options: Indigenous knowledge linked it to immune support and cancer-related symptoms
questions.expected: Indigenous knowledge linked it to immune support and cancer-related symptoms
questions.memo: Traditional Xhosa and Sotho healers used Sutherlandia for many conditions including cancer-related ones. Clinical trials underway.

questions.question: The MAIN risk of using untested traditional remedies is:
options: Unknown active doses, side effects or interactions with other medicine
questions.expected: Unknown active doses, side effects or interactions with other medicine
questions.memo: Traditional remedies CAN be effective, but without testing the dose and interactions are uncertain — some are dangerous with prescription drugs (especially ARVs).

questions.question: True or false: A patient on antiretroviral (ARV) therapy for HIV should always check before adding herbal remedies.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Some herbs affect liver enzymes that process ARVs, changing the drug level in blood. Always tell the doctor.

questions.question: Stem-cell therapies for tissue repair (e.g. burn skin grafts) work by:
options: Growing new tissue from stem cells to replace damaged tissue
questions.expected: Growing new tissue from stem cells to replace damaged tissue
questions.memo: Skin stem cells can be cultured on a scaffold to make sheets of new skin — used for severe burn victims.

questions.question: Why does a doctor advise a patient to FINISH a full course of antibiotics?
options: Stopping early lets surviving bacteria multiply and develop resistance
Antibiotics get tastier near the end
questions.expected: Stopping early lets surviving bacteria multiply and develop resistance
questions.memo: Symptoms improve before all bacteria are killed. Stopping early = weakest bacteria die, stronger ones survive → resistance.

questions.question: Vaccines have eradicated which disease worldwide?
questions.expected: Smallpox
questions.memo: Smallpox was declared eradicated by the WHO in 1980 — a triumph of global vaccination. Polio is close.

questions.question: The benefit of plant tissue culture for SA conservation includes:
options: Producing many copies of rare/endangered plants for replanting
questions.expected: Producing many copies of rare/endangered plants for replanting
questions.memo: Endangered SA plants like some cycads and orchids are propagated by tissue culture to support conservation and reduce wild harvesting.

questions.question:
The table shows hospital infection survival rates before and after antibiotic discovery. What is the MAIN message?

| Period         | Survival after major surgery |
|----------------|-----------------------------|
| Pre-1940       | 50%                         |
| Post-1940      | 95%                         |
options: Antibiotics massively reduced deaths from post-surgery infection
questions.expected: Antibiotics massively reduced deaths from post-surgery infection
questions.memo: Penicillin became widely available in the 1940s. Survival after surgery jumped — many infections that were once fatal became treatable.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why indigenous knowledge and modern science can complement each other.
questions.expected: Indigenous knowledge identifies useful plants, and science tests and standardises them for safety.
questions.memo: Two-way street: IK guides discovery (saves time); science validates and ensures dose/safety. SA has formal biodiversity benefit-sharing laws to protect IK contributors.
options: Indigenous knowledge is just superstition, but science can borrow a few lucky guesses from it.
Indigenous knowledge identifies useful plants, and science tests and standardises them for safety.
Science replaces indigenous knowledge entirely once a remedy has been proven to work.
They cannot complement each other because traditional and modern methods always contradict.

questions.question: True or false: Blood transfusions today are screened for HIV and Hepatitis before being given.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: SA's blood services screen every unit for HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis. Decades ago this didn't happen and people contracted infections from transfusions.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ETHICAL benefit-sharing is important when scientists use indigenous knowledge to develop a drug.
questions.expected: The community shared the knowledge enabling the discovery, so they deserve fair benefits.
questions.memo: SA's Biodiversity Act requires benefit-sharing agreements (e.g. the Khoisan-Hoodia agreement). It's a justice and trust issue.
options: Benefit-sharing is only a polite gesture, since the community contributed nothing of value.
It is needed so the community can be paid to keep the knowledge secret from rivals.
Sharing benefits is unnecessary because the knowledge becomes public once published.
The community shared the knowledge enabling the discovery, so they deserve fair benefits.

LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A1.title: Support systems in plants
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A1.description: Herbaceous vs woody support; xylem (lignified), sclerenchyma, collenchyma; turgor pressure.
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A1.caps_topic: Support and transport systems in plants
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A1.recovery_strategy: Soft plants stand by water pressure (turgor). Woody plants stand by lignified xylem. Loss of water → wilting.

questions.question: Soft (herbaceous) plants stay upright mainly because of:
questions.expected: Turgor pressure inside cells
questions.memo: Water in vacuoles pushes against cell walls → cells become firm (turgid) → stem holds itself up. Lose water → wilting.

questions.question: Which substance makes wood rigid in trees?
questions.expected: Lignin in xylem cell walls
questions.memo: Lignin is deposited in secondary cell walls of xylem (and sclerenchyma) → strong, woody support.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma differs from collenchyma in that sclerenchyma:
options: Has lignified cell walls and is found in mature/woody tissue
questions.expected: Has lignified cell walls and is found in mature/woody tissue
questions.memo: Collenchyma = flexible support in growing parts. Sclerenchyma = rigid support in mature parts (lignified, often dead at maturity).

questions.question: When a plant cell loses water, it becomes:
questions.expected: Flaccid (limp)
questions.memo: Turgid = full of water (firm). Flaccid = lost water (limp). Plasmolysed = lost so much water the membrane peels off the wall.

questions.question: Why does lettuce in a fridge stay crisp longer in a sealed container with water?
options: The lettuce cells stay turgid by absorbing water and keeping cell walls tense
questions.expected: The lettuce cells stay turgid by absorbing water and keeping cell walls tense
questions.memo: Crispy = turgid. Limp = flaccid. Keep water available + keep humidity high to prevent evaporation from the leaf.

questions.question: Which support tissue is BEST suited for the soft, flexible petiole (leaf stalk) of a young plant?
questions.expected: Collenchyma
questions.memo: Collenchyma has uneven thick walls but is still alive and flexible — ideal for growing parts that need support but mustn't be rigid.

questions.question: True or false: All plants rely on wood for support.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Soft (herbaceous) plants like lettuce, tomatoes and ferns rely on turgor + collenchyma — no lignin or wood.

questions.question: The thick secondary cell wall of xylem is mainly made of:
questions.expected: Cellulose and lignin
questions.memo: Cellulose fibres form the framework; lignin is added in layers between fibres → super-strong rigid wall.

questions.question:
Look at the cross-section of a young stem. Which tissue lies in a ring just inside the epidermis and provides flexible support?
[Diagram: stem cross-section with labelled layers]
questions.expected: Collenchyma
questions.memo: Collenchyma forms a continuous flexible support ring under the epidermis in many young stems — feel a celery stalk's tough outer 'string' = bundles of collenchyma.

questions.question: Why does a wilting indigenous SA succulent (e.g. spekboom) wilt less easily than a soft herbaceous plant?
options: It stores large amounts of water in fleshy leaves and stems
questions.expected: It stores large amounts of water in fleshy leaves and stems
questions.memo: Succulents are built for SA's dry biomes — water-storing tissue + waxy cuticle + reduced surface area minimise water loss.

questions.question: An adaptation of woody plants for living in windy areas is:
options: Flexible bending of the lignified stem without breaking
questions.expected: Flexible bending of the lignified stem without breaking
questions.memo: Wood is strong but not brittle — it flexes and recovers. Tall woody plants in windy areas (Karoo, coastal) survive wind by bending.

questions.question: True or false: Loss of turgor in plant cells is reversible if water is added.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Add water → vacuoles refill → cells become turgid again → plant 'perks up'. (Plasmolysis can sometimes be reversed too, if not too severe.)

questions.question: Which is NOT a function of plant support tissues?
questions.expected: Photosynthesis
questions.memo: Photosynthesis is the job of chloroplast-rich tissue (mesophyll). Support tissue holds the plant upright so the leaves CAN reach light.

questions.question: Why is xylem suitable for BOTH transport and support?
questions.expected: Xylem is hollow for water flow and has thick lignified walls that give support.
questions.memo: Two-for-one: structure (rigid wall) AND function (transport channel). Beautiful example of evolutionary efficiency.
options: Xylem cells are alive and flexible, bending to both carry water and hold the plant up.
Xylem is hollow for water flow and has thick lignified walls that give support.
Xylem stores sugar that fuels growth, which is what makes the stem stand upright.
Xylem is filled with air pockets that float the plant upward and carry water along.

questions.question: A wilted plant left in the sun for many hours may not recover when watered because:
options: Cells have plasmolysed and some have died from severe dehydration
Water has evaporated from the soil
questions.expected: Cells have plasmolysed and some have died from severe dehydration
questions.memo: Brief wilting is reversible (just flaccid). Prolonged severe wilting → plasmolysis → cell death = irreversible damage.

questions.question: The 'rings' you see in a tree trunk cross-section are mostly:
questions.expected: Annual layers of secondary xylem (wood)
questions.memo: Each year the cambium adds a new layer of xylem. Wide rings = good year (rain, warmth). Narrow rings = drought year — useful for past climate reconstruction.

questions.question: The 'bark' on the outside of a tree is mainly made of:
options: Dead cork cells full of waterproof suberin
questions.expected: Dead cork cells full of waterproof suberin
