questions.memo: Bark = the outer protective layer, mostly dead cork cells. Protects from water loss, pests, fire (in fynbos species especially).

questions.question: Why does a fynbos plant in the Cape often grow short and dense rather than tall?
options: Adaptation to wind, fire and poor soils — shorter plants resist wind and recover faster after fire
Plants don't grow tall in SA
questions.expected: Adaptation to wind, fire and poor soils — shorter plants resist wind and recover faster after fire
questions.memo: Fynbos is a fire-adapted biome — many species resprout from underground bulbs/lignotubers after fire. Tall woody plants are at greater fire risk.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a plant relying only on turgor cannot grow very tall.
questions.expected: Turgor cannot support the plant's weight over many metres, so tall plants need lignin.
questions.memo: Tall plants need rigid lignified xylem (wood). Tree-tall + turgor only would crumple in the first strong wind.
options: Turgor cannot support the plant's weight over many metres, so tall plants need lignin.
Turgor pressure pushes downward, which would crush a tall plant from above.
Tall plants run out of water before turgor can ever reach the top branches.
Turgor only works at night, so a plant relying on it could not grow during the day.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how a cabbage stem combines two support strategies.
questions.expected: The cabbage uses turgor in its parenchyma plus collenchyma and xylem for extra support.
questions.memo: Real plants usually combine strategies. Cabbage = mostly turgor + collenchyma; an oak = mostly lignified xylem.
options: The cabbage relies only on turgor, with no support tissue helping at all.
The cabbage uses lignified xylem like an oak tree, with no turgor involved.
The cabbage uses turgor in its parenchyma plus collenchyma and xylem for extra support.
The cabbage uses its waxy leaf coating and its roots as its two support strategies.

LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A2.title: Plant transport and transpiration
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A2.description: Xylem/phloem structure; transpiration pull theory; translocation; environmental factors affecting transpiration.
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A2.caps_topic: Support and transport systems in plants
LSC.G10.S2.PTRN.A2.recovery_strategy: Xylem = WATER, root→leaf, one-way. Phloem = SUGAR, both directions. Transpiration rises with light, temperature, wind; falls with humidity.

questions.question: Transpiration is the:
options: Loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through stomata
Movement of sugars in the phloem
Uptake of minerals by the roots
questions.expected: Loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through stomata
questions.memo: Liquid water in leaf cells evaporates → vapour leaves through stomata in the leaf surface. The 'engine' that pulls water up the plant.

questions.question: The MAJORITY of transpiration in a typical plant happens through:
questions.expected: Stomata on leaves
questions.memo: Stomata = pores in the leaf surface. The leaf has huge total surface area + many stomata → main route of water loss.

questions.question: The 'transpiration pull' theory says water moves up the xylem because:
options: Evaporation from leaves pulls a continuous water column up due to cohesion
Wind blows water up the stem
questions.expected: Evaporation from leaves pulls a continuous water column up due to cohesion
questions.memo: Water molecules stick to each other (cohesion) and to xylem walls (adhesion). As water vapour leaves the leaves, the whole column is pulled up like a straw.

questions.question: Which mineral does the phloem mainly transport?
questions.expected: Sucrose (sugar)
questions.memo: Phloem moves dissolved sugar from 'sources' (photosynthesising leaves) to 'sinks' (roots, fruits, growing tips). This is translocation.

questions.question: True or false: Xylem transport is two-way (up AND down).
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Xylem = one-way only (root → leaf). Phloem can move in BOTH directions depending on where sugar is needed.

questions.question: Which environmental factor INCREASES the rate of transpiration?
questions.expected: A windy day
questions.memo: Wind blows the layer of humid air off the leaf → keeps the gradient steep → transpiration speeds up.

questions.question: Which environmental factor DECREASES transpiration?
options: High humidity in the surrounding air
questions.expected: High humidity in the surrounding air
questions.memo: High humidity = less gradient between leaf and air → water doesn't leave the stomata as fast.

questions.question: The graph shows transpiration rate vs time of day. The rate is high at midday and low at night. The MAIN reason for low night-time transpiration is:

data.description: Transpiration rate: 6am low, 9am medium, 12pm high, 3pm high, 6pm medium, 9pm low, 12am very low

options: Stomata close at night to reduce water loss
Roots stop taking up water at night
questions.expected: Stomata close at night to reduce water loss
questions.memo: Most plants close their stomata at night — no photosynthesis happening → no need to take in CO2 → save water.

questions.question: Plants in dry biomes often have FEWER stomata, or stomata sunken into pits. This is because:
options: Both reduce water loss in dry conditions
questions.expected: Both reduce water loss in dry conditions
questions.memo: Karoo plants, succulents and grasses often hide stomata in pits or have a thicker cuticle. Less surface exposed → less transpiration.

questions.question: A pupil tests transpiration in a plant by weighing it over a day. The mass DROPS by 3 g. Why?

data.description: Plant mass at 8am: 250 g. Plant mass at 5pm: 247 g.

options: Water has been lost as vapour during transpiration
questions.expected: Water has been lost as vapour during transpiration
questions.memo: The lost mass is water leaving as vapour through stomata. A simple, elegant practical to demonstrate transpiration.

questions.question: Why do xylem vessels have thick walls?
options: To resist the negative pressure of the water column being pulled up
questions.expected: To resist the negative pressure of the water column being pulled up
questions.memo: Transpiration pull creates tension (negative pressure) in the water column. Thin walls would collapse — thick lignified walls don't.

questions.question: What are GUARD CELLS?
options: Pairs of cells that open and close the stoma
questions.expected: Pairs of cells that open and close the stoma
questions.memo: Guard cells flank each stoma. When turgid → bend apart → stoma open. When flaccid → close → stoma shut.

questions.question: Stomata open and close to balance:
options: Letting CO2 in for photosynthesis vs limiting water loss
questions.expected: Letting CO2 in for photosynthesis vs limiting water loss
questions.memo: Stomata = the plant's main trade-off. Open = photosynthesis works but water lost. Closed = water saved but photosynthesis slows.

questions.question: Translocation refers to:
options: The movement of sugars in the phloem
questions.expected: The movement of sugars in the phloem
questions.memo: Translocation = sugar transport (phloem). Distinct from transpiration (xylem water).

questions.question: True or false: Phloem transport requires energy (it is active).
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Loading sucrose into sieve tubes uses active transport (ATP). Once loaded, water follows by osmosis and the pressure flow carries the sugar along.

questions.question: Why does a leafy cutting placed in coloured water show the colour rising through the stem?
options: The dye is pulled up the xylem along with the water column
The dye is alive and crawls up
Cutting the stem injects the dye
questions.expected: The dye is pulled up the xylem along with the water column
questions.memo: Classic practical: celery + food colouring. The dyed water column moves up the xylem and stains the leaf veins.

questions.question: Ringing (removing a strip of bark) a branch kills the leaves above the ring eventually because:
options: Phloem is in the bark — removing it cuts off sugar transport to and from above the ring
questions.expected: Phloem is in the bark — removing it cuts off sugar transport to and from above the ring
questions.memo: Phloem sits just inside the bark. Cutting it breaks sugar flow between roots and leaves. Trees girdled this way slowly die — a sad orchard problem.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how stomata closing helps a plant during a hot dry day.
questions.expected: Closing the stomata reduces transpiration, conserving water and helping avoid wilting.
questions.memo: Trade-off: closing stomata also slows photosynthesis — but in extreme conditions surviving is more important than growing.
options: Closing the stomata reduces transpiration, conserving water and helping avoid wilting.
Closing the stomata lets the plant take in more water vapour from the hot air.
Closing the stomata cools the plant by trapping heat inside the leaf.
Closing the stomata speeds up photosynthesis so the plant can grow in the heat.

questions.question: Predict: A pupil sets up two identical leafy shoots — one in still air, one in a fan-blown stream. After 1 hour, which has lost more water?
options: The shoot in the fan-blown air, because wind speeds up transpiration
questions.expected: The shoot in the fan-blown air, because wind speeds up transpiration
questions.memo: Wind blows humid air away from the leaf surface, keeping the diffusion gradient steep → transpiration rises.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why xylem and phloem TOGETHER make a complete circulatory system for a plant.
questions.expected: Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries sugars from leaves to the rest.
questions.memo: Two opposite directions of bulk flow keep every cell supplied. Cut either one and the plant fails.
options: Both xylem and phloem carry water upward, doubling the supply to the leaves.
Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries sugars from leaves to the rest.
Xylem carries sugars down while phloem carries water up to the leaves.
Phloem carries blood around the plant while xylem pumps it like a heart.

LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A1.title: Animal support — the human skeleton
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A1.description: Skeleton functions; axial vs appendicular; long bone structure; joint types.
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A1.recovery_strategy: Axial = skull, ribs, vertebrae. Appendicular = limbs + girdles. Long bones: compact outside, spongy inside, marrow makes blood cells.

questions.question: Which is NOT a function of the human skeleton?
questions.expected: Photosynthesis
questions.memo: Skeleton roles: support, protection, movement (with muscles), blood-cell formation, mineral storage. Photosynthesis is for plants.

questions.question: The axial skeleton includes:
questions.expected: Skull, vertebral column and ribs
questions.memo: Axial = centre line (head + spine + ribs + sternum). Appendicular = limbs + girdles.

questions.question: Which bone is part of the APPENDICULAR skeleton?
questions.expected: Femur (thigh bone)
questions.memo: Femur = part of the leg → appendicular. Skull, sternum, vertebrae = axial.

questions.question: Bone marrow's MAIN job is:
options: Producing red and white blood cells
questions.expected: Producing red and white blood cells
questions.memo: Red bone marrow (mainly in spongy bone) makes blood cells. This is haematopoiesis. Diseased marrow → leukaemia.

questions.question: A ball-and-socket joint is found at the:
questions.expected: Shoulder and hip
questions.memo: Ball-and-socket = wide range of movement in many directions. Shoulder and hip are the main examples in the body.

questions.question: A hinge joint is found at the:
questions.expected: Elbow and knee
questions.memo: Hinge joint = movement in one plane (open/close). Elbow, knee, finger joints all work this way.

questions.question:
On the long-bone diagram, which letter labels the hard outer layer that gives strength?
[Diagram: long bone with A=compact bone outer, B=spongy bone, C=marrow cavity, D=epiphysis]
questions.expected: A
questions.memo: Compact (cortical) bone = dense outer shell. Spongy (cancellous) bone = inside, with marrow. Cavity = central hollow.

questions.question: Why do birds have HOLLOW bones?
options: To reduce weight for flight while still being strong
questions.expected: To reduce weight for flight while still being strong
questions.memo: Hollow tubes are nearly as strong as solid ones but much lighter. Excellent adaptation for flight — same engineering as bike frames.

questions.question:
Match each function to the part of the skeleton:
1. Protects the brain
2. Protects heart and lungs
3. Allows the leg to move at the knee

A. Hinge joint
B. Rib cage
C. Skull
questions.memo: Skull → brain. Rib cage → heart and lungs. Hinge joint at knee → bending.

questions.question: Cartilage at the end of bones in a joint helps:
questions.expected: Reduce friction and absorb shock
questions.memo: Articular cartilage = smooth, springy. Damaged cartilage (arthritis) → bone rubs on bone → pain.

questions.question: True or false: All adult bones contain bone marrow that produces blood cells.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: In adults, only some bones (sternum, hips, vertebrae, skull) still make blood. Long bones in arms/legs often have yellow (fatty) marrow instead.

questions.question: The vertebral column has natural curves. The MAIN reason is:
options: To absorb shock and balance the weight of the head
questions.expected: To absorb shock and balance the weight of the head
questions.memo: S-shaped spine acts like a spring — absorbs impact when walking/running. A straight column would jar the brain with every step.

questions.question: Synovial fluid in a joint serves to:
questions.expected: Lubricate the joint surfaces
questions.memo: Synovial fluid is a slippery, viscous fluid in a joint capsule — like oil in a hinge. Reduces wear and friction.

questions.question: Which joint allows you to turn your head from side to side?
options: Pivot joint between the first two vertebrae
questions.expected: Pivot joint between the first two vertebrae
questions.memo: Atlas (C1) and Axis (C2) form a pivot joint at the top of the spine — neck rotation.

questions.question: The pelvis protects which organs?
options: The reproductive and lower urinary organs
questions.expected: The reproductive and lower urinary organs
questions.memo: Pelvis = bony bowl that protects the bladder, parts of the gut, and reproductive organs. Also supports body weight in standing/walking.

questions.question: Why is the femur the longest and strongest bone in the body?
options: It supports the body's weight and powerful leg muscles attach to it
It is closest to the heart
questions.expected: It supports the body's weight and powerful leg muscles attach to it
questions.memo: When you walk or run, the femur takes huge forces. Its size and density match its job.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why an athlete in a contact sport benefits from a strong skeleton.
questions.expected: Strong bones support the body and resist impact, and anchor muscles for more power.
questions.memo: Muscles attach via tendons to bone — bone density matters for force generation as well as protection. Why weight-bearing exercise strengthens bone.
options: Strong bones store extra calcium that the athlete burns directly as energy during play.
Strong bones make the athlete heavier, so opponents cannot push them over.
Strong bones support the body and resist impact, and anchor muscles for more power.
Strong bones produce the hormones that make the athlete's muscles contract faster.

questions.question: Children's bones break less catastrophically than adults' because:
options: Their bones contain more collagen (flexible protein) and are still growing
questions.expected: Their bones contain more collagen (flexible protein) and are still growing
questions.memo: Young bones are more elastic — 'greenstick' fractures bend rather than snap clean. With age, bones become more brittle (less collagen).

questions.question: True or false: Bones are dead — they do not change after you stop growing.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Bone is living tissue — constantly remodelled. Weight-bearing exercise increases density; inactivity (e.g. astronauts) loses bone mass.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the structure of compact bone (Haversian system) makes it strong.
questions.expected: Concentric layers (Haversian systems) around blood vessels make it strong and able to repair.
questions.memo: Mineralised + tube-shaped → strong against compression and bending. Blood supply keeps the cells alive and lets the bone heal after a fracture.
options: Compact bone is solid and lifeless throughout, which is what makes it hard.
Compact bone is filled with soft marrow that cushions every impact like a sponge.
Compact bone is made of flexible cartilage layers that bend rather than break.
Concentric layers (Haversian systems) around blood vessels make it strong and able to repair.

LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A2.title: Bone disorders and indigenous knowledge of plant remedies
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A2.description: Osteoporosis, rickets, arthritis; indigenous plant-based treatments; links to modern medicine.
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A2.recovery_strategy: Rickets = soft bones in children (Vit D/Ca). Osteoporosis = thinning bones in adults. Arthritis = joint inflammation.

questions.question: Rickets is caused by:
questions.expected: Vitamin D and calcium deficiency
questions.memo: Vit D needed for calcium absorption. Lack → bones don't mineralise properly → soft, bowed legs in children.

questions.question: Osteoporosis is most common in:
questions.expected: Older adults, especially post-menopausal women
questions.memo: Bone density falls with age and falls more sharply in women after menopause (oestrogen drop). Hip and wrist fractures are common.

questions.question: Arthritis is mainly:
options: Inflammation of joints causing pain and stiffness
questions.expected: Inflammation of joints causing pain and stiffness
questions.memo: Arthritis affects joints. Two main types: osteoarthritis (wear of cartilage) and rheumatoid (autoimmune).

questions.question: Which food group helps PREVENT osteoporosis?
questions.expected: Dairy and other calcium-rich foods
questions.memo: Dairy, leafy greens, sardines (with bones), fortified plant milks. Combined with Vitamin D + weight-bearing exercise.

questions.question: True or false: Sunshine on the skin helps prevent rickets.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: UV light triggers Vit D production in skin. SA has abundant sunlight — rickets is rare except where skin coverage is heavy or diet is very poor.

questions.question: Weight-bearing exercise helps prevent osteoporosis because:
options: It signals bones to lay down more mineral, increasing density
Exercise has no effect on bone
questions.expected: It signals bones to lay down more mineral, increasing density
questions.memo: Bone responds to loading (Wolff's Law) — stress → stronger bone. Why walking, running and weight training matter for bone health.

questions.question:
The table shows bone-fracture rates per 1000 women per year by age. Which trend does it show?

| Age   | Fractures |
|-------|-----------|
| 30–40 | 1         |
| 50–60 | 5         |
| 70–80 | 25        |
options: Fracture risk rises sharply with age (osteoporosis)
questions.expected: Fracture risk rises sharply with age (osteoporosis)
questions.memo: Bone density falls with age — fracture risk rises exponentially. This is why screening (DEXA) is recommended for older women.

questions.question: True or false: Smoking and excessive alcohol can WORSEN osteoporosis.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Both interfere with bone-forming cells (osteoblasts). Smoking also lowers oestrogen levels in women — extra risk.

questions.question: Indigenous Zulu healers have traditionally used the bark of Sclerocarya birrea (marula) for:
questions.expected: Pain relief including joint pain
questions.memo: Marula bark has long been used for inflammation and joint pain. Scientific studies have found anti-inflammatory compounds.

questions.question: Why should a patient with osteoporosis tell their doctor about ALL the herbal remedies they take?
options: Some herbs interact with prescription medication or affect bone health
questions.expected: Some herbs interact with prescription medication or affect bone health
questions.memo: Some herbs raise/lower oestrogen, blood thinning, or interact with bone-density drugs. Disclosure prevents harm.

questions.question: Aspirin, used for arthritis pain, was originally derived from:
questions.expected: Willow tree bark (traditional remedy)
questions.memo: Willow bark contains salicin. Indigenous use → scientists isolated and synthesised acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in the 1800s. Great IK → science example.

questions.question: Which is the BEST scientific way to evaluate a traditional remedy for arthritis?
options: A controlled clinical trial comparing it to a placebo
Reading about it in old books
questions.expected: A controlled clinical trial comparing it to a placebo
questions.memo: Anecdotes ≠ evidence. A blinded, controlled trial removes bias and tests if the remedy works better than nothing.

questions.question: Treatment of osteoporosis often includes:
options: Calcium + Vit D supplements + exercise + sometimes bisphosphonate drugs
questions.expected: Calcium + Vit D supplements + exercise + sometimes bisphosphonate drugs
questions.memo: Multi-pronged approach: nutrition + exercise + medication if needed. Prevent falls (hip fractures are dangerous in elderly).

questions.question: True or false: Rickets has almost disappeared in countries with diet fortification and good sunlight, but is making a comeback in some.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Resurgence linked to indoor lifestyles, poor diet, heavy sun protection. Public-health messaging matters.

questions.question: Why do older people often shrink (lose height)?
options: Vertebrae lose height due to osteoporosis and compressed discs
questions.expected: Vertebrae lose height due to osteoporosis and compressed discs
questions.memo: Bone loss in the spine + thinning of intervertebral discs. Can be reduced by exercise, calcium and avoiding smoking.

questions.question: Compare osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis briefly.
questions.expected: Osteoarthritis is wear of joint cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune attack.
questions.memo: Different causes, different treatments. Osteo = pain relief + joint replacement if severe. Rheumatoid = immune-modifying drugs.
options: Osteoarthritis is wear of joint cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune attack.
Both are caused by the immune system attacking the joints, just at different ages.
Osteoarthritis is an infection of the bone; rheumatoid arthritis is caused by old age.
Osteoarthritis affects only children, while rheumatoid arthritis affects only the elderly.

questions.question: Why is the FALL — not the osteoporosis itself — often the cause of death in elderly patients?
options: Fractures from falls (especially hip) can lead to immobility, pneumonia and complications
Old people are made of glass
questions.expected: Fractures from falls (especially hip) can lead to immobility, pneumonia and complications
questions.memo: A hip fracture can confine an elderly patient to bed → muscle wasting → pneumonia → death. Fall-prevention (vision, balance, home hazards) saves lives.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a balanced indigenous AND modern medical approach is often best for chronic bone conditions.
questions.expected: IK offers accessible, cultural value while modern medicine offers tested treatment for severe cases.
questions.memo: Many SA patients use both. Mutual respect + open communication between healer and doctor → better outcomes.
options: Indigenous remedies are always more effective, so modern medicine should be avoided.
IK offers accessible, cultural value while modern medicine offers tested treatment for severe cases.
Only modern medicine works, so indigenous remedies should never be used at all.
The two should never be combined because mixing them is always dangerous.

questions.question: True or false: Children playing outside in the sun get free Vitamin D.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: 15–30 minutes of sun exposure on arms/legs a few times a week is enough for most kids. Balance with sun safety (no burns).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why diet quality at age 15 affects bone strength at age 70.
questions.expected: Peak bone mass is built in youth, so a higher peak means less osteoporosis risk later.
questions.memo: Teens who eat well + exercise have stronger skeletons their whole life. Skipping milk and sun in adolescence is a long-term cost.
options: Bones stop changing after birth, so age 15 diet has no effect on age 70.
Peak bone mass is built in youth, so a higher peak means less osteoporosis risk later.
Eating well at 15 makes bones grow until age 70, so they never stop getting denser.
Diet at 15 matters only because it sets eating habits, not because of bone itself.

LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A3.title: Muscles and movement
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A3.description: Skeletal/smooth/cardiac muscle; antagonistic pairs (biceps + triceps); tendons and ligaments.
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A3.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.ASUP.A3.recovery_strategy: Tendon = muscle→bone. Ligament = bone→bone. Muscles only PULL. Pairs work in opposition.

questions.question: Tendons attach:
questions.expected: Muscle to bone
questions.memo: Tendon = muscle to bone (transmits the pull). Ligament = bone to bone (stabilises a joint).

questions.question: Ligaments attach:
questions.expected: Bone to bone
questions.memo: Ligaments hold joint bones together. Tear a ligament (e.g. ACL in the knee) → joint becomes unstable.

questions.question: Which muscle type is under voluntary (conscious) control?
questions.expected: Skeletal muscle
questions.memo: Skeletal = voluntary (move when you decide). Smooth (gut, vessels) and cardiac (heart) = involuntary.

questions.question: The biceps and triceps are an example of:
questions.expected: An antagonistic pair
questions.memo: Antagonistic pair = opposite actions. Biceps bends elbow; triceps straightens elbow.

questions.question: When you bend your arm at the elbow:
options: The biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes
questions.expected: The biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes
questions.memo: Muscles only PULL. To bend the arm, biceps shorten while triceps lengthen. To straighten, the opposite happens.

questions.question: Why do muscles need to work in antagonistic pairs?
options: Because muscles can only PULL, not push — opposing muscles are needed to reverse the movement
questions.expected: Because muscles can only PULL, not push — opposing muscles are needed to reverse the movement
questions.memo: A muscle shortens when it contracts. To move a joint back, another muscle must pull in the opposite direction.

questions.question:
On the labelled arm diagram, which muscle is the biceps and what does it do?
[Diagram: arm bent showing two muscles, one bulging on the top of the upper arm]
questions.expected: Top muscle, bends the elbow
questions.memo: Biceps (top) flexes the elbow. Triceps (bottom) extends it.

questions.question: Smooth muscle is found in:
questions.expected: The gut and blood-vessel walls
questions.memo: Smooth muscle = involuntary, slow, sustained. Pushes food through the gut (peristalsis), narrows arteries to control blood pressure.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle is special because:
options: It contracts rhythmically without tiring and is found only in the heart
questions.expected: It contracts rhythmically without tiring and is found only in the heart
questions.memo: Heart muscle has its own pacemaker (SA node). Contracts ~70 times a minute for life. Cells linked by intercalated discs.

questions.question:
Match each muscle type to its location:
1. Skeletal  2. Smooth  3. Cardiac

A. Heart only
B. Attached to bones, moves limbs
C. Walls of gut and blood vessels
questions.memo: Skeletal = limbs. Smooth = gut + vessels. Cardiac = heart only.

questions.question: An Achilles tendon injury happens when:
options: The tendon connecting calf muscle to heel bone tears
questions.expected: The tendon connecting calf muscle to heel bone tears
questions.memo: Achilles is the largest tendon in the body. Rupture (often in older runners) = sudden 'snap' + inability to push off — surgery often needed.

questions.question: An ACL tear in the knee is an injury to a:
questions.expected: Ligament (anterior cruciate)
questions.memo: ACL = ligament inside the knee joint. Tear = unstable knee. Famous sports injury (rugby, soccer, netball).

questions.question: True or false: When you 'flex' your bicep, the muscle gets shorter and thicker.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Muscle filaments slide past each other → muscle shortens, bulges in the middle. Antagonist (triceps) lengthens at the same time.

questions.question: Muscle fatigue during prolonged exercise is partly due to:
options: Build-up of lactic acid from anaerobic respiration
questions.expected: Build-up of lactic acid from anaerobic respiration
questions.memo: When O2 supply can't keep up, cells use anaerobic respiration → lactic acid builds up → 'burn' + fatigue. (Aerobic respiration covered in Grade 11.)

questions.question: Why do athletes warm up muscles before intense exercise?
options: Warm muscles are more flexible, reducing tear and strain risk
questions.expected: Warm muscles are more flexible, reducing tear and strain risk
questions.memo: Warm-up raises muscle temperature → enzyme activity rises → fibres slide more smoothly. Reduces injury risk.

questions.question: Why is regular exercise good for skeletal muscles AND bones?
questions.expected: Exercise stresses bones and muscles, signalling them to grow stronger and denser.
questions.memo: Use it or lose it. Inactivity → bone loss, muscle wasting. Activity = adaptation = stronger system.
options: Exercise stresses bones and muscles, signalling them to grow stronger and denser.
Exercise wears bones and muscles down, so they slowly become weaker over time.
Exercise only burns fat and has no real effect on the bones or muscles themselves.
Exercise adds new bones and muscles to the body that were not there before.

questions.question: Some traditional SA athletes use stretching and balance routines passed down through their families. Why are these still useful today?
options: Stretching improves flexibility and reduces injury risk — modern sports science confirms this
questions.expected: Stretching improves flexibility and reduces injury risk — modern sports science confirms this
questions.memo: Indigenous practices often have built-in functional value. Sports science can validate and refine them.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a person with weak quadriceps muscles often has knee pain.
questions.expected: The quadriceps help stabilise the knee, so when they are weak the joint bears uneven force and its structures get strained, causing pain.
questions.memo: Strengthening exercise (squats, leg extensions) is often a first-line treatment for knee pain in healthy joints.
options: The quadriceps help stabilise the knee, so when they are weak the joint bears uneven force and its structures get strained, causing pain.
Weak quadriceps cannot produce lactic acid, and the build-up of toxins in the joint is what causes the knee pain.
Weak quadriceps stretch the kneecap bone until it cracks, which is the direct source of the pain.
Pain comes only from the cartilage wearing out with age; the strength of the quadriceps has no effect on the knee.

questions.question: True or false: Muscles can only get bigger by lifting heavier weights, never by simple movements.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Body-weight movements (push-ups, squats), resistance bands, and increased repetition all grow muscle. The principle is progressive overload — push beyond what you're used to.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how muscles, tendons, bones and joints work TOGETHER in a single movement (e.g. lifting a bag).
questions.expected: Muscles contract and pull on tendons, the tendons transmit the pull to bones, and the bones move at joints to lift the bag.
questions.memo: It's a chain: muscle pull → tendon → bone lever → joint pivot → movement. One weak link slows the whole motion.
options: The bones contract on their own to lift the bag, and the muscles simply cushion the joint while it moves.
Tendons contract and shorten to lift the bag, while muscles act as the rigid levers the bag rests on.
Muscles contract and pull on tendons, the tendons transmit the pull to bones, and the bones move at joints to lift the bag.
Joints generate the force, the muscles store it as fat, and the tendons release it slowly to raise the bag.

LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A1.title: Heart structure, circulation and the cardiac cycle
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A1.description: Heart chambers, valves, vessels; double circulation; left ventricle wall; cardiac cycle phases; SA/AV nodes; pulse and exercise.
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A1.recovery_strategy: RIGHT side = DEoxygenated (body→lungs). LEFT side = OXYGENATED (lungs→body). Left ventricle thicker for whole-body pump. Cycle: atria→ventricles→relax. SA node = pacemaker.

questions.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.memo: Two atria (top), two ventricles (bottom). Right side = deoxygenated; left side = oxygenated.

questions.question: Blood enters the heart through the:
questions.expected: Atria
questions.memo: Atria receive blood. Ventricles pump blood OUT. Vena cavae → right atrium; pulmonary veins → left atrium.

questions.question: The aorta carries blood from the:
questions.expected: Left ventricle to the body
questions.memo: Aorta = the body's main artery. Carries oxygenated blood from left ventricle to the systemic circulation.

questions.question: The pulmonary artery carries:
options: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
Oxygenated blood from the heart to the body
questions.expected: Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
questions.memo: Pulmonary artery is the EXCEPTION: arteries usually carry oxygenated blood, but the pulmonary artery carries DEoxygenated blood.

questions.question: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right ventricle wall?
options: It pumps blood to the whole body, needing more force
It is closer to the lungs
questions.expected: It pumps blood to the whole body, needing more force
questions.memo: Left ventricle drives the systemic circuit (high pressure, whole body). Right ventricle drives the pulmonary circuit (low pressure, just to the nearby lungs).

questions.question:
Identify the structure labelled 'X' (the muscular pump on the left, with thick wall).
[Diagram: heart with chambers labelled W=right atrium, X=left ventricle, Y=right ventricle, Z=left atrium]
questions.expected: Left ventricle
questions.memo: Thickest wall = left ventricle. Sits on the LEFT side of the heart (from the patient's perspective).

questions.question: The AV (atrioventricular) valves PREVENT:
questions.expected: Back-flow from ventricles to atria
questions.memo: When ventricles contract, the AV valves snap shut → blood goes out into the arteries, not back into the atria. Faulty valve → murmur, fatigue.

questions.question: Double circulation means:
options: Blood passes through the heart TWICE per body circuit (pulmonary + systemic)
Blood circulates only on rest days
Blood goes only to the lungs
questions.expected: Blood passes through the heart TWICE per body circuit (pulmonary + systemic)
questions.memo: Body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body. Two loops = pulmonary + systemic. Allows high pressure to body + low pressure to delicate lungs.

questions.question:
Order the cardiac cycle events:
(a) Atria contract
(b) Ventricles contract
(c) All chambers relax (diastole)
(d) Blood enters atria from veins
questions.expected: d → a → b → c
questions.memo: Blood fills atria (during diastole) → atria contract (atrial systole) → ventricles contract (ventricular systole) → all chambers relax (diastole) → cycle repeats.

questions.question: The pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.expected: SA (sinoatrial) node
questions.memo: SA node in the right atrium generates the electrical signal that starts each heartbeat. AV node relays the signal to the ventricles after a short delay.

questions.question: An artificial pacemaker is fitted when:
options: The natural pacemaker (SA node) fails or beats irregularly
questions.expected: The natural pacemaker (SA node) fails or beats irregularly
questions.memo: Pacemaker = small electronic device that delivers regular electrical impulses to keep the heart beating reliably.

questions.question: Pulse rate measures:
options: The number of heartbeats per minute
questions.expected: The number of heartbeats per minute
questions.memo: Each heartbeat sends a pressure wave down the arteries — you feel it as pulse at the wrist or neck. Normal resting adult: ~60–80 bpm.

questions.question: True or false: Pulse rate INCREASES during exercise.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Working muscles need more O2 and produce more CO2 → heart beats faster to deliver O2 and remove CO2.

questions.question: A pupil records her pulse: resting 70 bpm, immediately after a sprint 160 bpm. Why does pulse rise?

data.description: Resting pulse 70 bpm; post-sprint pulse 160 bpm

options: Muscles need more O2 and to remove CO2 faster
questions.expected: Muscles need more O2 and to remove CO2 faster
questions.memo: Higher heart rate = more cardiac output = more O2 delivered + more CO2 removed per minute. Athletes recover faster (lower 'recovery pulse').

questions.question: Semilunar valves are found at the:
options: Exits of the ventricles into the aorta and pulmonary artery
questions.expected: Exits of the ventricles into the aorta and pulmonary artery
questions.memo: Semilunar valves prevent backflow of blood from the arteries into the ventricles when ventricles relax.

questions.question: Why does the LEFT side of the heart NEVER mix blood with the RIGHT side?
options: The septum (wall) between them keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate
The blood is too thick to mix
questions.expected: The septum (wall) between them keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate
questions.memo: Septum prevents mixing — essential for efficient gas exchange. A 'hole in the heart' (septal defect) is a serious birth condition.

questions.question: Identify the phase of the cardiac cycle where ventricles contract and push blood out of the heart.
questions.expected: Ventricular systole
questions.memo: Systole = contract. Diastole = relax. Ventricular systole = the strong heart squeeze that creates your pulse.

questions.question: Why does a fit athlete have a LOWER resting pulse than an unfit person?
options: A trained heart pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats per minute
questions.expected: A trained heart pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats per minute
questions.memo: Endurance training makes the heart muscle stronger and the chambers slightly larger → higher stroke volume → lower resting pulse to deliver the same output.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why double circulation in mammals is more efficient than the single circulation in a fish.
questions.expected: Double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and lets the heart pump at high pressure to the body but gentler to the lungs.
questions.memo: Mammals (and birds) are 'high-performance' animals — high O2 demand for warm-bloodedness needs the more efficient double circulation.
options: Double circulation lets oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix freely, which warms the blood faster than a fish can.
Double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate and lets the heart pump at high pressure to the body but gentler to the lungs.
Double circulation means blood passes through the heart only once, so it travels around the body more quickly than in a fish.
Double circulation is more efficient only because mammals have more blood than fish, not because of how it is routed.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences what the SA and AV nodes do in coordinating the heartbeat.
questions.expected: The SA node generates the signal that starts each beat and sets the rate, and the AV node relays it to the ventricles after a short delay.
questions.memo: Timing matters: if atria and ventricles contracted at the same time, the valves wouldn't have time to fill properly. The delay ensures efficient pumping.
options: The SA node only controls breathing rate, while the AV node is what actually starts each heartbeat.
Both nodes fire at exactly the same instant so the atria and ventricles contract together for maximum force.
The AV node sets the heart rate and the SA node pumps the blood out of the ventricles into the arteries.
The SA node generates the signal that starts each beat and sets the rate, and the AV node relays it to the ventricles after a short delay.

LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A2.title: Blood vessels, blood composition and lymph
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A2.description: Arteries, veins, capillaries; red/white cells, platelets, plasma; lymphatic system.
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A2.recovery_strategy: Arteries: thick walls, away from heart. Veins: thin walls, valves, toward heart. Capillaries: one-cell-thick, exchange. Pulmonary artery is the exception.

questions.question: Arteries usually carry:
options: Oxygenated blood away from the heart
questions.expected: Oxygenated blood away from the heart
questions.memo: Arteries = away from heart. Most carry oxygenated blood — pulmonary artery is the exception (carries deoxygenated blood to lungs).

questions.question: Veins carry blood:
questions.expected: Toward the heart
questions.memo: Veins return blood TO the heart. Most carry deoxygenated blood — pulmonary vein is the exception (carries oxygenated blood from lungs).

questions.question: Capillaries are special because:
options: Their walls are only one cell thick, so substances can diffuse in and out
questions.expected: Their walls are only one cell thick, so substances can diffuse in and out
questions.memo: Capillaries = the exchange vessels. One-cell-thick walls + huge total surface area → O2, CO2, glucose, waste all diffuse across.

questions.question: Why do veins have valves but arteries do not?
options: Veins carry blood at low pressure and need to prevent back-flow against gravity
Arteries are too small for valves
questions.expected: Veins carry blood at low pressure and need to prevent back-flow against gravity
questions.memo: Artery walls are thick + elastic + blood is at high pressure → no back-flow risk. Veins are low pressure → valves stop blood from pooling, especially in the legs.

questions.question:
On the artery-vein-capillary diagram, which vessel has the thickest muscular wall?
[Diagram: 3 vessel cross-sections]
questions.expected: Artery (left)
questions.memo: Arteries have thick smooth-muscle + elastic walls to handle the high pressure pulses from the heart.

questions.question: Red blood cells transport:
questions.expected: Oxygen, using haemoglobin
questions.memo: Red cells contain haemoglobin (iron-rich pigment). Each Hb molecule binds 4 O2. Anaemia = too little Hb → tired, breathless.

questions.question: White blood cells are part of the body's:
questions.expected: Defence system (fight infection)
questions.memo: White cells (phagocytes, lymphocytes) engulf invaders and make antibodies. Low white-cell count → poor immunity.

questions.question: Platelets are MOST important for:
questions.expected: Clotting at a wound
questions.memo: Platelets stick to wound + release clotting factors → fibrin mesh forms → clot stops bleeding. Low platelets = bleeding disorder.

questions.question: Plasma is mostly:
options: Water with dissolved proteins, salts, nutrients, hormones, waste
questions.expected: Water with dissolved proteins, salts, nutrients, hormones, waste
questions.memo: Plasma = about 55% of blood. It's the watery medium that carries everything that isn't a blood cell.

questions.question:
Match the blood component to its function:
1. Red blood cells  2. White blood cells  3. Platelets  4. Plasma

A. Clotting
B. Carries O2
C. Defence
D. Carries dissolved substances
questions.memo: RBC → O2. WBC → defence. Platelets → clotting. Plasma → dissolved transport.

questions.question: Which feature of a red blood cell increases its O2-carrying ability?
options: No nucleus + biconcave disc shape gives more haemoglobin and faster diffusion
questions.expected: No nucleus + biconcave disc shape gives more haemoglobin and faster diffusion
questions.memo: No nucleus = more room for haemoglobin. Biconcave shape = large surface area for fast O2 uptake/release.

questions.question:
The pie chart shows blood is 55% plasma, 44% red cells, 1% white cells and platelets. Which component takes up the MOST of the blood?
[Pie chart of blood composition]
questions.expected: Plasma
questions.memo: Plasma is the largest portion at 55%. Most of the rest is red cells. White cells and platelets are a tiny but vital fraction.

questions.question: The lymphatic system mainly:
options: Returns excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream and fights infection
questions.expected: Returns excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream and fights infection
questions.memo: Lymph vessels collect leaked fluid from tissues → return it to blood via the subclavian vein. Lymph nodes filter for infection (swollen 'glands' when sick).

questions.question: Which condition can result from a LOW red blood cell count?
questions.expected: Anaemia — fatigue, breathlessness, pale skin
questions.memo: Common causes: iron deficiency, blood loss, vitamin B12 deficiency, malaria. Treatment depends on cause.

questions.question: True or false: A blood transfusion requires the donor blood group to match the recipient.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Wrong-group transfusion → recipient's antibodies attack donor cells → potentially fatal. Universal donor = O-negative; universal recipient = AB-positive.

questions.question: Why are capillaries arranged in DENSE networks in active tissues like muscle?
options: Active tissues need fast O2 supply and waste removal — more capillaries = more exchange surface
questions.expected: Active tissues need fast O2 supply and waste removal — more capillaries = more exchange surface
questions.memo: More demand = more capillaries. Training increases capillary density in trained muscles — one of many endurance adaptations.

questions.question: Why is the pulmonary VEIN unusual?
options: It carries OXYGENATED blood, while most veins carry deoxygenated
questions.expected: It carries OXYGENATED blood, while most veins carry deoxygenated
questions.memo: Pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood from lungs to left atrium. Pulmonary artery = the matching exception going the other way.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how a wound stops bleeding and starts to heal.
questions.expected: Platelets clot the wound and white blood cells fight infection, while skin cells divide to seal and rebuild the tissue.
questions.memo: Clot stops bleeding → immune response prevents infection → mitosis rebuilds tissue. All three systems in one healing.
options: Platelets clot the wound and white blood cells fight infection, while skin cells divide to seal and rebuild the tissue.
Red blood cells stick together to plug the cut, and the wound heals once the bleeding simply dries up on its own.
The wound stops bleeding only because the blood vessels turn to bone, sealing the cut permanently.
White blood cells form the clot that stops bleeding, and platelets then fight off any infection in the wound.

questions.question: An athletic SA athlete training at high altitude (e.g. in Lesotho's mountains) develops more red blood cells. Why?
options: Less O2 at high altitude triggers production of more RBCs to compensate
Altitude makes blood thicker by gravity
questions.expected: Less O2 at high altitude triggers production of more RBCs to compensate
questions.memo: Body senses low O2 → kidneys release EPO → bone marrow makes more RBCs. When the athlete returns to lower altitude, the extra RBCs boost performance.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the structure of an artery (thick, muscular, elastic wall) MATCHES its function.
questions.expected: Arteries receive blood at high pressure, so thick elastic walls withstand and recoil with each beat to smooth the flow.
questions.memo: Elastic recoil = smooths the pulse so blood arrives at organs steadily. Muscle control = lets the body redirect blood (e.g. dilate arteries to skin when hot).
options: Arteries carry blood at low pressure, so their thin walls let oxygen leak out easily to the tissues nearby.
Artery walls are thick simply to make them heavy enough to anchor the blood vessels in place inside the body.
Arteries receive blood at high pressure, so thick elastic walls withstand and recoil with each beat to smooth the flow.
Arteries have valves in their thick walls to stop blood flowing backwards, which is their main structural job.

LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A3.title: Cardiovascular disease and lifestyle
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A3.description: Hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart attack, stroke; risk factors; lifestyle prevention; data interpretation.
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A3.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G10.S2.CIRC.A3.recovery_strategy: Heart attack = blocked coronary artery. Stroke = blocked or burst vessel in brain. HDL = good, LDL = bad. Risk drops with no smoking, exercise, low saturated fat.

questions.question: Hypertension is:
questions.expected: High blood pressure
questions.memo: BP measured as systolic/diastolic. >140/90 mmHg = hypertensive. Major risk factor for stroke and heart attack.

questions.question: A heart attack happens when:
options: A coronary artery is blocked, starving heart muscle of oxygen
questions.expected: A coronary artery is blocked, starving heart muscle of oxygen
questions.memo: Coronary arteries supply heart muscle. Blocked by atherosclerotic plaque + blood clot → muscle dies (infarction).

questions.question: A stroke happens when:
options: Blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts
questions.expected: Blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bursts
questions.memo: Two types: ischaemic (blocked artery) and haemorrhagic (burst vessel). Brain cells die quickly without O2.

questions.question: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of:
options: Fatty plaques in artery walls, narrowing them
questions.expected: Fatty plaques in artery walls, narrowing them
questions.memo: Cholesterol + cells + fibrous tissue build up on artery walls → flow restricted → blood clots can form → stroke or heart attack.

questions.question: Which is a MAJOR risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
questions.expected: Smoking
questions.memo: Smoking damages artery walls, raises BP, lowers HDL. Quitting cuts CVD risk dramatically within 1–5 years.

questions.question: HDL cholesterol is often called 'good' because it:
options: Carries excess cholesterol back to the liver for disposal
questions.expected: Carries excess cholesterol back to the liver for disposal
questions.memo: HDL = High-Density Lipoprotein. Sweeps cholesterol back to liver. Higher HDL = lower CVD risk.

questions.question: LDL cholesterol is 'bad' because it:
options: Deposits cholesterol in artery walls, forming plaques
Carries it back to the liver
questions.expected: Deposits cholesterol in artery walls, forming plaques
questions.memo: LDL = Low-Density Lipoprotein. Drops off cholesterol in artery walls → plaques. Lifestyle and statins lower LDL.

questions.question: Which is the SINGLE most effective lifestyle change to reduce CVD risk?
questions.expected: Quit smoking
questions.memo: Quitting smoking has rapid and large benefits across multiple risk factors. Other big ones: regular exercise, healthy diet, weight management.

questions.question:
The table shows CVD death rates per 100 000 in 4 SA provinces. Which province has the HIGHEST?

| Province        | CVD deaths per 100 000 |
|-----------------|------------------------|
| Eastern Cape    | 180                    |
| Free State      | 220                    |
| KwaZulu-Natal   | 165                    |
| Western Cape    | 200                    |
questions.expected: Free State
questions.memo: Read the highest value: 220 in Free State. SA provinces vary by lifestyle, access to healthcare, and demographics.

questions.question: True or false: Regular exercise can reduce blood pressure.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Aerobic exercise (walking, jogging, swimming) lowers resting BP by 5–10 mmHg over weeks. As effective as some medications.

questions.question: Why does eating less salt help lower blood pressure?
options: Less salt → less water retained → lower blood volume → lower pressure
Salt has nothing to do with BP
questions.expected: Less salt → less water retained → lower blood volume → lower pressure
questions.memo: Sodium pulls water into the bloodstream. SA has high average salt intake — cutting back helps national BP statistics.

questions.question: A blood pressure of 180/110 is:
questions.expected: Severe hypertension — urgent care needed
questions.memo: Normal: ~120/80. >140/90 = hypertension. >180/110 = hypertensive crisis. Patient needs medical attention.

questions.question: Symptoms of a heart attack often include:
options: Chest pain that may spread to arm or jaw, sweating, shortness of breath
questions.expected: Chest pain that may spread to arm or jaw, sweating, shortness of breath
questions.memo: Classic symptoms. Women sometimes have less obvious symptoms (nausea, back pain). Treat as emergency — call 10177 in SA.

questions.question: FAST is a quick way to spot a stroke. It stands for:
options: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency
questions.expected: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency
questions.memo: FAST helps the public spot strokes early. The faster the treatment, the more brain can be saved.

questions.question: Why is OBESITY a major CVD risk factor?
options: Extra weight strains the heart, raises BP and worsens cholesterol
Obesity has no link to CVD
questions.expected: Extra weight strains the heart, raises BP and worsens cholesterol
questions.memo: Obesity raises BP, blood sugar (diabetes risk), and unfavourable lipids. Weight loss reverses many of these.

questions.question: True or false: A family history of heart disease means YOU will definitely get heart disease.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Family history raises your risk but doesn't determine fate. Lifestyle (diet, exercise, no smoking) plays a major role even with genetic risk.

questions.question: A patient is told to take statins for high cholesterol. Statins work by:
options: Reducing the liver's production of cholesterol
questions.expected: Reducing the liver's production of cholesterol
questions.memo: Statins block an enzyme the liver uses to make cholesterol. LDL falls → CVD risk drops. Combined with lifestyle change.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why CVD is a major public-health problem in SA.
questions.expected: Risk factors like high salt intake, smoking and obesity are common in SA, making CVD a leading cause of death in adults.
questions.memo: Health system challenge: prevention (education, screening) + treatment + lifestyle change. Multiple government programmes target diet, smoking, exercise.
options: CVD is mainly an infectious disease spread between people, which is why it is so common in South Africa.
CVD is a problem only for the elderly, so it has little real impact on South Africa's overall public health.
Risk factors like high salt intake, smoking and obesity are common in SA, making CVD a leading cause of death in adults.
CVD is rare in South Africa, but it gets attention because treatment is unusually expensive for the few affected.

questions.question: A pupil's father is told his cholesterol is 6 mmol/L (above 5 = high). Suggest a one-month plan.
options: Cut saturated fats, eat more vegetables and fish, exercise 30 min/day, recheck
questions.expected: Cut saturated fats, eat more vegetables and fish, exercise 30 min/day, recheck
questions.memo: Lifestyle change is the first line. If cholesterol stays high after months of effort, the doctor may prescribe statins.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why young people should also pay attention to CVD risk factors, not just older adults.
questions.expected: CVD develops over decades, so plaques start building in young arteries and healthy habits begun young prevent later damage.
questions.memo: Atherosclerosis can begin in the teens. Smoking, obesity and high LDL in youth → heart attack risk in 40s/50s. Public-health message: start young.
options: CVD develops over decades, so plaques start building in young arteries and healthy habits begun young prevent later damage.
Young people cannot develop any artery damage, so paying attention to risk factors before middle age makes no difference.
CVD is purely genetic, so a young person's diet and smoking habits have no effect on their later heart-attack risk.
Young hearts repair all damage overnight, so risk factors only begin to matter once a person stops growing.

LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A1.title: Biosphere, biomes and ecosystems
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A1.description: Biosphere, biome, ecosystem definitions; SA biomes; abiotic vs biotic factors.
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A1.recovery_strategy: Biosphere = all life + non-life on Earth. Biome = large climate-life region. Ecosystem = community + its abiotic environment. Abiotic = non-living; Biotic = living.

questions.question: The biosphere is:
options: All life on Earth and the parts of Earth where life exists
questions.expected: All life on Earth and the parts of Earth where life exists
questions.memo: Biosphere = the thin zone of life: surface land, oceans, lower atmosphere. Everything else is non-living.

questions.question: A biome is BEST described as:
options: A large geographical region with similar climate and characteristic life forms
All the animals in a forest
questions.expected: A large geographical region with similar climate and characteristic life forms
questions.memo: Biome = continent-scale. SA examples: Fynbos, Savanna, Grassland, Karoo. Defined by climate + dominant plants.

questions.question: An ecosystem includes:
options: A community of living things + their non-living environment
questions.expected: A community of living things + their non-living environment
questions.memo: Ecosystem = biotic + abiotic. Can be tiny (a puddle) or vast (the Kruger Park).

questions.question: Which is an ABIOTIC factor?
questions.expected: Soil pH
questions.memo: Abiotic = non-living. Soil, water, light, temperature, pH, wind, gases. Biotic = living organisms.

questions.question: Which is a BIOTIC factor?
options: Numbers of zebras in a savanna
questions.expected: Numbers of zebras in a savanna
questions.memo: Biotic = living things and their effects (predation, competition, disease). Zebras count as biotic.

questions.question: The Fynbos biome is found mainly in:
questions.expected: The south-western Cape
questions.memo: Fynbos = SA's smallest but most biodiverse biome. Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms.

questions.question: The Savanna biome is characterised by:
options: Grassland with scattered trees, summer rainfall, large mammals
questions.expected: Grassland with scattered trees, summer rainfall, large mammals
questions.memo: Classic SA savanna: Acacia + grass + zebra/giraffe/lion. Covers Limpopo, Mpumalanga, parts of North West.

questions.question:
Match SA biomes to features:
1. Fynbos  2. Savanna  3. Succulent Karoo  4. Grassland

A. Highveld, summer rain, dominated by grasses
B. Western Cape, fire-adapted shrubs
C. Trees + grass, large game
D. Dry, water-storing plants (succulents)
questions.memo: Fynbos = Western Cape shrubs. Savanna = trees + grass + game. Succulent Karoo = dry, succulents. Grassland = highveld grasses.

questions.question: True or false: A biome and an ecosystem are the same thing.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Biome is larger and defined by climate + plant type. An ecosystem is a smaller unit (could be a pond, a kelp forest, a tree).

questions.question: The level above ecosystem is:
questions.expected: Biome
questions.memo: Hierarchy: organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere.

questions.question:
The graph shows rainfall in two SA biomes by season. Which biome has the highest annual rainfall?

| Biome    | Annual rainfall (mm) |
|----------|----------------------|
| Forest   | 1200                 |
| Savanna  | 600                  |
| Karoo    | 200                  |
questions.expected: Forest
questions.memo: Forest biome is the smallest in SA — found in areas with high rainfall (e.g. Knysna, Tsitsikamma). Saved by Cape mountains catching moist air.

questions.question: A population is:
options: All the members of one species in an area
questions.expected: All the members of one species in an area
questions.memo: Population = same species. Community = all populations together. Ecosystem = community + abiotic.

questions.question: A community is:
options: All the populations of different species living together in an area
questions.expected: All the populations of different species living together in an area
questions.memo: Community = all the species and their interactions in a place. Add the abiotic environment = ecosystem.

questions.question: Why are abiotic factors important for life in a biome?
questions.expected: Abiotic factors such as temperature, rainfall, soil and light decide which species can live there, so different combinations support different biomes.
questions.memo: Climate is the master variable. High rain + warm → forest. Low rain → desert. SA's biomes correlate strongly with rainfall + temperature gradients.
options: Abiotic factors matter only for plants; animals are unaffected by temperature, rainfall or soil conditions.
Abiotic factors are created by the animals living in a biome, so they follow rather than shape which species survive.
Abiotic factors such as temperature, rainfall, soil and light decide which species can live there, so different combinations support different biomes.
Abiotic factors are unimportant because living things can adapt to live anywhere regardless of climate or soil.

questions.question: Niche refers to:
options: The role and 'job' of a species in an ecosystem
questions.expected: The role and 'job' of a species in an ecosystem
questions.memo: Niche = how it makes a living: what it eats, when it's active, who eats it. Two species rarely share an identical niche.

questions.question: Habitat refers to:
options: The physical place where an organism lives
questions.expected: The physical place where an organism lives
questions.memo: Habitat = address. Niche = job/role. A meerkat's habitat is the Kalahari; its niche includes diet of insects, daytime activity, alarm-call role.

questions.question: Why is the Cape Floral Kingdom famous worldwide?
options: It is the smallest of six floral kingdoms but has the highest plant density per area
questions.expected: It is the smallest of six floral kingdoms but has the highest plant density per area
questions.memo: Cape Floral Kingdom (mainly Fynbos) has ~9000 species, ~70% endemic. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: True or false: Decomposers are a biotic factor.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Decomposers (fungi, bacteria) are living. They are biotic. They recycle nutrients from dead material back into the ecosystem.

questions.question: Why does an ecosystem need BOTH biotic and abiotic components?
questions.expected: Living organisms depend on abiotic resources like water and light, and living things in turn shape those abiotic conditions.
questions.memo: Two-way relationship. Forest creates its own microclimate; soil nutrients depend on decomposition by organisms.
options: An ecosystem needs only biotic components, since living things make all the water and minerals they require themselves.
Living organisms depend on abiotic resources like water and light, and living things in turn shape those abiotic conditions.
Abiotic and biotic components never affect each other; they simply exist side by side in the same place.
Only abiotic factors matter, because rocks, water and air would form a complete ecosystem without any organisms.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA has such varied biomes in a relatively small area.
questions.expected: SA has large gradients in rainfall, temperature and altitude over short distances, so different climates support many biomes side by side.
questions.memo: From the Cape's winter rainfall to the Lowveld's hot wet summers, SA's geography produces 8+ biomes — a global biodiversity hotspot.
options: SA has uniform climate everywhere, so its many biomes are caused by differences in animal species, not the environment.
SA's biomes are all the same biome that people have simply given different names across the provinces.
SA has only a few biomes spread evenly, because its climate barely changes from one region to the next.
SA has large gradients in rainfall, temperature and altitude over short distances, so different climates support many biomes side by side.

LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A2.title: Energy flow, food chains and food webs
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A2.description: Food chains/webs; energy pyramids; producers, consumers, decomposers; ~10% energy transfer.
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A2.recovery_strategy: Arrows point in direction energy FLOWS (eaten → eater). Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary. Only ~10% energy passes up each level.

questions.question: A food chain ARROW points:
options: From the organism being eaten to the one that eats it (direction of energy flow)
questions.expected: From the organism being eaten to the one that eats it (direction of energy flow)
questions.memo: Arrow = energy flow. Grass → zebra → lion. Grass is the energy source for zebra; zebra for lion.

questions.question: A producer is an organism that:
options: Makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
questions.expected: Makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
questions.memo: Producers = green plants and some bacteria. They feed everything else. Base of every food chain.

questions.question: A primary consumer eats:
questions.expected: Producers (plants)
questions.memo: Primary consumers = herbivores (zebra, antelope, caterpillars). They directly eat producers.

questions.question: A secondary consumer eats:
questions.expected: Primary consumers (herbivores)
questions.memo: Secondary consumer = small/medium carnivore. Snake eats mouse = secondary consumer.

questions.question: Decomposers are important because they:
options: Break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil
questions.expected: Break down dead material and return nutrients to the soil
questions.memo: Fungi + bacteria. Without them, nutrients would be locked in dead bodies and the ecosystem would collapse.

questions.question:
Order this food chain from producer to top predator:
(a) Lion (b) Grass (c) Zebra
questions.expected: b → c → a
questions.memo: Grass (producer) → Zebra (primary consumer) → Lion (top consumer). Always start with the producer.

questions.question:
On the savanna food web diagram, which organism is a TERTIARY consumer?
[Diagram: grass→zebra→lion→vulture]
questions.expected: Vulture (eats lion remains)
questions.memo: Producer→primary→secondary→tertiary. Vulture eating lion remains makes it tertiary. (Scavengers don't fit neatly — flexibility in food webs.)

questions.question: Roughly what % of energy passes from one trophic level to the next?
questions.expected: About 10%
questions.memo: 10% rule (approximate). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), undigested, or stored in inedible parts. This is why food chains rarely have more than 4–5 levels.

questions.question: Why do food chains usually have only 4–5 trophic levels?
options: So much energy is lost at each level that there isn't enough left for a higher consumer
questions.expected: So much energy is lost at each level that there isn't enough left for a higher consumer
questions.memo: 10% energy passed up each level means after 4–5 levels, very little remains. Top predators are usually rare for this reason.

questions.question: An energy pyramid has producers at the:
questions.expected: Base (widest level)
questions.memo: Wide base of producers → narrower steps up. Reflects the 10% energy rule.

questions.question: The energy at producer level is 10000 kJ. Roughly how much energy reaches secondary consumers?
questions.expected: 100 kJ
questions.memo: Producer 10000 → primary 1000 (10%) → secondary 100 (10% of 1000) → tertiary ~10. Each step loses 90%.

questions.question: Which is a likely PRIMARY consumer in a SA grassland ecosystem?
questions.expected: Zebra
questions.memo: Zebra (herbivore) eats grass = primary consumer. Lion and vulture are higher up. Grass is the producer.

questions.question: True or false: A food WEB shows more realistic feeding relationships than a food chain.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Real ecosystems have many overlapping food chains. A food web shows all of them together — most organisms eat (and are eaten by) several others.

questions.question: If lions decline sharply in a savanna ecosystem, which effect is MOST likely?
options: Herbivore numbers may rise initially, then overgrazing damages the vegetation
questions.expected: Herbivore numbers may rise initially, then overgrazing damages the vegetation
questions.memo: Top predators control herbivore numbers. Remove them → too many herbivores → overgrazing → habitat damage. Classic 'trophic cascade'.

questions.question: Why is energy flow through an ecosystem ONE-WAY, but nutrient flow is cyclic?
questions.expected: Energy enters as sunlight and is lost as heat so it cannot be reused, while nutrients are recycled by decomposers back into the soil.
questions.memo: Energy = one-way (input from sun, output as heat). Nutrients = round-and-round forever. Decomposers close the nutrient loop.
options: Energy enters as sunlight and is lost as heat so it cannot be reused, while nutrients are recycled by decomposers back into the soil.
Both energy and nutrients are recycled endlessly, so the sun's input is only needed to start the very first food chain.
Energy is recycled by decomposers, but nutrients are lost as heat and must be replaced by sunlight each time.
Energy and nutrients both flow one way and are lost forever, which is why ecosystems eventually run down completely.

questions.question: In an ocean food web, plankton are typically:
questions.expected: Producers (phytoplankton) and primary consumers (zooplankton)
questions.memo: Phytoplankton = microscopic plant-like producers. Zooplankton = microscopic animal-like primary consumers. Foundation of ocean ecosystems.

questions.question: True or false: Removing top predators can lead to a SHORTER food chain over time.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Without top predators, the highest remaining level becomes the 'top'. Food chain shortens. Removing lions, leopards, wild dogs etc. has this effect in SA reserves.

questions.question: Why does a pyramid of NUMBERS sometimes appear inverted (more consumers than producers)?
options: A single large tree can feed many small insect herbivores, making producers fewer than consumers in number
questions.expected: A single large tree can feed many small insect herbivores, making producers fewer than consumers in number
questions.memo: Pyramid of NUMBERS counts individuals, ignoring size. Pyramid of BIOMASS or ENERGY is usually upright.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why producers are 'the base' of every food chain.
questions.expected: Producers convert sunlight into the chemical energy stored in food, and all other organisms depend directly or indirectly on that energy.
questions.memo: Photosynthesis captures the energy that fuels everything else. No producers = no food = no ecosystem.
options: Producers are the base because they are the largest organisms and physically support the smaller ones above them.
Producers convert sunlight into the chemical energy stored in food, and all other organisms depend directly or indirectly on that energy.
Producers are the base only because there are more of them; any organism could replace them as the foundation.
Producers feed on dead matter and pass the energy upward, which is why they sit at the bottom of the chain.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a humans-eat-meat diet uses more energy from the ecosystem than a humans-eat-plants diet.
questions.expected: Eating meat puts us higher up the food chain where about 90% of energy is lost at each step, so eating plants directly is more efficient.
questions.memo: Same reason as why food chains are short. A vegetarian diet supports more people from the same land. This is also why beef farming has a high environmental footprint.
options: A meat diet uses less energy because animals concentrate the sun's energy, making meat the more efficient food source.
Both diets use the same energy, since the total energy in an ecosystem stays constant no matter what we eat.
Eating meat puts us higher up the food chain where about 90% of energy is lost at each step, so eating plants directly is more efficient.
A plant diet uses more energy because plants must first be eaten by animals before humans can digest them.

LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A3.title: Nutrient cycles — carbon, nitrogen, water
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A3.description: C, N, water cycles; human disturbances at key steps (deforestation, combustion, fertilisers).
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A3.recovery_strategy: Carbon: photosynthesis ↔ respiration + combustion. Water: evaporation → condensation → precipitation. Nitrogen: fixation → nitrification → uptake → denitrification.

questions.question: In the carbon cycle, plants take in CO2 by:
questions.expected: Photosynthesis
questions.memo: Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2. Plants pull carbon out of the air to make food.

questions.question: Respiration RELEASES which gas back to the air?
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide
questions.memo: Respiration: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Plants AND animals respire. Reverse of photosynthesis.

questions.question: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) adds:
questions.expected: CO2 to the atmosphere
questions.memo: Combustion releases CO2 that was locked up millions of years ago. Main human driver of climate change.

questions.question: Decomposers in the carbon cycle return carbon to the atmosphere by:
options: Respiration as they break down dead material
questions.expected: Respiration as they break down dead material
questions.memo: Bacteria and fungi respire as they decompose. They convert dead biomass back to CO2.

questions.question:
On the labelled carbon cycle, which arrow shows the largest human disturbance?
[Diagram: carbon cycle with arrows]
questions.expected: Combustion of fossil fuels
questions.memo: Burning fossil fuels adds CO2 faster than natural cycles can absorb it → rising atmospheric CO2 → climate change.

questions.question: Most of the water vapour in the atmosphere comes from:
options: Evaporation from oceans, lakes, and rivers + transpiration from plants
questions.expected: Evaporation from oceans, lakes, and rivers + transpiration from plants
questions.memo: Together: evapotranspiration. Oceans contribute the largest single share, but plants are very important too.

questions.question: True or false: Cutting down a forest reduces local rainfall in the long run.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Forests transpire a lot of water, contributing to local rain. Remove forest → less transpiration → less rain → harder to regrow.

questions.question: In the nitrogen cycle, which group of organisms fixes nitrogen from N2 gas into a form plants can use?
options: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in root nodules of legumes, or free-living in soil)
questions.expected: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in root nodules of legumes, or free-living in soil)
questions.memo: Legumes (beans, peas, lucerne) host Rhizobium in root nodules — they fix N2 → NH3 → NH4+. Why farmers rotate legumes into fields.

questions.question: Nitrification is the conversion of:
questions.expected: Ammonium (NH4+) into nitrite (NO2-) and nitrate (NO3-)
questions.memo: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise NH4+ → NO2- → NO3-. Nitrate is the form most plants prefer.

questions.question: Denitrifying bacteria turn:
options: Nitrate back into nitrogen gas (released to air)
questions.expected: Nitrate back into nitrogen gas (released to air)
questions.memo: Denitrification closes the loop — N is returned to the atmosphere. Happens in waterlogged soils where O2 is low.

questions.question: Why can't plants use the N2 gas in air directly?
options: The triple bond in N2 is very strong — only specialised bacteria (and lightning) can break it
There is no N2 in the air
questions.expected: The triple bond in N2 is very strong — only specialised bacteria (and lightning) can break it
questions.memo: N≡N is one of the strongest bonds in nature. Plants need pre-broken N (ammonium or nitrate) from bacteria, lightning or fertilisers.

questions.question: How does heavy fertiliser use disrupt the nitrogen cycle?
options: Excess nitrate washes into rivers → eutrophication and ocean dead zones
questions.expected: Excess nitrate washes into rivers → eutrophication and ocean dead zones
questions.memo: Global problem: excess N from agriculture creates 'dead zones' in oceans where O2 is depleted by decomposing algal blooms.

questions.question: In the water cycle, water vapour cools and forms:
questions.expected: Clouds (condensation)
questions.memo: Warm moist air rises → cools → vapour condenses on tiny particles → cloud droplets. Cloud droplets grow → precipitation.

questions.question: True or false: Photosynthesis and respiration together drive the carbon cycle's biological loop.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from atmosphere → respiration adds it back. Two-way biological flux of carbon.

questions.question: Why does paving over soil reduce the water cycle?
options: Concrete prevents infiltration — water runs off instead of recharging groundwater
questions.expected: Concrete prevents infiltration — water runs off instead of recharging groundwater
questions.memo: Urbanisation = less infiltration → more flooding + falling groundwater levels. SA cities like Cape Town have struggled with both.

questions.question: Which forest's destruction has the BIGGEST impact on global carbon cycling?
questions.expected: The Amazon rainforest
questions.memo: Amazon stores huge carbon AND drives a lot of global rainfall. Deforestation = double climate hit.
