questions.question: Soils in over-farmed SA areas often become low in nitrogen because:
options: Crops removed each season take nitrogen out faster than fixation puts it back
questions.expected: Crops removed each season take nitrogen out faster than fixation puts it back
questions.memo: Removing harvest = removing N. Solutions: legume rotation, fertiliser, composting. Sustainable farming balances inputs and outputs.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why decomposers are essential to BOTH the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
questions.expected: Decomposers break down dead material, releasing CO2 by respiration and returning nitrogen to the soil for plants to reuse.
questions.memo: Without decomposers, nutrients stay locked in dead bodies. Forests would fill with dead leaves, the cycle stops.
options: Decomposers lock carbon and nitrogen away permanently in dead bodies, which is why both elements run out over time.
Decomposers only matter to the carbon cycle; nitrogen is recycled entirely by lightning and never by living things.
Decomposers build dead material into new living tissue directly, bypassing both the carbon and nitrogen cycles.
Decomposers break down dead material, releasing CO2 by respiration and returning nitrogen to the soil for plants to reuse.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why GROWING ATMOSPHERIC CO2 is a global problem.
questions.expected: Rising CO2 traps heat in the atmosphere, warming the planet and driving sea-level rise, droughts, heatwaves and ecosystem disruption.
questions.memo: Greenhouse effect. Pre-industrial CO2 ~280 ppm; today ~420 ppm. SA already experiences hotter, drier conditions in many provinces.
options: Rising CO2 traps heat in the atmosphere, warming the planet and driving sea-level rise, droughts, heatwaves and ecosystem disruption.
Rising CO2 is a problem because the gas is poisonous to breathe, suffocating people directly at current levels.
Rising CO2 cools the planet by blocking sunlight, causing widespread freezing and crop failure worldwide.
Rising CO2 destroys the ozone layer, and the extra ultraviolet rays are the main cause of global warming.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how planting trees can help offset some carbon emissions.
questions.expected: Trees take in CO2 through photosynthesis and store the carbon in their wood for decades, removing some carbon from the atmosphere.
questions.memo: Forests = carbon sinks. Reforestation + protection of existing forests is part of climate-change response. Note: NOT a full replacement for cutting emissions.
options: Trees release oxygen that pushes CO2 out of the atmosphere into space, removing it from the climate system.
Trees take in CO2 through photosynthesis and store the carbon in their wood for decades, removing some carbon from the atmosphere.
Trees cool the planet only by providing shade, not by removing any carbon dioxide from the air.
Trees absorb CO2 and convert it into nitrogen, which is then locked safely in the soil around their roots.

LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A4.title: Ecological field study and seasonal change
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A4.description: Design simple field studies (abiotic + biotic); compare seasons; succession.
LSC.G10.S3.ECO.A4.recovery_strategy: Field study: list abiotic + biotic factors, sample the same way, repeat across seasons. Succession = orderly replacement over time (pioneer → climax).

questions.question: In a field study, which is an ABIOTIC measurement?
questions.expected: Air temperature
questions.memo: Abiotic = non-living. Temperature, light, soil pH, soil moisture, humidity, wind speed.

questions.question: In a field study, which is a BIOTIC measurement?
options: Number of zebras counted in a 100 m² plot
questions.expected: Number of zebras counted in a 100 m² plot
questions.memo: Biotic = living organisms and their effects. Count, list, identify species.

questions.question: A quadrat is used to:
options: Sample a fixed area to estimate species abundance
questions.expected: Sample a fixed area to estimate species abundance
questions.memo: Quadrat = square frame (e.g. 1 m²). Place randomly, count plants inside. Repeat many times → estimate density over a larger area.

questions.question: A line transect is used to:
options: Record changes in species along a line (e.g. across a beach)
questions.expected: Record changes in species along a line (e.g. across a beach)
questions.memo: Transect captures gradients. Classic example: beach transect from waterline up into dunes shows zoned vegetation.

questions.question: Why must samples in a field study be taken in the SAME way at each site?
options: So results can be fairly compared — different methods would give different counts
questions.expected: So results can be fairly compared — different methods would give different counts
questions.memo: Controlled variables = fair test. Same quadrat size, same time of day, same recording rules → comparable data.

questions.question: Why are field studies often repeated over two SEASONS?
options: Many species and abiotic factors change between seasons; comparing reveals patterns
questions.expected: Many species and abiotic factors change between seasons; comparing reveals patterns
questions.memo: SA has strong seasonal differences (summer/winter rainfall, growth seasons). One snapshot misses the variation.

questions.question: True or false: Random sampling reduces bias in a field study.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Random placement avoids picking only 'interesting' spots. Throw a quadrat over your shoulder, or use random co-ordinates.

questions.question:
The table compares species counts in summer and winter at one site. Which season had more species?

| Season  | # species |
|---------|-----------|
| Summer  | 23        |
| Winter  | 11        |
questions.expected: Summer
questions.memo: Read the numbers: 23 > 11. Many species are dormant in winter (especially insects, migrating birds, deciduous plants).

questions.question: Ecological succession is:
options: The orderly change of a community over time, leading to a stable climax community
questions.expected: The orderly change of a community over time, leading to a stable climax community
questions.memo: Bare rock → pioneer (lichens, moss) → grasses → shrubs → forest. Each step changes the environment → next species can live there.

questions.question: Which are typically the FIRST organisms to colonise bare rock (pioneers)?
questions.expected: Lichens and mosses
questions.memo: Lichens break down rock + add organic matter → soil forms → grasses can take over. Slow but essential first step.

questions.question: A climax community is:
options: The stable end-stage community of succession
questions.expected: The stable end-stage community of succession
questions.memo: Climax = balanced, mature community that maintains itself. Depends on climate (e.g. fynbos climax in Cape; savanna climax in Limpopo).

questions.question: Why does the diversity of life usually INCREASE during succession?
questions.expected: Each new community changes the environment, creating more habitats and niches over time so that more species can live there.
questions.memo: Build-up of organic matter, shade, microclimates → more niches → more species. Until disturbance resets it.
options: Diversity increases because the first pioneer species reproduce faster as the years go by, with no change to the habitat.
Diversity increases only because more sunlight reaches the ground over time, which has nothing to do with new species.
Each new community changes the environment, creating more habitats and niches over time so that more species can live there.
Diversity actually stays the same throughout succession; only the sizes of the existing organisms increase.

questions.question: Fire in a fynbos area is followed by:
options: Many seeds germinating and resprouting from underground storage
questions.expected: Many seeds germinating and resprouting from underground storage
questions.memo: Fynbos is fire-adapted. Many species have fire-stimulated seeds or sprout from bulbs/lignotubers. Fire is part of the natural cycle.

questions.question: A pupil records soil moisture at 9 am and at 3 pm in summer. What is the LIKELY pattern?
options: Soil drier at 3 pm due to evaporation during the heat of day
questions.expected: Soil drier at 3 pm due to evaporation during the heat of day
questions.memo: Sun + heat = evaporation. Why ecologists time measurements (e.g. early morning) to standardise comparisons.

questions.question: True or false: Designed field studies must specify a clear question or hypothesis BEFORE data is collected.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Without a question, the data has no purpose. Hypothesis → design → collect → analyse → conclude.

questions.question: Why are mark-and-recapture studies useful for mobile animals?
options: Counting all individuals is impractical — recapture data lets you estimate the total population
questions.expected: Counting all individuals is impractical — recapture data lets you estimate the total population
questions.memo: Catch a sample → mark them → release. Catch again later → proportion marked tells you total population size (Lincoln index).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how human disturbance can RESET ecological succession.
questions.expected: Activities like clearing, ploughing, fire or pollution destroy the existing community, so succession restarts from pioneer species.
questions.memo: Old fields, mine dumps, areas cleared by alien plant removal — all go through secondary succession back to something like their climax.
options: Activities like clearing, ploughing, fire or pollution destroy the existing community, so succession restarts from pioneer species.
Human disturbance speeds succession straight to the climax community, skipping all the earlier pioneer stages.
Human disturbance has no real effect, because an ecosystem always stays frozen at whatever stage it has reached.
Human disturbance permanently ends succession, so the land can never support living communities again.

questions.question: Which is a major SOURCE of error in a field study?
options: Incorrect species identification, inconsistent quadrat placement, weather differences
questions.expected: Incorrect species identification, inconsistent quadrat placement, weather differences
questions.memo: Common errors. Mitigations: use ID guides + experts, randomise placement, repeat on similar weather days.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a STUDY at JUST ONE site cannot represent a whole biome.
questions.expected: One site has its own particular soil, slope, history and microclimate, so multiple sites must be sampled to draw conclusions about the biome.
questions.memo: Replication across the biome is essential. A single hectare of fynbos near Cape Town can't speak for fynbos at Cederberg or the Cape Peninsula.
options: One site is enough to represent a whole biome, because every part of a biome is identical to every other part.
One site has its own particular soil, slope, history and microclimate, so multiple sites must be sampled to draw conclusions about the biome.
A single site cannot represent a biome only because one researcher might make mistakes, not because the site itself varies.
Studying one site is best, since adding more sites just introduces confusing differences that should be avoided.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why long-term ecological monitoring matters for SA biodiversity.
questions.expected: Slow changes like drought, climate change and invasive species take years to show, so long-term monitoring detects them and guides conservation.
questions.memo: SA programmes like SAEON do exactly this. Without long-term data, slow declines can go unnoticed until it's too late.
options: Long-term monitoring is unnecessary, because a single survey captures everything important about an ecosystem at once.
Long-term monitoring matters only for counting how many tourists visit reserves each year, not for biodiversity.
Slow changes like drought, climate change and invasive species take years to show, so long-term monitoring detects them and guides conservation.
Long-term monitoring is useful only after a species has already gone extinct, to confirm that the loss happened.

LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A1.title: Biodiversity, taxonomy and binomial naming
LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A1.description: Biodiversity; taxonomic hierarchy; five-kingdom system; binomial nomenclature; dichotomous keys.
LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A1.recovery_strategy: Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup. Genus capitalised, species lowercase, both italic: *Homo sapiens*. Dichotomous key gives two choices at each step.

questions.question: Biodiversity refers to:
options: The variety of life on Earth, at all levels
questions.expected: The variety of life on Earth, at all levels
questions.memo: Includes diversity of genes, species and ecosystems. SA is one of the most biodiverse countries.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks from broadest to most specific?
options: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Phylum, Kingdom
Class, Order, Kingdom, Family, Phylum, Genus, Species
Phylum, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Kingdom, Species
questions.expected: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.memo: Mnemonic: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup. KPCOFGS.

questions.question: In the five-kingdom system, which kingdom includes bacteria?
questions.expected: Monera (Prokaryotae)
questions.memo: Bacteria are prokaryotes (no nucleus). All other kingdoms = eukaryotes. Note: modern biology splits Monera into Archaea + Bacteria.

questions.question: Fungi are placed in a SEPARATE kingdom from plants because:
options: They do not photosynthesise — they absorb nutrients from dead/living material
questions.expected: They do not photosynthesise — they absorb nutrients from dead/living material
questions.memo: Fungi: cell walls of CHITIN (not cellulose), no chlorophyll, heterotrophic by absorption. Mushrooms, yeast, moulds.

questions.question: Protista is the kingdom for:
options: Mostly single-celled eukaryotes (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium, algae)
questions.expected: Mostly single-celled eukaryotes (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium, algae)
questions.memo: Protista is a 'catch-all' kingdom for eukaryotic organisms that don't fit Plantae, Animalia, or Fungi.

questions.question: Which is the correct binomial name format?
questions.expected: *Homo sapiens* (genus capitalised, species lowercase, italic)
questions.memo: Two-word Latin name. Genus = capital. Species = lowercase. Both italic (or underlined when handwritten).

questions.question:
Match the organism to its kingdom:
1. Mushroom  2. Lion  3. Maize  4. E. coli

A. Plantae
B. Monera
C. Animalia
D. Fungi
questions.memo: Mushroom = Fungi. Lion = Animalia. Maize = Plantae. E. coli = Monera (bacteria).

questions.question: Two species in the same genus are MORE closely related than two species in the same:
questions.expected: Family
questions.memo: Going UP the hierarchy = less related. Two species in the same Family share less than two species in the same Genus.

questions.question: A dichotomous key works by:
options: Offering two choices at each step, guiding you to one identification
questions.expected: Offering two choices at each step, guiding you to one identification
questions.memo: 'Di' = two. Each step splits the options in half. Good keys use easily observable features.

questions.question: Using this key: Step 1 — Has feathers? Yes → bird, No → step 2. Step 2 — Has fur? Yes → mammal, No → reptile. A bat would be:
questions.expected: A mammal (has fur, no feathers)
questions.memo: Don't be tricked by behaviour. Bats fly but have fur and feed their young milk → mammal. Always check the key features.

questions.question:
Using the taxonomic pyramid, which letter represents the GENUS for Panthera leo (lion)?
[Diagram: KPCOFGS pyramid with example of lion]
questions.expected: F (Panthera)
questions.memo: Genus = Panthera. Species = leo. Family = Felidae. So in KPCOFGS order, genus comes 6th = letter F (if labelled K=A, P=B, etc.).

questions.question: True or false: Two organisms with the SAME genus name are always the same species.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Same genus = related, but different species. Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) share a genus, not a species.

questions.question: Why do scientists worldwide use Latin binomial names?
options: A single standard avoids confusion that comes from different common names in different languages
questions.expected: A single standard avoids confusion that comes from different common names in different languages
questions.memo: A leopard is 'leopard' in English, 'luiperd' in Afrikaans, 'ingwe' in Zulu — but Panthera pardus everywhere in science.

questions.question: Carl Linnaeus is famous for:
options: Creating the binomial naming system in the 1700s
questions.expected: Creating the binomial naming system in the 1700s
questions.memo: Linnaeus standardised biological naming and classification. The basis of modern taxonomy.

questions.question: Modern classification uses what besides physical features to decide relationships?
questions.expected: DNA sequence comparison
questions.memo: Molecular phylogenetics has changed the tree of life — sometimes a 'plant'-like organism turns out to be more closely related to fungi (etc.).

questions.question: Why is biodiversity often measured at three different LEVELS (genetic, species, ecosystem)?
questions.expected: Each level adds different information: genetic = variation within a species, species = number of kinds, ecosystem = range of habitats.
questions.memo: All three matter. Loss at any level reduces resilience — e.g. cheetahs have low genetic diversity, making them vulnerable to disease.
options: The three levels all measure the same thing, so any one of them on its own gives the complete picture of biodiversity.
Each level adds different information: genetic = variation within a species, species = number of kinds, ecosystem = range of habitats.
Biodiversity is measured at three levels only to make reports longer; the species count alone is what truly matters.
Genetic diversity means the number of species, species diversity means the number of habitats, and ecosystem diversity means total population.

questions.question: Why are CLOSE relatives sometimes placed in DIFFERENT taxonomic groups based on DNA?
options: DNA reveals true evolutionary relationships that physical similarity can hide
questions.expected: DNA reveals true evolutionary relationships that physical similarity can hide
questions.memo: Convergent evolution makes unrelated species look similar (e.g. sharks and dolphins). DNA cuts through that to reveal true relatedness.

questions.question: True or false: Viruses are placed in a Kingdom of their own.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Viruses are NOT classified into a Kingdom because they are not cellular. They have their own separate classification (e.g. by genome type).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why TAXONOMY is important for conservation.
questions.expected: You cannot protect a species you cannot identify, and taxonomy reveals what species exist and which most need protection.
questions.memo: New species are still being discovered. Cryptic species sometimes turn out to be highly endangered — taxonomy helps prioritise.
options: Taxonomy tells us only what a species looks like, which has no bearing on deciding what to conserve.
Taxonomy is about naming fossils of extinct species, so it is irrelevant to protecting living ones today.
Conservation works best when species are left unidentified, so taxonomy actually slows protection efforts down.
You cannot protect a species you cannot identify, and taxonomy reveals what species exist and which most need protection.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how a dichotomous key helps a Grade 10 pupil identify an unknown insect.
questions.expected: The key gives two clear choices at each step, narrowing the possibilities until the pupil reaches a single identification.
questions.memo: Practical skill — used in biology, medicine (e.g. diagnosis trees), and engineering. Universal pattern: divide and conquer.
options: The key gives two clear choices at each step, narrowing the possibilities until the pupil reaches a single identification.
The key lists every insect species alphabetically so the pupil scrolls through until a matching picture appears.
The key offers many open-ended questions at once, and the pupil guesses the answer that feels most likely.
The key tells the pupil the answer immediately without any steps, simply by scanning the insect's colour.

LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A2.title: South African biodiversity and conservation
LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A2.description: SA as megadiverse; Cape Floral Kingdom; threats; conservation responses (national parks, CITES, Red List).
LSC.G10.S4.BIO.A2.recovery_strategy: Endemic = found ONLY in one place. Endangered = at risk of extinction. SA's Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the six floral kingdoms but most species per area.

questions.question: South Africa is one of the world's how-many MEGADIVERSE countries?
questions.memo: SA is one of 17 megadiverse countries (UN classification). Despite being small, it holds a huge fraction of global species.

questions.question: An ENDEMIC species is one that:
options: Is found ONLY in one place / region
Is found everywhere in the world
questions.expected: Is found ONLY in one place / region
questions.memo: Endemism = unique to a region. Cape Floral Kingdom is famously high in endemic plants — ~70% of species occur nowhere else.

questions.question: An ENDANGERED species is one that:
options: Faces a high risk of extinction in the wild
questions.expected: Faces a high risk of extinction in the wild
questions.memo: IUCN Red List categories: Least Concern → Near Threatened → Vulnerable → Endangered → Critically Endangered → Extinct in Wild → Extinct.

questions.question: The Cape Floral Kingdom is mainly the:
options: Fynbos biome of the south-western Cape
questions.expected: Fynbos biome of the south-western Cape
questions.memo: Smallest of the world's 6 floral kingdoms but with the most plant species per area. UNESCO World Heritage Site.

questions.question: True or false: Fynbos has more plant species per area than the Amazon.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Per unit area, Fynbos beats most other biomes — about 9000 plant species in a region smaller than England.

questions.question: The BIGGEST threat to biodiversity in South Africa is:
questions.expected: Habitat loss (farming, urbanisation, mining)
questions.memo: Habitat loss leads globally. Other major SA threats: invasive species, poaching (rhino, abalone), climate change.

questions.question: An INVASIVE alien species is:
options: A species from another region that spreads aggressively and harms native ecosystems
questions.expected: A species from another region that spreads aggressively and harms native ecosystems
questions.memo: SA examples: Black Wattle, Port Jackson, Lantana, Rooikrans. Use water, displace native species, increase fire risk.

questions.question: Why are RHINO POACHED in South Africa?
options: Their horns sell for high prices in illegal Asian markets
questions.expected: Their horns sell for high prices in illegal Asian markets
questions.memo: Despite the horn being keratin (same as fingernails), it's wrongly believed to have medicinal value. Demand drives poaching. SA hosts ~80% of African rhinos.

questions.question: CITES is an international agreement that:
options: Regulates trade in endangered species to prevent extinction from trade
questions.expected: Regulates trade in endangered species to prevent extinction from trade
questions.memo: CITES (since 1975) lists species in Appendix I (no trade), II (limited trade) or III. SA participates actively.

questions.question: The IUCN Red List is used to:
options: Categorise species by their extinction risk
questions.expected: Categorise species by their extinction risk
questions.memo: Red List is the global authority on conservation status. Updated regularly based on field studies.

questions.question: The graph shows white-rhino population trend in SA: 18000 in 2010, 14000 in 2020. The trend is:
questions.expected: Declining due mostly to poaching
questions.memo: White rhino numbers in SA have dropped sharply since 2010. Conservation efforts continue, including dehorning and intensive protection.

questions.question: Why is the loss of a SINGLE plant species potentially serious for an ecosystem?
options: Other species may depend on it for food, shelter, or pollination — its loss can cascade
Other species can replace it instantly
Losing one plant has no effect
questions.expected: Other species may depend on it for food, shelter, or pollination — its loss can cascade
questions.memo: Loss of a 'keystone' species can collapse a whole food web. Many SA plants have specialised pollinators that fail without them.

questions.question: SANParks (South African National Parks) manages:
options: A network of protected areas including Kruger, Table Mountain, Addo
questions.expected: A network of protected areas including Kruger, Table Mountain, Addo
questions.memo: SANParks is a key conservation body. Protected areas safeguard >9 million hectares of biodiversity.

questions.question: True or false: Removing alien invasive plants from a fynbos area benefits both biodiversity AND water supply.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Aliens like Black Wattle use far more water than fynbos. Removing them frees up water (relevant to Cape Town's water crisis) AND lets fynbos return.

questions.question: Why is climate change a growing biodiversity threat in SA?
options: Many SA species are already at climatic limits — even small warming can push them past survival
Climate change does not affect SA
questions.expected: Many SA species are already at climatic limits — even small warming can push them past survival
questions.memo: Mountain species, fynbos species, and many endemics have nowhere to go if their habitat gets too hot or dry. SA could lose dozens of endemic species under high-warming scenarios.

questions.question: Which is a CONSUMER-LEVEL action that helps conserve biodiversity?
options: Avoiding products from illegal wildlife trade (e.g. ivory, rhino horn)
Buying more alien plants for gardens
questions.expected: Avoiding products from illegal wildlife trade (e.g. ivory, rhino horn)
questions.memo: Demand drives poaching. Refusing to buy / passing the message + supporting reserves = real impact.

questions.question: Why is a private nature reserve (e.g. in a farming area) valuable even though it is small?
options: Many small reserves combined link fragmented habitats and protect species locally
Small reserves are worse than none
questions.expected: Many small reserves combined link fragmented habitats and protect species locally
questions.memo: Biodiversity corridors — networks of small + large reserves linked by 'stepping stones' allow species to move + cope with change.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA's Cape Floral Kingdom is a global conservation priority.
questions.expected: It is the smallest floral kingdom yet holds thousands of unique species found nowhere else, so losing fynbos would be a global extinction.
questions.memo: 70% of species endemic. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Under huge pressure from urbanisation, alien plants, fire-frequency changes.
options: The Cape Floral Kingdom is one of the largest floral kingdoms, so it simply contains more species than the rest.
It is a priority only because it is beautiful, even though its species are also common elsewhere in the world.
It is the smallest floral kingdom yet holds thousands of unique species found nowhere else, so losing fynbos would be a global extinction.
It matters because the plants there grow faster than anywhere else, making it valuable for farming and timber.

questions.question: True or false: Working for ecotourism can support both jobs AND biodiversity.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Ecotourism funds reserves + employs local communities → biodiversity is worth more alive than poached.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting biodiversity is important for HUMANS too — not just wildlife.
questions.expected: Healthy ecosystems give humans clean water, crop pollination, climate regulation and medicines, so losing biodiversity weakens services we rely on.
questions.memo: We are part of nature, not above it. Many of our medicines come from plants/animals/fungi (penicillin, aspirin, recent cancer drugs from yew tree).
options: Biodiversity matters to humans only as scenery, providing no practical benefits to our health or survival.
Healthy ecosystems give humans clean water, crop pollination, climate regulation and medicines, so losing biodiversity weakens services we rely on.
Protecting biodiversity benefits only wild animals, since humans live apart from nature and do not depend on it.
Humans are harmed by biodiversity, so reducing the number of species actually makes life safer for people.

LSC.G10.S4.HOL.A1.title: History of life, mass extinctions and South African fossil sites
LSC.G10.S4.HOL.A1.description: Fossil formation; major events in life's history; five mass extinctions; SA Karoo + Cradle of Humankind.
LSC.G10.S4.HOL.A1.recovery_strategy: Simple cells (3.8 Gya) → photosynthesis → O2 → Cambrian (~540 Mya) → dinosaurs (Mesozoic) → mammals (Cenozoic). End-Permian (252 Mya) = biggest (volcanic). End-Cretaceous (66 Mya) = killed dinosaurs (asteroid).

questions.question: A fossil is BEST defined as:
options: The preserved remains or traces of organisms from the past
questions.expected: The preserved remains or traces of organisms from the past
questions.memo: Includes bones, shells, impressions, footprints (trace fossils), and even DNA in some cases.

questions.question: Most fossils form by:
options: Slow burial in sediment, with minerals replacing hard parts over time
questions.expected: Slow burial in sediment, with minerals replacing hard parts over time
questions.memo: Permineralisation: minerals seep into bone or shell → stone replica of original structure. Usually takes thousands to millions of years.

questions.question: Which type of organism is MOST likely to fossilise?
options: One with hard parts (shell, bone) buried quickly in sediment
A jellyfish dying in deep ocean
A leaf eaten by a snail
questions.expected: One with hard parts (shell, bone) buried quickly in sediment
questions.memo: Soft parts decompose. Hard parts last. Quick burial = no scavengers, no weathering. That's why most fossils are skeletons / shells.

questions.question:
Order from EARLIEST to LATEST in the history of life:
(a) Cambrian explosion of multicellular life
(b) First single-celled life
(c) Dinosaurs
(d) Mammals dominate
questions.expected: b → a → c → d
questions.memo: Simple cells (~3.8 Gya) → Cambrian explosion (~540 Mya) → dinosaurs (~250 Mya in Triassic) → mammals dominate (last ~66 Mya).

questions.question: Which event RAISED atmospheric oxygen and made complex life possible?
options: Photosynthesising bacteria (Great Oxygenation Event ~2.4 billion years ago)
The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs
questions.expected: Photosynthesising bacteria (Great Oxygenation Event ~2.4 billion years ago)
questions.memo: Cyanobacteria producing O2 fundamentally changed Earth's atmosphere. Without it, no animals/plants as we know them.

questions.question: Approximately how many MASS extinctions have there been in Earth's history?
questions.expected: Five major ones
questions.memo: Five: end-Ordovician, Late Devonian, end-Permian, end-Triassic, end-Cretaceous. Many minor extinctions too. Some scientists say we are in a sixth (human-caused).

questions.question: Which mass extinction is famous for KILLING THE DINOSAURS?
questions.expected: End-Cretaceous (~66 million years ago)
questions.memo: End-Cretaceous extinction killed non-bird dinosaurs (plus many marine species). Caused by a massive asteroid impact + huge volcanism in India.

questions.question: The LARGEST mass extinction (95% of marine species lost) was the:
questions.expected: End-Permian (~252 million years ago)
questions.memo: Sometimes called 'The Great Dying'. Caused mainly by massive Siberian Traps volcanism → climate chaos. Took millions of years to recover.

questions.question: After the end-Cretaceous extinction, which group expanded rapidly to fill the dinosaurs' niches?
questions.expected: Mammals
questions.memo: Mammals had existed since the Triassic, but stayed small. Once dinosaurs were gone, mammals diversified into huge variety, including primates and us.

questions.question: True or false: All mass extinctions had a single cause.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most had multiple causes combining (volcanism + climate change + sea-level + asteroid). Rarely just one trigger.

questions.question: South Africa's Karoo Basin is famous for fossils from which period?
questions.expected: Permian–Triassic (250+ million years ago)
questions.memo: Karoo rocks preserve life before, during and after the end-Permian extinction — a globally unique record of mammal-like reptiles (therapsids).

questions.question: The Cradle of Humankind near Johannesburg includes fossil sites like:
options: Sterkfontein and Malapa (Australopithecus and Homo fossils)
questions.expected: Sterkfontein and Malapa (Australopithecus and Homo fossils)
questions.memo: UNESCO World Heritage Site. Sterkfontein = 'Mrs Ples'. Malapa = Australopithecus sediba. Rising Star = Homo naledi.

questions.question: True or false: The 'Mrs Ples' fossil is from a species in the genus Homo.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Mrs Ples is Australopithecus africanus, NOT Homo. Found by Robert Broom in 1947 at Sterkfontein.

questions.question: Homo naledi was discovered in:
options: The Rising Star cave system in SA (announced 2015)
questions.expected: The Rising Star cave system in SA (announced 2015)
questions.memo: Discovery led by Lee Berger and team. Hundreds of fossils, mosaic of features. Status of species still debated.

questions.question: Fossils help scientists understand:
options: What species existed in the past, how life evolved, and ancient environments
questions.expected: What species existed in the past, how life evolved, and ancient environments
questions.memo: Fossils = the main evidence for the history of life. They date and order species + reveal climate of the past.

questions.question: Why do we say we may be in a SIXTH mass extinction NOW?
options: Current species extinction rates from human activity are 100s to 1000s times higher than the natural background
questions.expected: Current species extinction rates from human activity are 100s to 1000s times higher than the natural background
questions.memo: Habitat loss, climate change, pollution, hunting → mass extinction at human time-scale. Reversible if we act, much harder if we don't.

questions.question: The fossil record is INCOMPLETE because:
options: Most organisms die without fossilising; many fossils erode before discovery
questions.expected: Most organisms die without fossilising; many fossils erode before discovery
questions.memo: Fossilisation is rare. We have snapshots from certain places and times. New finds (like Naledi) regularly change our picture.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why South African fossil sites are globally important.
questions.expected: The Karoo preserves a continuous record across the end-Permian extinction, and the Cradle of Humankind holds key hominin fossils of our origins.
questions.memo: Both UNESCO sites. SA scientists like Robert Broom, Phillip Tobias, Lee Berger have led major discoveries.
options: SA fossil sites are important only because they are easy for tourists to reach, not for any scientific reason.
The Karoo preserves a continuous record across the end-Permian extinction, and the Cradle of Humankind holds key hominin fossils of our origins.
SA's sites mainly preserve dinosaur footprints, which is why they attract worldwide scientific attention.
SA fossils are valuable because they are the oldest rocks on Earth, even though they contain few actual fossils.

questions.question:
The chart shows estimated extinction rates per million years. The peak around 252 Mya represents:

| Time (Mya) | Extinction rate |
|------------|-----------------|
| 444        | high            |
| 372        | high            |
| 252        | very high       |
| 201        | high            |
| 66         | high            |
questions.expected: The end-Permian mass extinction (the largest)
questions.memo: 252 Mya peak = end-Permian. Five peaks = five mass extinctions.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why studying mass extinctions of the past helps us today.
questions.expected: Mass extinctions show how life responds to rapid environmental change, helping us predict and mitigate today's biodiversity crisis.
questions.memo: Past as prologue. The end-Permian, in particular, was driven by greenhouse warming — directly relevant to today.
options: Mass extinctions show how life responds to rapid environmental change, helping us predict and mitigate today's biodiversity crisis.
Past extinctions teach us nothing useful, because the conditions then were completely unlike anything we face now.
Studying mass extinctions only helps us date old rocks, which has no link to present-day conservation problems.
Mass extinctions prove that life always recovers quickly, so today's biodiversity losses need no real concern.

LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A1.title: Classification of microorganisms — viruses, bacteria, protists, fungi
LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A1.description: Cellular features that distinguish the four microbe groups; examples for each.
LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A1.recovery_strategy: Virus = no cell. Bacteria = prokaryote. Protist = eukaryote single-celled. Fungi = eukaryote with chitin walls + absorptive feeding.

questions.question: A virus differs from all true cells because:
options: It has no cytoplasm or organelles — just nucleic acid in a protein coat
It is bigger than a cell
It is a type of bacterium
questions.expected: It has no cytoplasm or organelles — just nucleic acid in a protein coat
questions.memo: Viruses can't reproduce on their own — they hijack living cells. That's why they're not classified in any of the kingdoms.

questions.question: Bacteria are PROKARYOTES, meaning:
options: They have no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles
questions.expected: They have no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles
questions.memo: Bacterial DNA floats free in the cytoplasm. No nucleus, no mitochondria, no ER. Some have cell walls (peptidoglycan).

questions.question: Which is true of Protista?
questions.expected: Eukaryotic, mostly single-celled (Amoeba, Paramecium, algae)
questions.memo: Protists are a 'catch-all' eukaryote group — diverse modes of feeding, locomotion, reproduction.

questions.question: Fungi differ from plants because they:
options: Have chitin (not cellulose) walls and absorb nutrients (not photosynthesise)
questions.expected: Have chitin (not cellulose) walls and absorb nutrients (not photosynthesise)
questions.memo: Fungi: chitin walls (like insect exoskeletons), no chlorophyll, heterotrophic by absorption. Include yeasts, moulds, mushrooms.

questions.question: True or false: Viruses are technically alive.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most biologists don't classify viruses as alive — they can't reproduce or metabolise without a host cell. They're 'on the edge of life'.

questions.question:
Match each microbe to its group:
1. HIV  2. E. coli  3. Amoeba  4. Yeast

A. Bacterium
B. Virus
C. Fungus
D. Protist
questions.memo: HIV = virus. E. coli = bacterium. Amoeba = protist. Yeast = fungus.

questions.question: Bacteria reproduce mainly by:
options: Binary fission (one cell splits into two)
questions.expected: Binary fission (one cell splits into two)
questions.memo: Binary fission can be very fast — some bacteria divide every 20 minutes under good conditions. One bacterium → billions in hours.

questions.question:
Look at the four microbe diagrams (virus = small protein coat with DNA/RNA; bacterium = oval with no nucleus; protist = larger cell with nucleus; fungus = chain of cells with nuclei). Which is the bacterium?
[Diagram: 4 microbe types side-by-side]
questions.expected: Bacterium (oval, no nucleus)
questions.memo: Key feature for bacterium: prokaryote = no membrane-bound nucleus. The DNA floats free in cytoplasm.

questions.question: Algae are usually classified in:
options: Protista (or Plantae for some multicellular forms)
questions.expected: Protista (or Plantae for some multicellular forms)
questions.memo: Single-celled algae (e.g. diatoms) = protists. Larger multicellular algae (e.g. kelp) sometimes placed in Plantae.

questions.question: True or false: All fungi are single-celled.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Yeasts ARE single-celled. Most other fungi (moulds, mushrooms) are multicellular — networks of thread-like hyphae.

questions.question: The flu virus contains its genetic material as:
questions.expected: RNA (an RNA virus)
questions.memo: Many serious viruses (influenza, HIV, SARS-CoV-2) are RNA viruses. RNA mutates faster → why flu vaccines change yearly.

questions.question: Which feature do all four microbe groups SHARE?
questions.expected: They are microscopic
questions.memo: 'Micro' = small, usually needing a microscope. Otherwise the four groups differ in cellular organisation.

questions.question: Why are viruses NOT classified into a Kingdom in the five-kingdom system?
options: They are not cellular and don't fit the criteria for any cellular kingdom
questions.expected: They are not cellular and don't fit the criteria for any cellular kingdom
questions.memo: Kingdoms require cells. Viruses have their own separate classification system (Baltimore classification by genome type).

questions.question: A pupil sees a 'string of beads' shape under the microscope. The cells are linked end-to-end. The microbe is most likely:
questions.expected: A streptococcal bacterium (cocci in chains)
questions.memo: Bacterial shapes: cocci (round), bacilli (rod), spirilla (spiral). Chains/clusters give species names: strepto- (chain), staphylo- (cluster).

questions.question: Bacterial cell walls contain:
questions.expected: Peptidoglycan
questions.memo: Bacterial walls = peptidoglycan. Plant walls = cellulose. Fungal walls = chitin. Lignin = woody plants. Antibiotics like penicillin target peptidoglycan.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why understanding microbe classification matters for medicine.
questions.expected: Different microbe groups need different treatments, so correct identification ensures the right drug is used against the pathogen.
questions.memo: Treating viral flu with antibiotics doesn't help (and worsens resistance). Doctors classify the pathogen before prescribing.
options: Classification does not affect treatment, because one general antibiotic works equally well against any microbe.
Classification matters only for naming microbes in textbooks, not for choosing how to treat an infection.
All microbes are treated with antivirals, so identifying the exact group makes no difference to the cure.
Different microbe groups need different treatments, so correct identification ensures the right drug is used against the pathogen.

questions.question: Which microbe group includes Plasmodium, the cause of malaria?
questions.expected: Protista
questions.memo: Plasmodium is a protist. Carried by Anopheles mosquitoes. Malaria treatment uses antimalarial drugs, not antibiotics.

questions.question: True or false: Most bacteria are harmful to humans.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most bacteria are harmless or beneficial — gut microbes (digestion + immunity), nitrogen-fixing bacteria, food bacteria (yoghurt, cheese). Only a small fraction cause disease.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why VIRUSES are hard to treat compared to bacterial infections.
questions.expected: Viruses hide inside host cells and use the cell's own machinery to replicate, so drugs that kill them often harm host cells too.
questions.memo: Bacteria can be targeted by drugs that attack peptidoglycan walls (no human equivalent). Viruses don't have such unique targets.
options: Viruses hide inside host cells and use the cell's own machinery to replicate, so drugs that kill them often harm host cells too.
Viruses are simply larger than bacteria, so the same antibiotics work but much higher doses are needed.
Viruses are harder to treat because they live only in the bloodstream where drugs cannot reach them at all.
Viruses can be killed easily with antibiotics, but people just take them too late for the medicine to work.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how microbes BUILD the foundation of most ecosystems.
questions.expected: Decomposer bacteria and fungi recycle nutrients from dead matter, and photosynthetic microbes produce a huge share of the world's oxygen.
questions.memo: Without decomposers, nutrient cycles fail. Phytoplankton (mostly protists) make about half of Earth's O2.
options: Microbes only cause disease, so they take from ecosystems rather than building or supporting them in any way.
Microbes build ecosystems only by being eaten, since they cannot recycle nutrients or produce oxygen themselves.
Decomposer bacteria and fungi recycle nutrients from dead matter, and photosynthetic microbes produce a huge share of the world's oxygen.
Microbes matter mainly because larger animals could not exist without microbes physically holding the soil together.

LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A2.title: Microorganisms in disease, food and biotechnology
LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A2.description: Microbe-caused diseases; food fermentation; antibiotics and resistance; vaccines; sewage; SA context.
LSC.G11.S4.MICR.A2.recovery_strategy: TB = bacterium (Mycobacterium tuberculosis). HIV = virus. Cholera = bacterium. Malaria = protist. Antibiotics target bacteria. Vaccines train the immune system.

questions.question: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by:
questions.expected: A bacterium (Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
questions.memo: TB = bacterial lung infection. Major SA public-health problem, often co-infecting people with HIV.

questions.question: HIV is:
options: A virus that infects immune (CD4) cells
questions.expected: A virus that infects immune (CD4) cells
questions.memo: HIV destroys CD4 T-cells → immune system weakens → opportunistic infections (TB, pneumonia). ARV treatment + U=U.

questions.question: Cholera is caused by:
options: A bacterium spread via contaminated water (Vibrio cholerae)
questions.expected: A bacterium spread via contaminated water (Vibrio cholerae)
questions.memo: Cholera causes severe diarrhoea — dehydration is the main killer. Treatment: rehydration + antibiotics. Prevention: clean water + sanitation.

questions.question: Malaria is spread by:
questions.expected: Female Anopheles mosquitoes carrying Plasmodium
questions.memo: The mosquito is the vector; the protist Plasmodium is the actual cause. Endemic in low-altitude tropical/sub-tropical SA areas (Limpopo, Mpumalanga, KZN).

questions.question: Yeast is used to make bread because it:
options: Ferments sugars, producing CO2 that makes the dough rise
questions.expected: Ferments sugars, producing CO2 that makes the dough rise
questions.memo: Anaerobic respiration in yeast: sugar → ethanol + CO2. CO2 bubbles puff the dough up. Alcohol evaporates during baking.

questions.question: Sorghum beer (umqombothi) in SA is made by:
options: Letting yeasts and bacteria ferment a sorghum-malt mash
questions.expected: Letting yeasts and bacteria ferment a sorghum-malt mash
questions.memo: Traditional sour beer fermented in clay pots. Microbial mix (lactic-acid bacteria + yeast) gives sour + alcoholic profile. Cultural significance across SA.

questions.question: Amasi (fermented milk) is made by:
questions.expected: Lactic-acid bacteria fermenting milk sugars
questions.memo: Same family of bacteria as yoghurt. Lactic acid lowers pH → milk thickens + sours. Long shelf-life without refrigeration.

questions.question: True or false: Antibiotics work against viral infections like the flu.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Antibiotics target bacterial structures viruses don't have. Misuse drives antibiotic resistance — a major SA + global problem.

questions.question: MDR-TB (multi-drug-resistant TB) means:
options: The TB bacterium has evolved resistance to more than one first-line antibiotic
TB has spread to multiple people
questions.expected: The TB bacterium has evolved resistance to more than one first-line antibiotic
questions.memo: Major SA problem. Caused by stopping antibiotics early, incomplete courses, poor adherence. XDR-TB = even worse.

questions.question: Vaccines work by:
options: Training the immune system to recognise and fight a pathogen quickly if exposed
Killing all bacteria in the body
questions.expected: Training the immune system to recognise and fight a pathogen quickly if exposed
questions.memo: Memory cells made after vaccination = quick response on real infection. Why polio is nearly eradicated, why smallpox is gone.

questions.question: Sewage treatment uses bacteria to:
options: Break down organic waste into safer compounds
questions.expected: Break down organic waste into safer compounds
questions.memo: Aerobic + anaerobic stages use microbial communities. Without microbes, treating sewage would be impossible.

questions.question:
The table shows TB infection rates in 4 provinces. Which province has the HIGHEST burden?

| Province        | TB cases per 100 000 |
|-----------------|----------------------|
| Western Cape    | 681                  |
| KwaZulu-Natal   | 685                  |
| Eastern Cape    | 762                  |
| Gauteng         | 555                  |
questions.expected: Eastern Cape
questions.memo: Eastern Cape has the highest reported TB rate. Several factors: poverty, overcrowding, HIV co-infection.

questions.question: An antibiotic course should be FINISHED even when symptoms improve because:
options: Some bacteria survive longer — stopping early allows resistance to develop
questions.expected: Some bacteria survive longer — stopping early allows resistance to develop
questions.memo: Survival of the toughest = natural selection in action. Always finish the course. Major message in SA's TB programmes.

questions.question: ARV (antiretroviral) therapy for HIV works by:
options: Blocking the virus's ability to replicate, lowering viral load
questions.expected: Blocking the virus's ability to replicate, lowering viral load
questions.memo: ARVs target different viral steps. Effective enough that viral load becomes undetectable + untransmittable (U=U).

questions.question: Penicillin was discovered by:
questions.expected: Alexander Fleming (from a Penicillium mould)
questions.memo: Fleming, 1928. The first antibiotic. Saved millions of lives during and after WW2.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why HIV co-infection makes TB worse in SA.
questions.expected: HIV weakens the immune system that normally controls TB bacteria, so people with HIV are far more likely to develop active TB.
questions.memo: TB is the leading cause of death in HIV-positive South Africans. Co-treatment programmes target both at once.
options: HIV makes TB worse only because the two infections spread through the same coughing, not through the immune system.
HIV weakens the immune system that normally controls TB bacteria, so people with HIV are far more likely to develop active TB.
HIV directly feeds the TB bacteria, making them multiply faster regardless of how strong the immune system is.
HIV and TB are unrelated, so having both at once is no worse than having either infection on its own.

questions.question: Genetically engineered microbes can be used in biotechnology to:
options: Produce useful proteins like human insulin
questions.expected: Produce useful proteins like human insulin
questions.memo: Insulin for diabetics has been produced by genetically modified E. coli since the 1980s. Cheaper + more reliable than animal sources.

questions.question: True or false: Good handwashing reduces the spread of many microbial infections.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Soap breaks lipid envelopes (many viruses) + washes bacteria off hands. Simple, cheap, effective. Lifesaver in clinic settings.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why vaccination of MANY people (not just one) protects a community.
questions.expected: When most people are immune, the pathogen struggles to spread, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as babies and the immunocompromised.
questions.memo: Herd-immunity threshold varies by disease (measles ~95%, polio ~80%). When coverage drops, outbreaks return.
options: When most people are immune, the pathogen struggles to spread, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as babies and the immunocompromised.
The vaccine spreads from a vaccinated person to others nearby, immunising the whole community through contact.
Vaccinating many people uses up all the pathogen in the area so there is none left to infect anyone.
Each vaccinated person only protects themselves; numbers make no difference to how easily the disease spreads.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why microbial biotechnology is becoming MORE important for SA.
questions.expected: Microbes make products like medicines, foods and biofuels cheaply, and SA's biotech sector creates jobs while tackling health and environmental challenges.
questions.memo: From insulin to mine bioremediation to indigenous fermented foods — microbes are at the heart of modern biotech.
options: Biotechnology only matters overseas; SA has no role in producing biotech products or benefiting from them.
Microbes make products like medicines, foods and biofuels cheaply, and SA's biotech sector creates jobs while tackling health and environmental challenges.
Microbes are only useful for causing disease, so studying them protects SA but produces nothing valuable.
Biotechnology replaces all microbes with chemicals, which is why it is becoming more important worldwide.

LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A1.title: Bryophytes and pteridophytes — mosses and ferns
LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A1.description: Non-vascular vs vascular non-seed plants; water dependence; alternation of generations.
LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A1.recovery_strategy: Mosses = no vascular tissue, no real roots (rhizoids), water for fertilisation. Ferns = vascular but still no seeds, reproduce by spores. Both need water for sperm to swim.

questions.question: Bryophytes include:
questions.expected: Mosses, liverworts, hornworts
questions.memo: Bryophytes = the simplest land plants. Small, close to the ground, common in damp shaded places.

questions.question: Mosses lack:
options: True roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue
questions.expected: True roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue
questions.memo: Mosses have leaf-like and stem-like parts but no true xylem/phloem. They absorb water across their whole surface via diffusion.

questions.question: Mosses anchor themselves to a surface using:
questions.expected: Rhizoids (hair-like structures)
questions.memo: Rhizoids look like tiny roots but lack vascular tissue. They mainly anchor — water absorption is across the whole moss surface.

questions.question: Why are MOSSES restricted to damp habitats?
options: Sperm cells must swim through a film of water to reach eggs
questions.expected: Sperm cells must swim through a film of water to reach eggs
questions.memo: External fertilisation = water dependence. Why mosses thrive on forest floors, stream banks, after rain.

questions.question: Pteridophytes include:
questions.expected: Ferns and horsetails
questions.memo: Pteridophytes = vascular spore plants. Bigger than mosses, can be tree-sized in tropics. Common in SA forests and wet places.

questions.question: Ferns have:
options: True roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue, but reproduce by spores
questions.expected: True roots, stems and leaves with vascular tissue, but reproduce by spores
questions.memo: Ferns are intermediate: vascular like seed plants, but spores like mosses. The leaves (fronds) bear spore-producing sori on the underside.

questions.question: Ferns still depend on water for reproduction because:
options: Their sperm cells need to swim to fertilise the egg
questions.expected: Their sperm cells need to swim to fertilise the egg
questions.memo: Like mosses, ferns have flagellated sperm needing free water. So ferns still need moist conditions.

questions.question: True or false: Mosses reproduce by seeds.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Mosses reproduce by spores (not seeds). Seeds = innovation of gymnosperms and angiosperms (later in evolution).

questions.question:
On the moss diagram, which structure produces spores?
[Diagram: moss with leafy gametophyte, stalk, spore capsule on top]
options: The spore capsule (top of the stalk)
questions.expected: The spore capsule (top of the stalk)
questions.memo: Spore capsule (sporangium) sits on a stalk above the green leafy gametophyte. Spores released → new mosses grow.

questions.question:
Match the feature to the plant group:
1. Has true vascular tissue
2. Sperm needs to swim
3. Has rhizoids, not roots

A. Both mosses and ferns
B. Ferns only
C. Mosses only
questions.memo: True vascular = ferns only. Sperm swims in both. Rhizoids only in mosses.

questions.question: Mosses can act as PIONEER species because:
options: They colonise bare rock and start soil formation
questions.expected: They colonise bare rock and start soil formation
questions.memo: Mosses release acids that break down rock + trap dust → thin soil layer → seeds can grow. Key step in primary succession.

questions.question: Why are ferns LARGER than mosses?
options: Vascular tissue lets them transport water + nutrients further, supporting bigger size
questions.expected: Vascular tissue lets them transport water + nutrients further, supporting bigger size
questions.memo: Vascular tissue = the key innovation that let plants grow tall on land. Mosses are limited to centimetres; tree ferns reach 10+ metres.

questions.question: True or false: Spores from ferns can be dispersed by wind.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Spores are tiny, lightweight — easily carried by wind. That's how ferns colonise distant locations even without seeds.

questions.question: Alternation of generations means:
options: A plant's life cycle alternates between haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) stages
questions.expected: A plant's life cycle alternates between haploid (gametophyte) and diploid (sporophyte) stages
questions.memo: Gametophyte (n) → gametes → fertilisation → sporophyte (2n) → meiosis → spores → gametophyte (n). Two generations alternate.

questions.question: In moss life cycle, the GREEN leafy part you see is the:
questions.expected: Gametophyte (haploid)
questions.memo: In mosses, the dominant visible generation is the gametophyte. In ferns and seed plants, the visible generation is the sporophyte.

questions.question: In fern life cycle, the BIG leafy fern you see is the:
questions.expected: Sporophyte (diploid)
questions.memo: Opposite of mosses. Big ferns = sporophyte. The gametophyte is a tiny heart-shaped 'prothallus' easily missed.

questions.question: Tree ferns are found in SA's:
options: Coastal forests in KwaZulu-Natal and Tsitsikamma
questions.expected: Coastal forests in KwaZulu-Natal and Tsitsikamma
questions.memo: Wet, sheltered forest = ideal for tree ferns (Cyathea dregei). Iconic SA forest species.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why bryophytes are considered the FIRST true land plants in evolution.
questions.expected: Bryophytes were among the earliest plants on land with adaptations like a cuticle, but they stay small and still need water for reproduction.
questions.memo: First step out of water ~470 million years ago. Vascular plants followed; seeds and flowers came much later.
options: Bryophytes were the largest, most advanced plants and fully escaped the need for water in reproduction.
Bryophytes evolved after flowering plants, making them the most recent group to colonise land.
Bryophytes were among the earliest plants on land with adaptations like a cuticle, but they stay small and still need water for reproduction.
Bryophytes lived only in the oceans and never actually colonised land, so they cannot be true land plants.

questions.question: True or false: Ferns and mosses can both live in completely dry deserts.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Both need free water for fertilisation. Some species can tolerate dry seasons (resurrection plants) but most require regular moisture.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why bryophytes and pteridophytes are important indicators of HEALTHY forest ecosystems.
questions.expected: They are sensitive to moisture, light and air quality, so a diverse community of mosses and ferns usually indicates a damp, undisturbed forest.
questions.memo: Same reason lichens indicate clean air. Ecologists use bryophyte counts to assess forest condition in fynbos-margin and KZN forests.
options: They survive in any conditions and thrive even in polluted, dry, disturbed areas, so their presence tells us little.
They are sensitive to moisture, light and air quality, so a diverse community of mosses and ferns usually indicates a damp, undisturbed forest.
They only grow where the soil has been heavily disturbed, so lots of them signals a damaged forest.
They produce the oxygen the forest needs, so counting them measures how much air a forest makes.

LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A2.title: Gymnosperms and angiosperms — seed plants
LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A2.description: Gymnosperms = naked seeds (cycads, conifers); angiosperms = flowering plants; monocot vs dicot; SA examples.
LSC.G11.S4.PLNT.A2.recovery_strategy: Gymnosperm = naked seeds in cones. Angiosperm = seeds in fruits. Monocot: 1 cotyledon, parallel veins, fibrous roots. Dicot: 2 cotyledons, net veins, tap root.

questions.question: Gymnosperms include:
questions.expected: Pines, cycads, conifers
questions.memo: Gymnos = naked, sperma = seeds. Their seeds sit naked on cone scales (no fruit).

questions.question: Angiosperms (flowering plants) bear seeds:
questions.expected: Inside a fruit
questions.memo: Angio = vessel, sperma = seeds. Seeds develop INSIDE the ovary, which becomes the fruit. Major innovation.

questions.question: True or false: Gymnosperms have flowers.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Gymnosperms reproduce by cones, NOT flowers. Pine cones, cycad cones — flower-free. Flowers are the angiosperm innovation.

questions.question: South African indigenous cycads (Encephalartos) are:
questions.expected: Ancient gymnosperms, many highly endangered
questions.memo: SA hosts ~50% of the world's cycad species. Many are critically endangered due to illegal collecting. CITES-protected.

questions.question: Which group has the GREATEST diversity of plant species?
questions.expected: Angiosperms
questions.memo: About 300,000 angiosperm species — more than all other plant groups combined. Flowers + fruits drove huge evolutionary success.

questions.question: A monocot has:
options: 1 cotyledon, parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots
2 cotyledons, net leaf veins, tap root
questions.expected: 1 cotyledon, parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots
questions.memo: Monocots: grasses, maize, palms, lilies, orchids. Parallel veins are the easiest field check.

questions.question: A dicot has:
questions.expected: 2 cotyledons, net veins, tap root
questions.memo: Dicots: beans, daisies, oaks, most trees, most fynbos. Net veins distinguish from grasses.

questions.question: Maize (mealies, pap) is a:
questions.expected: Monocot
questions.memo: Maize is a grass. Parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots, single cotyledon. Same as wheat, rice, sorghum.

questions.question: Marula (Sclerocarya birrea) is a:
questions.expected: Dicot angiosperm
questions.memo: Marula = SA indigenous tree, dicot. Famous fruit, traditional uses. Cultural significance in many SA communities.

questions.question:
Match the plant to its category:
1. Pine  2. Cycad  3. Rose  4. Grass

A. Monocot angiosperm
B. Dicot angiosperm
C. Gymnosperm (cones)
D. Gymnosperm (cones)
questions.memo: Pine + Cycad = gymnosperms. Rose = dicot. Grass = monocot.

questions.question: Looking at a leaf, you see clear parallel veins running from base to tip. The plant is a:
questions.expected: Monocot
questions.memo: Parallel veins = monocot signature. Net (reticulate) veins = dicot. Reliable field check.

questions.question: Fynbos plants (proteas, ericas) are mostly:
questions.expected: Dicot angiosperms
questions.memo: Most fynbos species are dicots — proteaceae, ericaceae, fabaceae. Famous for bird-pollinated flowers + fire-adapted biology.

questions.question: True or false: Conifers are angiosperms because they have seeds.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Conifers = gymnosperms. Having seeds is necessary but not sufficient — they must be in a fruit to be angiosperm.

questions.question: Why is the seed an EVOLUTIONARY innovation?
options: It contains an embryo + food store + protective coat — can survive harsh conditions and disperse
questions.expected: It contains an embryo + food store + protective coat — can survive harsh conditions and disperse
questions.memo: Seeds let plants spread far + wait for good conditions. They were a huge advance over spores in dry climates.

questions.question: Why are FLOWERS an evolutionary advantage over cones?
options: They attract animal pollinators, increasing efficient cross-pollination
questions.expected: They attract animal pollinators, increasing efficient cross-pollination
questions.memo: Insect/bird pollination is much more targeted than wind. Flowers + fruits + animal partners → angiosperm explosion of diversity.

questions.question:
On the labelled angiosperm leaf, the network-like vein pattern shows it is a:
[Diagram: dicot leaf with net venation]
questions.expected: Dicot
questions.memo: Net venation = dicot. Parallel = monocot. Easy to remember.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why FRUIT is an angiosperm advantage in seed dispersal.
questions.expected: Animals eat the fleshy fruit and carry the seeds far away, dropping them in their droppings, which spreads seeds wider than wind alone.
questions.memo: Fruit = bribe for the disperser. Bigger range = better chance of finding new habitat + reduces competition with parent.
options: Animals eat the fleshy fruit and carry the seeds far away, dropping them in their droppings, which spreads seeds wider than wind alone.
Fruit makes the seed heavier so it falls straight down and germinates right beside the parent plant.
Fruit feeds the seedling for years after germination, so dispersal distance does not matter.
Fruit poisons animals that eat it, keeping seeds safely near the parent where conditions are known.

questions.question: True or false: Cycads are one of the OLDEST living seed-plant groups.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Cycads existed in the time of dinosaurs (~280 Mya). They are living fossils. SA has globally important cycad diversity.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ANGIOSPERMS dominate most modern ecosystems.
questions.expected: Flowers attract animal pollinators for efficient reproduction and fruits disperse seeds widely, letting angiosperms diversify into nearly every habitat.
questions.memo: 300,000+ species. Cover most land area. Provide most of our food.
options: They are the tallest plants and simply shade out all competitors, which is why they dominate every habitat.
They reproduce only by spores carried on the wind, allowing them to spread faster than any other group.
They have no need for pollinators or seeds, relying instead on splitting in two to multiply rapidly.
Flowers attract animal pollinators for efficient reproduction and fruits disperse seeds widely, letting angiosperms diversify into nearly every habitat.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting indigenous SA gymnosperms (cycads) is important.
questions.expected: Many SA cycads are critically endangered and found nowhere else, so losing them means global extinction and the loss of an ancient evolutionary lineage.
questions.memo: Illegal collecting is a major threat. CITES + national law + DNA-tagging fight poaching of these living fossils.
options: Many SA cycads are critically endangered and found nowhere else, so losing them means global extinction and the loss of an ancient evolutionary lineage.
SA cycads are common everywhere in the world, so protecting them is just a local preference, not a global concern.
Cycads are recently evolved plants, so their loss would remove only a young branch of the plant family.
Cycads can easily be regrown in any garden, so wild populations do not need protection.

LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A1.title: Flower structure and pollination
LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A1.description: Flower parts; pollination types (wind, insect, bird); SA pollinators.
LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A1.recovery_strategy: Male = stamen (anther + filament). Female = carpel (stigma + style + ovary). Wind-pollinated = small/dull/no nectar. Insect/bird-pollinated = colourful, nectar, scent.

questions.question: The MALE part of a flower is the:
questions.expected: Stamen (anther + filament)
questions.memo: Stamen = filament (stalk) + anther (top sac that makes pollen). Many stamens per flower usually.

questions.question: The FEMALE part of a flower is the:
questions.expected: Carpel (stigma + style + ovary)
questions.memo: Carpel (pistil) = stigma (top) + style (neck) + ovary (base with ovules). Pollen lands on stigma.

questions.question: Pollen is produced in the:
questions.expected: Anther
questions.memo: Anther is the pollen factory. Pollen = male gametes packaged for transport.

questions.question:
On the labelled flower diagram, which structure is the OVARY?
[Diagram: flower cross-section with labels A=petal, B=stamen, C=stigma, D=ovary at base]
questions.expected: D (base of carpel)
questions.memo: Ovary = swollen base of the carpel, containing ovules (which become seeds). Becomes the fruit after fertilisation.

questions.question: The petals function mainly to:
options: Attract pollinators with colour and scent
questions.expected: Attract pollinators with colour and scent
questions.memo: Big colourful petals + nectar guides + scent → tempt insects, birds, bats. Why insect-pollinated flowers are bright.

questions.question: Sepals are:
options: Leaf-like structures that protected the flower bud
questions.expected: Leaf-like structures that protected the flower bud
questions.memo: Sepals = the green outer cup around a flower bud. Together they form the calyx.

questions.question: POLLINATION is:
options: The transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.expected: The transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
questions.memo: Pollination ≠ fertilisation. Pollination is movement of pollen. Fertilisation happens later after pollen grows down to the ovule.

questions.question: Wind-pollinated flowers usually have:
options: Small, dull, no scent, no nectar, lots of light pollen
questions.expected: Small, dull, no scent, no nectar, lots of light pollen
questions.memo: No need to attract animals → small + drab + lots of pollen. Grasses, maize, oaks. Hayfever sufferers know about wind-blown pollen.

questions.question: Insect-pollinated flowers usually:
options: Have bright petals, scent, nectar, and sticky pollen
questions.expected: Have bright petals, scent, nectar, and sticky pollen
questions.memo: Reward (nectar) + advertising (colour + scent) + sticky pollen for the bee's body → efficient transport.

questions.question: SA proteas are often pollinated by:
questions.expected: Sunbirds and Cape Sugarbirds
questions.memo: Long-tubed protea flowers + nectar = ideal for long-beaked sunbirds. Classic SA pollinator partnership.

questions.question: Cross-pollination is:
options: Pollen transfer between flowers on DIFFERENT plants of the same species
questions.expected: Pollen transfer between flowers on DIFFERENT plants of the same species
questions.memo: Cross-pollination = genetic mixing → variation → adaptability. Most flowering plants favour cross over self-pollination.

questions.question: Self-pollination has the DISADVANTAGE of:
questions.expected: Less genetic variation → less adaptability
questions.memo: Self-pollination = essentially cloning. Quick, but populations can't adapt as well to changing conditions or disease.

questions.question: True or false: Wind-pollinated plants tend to release HUGE amounts of pollen.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Wind is unreliable — most pollen blows away into nowhere. Plants compensate by producing pollen in enormous quantities.

questions.question: A flower in SA has long red tubular petals + lots of nectar + no scent. Which pollinator is MOST likely?
options: A bird (sunbird) — birds see red well, can hover, don't rely on scent
questions.expected: A bird (sunbird) — birds see red well, can hover, don't rely on scent
questions.memo: Red + no scent (birds can't smell) + long tube (long beak) + abundant nectar = bird syndrome. SA proteas, Aloe.

questions.question: Why are honeybees critical for SA agriculture?
options: They pollinate many fruit and seed crops, supporting farmers' yields
questions.expected: They pollinate many fruit and seed crops, supporting farmers' yields
questions.memo: Apples, pears, almonds, sunflowers — all need bees. Bee decline = food-security concern. SA hosts indigenous Cape honeybees.

questions.question:
Match the pollinator to the flower feature:
1. Wind  2. Insect  3. Bird  4. Bat

A. Long red tubular flowers, no scent
B. White/pale flowers, strong night scent
C. Small dull flowers, no nectar
D. Bright colours, scent, nectar guides
questions.memo: Wind = drab. Insect = colourful + scent. Bird = red + no scent. Bat = night + pale + strong scent.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why some plants have FLOWERS open at night.
questions.expected: Night flowers attract nocturnal pollinators like moths and bats, and are often pale or white with a strong scent to be found in the dark.
questions.memo: Each pollinator group = a 'syndrome' of flower traits. Co-evolution of plants + pollinators.
options: Night flowers stay closed in daylight to avoid bees, but this gives them no real pollination advantage.
Opening at night protects the flower from sunlight damage; pollination still happens during the day.
Night flowers attract nocturnal pollinators like moths and bats, and are often pale or white with a strong scent to be found in the dark.
Plants open flowers at night because photosynthesis stops, so the petals have nothing else to do.

questions.question: True or false: Pollination must always happen before fertilisation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Pollination = pollen arrives at stigma. Fertilisation = sperm reaches egg inside ovule. One leads to the other.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how plants and their POLLINATORS are an example of co-evolution.
questions.expected: Plants evolve flower features that attract specific pollinators, and those pollinators evolve traits to exploit the flowers, so each shapes the other's evolution.
questions.memo: Sunbirds + proteas, fig wasps + figs, orchids + their specific moth — countless examples worldwide.
options: Only the plant changes over time; pollinators stay exactly the same and are simply used by the flowers.
Plants and pollinators evolve separately and never influence each other's traits.
Co-evolution means the plant and pollinator are actually the same species changing form.
Plants evolve flower features that attract specific pollinators, and those pollinators evolve traits to exploit the flowers, so each shapes the other's evolution.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a decline in INSECT POLLINATORS is a serious problem.
questions.expected: Many wild plants and crops depend on insect pollination for seeds and fruit, so losing pollinators would reduce food supply and damage ecosystems.
questions.memo: Pesticides, habitat loss, climate change → global pollinator decline. SA monitors honeybee health, supports indigenous bee research.
options: Many wild plants and crops depend on insect pollination for seeds and fruit, so losing pollinators would reduce food supply and damage ecosystems.
Insects mainly damage crops, so fewer pollinators would actually increase harvests for farmers.
Wind can replace all insect pollination instantly, so a decline in pollinators changes nothing.
Pollinators only matter for flowers in gardens, not for the crops that feed people.

LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A2.title: Fertilisation, fruit, seed and dispersal
LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A2.description: Double fertilisation; fruit from ovary, seed from ovule; seed structure; dispersal types; germination.
LSC.G11.S4.PREP.A2.recovery_strategy: Ovary → fruit. Ovule → seed. Double fertilisation: 2 sperm = 1 makes zygote, 1 makes endosperm. Germination needs water + warmth + O2.

questions.question: After pollen lands on the stigma, it grows a tube down through the:
questions.expected: Style to the ovary
questions.memo: Pollen tube delivers sperm nuclei to the ovule. Style is the connecting neck between stigma and ovary.

questions.question: In DOUBLE fertilisation:
options: Two sperm cells are used — one fertilises the egg, the other forms endosperm
questions.expected: Two sperm cells are used — one fertilises the egg, the other forms endosperm
questions.memo: Unique to angiosperms. Zygote becomes embryo. Endosperm (triploid) = food store for the developing seed.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the OVARY develops into the:
questions.expected: Fruit
questions.memo: Ovary → fruit (surrounds + protects the seeds). Ovule → seed. Mnemonic: 'ovary OUTSIDE, ovule INSIDE'.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the OVULE develops into the:
questions.expected: Seed
questions.memo: Ovule = the structure inside the ovary that becomes the seed.

questions.question:
On the labelled seed diagram, which is the EMBRYO (the part that becomes a new plant)?
[Diagram: seed cross-section with cotyledon, embryo, testa labelled]
options: The small structure with radicle and plumule
questions.expected: The small structure with radicle and plumule
questions.memo: Embryo = future root (radicle) + future shoot (plumule) + cotyledon(s) for food. The seed coat (testa) protects it all.

questions.question: The seed coat (testa) functions to:
options: Protect the embryo and limit water loss until conditions are right
questions.expected: Protect the embryo and limit water loss until conditions are right
questions.memo: Testa is tough + waterproof. Allows seeds to survive harsh conditions, sometimes for years.

questions.question: Wind-dispersed seeds usually:
options: Are light, with wings or hairs (e.g. dandelion, maple)
questions.expected: Are light, with wings or hairs (e.g. dandelion, maple)
questions.memo: Wind dispersal = needs light seeds + drag surface (wing, parachute) to float in air.

questions.question: Animal-dispersed seeds often have:
questions.expected: Fleshy fruit (eaten) or hooks/burrs (carried)
