questions.memo: Two animal strategies: eaten + pooped out (berries, marula) OR hooked onto fur (cocklebur, Tribulus terrestris devil's-thorn).

questions.question: Coconut seeds use which method of dispersal?
options: Water (they float, can drift between islands)
questions.expected: Water (they float, can drift between islands)
questions.memo: Coconuts have fibrous, light husks → float for months in salt water. That's how palms reached remote islands.

questions.question: Explosive (mechanical) dispersal happens when:
options: A ripe pod splits open suddenly, flinging seeds away
questions.expected: A ripe pod splits open suddenly, flinging seeds away
questions.memo: Examples: balsam, witchhazel, some legumes. Tension built up in the drying pod releases when it splits.

questions.question: Marula fruit in SA is mainly dispersed by:
questions.expected: Animals (elephants love the fruit)
questions.memo: Elephants, baboons, antelope eat the fruit + carry seeds far. (Yes — the 'elephants get drunk on marula' tale is mostly a myth.)

questions.question: Germination requires:
questions.expected: Water, warmth, oxygen (and sometimes light)
questions.memo: Water reactivates enzymes. Warmth = good for chemistry. Oxygen = respiration to release energy. Light required by some species only.

questions.question:
Order the steps of seed germination:
(a) Water absorbed (imbibition)
(b) Radicle emerges
(c) Enzymes activated, food store mobilised
(d) Shoot emerges
questions.expected: a → c → b → d
questions.memo: Water in → metabolism resumes → root grows down (first) → shoot grows up. Logical sequence.

questions.question: True or false: Some seeds NEED fire or smoke before they will germinate.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Many SA fynbos species (serotinous proteas, Erica) need fire-related cues. This is a key adaptation to fire-prone biome.

questions.question: Why are angiosperm seeds usually accompanied by ENDOSPERM?
options: It is a food store that feeds the embryo until the new plant can photosynthesise
questions.expected: It is a food store that feeds the embryo until the new plant can photosynthesise
questions.memo: Wheat endosperm = the flour we eat. Coconut endosperm = the liquid + meat. Stored energy for germination.

questions.question: Cotyledons (seed leaves) in some seeds:
options: Store food themselves (e.g. beans) and feed the seedling
questions.expected: Store food themselves (e.g. beans) and feed the seedling
questions.memo: Beans = food stored in COTYLEDONS (not endosperm). Maize = food stored in ENDOSPERM. Different strategies, same purpose.

questions.question: Why do farmers PLANT seeds at a specific depth?
options: Too deep → not enough O2 or light. Too shallow → not enough moisture or stability
questions.expected: Too deep → not enough O2 or light. Too shallow → not enough moisture or stability
questions.memo: Seed packets specify depth for a reason. Maize: ~5 cm. Carrots: <1 cm. Right depth balances conditions for germination.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SEED DORMANCY is useful.
questions.expected: Seeds stay dormant until conditions are right before germinating, so the seedling avoids wasting resources during drought, winter or fire.
questions.memo: Various dormancy triggers: temperature change, fire, fruit digestion. Some seeds stay viable for decades or even thousands of years.
options: Dormant seeds germinate immediately whatever the weather, so they never waste a growing season.
Dormancy means a seed is dead and can never grow, which protects the parent from competition.
Seeds stay dormant until conditions are right before germinating, so the seedling avoids wasting resources during drought, winter or fire.
Dormancy makes seeds heavier so they sink into the soil faster after falling.

questions.question: True or false: SEED BANKS preserve plant genetic diversity for the future.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Millennium Seed Bank (UK), SANBI Seed Bank (SA) store seeds against extinction. Critical insurance against climate change and habitat loss.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SEED + FRUIT together are an evolutionary success story.
questions.expected: Seeds carry the embryo with a food store and tough coat for protection, while fruit disperses the seed by wind, water or animals, widening the plant's range.
questions.memo: Both structures = innovations of seed plants. Angiosperms refined both → massive evolutionary success.
options: Seeds need no protection, and fruit's only job is to feed the parent plant, not to spread offspring.
Fruit traps the seed in place near the parent, while the seed coat blocks germination forever.
Seeds and fruit are the same structure, so having both is just a repeated, wasteful feature.
Seeds carry the embryo with a food store and tough coat for protection, while fruit disperses the seed by wind, water or animals, widening the plant's range.

LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A1.title: Invertebrate phyla — main groups
LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A1.description: Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Mollusca, Arthropoda, Echinodermata; SA examples.
LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A1.recovery_strategy: Arthropods = exoskeleton + jointed legs (insects, spiders, crabs). Molluscs = soft body, often shell. Annelids = segmented. Echinoderms = five-fold radial symmetry.

questions.question: Sponges belong to phylum:
questions.expected: Porifera
questions.memo: Porifera = 'pore-bearer'. Body is full of holes; water flows through, food is filtered out. No true tissues.

questions.question: Jellyfish and sea anemones are:
questions.expected: Cnidaria
questions.memo: Cnidarians have stinging cells (cnidocytes). Radial symmetry. Includes jellyfish, sea anemones, corals.

questions.question: Flatworms and tapeworms belong to:
questions.expected: Platyhelminthes
questions.memo: 'Platy' = flat. Many are parasites. Bilateral symmetry, no body cavity, simple gut.

questions.question: Roundworms (e.g. Ascaris) belong to:
questions.expected: Nematoda
questions.memo: Nematodes have round bodies, complete gut (mouth + anus). Many cause crop and human disease.

questions.question: Earthworms belong to:
questions.expected: Annelida (segmented worms)
questions.memo: Annelids = ringed/segmented worms (earthworms, leeches, marine worms). Bilateral symmetry, true body cavity (coelom).

questions.question: Snails, octopuses, and clams are:
questions.expected: Mollusca
questions.memo: Molluscs = soft body, often shell, muscular foot. Three main classes: gastropods (snails), bivalves (clams), cephalopods (octopuses).

questions.question: Insects, spiders, and crabs all belong to:
questions.expected: Arthropoda
questions.memo: Arthropods = exoskeleton (chitin) + jointed limbs + segmented body. Largest animal phylum by far.

questions.question: Starfish belong to:
questions.expected: Echinodermata
questions.memo: Echinoderms = 'spiny skin'. Five-fold radial symmetry. All marine. Includes starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers.

questions.question:
Match the phylum to a SA example:
1. Arthropoda  2. Mollusca  3. Annelida  4. Echinodermata

A. Earthworm
B. Cape rock lobster
C. Black mussel
D. Sea urchin
questions.memo: Lobster = arthropod. Mussel = mollusc. Earthworm = annelid. Sea urchin = echinoderm.

questions.question: True or false: All sponges live in the sea.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most sponges are marine, but some live in fresh water. Either way they are sessile (anchored) and filter feed.

questions.question: Which feature unites the Arthropoda?
questions.expected: A hard exoskeleton + jointed appendages
questions.memo: Exoskeleton protects + supports. Jointed limbs give precise movement. Must moult to grow.

questions.question: Why are arthropods the MOST diverse animal phylum?
options: Many adaptations + small size + winged flight let them exploit countless niches
questions.expected: Many adaptations + small size + winged flight let them exploit countless niches
questions.memo: Over 1 million described arthropod species — possibly 10 million total. Insects alone are 80% of known animal diversity.

questions.question: Cape rock lobster is harvested in SA and is a:
questions.expected: Crustacean (Arthropoda)
questions.memo: Crustaceans = aquatic arthropods. Cape rock lobster is over-exploited; strict quotas in place.

questions.question: Abalone (perlemoen), poached heavily in SA, is a:
questions.expected: Marine gastropod mollusc
questions.memo: Abalone = mollusc with a single spiral-style shell. Poached for Asian markets. Now critically endangered in SA waters.

questions.question: Why are earthworms IMPORTANT for soil health?
options: They mix and aerate soil, breaking down organic matter into humus
questions.expected: They mix and aerate soil, breaking down organic matter into humus
questions.memo: Charles Darwin himself wrote about earthworms. They are crucial for soil structure + fertility in farms and forests.

questions.question: True or false: Tapeworms are parasites that live in vertebrate intestines.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Tapeworms (Platyhelminthes) absorb nutrients directly from gut contents. Cause weight loss, malnutrition. Common in undercooked meat.

questions.question:
Look at the diagram showing 8 invertebrate phyla. Which feature unites the Echinodermata?
[Diagram: phyla overview chart]
questions.expected: Five-fold (pentaradial) symmetry
questions.memo: Five-armed starfish = the classic example. Echinoderms also have a water vascular system + tube feet.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why invertebrates make up MOST of animal life.
questions.expected: Invertebrates have far more species than vertebrates, especially insects and arthropods, occupying nearly every habitat and filling key ecological roles.
questions.memo: About 97% of animal species are invertebrates. Without them, no pollination, no decomposition, food webs collapse.
options: Invertebrates have far more species than vertebrates, especially insects and arthropods, occupying nearly every habitat and filling key ecological roles.
Invertebrates are rare and only survive in a few oceans, but each one is very large and long-lived.
Vertebrates actually outnumber invertebrates in species; invertebrates just look more common.
Invertebrates dominate only because they reproduce by splitting, unlike all other animals.

questions.question: True or false: Ticks (which cause disease in SA cattle) are a type of mollusc.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Ticks are ARACHNIDS (arthropoda), related to spiders and mites. Major SA livestock + human health problem (tick-bite fever).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting INVERTEBRATE diversity matters for humans.
questions.expected: Invertebrates pollinate crops, decompose waste, control pests and support food webs, so without them ecosystems and agriculture would collapse.
questions.memo: Insect decline = global concern. SA has many endemic invertebrate species under threat from habitat loss + pesticides.
options: Invertebrates are pests that harm humans, so reducing their diversity would improve agriculture.
Invertebrates pollinate crops, decompose waste, control pests and support food webs, so without them ecosystems and agriculture would collapse.
Humans depend only on vertebrates for food and services, so invertebrate diversity is irrelevant to us.
Invertebrates provide no ecosystem services; protecting them is purely for their own sake.

LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A2.title: Chordates — fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals
LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A2.description: Phylum Chordata; five vertebrate classes; defining features and evolutionary trends.
LSC.G11.S4.ANIM.A2.recovery_strategy: Fish = gills, fins, scales. Amphibian = moist skin, larvae in water. Reptile = scales, lay eggs on land. Birds = feathers, warm-blooded. Mammals = fur, milk, warm-blooded.

questions.question: A chordate must have, at some life stage:
options: A notochord (rod of cells) and dorsal nerve cord
questions.expected: A notochord (rod of cells) and dorsal nerve cord
questions.memo: Other features: pharyngeal slits (gill slits in embryo), post-anal tail. The notochord becomes the vertebral column in vertebrates.

questions.question: Fish are characterised by:
questions.expected: Gills, fins, scales, cold-blooded, aquatic
questions.memo: Two big fish groups: cartilaginous (sharks, rays — skeleton of cartilage) and bony (most fish). Both are ectothermic (cold-blooded).

questions.question: Amphibians like frogs:
options: Have moist skin, are cold-blooded, and larvae develop in water
questions.expected: Have moist skin, are cold-blooded, and larvae develop in water
questions.memo: Amphi = double life. Larvae (tadpoles) in water with gills → adults can move on land with lungs.

questions.question: Reptiles differ from amphibians because reptiles:
options: Have scales, lay eggs with shells on land
Have moist skin and water larvae
questions.expected: Have scales, lay eggs with shells on land
questions.memo: Reptile scales prevent water loss. Eggs with shells let them reproduce on land — no water needed.

questions.question: Birds are unique because they have:
questions.expected: Feathers and are warm-blooded
questions.memo: Feathers = unique to birds. Bird are descended from theropod dinosaurs — technically 'avian dinosaurs'.

questions.question: Mammals are distinguished by:
questions.expected: Fur/hair, mammary glands (milk), warm-blooded
questions.memo: Mammary glands give the group its name. Includes monotremes (egg-laying — platypus), marsupials (pouch), placental (everyone else).

questions.question: True or false: Whales are mammals, not fish.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Whales = warm-blooded, breathe air through lungs, give birth to live young that drink milk. Classic example of convergent evolution (look like fish, but aren't).

questions.question:
Order from earliest to latest in vertebrate evolution:
(a) Reptiles  (b) Fish  (c) Amphibians  (d) Mammals
questions.expected: b → c → a → d
questions.memo: Fish (~500 Mya) → amphibians (~370 Mya) → reptiles (~310 Mya) → mammals (~210 Mya). Birds split from reptiles much later.

questions.question:
Match the SA animal to its class:
1. African elephant  2. Nile crocodile  3. Cape robin  4. Carp

A. Bird
B. Mammal
C. Reptile
D. Fish
questions.memo: Elephant = mammal. Crocodile = reptile. Robin = bird. Carp = fish.

questions.question: Why was the AMNIOTIC EGG a key innovation?
options: It allowed reptiles and birds to reproduce on dry land without water
questions.expected: It allowed reptiles and birds to reproduce on dry land without water
questions.memo: Amniotic egg = internal water supply for the embryo + shell to prevent drying. Freed vertebrates from water dependence.

questions.question: WARM-BLOODED (endothermic) animals like birds and mammals can:
options: Stay active across a wide temperature range, including cold conditions
questions.expected: Stay active across a wide temperature range, including cold conditions
questions.memo: Endotherms generate heat from metabolism. Costs more energy (= more food), but means staying active in cold weather + at night.

questions.question: Reptiles are ECTOTHERMIC, meaning they:
options: Rely on environment for heat (basking in sun)
questions.expected: Rely on environment for heat (basking in sun)
questions.memo: Cold-blooded = misleading term. Reptiles regulate temperature by behaviour (sun vs shade). Inactive in cold periods.

questions.question: South African Big Five (lion, leopard, rhino, elephant, buffalo) are all:
questions.expected: Mammals
questions.memo: All five = large mammals — flagship species for SA tourism + conservation.

questions.question: Coelacanth, the 'living fossil' fish found off SA coast, is famous because:
options: It was thought extinct for 65 million years until rediscovered in 1938
questions.expected: It was thought extinct for 65 million years until rediscovered in 1938
questions.memo: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer discovered the first specimen off East London in 1938 — one of the most famous biological discoveries.

questions.question: True or false: Penguins are flightless birds.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: African penguins on the SA coast can't fly but are excellent swimmers. Their wings are modified into flippers.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how AMPHIBIANS still depend on water.
questions.expected: Their eggs and larvae must develop in water and their adult skin must stay moist for gas exchange, so they need ponds, streams or wet habitats.
questions.memo: Why amphibians are good indicators of pollution and habitat loss. Frog declines = warning of wetland health.
options: Adult amphibians breathe only through lungs and never need moisture once they leave the water.
Amphibians lay shelled eggs on dry land, so they have fully escaped any dependence on water.
Their eggs and larvae must develop in water and their adult skin must stay moist for gas exchange, so they need ponds, streams or wet habitats.
Amphibians only need water for drinking, just like mammals, and can reproduce anywhere.

questions.question: True or false: Bird wings and bat wings evolved from a common winged ancestor.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Birds and bats evolved wings independently (convergent evolution). Bird wings = modified forelimbs with feathers. Bat wings = modified forelimbs with skin membrane.

questions.question: Why do SA bird-watchers track SEASONAL migrants?
options: Migratory birds depend on multiple habitats — their numbers indicate environmental health across continents
questions.expected: Migratory birds depend on multiple habitats — their numbers indicate environmental health across continents
questions.memo: SA hosts huge populations of European/Asian migrant birds in summer. SABAP (SA Bird Atlas Project) tracks them.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the EVOLUTIONARY trends from fish to mammals show increasing INDEPENDENCE from water.
questions.expected: Fish need water to breathe and reproduce, amphibians still need it for eggs, reptiles have shelled eggs, and mammals develop embryos internally, fully independent of water.
questions.memo: A clear sequence: gills → lungs, naked eggs → shelled eggs → live birth. Each step freed vertebrates from water more.
options: All four groups depend equally on water; there is no real trend of increasing independence from fish to mammals.
Mammals are the most water-dependent because they live in the sea, while fish are the most independent.
Fish need water to breathe and reproduce, amphibians still need it for eggs, reptiles have shelled eggs, and mammals develop embryos internally, fully independent of water.
Independence from water decreases over time, so mammals need more water than the fish they evolved from.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA's vertebrate diversity is globally important.
questions.expected: SA has many endemic vertebrate species and hosts important global migrations, with diverse biomes supporting birds, fish, reptiles and mammals found nowhere else.
questions.memo: From the Cape parrot to the riverine rabbit to coelacanths — SA vertebrate biodiversity is a global treasure.
options: SA has very few vertebrate species and none that are unique, so its diversity matters only locally.
SA's vertebrates are all common species found across the whole world, so they are not globally special.
SA only matters for plant diversity; its vertebrate life is unremarkable compared to other countries.
SA has many endemic vertebrate species and hosts important global migrations, with diverse biomes supporting birds, fish, reptiles and mammals found nowhere else.

LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A1.title: Photosynthesis — process and pigments
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A1.description: Chloroplast structure; light + dark reactions; word equation; pigments.
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A1.recovery_strategy: Light reactions: in thylakoids, water split → O2 + ATP + NADPH. Calvin cycle: in stroma, CO2 fixed using ATP/NADPH → glucose. O2 comes from water, NOT CO2.

questions.question: The overall word equation for photosynthesis is:
options: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy)
questions.memo: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O → C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Light energy captured by chlorophyll powers the reaction.

questions.question: Photosynthesis takes place inside which organelle?
questions.expected: Chloroplast
questions.memo: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll. Found in mesophyll cells of leaves. Plants only — animals can't photosynthesise.

questions.question: Within a chloroplast, the LIGHT reactions happen in the:
questions.expected: Thylakoid membranes (where chlorophyll sits)
questions.memo: Thylakoids are stacked into grana. Embedded chlorophyll captures light. Like solar panels inside the chloroplast.

questions.question: The DARK reactions (Calvin cycle) happen in the:
questions.expected: Stroma (fluid surrounding thylakoids)
questions.memo: Stroma = chloroplast's 'cytoplasm'. Calvin cycle enzymes here use ATP + NADPH from light reactions to fix CO2.

questions.question: True or false: 'Dark reactions' must happen at night.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Misleading name. Calvin cycle doesn't need LIGHT directly, but needs ATP/NADPH from light reactions — so usually happens in the day too.

questions.question: Light reactions produce:
questions.expected: ATP, NADPH, and oxygen (from water)
questions.memo: Light + water (split) → ATP (energy) + NADPH (electrons) + O2 (waste from water-splitting).

questions.question: Calvin cycle (dark reactions) produces:
options: Glucose (sugar) from CO2 using ATP and NADPH
questions.expected: Glucose (sugar) from CO2 using ATP and NADPH
questions.memo: ATP + NADPH from light reactions are USED in the Calvin cycle to fix CO2 into glucose.

questions.question: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from:
questions.expected: Water (split during light reactions)
questions.memo: Important: O2 source = WATER, not CO2. Proven with isotope-labelled water experiments.

questions.question:
On the chloroplast diagram, which structure are the thylakoids stacked into?
[Diagram: chloroplast cross-section]
questions.expected: Grana
questions.memo: Grana = stacks of thylakoid discs (like a stack of coins). Multiple grana per chloroplast, linked by stroma lamellae.

questions.question: Chlorophyll is GREEN because it:
options: Reflects green light and absorbs red and blue
questions.expected: Reflects green light and absorbs red and blue
questions.memo: Pigments are coloured by what they REFLECT, not absorb. Chlorophyll captures most energy from red + blue wavelengths.

questions.question: Why do AUTUMN leaves turn yellow/orange?
options: Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing other pigments (carotenoids, xanthophylls) underneath
Leaves change colour because of cold
questions.expected: Chlorophyll breaks down, revealing other pigments (carotenoids, xanthophylls) underneath
questions.memo: Accessory pigments are always there. When chlorophyll is broken down, the green is gone and yellow/orange/red colours show through.

questions.question:
Order the steps of photosynthesis:
(a) ATP and NADPH made in light reactions
(b) Light energy captured by chlorophyll
(c) Glucose formed in Calvin cycle
(d) CO2 enters through stomata
questions.expected: b → a → d → c
questions.memo: Light absorbed → light reactions make energy carriers → CO2 brought in → Calvin cycle uses energy to make glucose.

questions.question: Glucose made by photosynthesis can be:
options: Used in respiration, stored as starch, or built into cellulose
questions.expected: Used in respiration, stored as starch, or built into cellulose
questions.memo: Glucose is the universal sugar. Stored in plants as starch (food reserve). Built into cellulose for cell walls.

questions.question: Why do PLANTS need both photosynthesis AND respiration?
options: Photosynthesis makes food; respiration releases energy from food. Plants need both.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis makes food; respiration releases energy from food. Plants need both.
questions.memo: Common misconception: plants only photosynthesise. They photosynthesise during the day, but respire 24/7 like any cell.

questions.question: True or false: The Calvin cycle uses ATP made in the light reactions.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: ATP and NADPH from light reactions power the Calvin cycle. Without them, no glucose can be made.

questions.question: Plants in deep ocean or dark forest must:
options: Have accessory pigments or large surface area to capture limited light
questions.expected: Have accessory pigments or large surface area to capture limited light
questions.memo: Red algae use phycoerythrin (red pigment) to capture light at depth. Forest plants grow large leaves to catch dim light.

questions.question: Stomata on leaves allow:
options: CO2 to enter and water vapour + O2 to leave
questions.expected: CO2 to enter and water vapour + O2 to leave
questions.memo: Stomata are gas-exchange pores. Open during day (for CO2 for photosynthesis), closed at night (to save water).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why photosynthesis is the BASE of nearly all food chains.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis captures solar energy and stores it as glucose, and all other organisms depend on this energy, directly as herbivores or indirectly as carnivores.
questions.memo: Without photosynthesis, no producers → no food → no consumers → no decomposers → no ecosystems.
options: Photosynthesis captures solar energy and stores it as glucose, and all other organisms depend on this energy, directly as herbivores or indirectly as carnivores.
Food chains start with herbivores, which make their own food without needing plants or sunlight.
Photosynthesis only provides oxygen, while the energy in food chains comes from the soil directly.
Carnivores get their energy straight from the sun, so plants are not really the base of food chains.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why early photosynthesising bacteria CHANGED the Earth's atmosphere.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis releases oxygen as a waste, and over millions of years bacteria built atmospheric O2 from low to high levels, enabling complex life.
questions.memo: Great Oxygenation Event ~2.4 Gya. Many anaerobic organisms died. Without it, no animals/plants as we know them.
options: Early bacteria removed all oxygen from the air, creating the low-oxygen atmosphere we breathe today.
Photosynthesis releases oxygen as a waste, and over millions of years bacteria built atmospheric O2 from low to high levels, enabling complex life.
Photosynthesising bacteria produced carbon dioxide that filled the atmosphere and warmed the early Earth.
Bacteria had no effect on the atmosphere; oxygen has always been present at today's levels.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why CHLOROPLASTS are thought to have evolved from a free-living bacterium.
questions.expected: Chloroplasts have their own DNA, ribosomes and two membranes like an engulfed cell, supporting the endosymbiotic theory that they were once free-living photosynthetic bacteria.
questions.memo: Same idea applies to mitochondria. Strong DNA + structural + biochemical evidence supports endosymbiotic theory.
options: Chloroplasts are made fresh by the nucleus each generation, with no DNA or history of their own.
Chloroplasts evolved from mitochondria inside the same cell, not from any outside organism.
Chloroplasts have their own DNA, ribosomes and two membranes like an engulfed cell, supporting the endosymbiotic theory that they were once free-living photosynthetic bacteria.
Chloroplasts are just folded pieces of the cell membrane and were never separate living things.

LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A2.title: Photosynthesis — limiting factors and applications
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A2.description: Light, CO2, temperature, water as limiting factors; rate graphs; greenhouse use; food security.
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.PHOT.A2.recovery_strategy: Limiting factor = the one in short supply that holds back the rate. Plot rate vs each factor — the flat plateau tells you which factor is limiting.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT typically a limiting factor for photosynthesis?
questions.expected: Oxygen concentration
questions.memo: Light, CO2, temperature, water, chlorophyll — all can limit photosynthesis. Oxygen is a product, not normally limiting.

questions.question: A 'limiting factor' is one that:
options: Is in short supply and slows down the rate of the process
questions.expected: Is in short supply and slows down the rate of the process
questions.memo: Whichever resource is scarcest sets the rate. Add more of it → rate rises until another factor becomes limiting.

questions.question: The graph shows photosynthesis rate vs light intensity at constant CO2. Rate rises with light, then PLATEAUS. The plateau means:

data.description: Photosynthesis rate vs light intensity: rises linearly then levels off

options: Light is no longer limiting — another factor (CO2 or temp) has become limiting
questions.expected: Light is no longer limiting — another factor (CO2 or temp) has become limiting
questions.memo: Plateau = you can't get more out by adding more of THIS factor. Whatever's left in short supply now controls the rate.

questions.question: At very HIGH temperature, photosynthesis rate FALLS because:
options: Enzymes that catalyse the Calvin cycle start to denature
questions.expected: Enzymes that catalyse the Calvin cycle start to denature
questions.memo: Rubisco and other enzymes have optimum temperatures (~25-35°C in most plants). Past this, denaturation slows or stops the cycle.

questions.question: Increasing CO2 in a greenhouse usually:
options: Increases photosynthesis rate up to a maximum
questions.expected: Increases photosynthesis rate up to a maximum
questions.memo: Commercial greenhouses often boost CO2 to ~1000 ppm (vs ~420 ppm outside). Faster growth + higher yields.

questions.question: Why do GREENHOUSES often have heating in winter?
options: To keep temperature in the optimal range for enzyme activity
questions.expected: To keep temperature in the optimal range for enzyme activity
questions.memo: Cold = slow enzymes = slow photosynthesis. Heating + controlled CO2 + supplementary lighting = year-round growing.

questions.question: True or false: Drought reduces photosynthesis even if light and CO2 are plenty.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Drought → stomata close to save water → CO2 can't enter → photosynthesis falls. Water is both a reactant AND a stomata regulator.

questions.question: A pupil measures photosynthesis by counting bubbles of O2 from pondweed. Bubbles per minute rise as light is brought closer, then plateau. The light reaches its plateau at 20 cm. What does this suggest?

data.description: Bubbles per minute: at 50 cm 5/min, at 30 cm 12/min, at 20 cm 20/min, at 10 cm 20/min, at 5 cm 20/min

options: Light is no longer limiting beyond 20 cm — CO2 or temperature now limits
questions.expected: Light is no longer limiting beyond 20 cm — CO2 or temperature now limits
questions.memo: Classic SA Grade 11 practical. Bubbles plateau = limiting factor shift. Add NaHCO3 to boost CO2 → see if rate rises.

questions.question: Why does adding sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3) to pondweed water often increase photosynthesis?
options: It releases CO2 into the water, removing CO2 as the limiting factor
questions.expected: It releases CO2 into the water, removing CO2 as the limiting factor
questions.memo: NaHCO3 = an easy way to boost dissolved CO2 in a practical. If rate rises when added, CO2 was limiting before.

questions.question: What is the OPTIMAL temperature for photosynthesis in most C3 plants?
questions.expected: About 25-30°C
questions.memo: Most temperate plants optimum is ~25-30°C. Above ~40°C, denaturation begins. Tropical plants can have higher optima.

questions.question: South African summer rainfall regions (e.g. Free State, Limpopo) grow maize because:
options: Light, warmth and rain coincide during the growing season
questions.expected: Light, warmth and rain coincide during the growing season
questions.memo: Crop choice = matching crop needs to climate. Maize loves the SA highveld's warm wet summers.

questions.question: True or false: Plants grown indoors under FLUORESCENT lighting can photosynthesise.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Plants respond to wavelength + intensity, not the source. Fluorescent + LED grow lights work — just need the right spectrum.

questions.question: Why does VERY LOW CO2 stop photosynthesis even with bright light?
options: CO2 is a reactant — no CO2 means no Calvin cycle, no glucose made
questions.expected: CO2 is a reactant — no CO2 means no Calvin cycle, no glucose made
questions.memo: Light reactions make ATP/NADPH all day, but no CO2 = no use for them. Calvin cycle halts.

questions.question: C4 plants (like maize, sugar cane) are ADAPTED to:
options: Hot, sunny climates — more efficient CO2 use
questions.expected: Hot, sunny climates — more efficient CO2 use
questions.memo: C4 plants have a CO2-concentrating mechanism → less wasted energy in hot conditions. Maize + sugar cane = major SA crops.

questions.question: Predict: If a forest is cut down for farmland, the local atmospheric CO2 will:
options: Rise — less photosynthesis to remove it, plus combustion if burned
questions.expected: Rise — less photosynthesis to remove it, plus combustion if burned
questions.memo: Deforestation contributes ~10-15% of global CO2 emissions. Trees removed AND often burned = double impact.

questions.question: Why is photosynthesis crucial for SA FOOD SECURITY?
options: All SA crops depend on photosynthesis — climate change affecting light, temperature, water threatens yields
questions.expected: All SA crops depend on photosynthesis — climate change affecting light, temperature, water threatens yields
questions.memo: Drought + heatwaves reduce yields. Why climate adaptation in agriculture matters in SA.

questions.question: An algal bloom in a dam suddenly DIES OFF. Why might O2 in the water then drop sharply?
options: Decomposers use O2 to break down the algae
questions.expected: Decomposers use O2 to break down the algae
questions.memo: Live algae make O2 by photosynthesis. Dead algae are decomposed by bacteria that consume O2 → fish kills.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a FARMER might add CO2 to a greenhouse.
questions.expected: Adding CO2 raises the rate of photosynthesis, giving faster growth and higher yields, which is profitable for crops like tomatoes and cucumbers.
questions.memo: Commercial CO2 enrichment in greenhouses can double or triple yields if other factors aren't limiting.
options: Extra CO2 slows photosynthesis, so farmers add it to keep plants small and easy to harvest.
Adding CO2 raises the rate of photosynthesis, giving faster growth and higher yields, which is profitable for crops like tomatoes and cucumbers.
CO2 is added only to keep insects away from the greenhouse, not to affect the plants.
Plants use CO2 for respiration at night, so extra CO2 helps them rest rather than grow.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the GRAPH of photosynthesis vs temperature is a 'bell curve' — rising then falling.
questions.expected: The rate rises with temperature as enzyme activity speeds up, then falls sharply at high temperatures because the enzymes denature.
questions.memo: Same enzyme response pattern as anywhere in biology. Optimum = peak = best performance.
options: The rate keeps rising forever as temperature increases because enzymes never stop speeding up.
The rate falls at high temperature because the plant runs out of CO2, not because of the enzymes.
The curve falls first then rises because cold temperatures destroy enzymes and heat repairs them.
The rate rises with temperature as enzyme activity speeds up, then falls sharply at high temperatures because the enzymes denature.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why understanding LIMITING FACTORS helps SA farmers and gardeners.
questions.expected: Knowing the limiting factor lets farmers add exactly what is needed, like water in drought or fertiliser in poor soil, avoiding wasted effort on factors that aren't the bottleneck.
questions.memo: Smart farming = identify the bottleneck. Common SA limit = water. Many smart-farming initiatives focus on irrigation efficiency.
options: Knowing the limiting factor lets farmers add exactly what is needed, like water in drought or fertiliser in poor soil, avoiding wasted effort on factors that aren't the bottleneck.
Farmers should add more of every factor at once, since limiting factors cannot be identified anyway.
Understanding limiting factors only helps in laboratories, not for real SA farms and gardens.
The limiting factor is always sunlight in SA, so farmers simply need to plant in shade.

LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A1.title: Human digestive system — structure and processes
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A1.description: Digestive tract; mechanical + chemical digestion; enzymes; absorption in villi; role of liver/pancreas.
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A1.recovery_strategy: Amylase (saliva, pancreas) → starch. Pepsin (stomach) → protein. Lipase (pancreas) → fat. Absorption mainly in small intestine via villi (huge surface area).

questions.question: Digestion in the MOUTH is mainly:
questions.expected: Mechanical (chewing) + chemical (amylase on starch)
questions.memo: Teeth break food up (more surface area for enzymes). Saliva contains amylase, which begins starch digestion.

questions.question: Salivary amylase digests:
questions.expected: Starch into maltose
questions.memo: Amylase = starch enzyme. Same enzyme made later by pancreas. Mnemonic: amylum (Latin for starch).

questions.question: Food moves from mouth to stomach through the:
questions.expected: Oesophagus (gullet)
questions.memo: Oesophagus uses muscular waves (peristalsis) to push food. Trachea = windpipe (separate tube to lungs).

questions.question: Pepsin in the stomach digests:
questions.expected: Protein into smaller peptides
questions.memo: Pepsin works in acid (pH ~2 from HCl). Other proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) finish the job in the small intestine.

questions.question: The stomach has HYDROCHLORIC ACID (HCl) mainly to:
options: Provide acidic conditions for pepsin AND kill bacteria
questions.expected: Provide acidic conditions for pepsin AND kill bacteria
questions.memo: Pepsin's optimum is pH ~2. The acid also kills most bacteria in food. Stomach lining = thick mucus to protect itself.

questions.question: Most ABSORPTION of nutrients happens in the:
questions.expected: Small intestine (especially through villi)
questions.memo: Small intestine = 5-7 m long + folds + villi + microvilli → HUGE surface area for absorption.

questions.question: Villi (finger-like projections in the small intestine) function to:
questions.expected: Increase surface area for absorption
questions.memo: Each villus has microvilli on top → multiplies surface area. Each villus has a capillary network + lacteal to receive nutrients.

questions.question:
On the labelled human digestive system, which organ is the small intestine?
[Diagram: digestive system with labels A=stomach, B=small intestine, C=large intestine, D=liver]
questions.expected: B (long coiled tube after stomach)
questions.memo: Order: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. Liver/pancreas/gall bladder = accessory.

questions.question: The PANCREAS produces:
options: Pancreatic juice with amylase, lipase, trypsin + sodium bicarbonate
questions.expected: Pancreatic juice with amylase, lipase, trypsin + sodium bicarbonate
questions.memo: Pancreas = digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, trypsin) + bicarbonate (neutralises stomach acid). Also makes hormones (insulin, glucagon).

questions.question: The LIVER produces BILE, which:
options: Emulsifies fats (breaks them into tiny droplets) for digestion
questions.expected: Emulsifies fats (breaks them into tiny droplets) for digestion
questions.memo: Bile from liver, stored in gallbladder, released into small intestine. Doesn't digest fats itself — makes them easier for lipase to attack.

questions.question:
Match the enzyme to its substrate:
1. Amylase  2. Pepsin  3. Lipase  4. Trypsin

A. Protein (stomach)
B. Protein (small intestine)
C. Starch
D. Fat
questions.memo: Amylase = starch. Pepsin (stomach) = protein. Lipase = fat. Trypsin (pancreas/small intestine) = protein.

questions.question: The LARGE intestine mainly:
options: Absorbs water from undigested food, forming faeces
questions.expected: Absorbs water from undigested food, forming faeces
questions.memo: Big role: water absorption. Without it, diarrhoea + dehydration follow. Cholera attacks this region.

questions.question: The APPENDIX:
options: Is a small pouch with minor immune function (mostly vestigial in humans)
questions.expected: Is a small pouch with minor immune function (mostly vestigial in humans)
questions.memo: In some herbivores (rabbits), the equivalent organ is huge and digests cellulose. In humans, it's a remnant. Inflamed = appendicitis = emergency.

questions.question:
Order the digestion of a piece of starchy bread:
(a) Amylase in mouth begins starch breakdown
(b) Glucose absorbed in small intestine
(c) Stomach acid stops salivary amylase, mainly mechanical action
(d) Pancreatic amylase finishes starch → maltose, then maltase → glucose
questions.expected: a → c → d → b
questions.memo: Mouth (salivary amylase) → stomach (acid stops it) → small intestine (pancreatic amylase + maltase) → absorption in villi.

questions.question: True or false: Bile contains digestive enzymes.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Bile contains bile salts that emulsify fat — no enzymes itself. Lipase from the pancreas does the actual fat digestion.

questions.question: Peristalsis is:
options: Wave-like muscle contractions that move food along the gut
questions.expected: Wave-like muscle contractions that move food along the gut
questions.memo: Smooth muscle in gut wall contracts in waves. Pushes food forward — you can swallow upside down because of peristalsis.

questions.question: Where do amino acids from digested protein go after absorption?
options: Into capillaries in the villi, then to the liver via the hepatic portal vein
questions.expected: Into capillaries in the villi, then to the liver via the hepatic portal vein
questions.memo: Hepatic portal vein takes nutrients straight to the liver, which processes them before they reach the rest of the body.

questions.question: Why are FATS absorbed differently from sugars and amino acids?
options: Fat droplets are too large for capillaries, so they enter lacteals (lymph vessels) in the villi
Fats only enter through the skin
questions.expected: Fat droplets are too large for capillaries, so they enter lacteals (lymph vessels) in the villi
questions.memo: Each villus has a central lacteal (lymph vessel) specifically for fats. They eventually reach the bloodstream via the lymphatic system.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the SMALL INTESTINE is so well adapted for absorption.
questions.expected: It is long with folds, villi and microvilli giving a huge surface area, and each thin-walled villus has a rich blood supply and lacteal for efficient absorption.
questions.memo: Structure follows function. Surface area + thin walls + good blood/lymph supply = maximum absorption.
options: It is short and smooth-walled, which slows food down so nutrients have time to soak in.
It absorbs nutrients through a single thick wall with no blood supply, relying on pressure alone.
It is long with folds, villi and microvilli giving a huge surface area, and each thin-walled villus has a rich blood supply and lacteal for efficient absorption.
Its main adaptation is strong muscles that grind food, while absorption happens in the stomach.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why HARD-TO-DIGEST FIBRE in our diet is still important.
questions.expected: Fibre adds bulk to faeces, helping move material through the large intestine, which prevents constipation and supports gut health.
questions.memo: Fibre is mostly cellulose. Humans can't digest it for energy, but the gut benefits from its bulk.
options: Fibre is fully digested for lots of energy, which is why it is an important part of the diet.
Fibre adds bulk to faeces, helping move material through the large intestine, which prevents constipation and supports gut health.
Fibre is absorbed into the blood where it builds muscle and repairs tissue.
Fibre has no real role and is only included to make meals feel filling.

LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A2.title: Balanced diet, malnutrition and diet-related diseases
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A2.description: Food groups; kwashiorkor; marasmus; obesity; type 2 diabetes; SA public-health context.
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.NUTR.A2.recovery_strategy: Kwashiorkor = protein deficiency. Marasmus = both energy + protein lacking. Obesity + Type 2 diabetes = excess + poor diet.

questions.question: A balanced diet includes:
options: Carbs, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre AND water in correct proportions
questions.expected: Carbs, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre AND water in correct proportions
questions.memo: All food groups in right amounts. No single food has everything. Variety is key.

questions.question: Carbohydrates are MAINLY used for:
questions.expected: Energy
questions.memo: Carbs = quick fuel. Glucose powers cells via respiration. Excess stored as glycogen (short-term) or fat (long-term).

questions.question: Proteins are mainly needed for:
questions.expected: Growth and repair of tissue
questions.memo: Body builds muscle, skin, enzymes, antibodies from amino acids. Children + pregnant women need extra protein.

questions.question: Kwashiorkor is caused by:
options: Severe protein deficiency, often with enough total calories
questions.expected: Severe protein deficiency, often with enough total calories
questions.memo: Common in children given only starchy food. Symptoms: swollen belly (oedema), hair colour changes, growth failure.

questions.question: Marasmus is caused by:
options: Severe shortage of total energy AND protein — overall starvation
questions.expected: Severe shortage of total energy AND protein — overall starvation
questions.memo: Marasmus = severe wasting. The child has not had enough of anything. Different from kwashiorkor (which has enough calories but no protein).

questions.question: Obesity is BEST defined as:
options: Excess body fat that increases risk of disease
questions.expected: Excess body fat that increases risk of disease
questions.memo: BMI > 30 is a rough cutoff. Causes: excess calories, low physical activity, sometimes genetic + hormonal factors.

questions.question: Type 2 diabetes is linked to:
options: Obesity + low physical activity + diet high in refined sugars
questions.expected: Obesity + low physical activity + diet high in refined sugars
questions.memo: Cells become less responsive to insulin → blood sugar stays high. SA has rising type 2 diabetes rates, especially in urban areas.

questions.question:
The table shows obesity rates by gender in SA. Which trend does it show?

| Year | Women | Men |
|------|-------|-----|
| 2003 | 27%   | 9%  |
| 2016 | 41%   | 11% |
options: Obesity has risen, especially among women
questions.expected: Obesity has risen, especially among women
questions.memo: SA obesity rates have climbed steeply. Women's rates are notably higher than men's — complex social, biological factors.

questions.question: True or false: Children with kwashiorkor often have a SWOLLEN belly.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Lack of protein → low blood plasma proteins → fluid leaks into tissues (oedema). The belly swells, masking real wasting.

questions.question: Iron-deficiency anaemia symptoms include:
questions.expected: Fatigue, pale skin, breathlessness
questions.memo: Low iron → low haemoglobin → less O2 carried. Common in girls/women in SA. Foods: spinach, liver, beans.

questions.question: A school-aged child who is mostly fed PAP (maize porridge) but very little meat or beans risks:
questions.expected: Kwashiorkor — protein deficiency
questions.memo: Maize is mostly starch — energy is adequate but protein quality is low. Combine pap with beans, meat, eggs or amasi for balance.

questions.question: Reading a food label, which information helps you choose between brands?
options: Total energy, sugar, saturated fat, sodium, per serving
questions.expected: Total energy, sugar, saturated fat, sodium, per serving
questions.memo: Look at SAME serving size when comparing. Sugar in grams. Sodium in mg. Watch for hidden sugars + salt in 'healthy' looking foods.

questions.question: Why is SA's 'sugar tax' on sugary drinks a public-health measure?
options: Higher prices reduce consumption → lower obesity + diabetes risk
questions.expected: Higher prices reduce consumption → lower obesity + diabetes risk
questions.memo: Health Promotion Levy (since 2018) on sugar-sweetened beverages. Evidence shows it reduces consumption.

questions.question: Calcium-deficient diet in adolescence puts a person at risk of:
options: Lower peak bone mass + osteoporosis later in life
questions.expected: Lower peak bone mass + osteoporosis later in life
questions.memo: Bones build up to age ~25-30, then slowly decline. Higher peak = more reserve before later loss.

questions.question: True or false: Vitamin A deficiency can cause BLINDNESS.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Vit A needed for retinal pigment + eye health. Severe deficiency = night blindness → permanent blindness. SA programmes supplement Vit A.

questions.question: Folate (folic acid) before/during pregnancy prevents:
options: Neural tube defects in the developing baby
questions.expected: Neural tube defects in the developing baby
questions.memo: Folate is needed for cell division in early embryo development. SA fortifies flour with folic acid since 2003.

questions.question: An athlete preparing for a marathon needs MORE:
questions.expected: Carbohydrates and water (and electrolytes)
questions.memo: Carbs = main fuel for endurance. Adequate water + sodium/potassium to replace sweat losses. Glycogen loading helps.

questions.question: Why do many SA people develop the 'DOUBLE BURDEN' of obesity AND undernutrition in the same household?
options: Energy-dense cheap foods cause obesity but lack quality protein and micronutrients
questions.expected: Energy-dense cheap foods cause obesity but lack quality protein and micronutrients
questions.memo: Common SA pattern: bread, oil, sugar fill bellies (and add fat) but lack iron, Vit A, quality protein. Income inequality + food environment.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how a BALANCED DIET reduces risk of disease.
questions.expected: A balanced diet supplies energy, building materials, vitamins and minerals in the right amounts, supporting growth, immunity and metabolism while avoiding obesity and deficiency.
questions.memo: Balance = both 'enough' and 'not too much'. Each food group has a role.
options: A balanced diet just means eating large amounts of every food, since more nutrients always mean better health.
Disease risk depends only on genes, so what you eat makes no difference to your health.
A balanced diet supplies energy, building materials, vitamins and minerals in the right amounts, supporting growth, immunity and metabolism while avoiding obesity and deficiency.
Cutting out whole food groups is the best way to prevent disease, regardless of nutrient balance.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why TYPE 2 DIABETES is a growing problem in urban SA.
questions.expected: Urban diets are richer in processed foods, refined sugars and saturated fats while activity is low, and both raise obesity and the risk of type 2 diabetes.
questions.memo: Globalisation of food environment. Health Promotion Levy + sugar-tax + clinic screening try to slow the trend.
options: Urban diets are richer in processed foods, refined sugars and saturated fats while activity is low, and both raise obesity and the risk of type 2 diabetes.
Type 2 diabetes is purely inherited, so urban lifestyle and diet have nothing to do with the rise.
City people eat far healthier than before, so the rise in diabetes must be caused by infection.
Diabetes only affects rural communities, so the urban increase is just better reporting of old cases.

LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A1.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A1.description: Aerobic: glycolysis → Krebs → ETC. Anaerobic: lactic acid in muscle, ethanol in yeast. ATP yields.
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A1.recovery_strategy: Aerobic = needs O2, ~36 ATP, CO2 + H2O. Anaerobic = no O2, only 2 ATP. Muscles → lactic acid. Yeast → ethanol + CO2.

questions.question: The overall equation for AEROBIC respiration is:
options: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP
questions.expected: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP
questions.memo: C6H12O6 + 6 O2 → 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + ~36 ATP. Reverse of photosynthesis word equation.

questions.question: Aerobic respiration produces about:
questions.expected: 36-38 ATP per glucose
questions.memo: Many ATPs vs anaerobic's 2. Why aerobic respiration is so favoured when oxygen is available.

questions.question: Anaerobic respiration in HUMAN muscle produces:
questions.expected: Lactic acid + 2 ATP
questions.memo: When muscles run short on O2 (sprint), they switch to lactic-acid fermentation. Build-up causes burn.

questions.question: Anaerobic respiration in YEAST produces:
questions.expected: Ethanol + CO2 + 2 ATP
questions.memo: Why yeast is used for beer/wine (ethanol) and bread (CO2 makes dough rise). Same yeast, different products.

questions.question: Most ATP from aerobic respiration is made in the:
questions.expected: Mitochondria (Krebs cycle + electron transport chain)
questions.memo: Glycolysis starts in cytoplasm (2 ATP). Krebs + ETC happen in mitochondria (lots more ATP).

questions.question:
Order the steps of aerobic respiration:
(a) Krebs cycle
(b) Glycolysis
(c) Electron transport chain
questions.expected: b → a → c
questions.memo: Glycolysis (cytoplasm) → Krebs (mitochondrial matrix) → ETC (inner mitochondrial membrane). Most ATP from ETC.

questions.question: True or false: Anaerobic respiration is more EFFICIENT than aerobic.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Aerobic gives ~36 ATP; anaerobic only 2 ATP per glucose. Anaerobic is FASTER but far less efficient.

questions.question: After intense exercise, what happens to the LACTIC ACID built up in muscles?
options: It is carried to the liver and oxidised back to pyruvate using oxygen (oxygen debt)
questions.expected: It is carried to the liver and oxidised back to pyruvate using oxygen (oxygen debt)
questions.memo: Oxygen debt = extra O2 needed after exercise to deal with lactic acid. Why you keep panting after stopping.

questions.question: Why do plants need to RESPIRE even though they photosynthesise?
options: Plant cells need ATP for processes like active transport and growth
questions.expected: Plant cells need ATP for processes like active transport and growth
questions.memo: Photosynthesis makes glucose (food). Respiration releases ATP from glucose. Plants do both — but respire 24/7.

questions.question: A pupil seals yeast + glucose + water in a flask, then measures CO2 release over 30 minutes. Why does CO2 rise?
options: Yeast respires the glucose, producing CO2
Glucose makes CO2 on its own
questions.expected: Yeast respires the glucose, producing CO2
questions.memo: Anaerobic respiration: glucose → ethanol + CO2 + 2 ATP. Bubble rate ~ respiration rate. Classic SA Grade 11 practical.

questions.question: Why do SPRINTERS rely heavily on anaerobic respiration?
options: Lungs and heart can't deliver enough O2 fast enough for very high power
questions.expected: Lungs and heart can't deliver enough O2 fast enough for very high power
questions.memo: Anaerobic is FAST but inefficient + builds lactic acid. Sprinters fatigue in seconds, not minutes.

questions.question: Marathon runners rely mainly on:
questions.expected: Aerobic respiration
questions.memo: Endurance = mostly aerobic. Trained marathoners can sustain a high % of their max aerobic capacity for hours.

questions.question: True or false: Mitochondria are 'the powerhouses of the cell'.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Famous metaphor. ATP production = a cell's energy. Why active cells (muscle, liver) have many mitochondria.

questions.question: Where does GLYCOLYSIS take place?
questions.expected: Cytoplasm
questions.memo: Glycolysis = splits glucose to two pyruvate. Doesn't need oxygen. Happens in cytoplasm of every cell.

questions.question: The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain happen in:
questions.expected: Mitochondria
questions.memo: Krebs cycle in matrix. ETC on inner membrane (cristae). Most ATP comes from ETC.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ATP is sometimes called the 'energy currency' of cells.
questions.expected: ATP is the energy form cells use to do work, made from food energy and spent on processes like muscle contraction and active transport.
questions.memo: Universal energy molecule. Every cell makes and uses ATP. ~30 kg of ATP turn over in your body every day.
options: ATP is the food we eat, which the body burns directly without converting it into anything else.
ATP is stored permanently like savings and is only spent once in a lifetime.
ATP is a waste product of respiration that cells must get rid of, like spending bad money.
ATP is the energy form cells use to do work, made from food energy and spent on processes like muscle contraction and active transport.

questions.question: Cells in the SA Highveld (altitude ~1700 m) adapt to lower air oxygen by:
options: Producing more red blood cells over time, increasing oxygen carrying capacity
questions.expected: Producing more red blood cells over time, increasing oxygen carrying capacity
questions.memo: Altitude adaptation. Living in Joburg increases haemoglobin. Why endurance athletes train at altitude.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why YEAST makes both BREAD rise AND beer.
questions.expected: Yeast does anaerobic respiration producing carbon dioxide and ethanol; the CO2 makes bread dough rise and the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.
questions.memo: One process, two products, two uses. Yeast is the world's most important industrial microbe.
options: Yeast does anaerobic respiration producing carbon dioxide and ethanol; the CO2 makes bread dough rise and the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.
Yeast makes bread rise with oxygen and makes beer with sugar, using two completely separate organisms.
Yeast produces only carbon dioxide, so beer's alcohol must come from added chemicals.
Yeast makes ethanol in bread and CO2 in beer, which is why bread tastes alcoholic.

questions.question: True or false: Some cells in the body NEVER stop respiring.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Cells respire 24/7. Brain and heart cells especially need a constant ATP supply. Why O2 cut-off causes brain damage in minutes.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MUSCLE FATIGUE happens during high-intensity exercise.
questions.expected: When oxygen can't be delivered fast enough, muscles respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid, whose build-up lowers pH and contributes to fatigue.
questions.memo: Lactic acid + ion imbalance + glycogen depletion. Recovery requires rest + O2.
options: Fatigue happens because muscles get too much oxygen, which poisons them during hard exercise.
When oxygen can't be delivered fast enough, muscles respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid, whose build-up lowers pH and contributes to fatigue.
Muscles tire because they run out of muscle cells, which must be regrown after exercise.
Fatigue is caused by water building up in the muscle, not by any change in acidity.

LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A2.title: Respiration vs photosynthesis; exercise effects
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A2.description: Comparison of the two processes; relationships; exercise effects on breathing/heart rate; oxygen debt.
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.RESP.A2.recovery_strategy: Plants do BOTH — photosynthesise (day) AND respire (24/7). Oxygen debt = the extra O2 needed after exercise to oxidise built-up lactic acid.

questions.question: Compare in 1 word: PHOTOSYNTHESIS releases what gas, while RESPIRATION uses it?
questions.expected: Oxygen
questions.memo: Photosynthesis releases O2 (waste from water). Respiration consumes O2 (in aerobic ETC). Perfect cycle.

questions.question:
Match each feature:
1. Reactants  2. Products  3. Energy flow

A. Photosynthesis: CO2 + H2O → glucose + O2 (uses light)
B. Respiration: glucose + O2 → CO2 + H2O (releases ATP)
C. Reactants of one = products of the other
questions.memo: Photosynthesis + respiration = mirror images. Each provides the inputs for the other.

questions.question: True or false: Plants RESPIRE only at night.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Plants respire 24/7. During the day photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration (net O2 out). At night only respiration happens (net CO2 out).

questions.question: On a sunny day, a leaf's NET gas exchange is:
options: More O2 OUT than in (photosynthesis exceeds respiration)
questions.expected: More O2 OUT than in (photosynthesis exceeds respiration)
questions.memo: Day: photo > resp → net O2 out, net CO2 in. Night: only respiration → net CO2 out, net O2 in.

questions.question: During EXERCISE, breathing rate rises because:
options: Working muscles need more O2 and produce more CO2
questions.expected: Working muscles need more O2 and produce more CO2
questions.memo: Brain senses rising CO2 (or low blood pH) → triggers faster + deeper breathing.

questions.question: Heart rate during exercise rises because:
options: More blood flow is needed to carry O2 to muscles + remove CO2
questions.expected: More blood flow is needed to carry O2 to muscles + remove CO2
questions.memo: Cardiac output (HR × stroke volume) can rise 5-6× in hard exercise. Training increases stroke volume → lower resting HR.

questions.question: The graph shows pulse rate before, during and after a 5-minute run. The DELAYED RETURN to resting after exercise is due to:

data.description: Pulse rate: resting 75 bpm; during exercise 160 bpm; 1 min after 130 bpm; 5 min after 90 bpm; 10 min after 75 bpm

options: Body still needs extra O2 to recover (oxygen debt)
questions.expected: Body still needs extra O2 to recover (oxygen debt)
questions.memo: Recovery rate = good fitness measure. Fitter athletes recover faster.

questions.question: Why does the body SWEAT during exercise?
options: To remove excess heat — evaporation cools the body
questions.expected: To remove excess heat — evaporation cools the body
questions.memo: Exercise = heat-producing. Sweat evaporates → carries heat away. Failure (heatstroke) is dangerous.

questions.question: True or false: Trained athletes have HIGHER resting heart rates than untrained.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Opposite. Trained heart pumps more per beat (higher stroke volume) → lower resting HR. Some athletes <50 bpm at rest.

questions.question: Why does the body PANT after intense exercise has stopped?
options: To bring in extra O2 to oxidise the lactic acid built up
questions.expected: To bring in extra O2 to oxidise the lactic acid built up
questions.memo: Oxygen debt repaid. Heavy breathing continues until lactic acid is cleared. Recovery time = fitness indicator.

questions.question: PHOTOSYNTHESIS provides BOTH:
options: The food (glucose) AND oxygen needed for respiration
questions.expected: The food (glucose) AND oxygen needed for respiration
questions.memo: Beautiful interlock: photosynthesis makes both ingredients for respiration. Respiration releases the inputs for photosynthesis. Cycle perfect.

questions.question: Respiration provides photosynthesis with:
questions.expected: CO2 (waste from respiration)
questions.memo: Respiratory waste CO2 + water are exactly what photosynthesis needs.

questions.question: An athlete COLLAPSES after a marathon. Possible causes include:
options: Dehydration, low blood sugar, heat exhaustion, salt imbalance
questions.expected: Dehydration, low blood sugar, heat exhaustion, salt imbalance
questions.memo: Endurance events stress every system. Recovery: rehydration + glucose + salt + cooling. Medical staff trained for this.

questions.question: Why does training INCREASE the body's ability to use OXYGEN?
options: More mitochondria in muscle, more capillaries, more haemoglobin
questions.expected: More mitochondria in muscle, more capillaries, more haemoglobin
questions.memo: Training adapts cells. VO2max (max O2 use) is a key fitness measure for endurance athletes.

questions.question: True or false: A leaf in the DARK still respires.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Plant cells respire all the time. In the dark, only respiration → net CO2 release.

questions.question: What is the COMPENSATION POINT in plants?
options: The light level where photosynthesis EQUALS respiration → no net gas exchange
questions.expected: The light level where photosynthesis EQUALS respiration → no net gas exchange
questions.memo: Below compensation point, respiration > photosynthesis → plant LOSES carbon. Why shaded plants struggle.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why PHOTOSYNTHESIS and RESPIRATION together support nearly all life on Earth.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis captures sunlight and stores it as chemical energy in food, and respiration releases that energy as ATP to power all the activities of living cells.
questions.memo: Sun → food → ATP → life. Without either process, life as we know it stops.
options: Both processes only produce waste gases and contribute nothing to the energy that powers life.
Respiration captures sunlight and photosynthesis releases the energy, which is the reverse of how it really works.
Photosynthesis captures sunlight and stores it as chemical energy in food, and respiration releases that energy as ATP to power all the activities of living cells.
Photosynthesis and respiration cancel each other out completely, so neither actually supports life.

questions.question: Why does FITNESS training improve recovery rate AFTER exercise?
options: Fitter people clear lactic acid faster, have better cardiovascular function and more mitochondria
questions.expected: Fitter people clear lactic acid faster, have better cardiovascular function and more mitochondria
questions.memo: Recovery HR after 1 min of rest is a classic fitness test. Drops by 25+ bpm = good fitness.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why CO2 levels in your blood control breathing rate.
questions.expected: When CO2 rises the blood becomes more acidic, brain centres detect this and trigger faster, deeper breathing to exhale the CO2.
questions.memo: CO2-driven breathing control. Holding your breath fails when CO2 builds up — not when O2 runs low.
options: Breathing rate is controlled by falling oxygen levels alone, with CO2 playing no role at all.
When CO2 rises the blood becomes more acidic, brain centres detect this and trigger faster, deeper breathing to exhale the CO2.
Rising CO2 makes the blood more alkaline, which signals the brain to slow breathing down.
The lungs sense CO2 directly and decide breathing rate without involving the brain.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the RELATIONSHIP between photosynthesis and respiration creates the OXYGEN CYCLE.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis releases O2 into the air while respiration uses O2 and returns CO2, and this balance keeps atmospheric O2 and CO2 levels stable.
questions.memo: Disruption of this balance (e.g. deforestation + fossil fuel burning) is shifting atmospheric composition → climate change.
options: Photosynthesis releases O2 into the air while respiration uses O2 and returns CO2, and this balance keeps atmospheric O2 and CO2 levels stable.
Both photosynthesis and respiration release oxygen, so oxygen keeps building up in the atmosphere over time.
Respiration releases O2 while photosynthesis uses it up, the reverse of how the cycle actually works.
Plants make oxygen and animals make carbon dioxide, but the two processes are unrelated and do not form a cycle.

LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A1.title: Gas exchange in mammals — lungs and ventilation
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A1.description: Respiratory pathway; ventilation mechanism; alveolar adaptations.
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A1.recovery_strategy: Inhalation: diaphragm contracts (flattens), intercostals contract, chest volume up → pressure drops → air rushes in. Alveoli: thin + moist + huge area + capillaries.

questions.question: Air enters the human respiratory system through the:
questions.expected: Nose or mouth
questions.memo: Nose preferred — filters dust, warms and moistens air. Mouth = backup.

questions.question: The order of structures from outside to alveoli is:
questions.expected: Nose → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
questions.memo: Nose/mouth → pharynx → larynx → trachea → left+right bronchi → bronchioles → alveolar sacs → alveoli.

questions.question: Gas exchange happens at the:
questions.expected: Alveoli
questions.memo: Alveoli = tiny air sacs at the end of bronchioles. Combined surface area of both lungs = ~70 m² (size of a tennis court).

questions.question: During INHALATION:
options: Diaphragm CONTRACTS (flattens), intercostals contract, chest volume increases
questions.expected: Diaphragm CONTRACTS (flattens), intercostals contract, chest volume increases
questions.memo: More volume → lower pressure inside chest → air rushes in down the pressure gradient.

questions.question: During EXHALATION (quiet breathing):
options: Diaphragm relaxes (domes up), intercostals relax, chest volume decreases
questions.expected: Diaphragm relaxes (domes up), intercostals relax, chest volume decreases
questions.memo: Smaller chest volume → higher pressure → air pushed out. Mostly passive — elastic recoil of lungs.

questions.question:
On the lung diagram, which structure is the diaphragm?
[Diagram: lungs + chest cavity with structures labelled]
options: The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs
questions.expected: The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs
questions.memo: Diaphragm = main breathing muscle. Hiccups = sudden involuntary diaphragm contractions.

questions.question: Alveoli are adapted for gas exchange because they have:
options: Thin walls (1 cell), huge surface area, moist lining, rich blood supply
questions.expected: Thin walls (1 cell), huge surface area, moist lining, rich blood supply
questions.memo: Four classic adaptations for efficient diffusion. Damage to these (emphysema, fibrosis) cripples gas exchange.

questions.question: Oxygen moves from alveoli into the blood by:
questions.expected: Diffusion down a concentration gradient
questions.memo: Air in alveolus is O2-rich; blood arriving is O2-poor. Net O2 moves into blood. No energy needed = passive.

questions.question: CO2 in blood is mostly carried as:
options: Bound to red blood cells only
questions.expected: Bicarbonate ions in plasma
questions.memo: CO2 + water → carbonic acid → bicarbonate (HCO3⁻). Most CO2 travels as HCO3⁻ in plasma. Some bound to haemoglobin or dissolved.

questions.question: True or false: Smoking destroys alveoli and lowers gas exchange efficiency.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Smoking → emphysema = alveoli walls break down → fewer, larger spaces with less surface area → breathlessness.

questions.question: TB (tuberculosis) affects which body system mainly?
questions.expected: Respiratory system
questions.memo: Pulmonary TB = the lung form (most common). Bacteria damage alveoli → coughing, blood, weight loss. SA has high TB rates.

questions.question: Asthma is BEST described as:
options: Narrowing and inflammation of bronchioles, making breathing difficult
questions.expected: Narrowing and inflammation of bronchioles, making breathing difficult
questions.memo: Bronchioles tighten + swell + produce mucus → wheezing, breathlessness. Inhalers open them up.

questions.question: Why does a person OUT OF BREATH after climbing stairs breathe DEEPER and FASTER?
options: Body needs more O2 in + CO2 out to meet exercise demand
questions.expected: Body needs more O2 in + CO2 out to meet exercise demand
questions.memo: Normal physiological response. Brain centres respond to rising CO2 + dropping O2 → ramp up ventilation.

questions.question: An inhaler used for asthma typically contains:
options: Bronchodilator drugs that relax bronchiole muscles
questions.expected: Bronchodilator drugs that relax bronchiole muscles
questions.memo: Quick-relief inhalers (salbutamol) open bronchioles in minutes. Steroid inhalers reduce inflammation longer-term.

questions.question: Which feature of the TRACHEA stops it from collapsing?
questions.expected: C-shaped rings of cartilage
questions.memo: C-shape keeps the windpipe open. The gap behind allows the oesophagus to expand when swallowing.

questions.question: CILIA in the airways function to:
options: Sweep mucus + trapped particles up to the throat
questions.expected: Sweep mucus + trapped particles up to the throat
questions.memo: Ciliated cells + mucus = the lung's escalator. Smoking paralyses cilia → mucus builds up → 'smoker's cough'.

questions.question: True or false: Alveoli have surfactant — a substance that prevents collapse.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Surfactant lowers surface tension inside alveoli, stopping them collapsing as you exhale. Premature babies often need surfactant therapy.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ALVEOLI are SO MUCH MORE EFFICIENT than just having one big lung cavity.
questions.expected: Millions of tiny alveoli give a huge combined surface area, and their thin walls close to capillaries make diffusion fast.
questions.memo: Surface-to-volume principle. Small structures multiplied = massive total area. Same principle as villi, root hairs, gills.
options: Alveoli warm the air before it reaches the blood, which speeds up gas exchange compared with a single cavity.
Millions of tiny alveoli give a huge combined surface area, and their thin walls close to capillaries make diffusion fast.
Alveoli actively pump oxygen into the blood, unlike a single lung cavity which relies only on diffusion.
One large cavity would actually exchange gases faster because air moves through it more freely.

questions.question: Why is air POLLUTION a big problem for human gas exchange?
options: Tiny particles + chemicals damage alveoli and bronchi
questions.expected: Tiny particles + chemicals damage alveoli and bronchi
questions.memo: PM2.5 particles reach deep into lungs. Big problem in SA mining towns and around coal stations. Lung cancer, asthma, TB worse.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the lungs are PROTECTED inside the rib cage.
questions.expected: The ribs form a bony cage that shields the soft lungs from injury, and they also move with the intercostal muscles to change chest volume for breathing.
questions.memo: Function + protection in one structure. Same evolutionary trick as the skull.
options: The rib cage is a solid, rigid shell whose only job is to protect the lungs from injury.
The ribs store oxygen and release it into the lungs while also shielding them from knocks.
The ribs form a bony cage that shields the soft lungs from injury, and they also move with the intercostal muscles to change chest volume for breathing.
The ribs protect the lungs but play no role in breathing, which is driven only by the diaphragm.

LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A2.title: Gas exchange in plants, fish and insects
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A2.description: Stomata; gills + countercurrent flow; insect tracheal system; surface area principle.
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.GAS.A2.recovery_strategy: Plants: stomata. Fish: gills (countercurrent). Insects: tracheae deliver O2 directly to cells (no blood transport).

questions.question: Plants exchange gases mainly through:
questions.expected: Stomata on leaves
questions.memo: Stomata = small pores, mostly on the underside of leaves. Open during the day for CO2 in; close at night to save water.

questions.question: Stomata are surrounded by:
options: A pair of guard cells that open/close the pore
questions.expected: A pair of guard cells that open/close the pore
questions.memo: Turgid guard cells bow apart → stoma opens. Flaccid → stoma closes. Why drought triggers stomatal closure.

questions.question: Fish exchange gases at the:
questions.expected: Gills
questions.memo: Water flows over gills; O2 diffuses from water into blood; CO2 leaves blood into water. Gills must stay moist.

questions.question: Countercurrent flow in fish gills means:
options: Water flows in opposite direction to blood, maintaining a O2 gradient along the gill length
Water flows in same direction as blood
questions.expected: Water flows in opposite direction to blood, maintaining a O2 gradient along the gill length
questions.memo: Countercurrent = far more efficient O2 extraction. Fish gills extract ~80% of available O2 vs ~25% for same-direction flow.

questions.question: Insects exchange gases through:
options: Tracheal system — tracheae deliver air directly to cells via spiracles
questions.expected: Tracheal system — tracheae deliver air directly to cells via spiracles
questions.memo: Insects have no blood transport of O2. Air enters spiracles (pores on body) → tracheae → tracheoles → cells.

questions.question: Why don't insects need LUNGS or blood transport for O2?
options: Tracheal system delivers air directly to cells, very efficient at small sizes
questions.expected: Tracheal system delivers air directly to cells, very efficient at small sizes
questions.memo: Tracheal system works well only at small body sizes. This may be why insects can't grow as large as mammals.

questions.question: Why are GILLS only used in WATER, not air?
options: Gill filaments collapse and stick together out of water → no surface area
Gills only work in salt water
questions.expected: Gill filaments collapse and stick together out of water → no surface area
questions.memo: Why fish suffocate out of water — even though air is more O2-rich. Surface area is lost when wet structure clumps.

questions.question: Stomata are usually MORE NUMEROUS on the:
questions.expected: Underside of the leaf
questions.memo: Underside is shaded + cooler + less wind exposure → reduces water loss while still allowing CO2 entry.

questions.question:
Match the organism to its main gas exchange surface:
1. Frog (adult)  2. Tilapia fish  3. Honey bee  4. Wheat plant

A. Tracheal system
B. Stomata
C. Gills
D. Lungs + moist skin
questions.memo: Frog adult = lungs + moist skin. Fish = gills. Bee = tracheal. Plant = stomata.

questions.question: True or false: All gas exchange surfaces share certain features (thin, moist, large area).
questions.expected: True
