questions.memo: Universal principles: thin walls for short diffusion distance, moisture (gases must dissolve to cross membranes), large surface area, good supply/transport on both sides.

questions.question: Adult amphibians (frogs) can exchange gases through:
questions.expected: Lungs AND moist skin
questions.memo: Frog skin is thin + moist + well-vascularised — significant gas exchange happens through skin. Why polluted water kills frogs fast.

questions.question:
Look at the diagram of a leaf cross-section. Which structure is a stoma?
[Diagram: leaf cross-section with cuticle, epidermis, mesophyll, stomata labelled]
options: The pore in the lower epidermis surrounded by guard cells
questions.expected: The pore in the lower epidermis surrounded by guard cells
questions.memo: Stoma = the actual opening. Stomata is the plural. Lower epidermis is where most are.

questions.question: Why is OPENING STOMATA always a TRADE-OFF for plants?
options: Open = CO2 in for photosynthesis but water vapour out (transpiration)
questions.expected: Open = CO2 in for photosynthesis but water vapour out (transpiration)
questions.memo: Central plant dilemma. Why drought-stressed plants close stomata + slow growth.

questions.question: Why are LUNGS more efficient than skin for gas exchange in larger animals?
options: Lungs have huge folded internal surface area + active ventilation + capillary supply
questions.expected: Lungs have huge folded internal surface area + active ventilation + capillary supply
questions.memo: Skin's surface area is limited by body shape. Lungs pack massive surface area inside the body.

questions.question: True or false: Some insects can SHUT spiracles to reduce water loss.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Important in desert insects. Some can stay closed for hours, opening briefly to breathe. Survival adaptation.

questions.question: Why do plants in DRY climates have FEWER stomata or stomata in PITS?
options: To reduce water loss via transpiration
questions.expected: To reduce water loss via transpiration
questions.memo: Karoo plants, fynbos, succulents = classic SA examples. Adaptation to dry conditions.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why FISH OUT OF WATER suffocate even though air has MORE oxygen than water.
questions.expected: Gills only work when wet; out of water the filaments stick together and lose surface area, so gas exchange stops.
questions.memo: Surprising fact for students. Same principle as why a wet sponge is much more porous than a dry, balled-up one.
options: Fish gills can only extract oxygen from water, so air simply contains the wrong kind of oxygen for them.
Out of water the gills dry out and the oxygen in air is too thin for the gills to absorb.
Fish suffocate because air pressure crushes the delicate gill filaments shut.
Gills only work when wet; out of water the filaments stick together and lose surface area, so gas exchange stops.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the INSECT TRACHEAL system limits insect size.
questions.expected: Insect tracheae rely on diffusion to carry oxygen to the cells, and beyond a certain size diffusion is too slow, which limits how large insects can grow.
questions.memo: Why insects are small. Ancient larger insects (like dragonflies the size of seagulls) lived when O2 was higher.
options: Insect tracheae rely on diffusion to carry oxygen to the cells, and beyond a certain size diffusion is too slow, which limits how large insects can grow.
Insects have tiny hearts that cannot pump blood far, so their bodies must stay small.
Tracheae actively pump oxygen so efficiently that insects could grow to any size if they had stronger muscles.
Insect lungs are too small to hold enough air, which is the only thing limiting insect size.

questions.question: True or false: Land plants need stomata MAINLY because of cuticle.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Waxy cuticle protects against water loss but also blocks gas. Stomata provide regulated openings — best of both worlds.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the SURFACE-AREA-TO-VOLUME ratio limits how big a single CELL can be for gas exchange.
questions.expected: As a cell grows its volume increases faster than its surface area, so eventually the surface cannot supply the inside fast enough, forcing larger organisms to use specialised exchange surfaces.
questions.memo: Universal biological principle. Why all organisms above microbial size need specialised exchange surfaces.
options: As a cell grows its surface area grows faster than its volume, so large cells exchange gases easily.
Cell size is limited only by the strength of the cell membrane, not by gas exchange.
As a cell grows its volume increases faster than its surface area, so eventually the surface cannot supply the inside fast enough, forcing larger organisms to use specialised exchange surfaces.
Large cells simply make more mitochondria, so surface area never limits how big a cell can be.

LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A1.title: Kidney structure and the nephron
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A1.description: Kidney location; nephron parts; ultrafiltration, reabsorption, secretion; urine formation.
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A1.recovery_strategy: Ultrafiltration in Bowman's capsule. Reabsorption in proximal tubule = useful stuff back. Secretion = extra waste added.

questions.question: Humans have how many kidneys?
questions.expected: 2 (left and right)
questions.memo: Located either side of the spine, just below the rib cage. Bean-shaped. Each contains ~1 million nephrons.

questions.question: Blood enters each kidney via the:
questions.expected: Renal artery
questions.memo: Renal artery brings O2 + waste in. Renal vein takes filtered blood out. Ureter carries urine to bladder.

questions.question: The functional unit of the kidney is called the:
questions.expected: Nephron
questions.memo: Each kidney has ~1 million nephrons. Each does the full filtering, reabsorption, and concentration job in miniature.

questions.question: Ultrafiltration happens at:
questions.expected: The Bowman's capsule (around the glomerulus)
questions.memo: Blood pushed through glomerular capillaries under pressure → small molecules (water, salts, glucose, urea) forced into Bowman's capsule.

questions.question: After filtration, USEFUL substances like glucose are reabsorbed in the:
questions.expected: Proximal convoluted tubule
questions.memo: PCT actively reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, salts, water. ALL glucose reabsorbed if blood sugar is normal.

questions.question: The LOOP of Henle's main role is to:
options: Create a salt gradient that concentrates urine and saves water
questions.expected: Create a salt gradient that concentrates urine and saves water
questions.memo: Long thin loop dipping into the medulla. Concentrates salt around itself → pulls water out of the collecting duct → concentrated urine.

questions.question: True or false: Healthy urine should contain GLUCOSE.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: All glucose is normally reabsorbed by PCT. Glucose in urine = sign of diabetes (blood sugar so high that PCT can't reabsorb it all).

questions.question: True or false: Healthy urine contains UREA.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Urea = main nitrogenous waste in mammals. Made by liver from old amino acids. Excreted in urine.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the nephron. Which structure is the GLOMERULUS?
[Diagram: nephron with labelled parts]
options: The tuft of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule
questions.expected: The tuft of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule
questions.memo: Glomerulus = ball of capillaries where filtration starts. Bowman's capsule wraps around it.

questions.question: Anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) acts on the:
options: Collecting duct, making it more permeable to water → concentrated urine
questions.expected: Collecting duct, making it more permeable to water → concentrated urine
questions.memo: Pituitary releases ADH when dehydrated → collecting duct reabsorbs more water → small amount of dark concentrated urine.

questions.question: If a person drinks lots of water, urine becomes:
questions.expected: Pale and dilute (large volume)
questions.memo: ADH falls when blood is over-watered. Collecting duct lets water pass through → more dilute urine.

questions.question: If a person is dehydrated, urine becomes:
questions.expected: Dark and concentrated (small volume)
questions.memo: ADH rises → collecting duct reabsorbs water → urine darker and smaller in volume. Universal sign of dehydration.

questions.question:
Sequence the path of urine:
(a) Collecting duct
(b) Renal pelvis
(c) Ureter
(d) Bladder
(e) Urethra
questions.expected: a → b → c → d → e
questions.memo: Tubules → renal pelvis (basin) → ureter (one each side) → bladder → urethra (one common exit).

questions.question: Glucose appears in urine when:
options: Blood glucose is so high that the PCT can't reabsorb it all (e.g. diabetes)
questions.expected: Blood glucose is so high that the PCT can't reabsorb it all (e.g. diabetes)
questions.memo: Renal threshold for glucose ~10 mmol/L. Glucose in urine = classic sign clinicians look for in diabetes.

questions.question: Protein in urine (proteinuria) usually indicates:
options: Kidney damage — filter letting protein through
questions.expected: Kidney damage — filter letting protein through
questions.memo: Normally protein is too big to pass through the glomerulus. If it appears in urine → filter damaged. Common in hypertension/diabetes.

questions.question: True or false: Urea is made by the LIVER, not the kidneys.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Liver breaks down excess amino acids → ammonia → urea (less toxic). Kidneys then filter urea out of blood.

questions.question: Why does the body NEED to make urea instead of leaving ammonia?
options: Ammonia is highly toxic; urea is much safer to carry and excrete
questions.expected: Ammonia is highly toxic; urea is much safer to carry and excrete
questions.memo: Fish (in water) excrete ammonia directly. Mammals (limited water) convert to urea or uric acid for safer storage and transport.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ULTRAFILTRATION needs HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE.
questions.expected: High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules through the filter into Bowman's capsule, and without it filtration cannot happen.
questions.memo: Why low blood pressure → reduced kidney output. Severe hypotension → acute kidney injury.
options: High pressure in the glomerulus forces small molecules through the filter into Bowman's capsule, and without it filtration cannot happen.
High blood pressure heats the blood so that wastes evaporate out into Bowman's capsule.
Ultrafiltration uses active transport, so blood pressure has little to do with it.
Low blood pressure actually improves filtration by giving molecules more time to pass through.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the LOOP OF HENLE helps the body SAVE WATER.
questions.expected: The loop builds a high salt concentration in the medulla, which draws water out of the collecting duct, producing concentrated urine and saving water.
questions.memo: Desert mammals have very long loops of Henle (kangaroo rat) → can excrete crystalline urine. Whales have short loops + drink no fresh water.
options: The loop of Henle filters the blood directly, removing extra water to make concentrated urine.
The loop builds a high salt concentration in the medulla, which draws water out of the collecting duct, producing concentrated urine and saving water.
The loop adds water to the urine so the body does not become too dehydrated.
The loop reabsorbs all the salt while letting the water pass straight out as dilute urine.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the KIDNEY balances WATER + SALT in the body.
questions.expected: The kidney filters all the blood and then adjusts how much water and salt are reabsorbed to suit the body's needs, controlled by hormones like ADH and aldosterone.
questions.memo: Kidneys = master regulators of body fluid balance. Why kidney failure has so many downstream effects.
options: The kidney always removes a fixed amount of water and salt regardless of what the body needs.
The kidney only filters waste and has no role in balancing water and salt in the body.
The kidney filters all the blood and then adjusts how much water and salt are reabsorbed to suit the body's needs, controlled by hormones like ADH and aldosterone.
The kidney balances water and salt purely by diffusion, with no hormonal control involved.

LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A2.title: Excretory disorders and treatments
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A2.description: Kidney failure; dialysis; transplants; lifestyle factors; SA dialysis access.
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G11.S2.EXCR.A2.recovery_strategy: Dialysis = machine filters blood. Transplant = donor kidney implanted. Major SA causes: diabetes + hypertension. Prevention = control BP + blood sugar.

questions.question: Kidney failure is BEST defined as:
options: Loss of kidney function so waste builds up in the blood
questions.expected: Loss of kidney function so waste builds up in the blood
questions.memo: Waste (urea, creatinine) accumulates → many symptoms across body systems. Without treatment, fatal.

questions.question: Common causes of kidney failure include:
questions.expected: Untreated hypertension and diabetes
questions.memo: High BP damages tiny glomerular vessels. High blood sugar damages filtration. SA has both as leading causes.

questions.question: Dialysis is a treatment that:
options: Uses a machine to filter waste from blood when kidneys fail
questions.expected: Uses a machine to filter waste from blood when kidneys fail
questions.memo: Two types: haemodialysis (blood pumped through filter, 3-4× a week) and peritoneal dialysis (fluid in abdomen).

questions.question: A kidney TRANSPLANT involves:
options: Replacing the failed kidneys with a donor kidney (from living or deceased donor)
questions.expected: Replacing the failed kidneys with a donor kidney (from living or deceased donor)
questions.memo: Transplant = best long-term outcome IF match found. Patient takes immune-suppressing drugs for life.

questions.question: Why must transplant patients take IMMUNE-SUPPRESSING drugs?
options: To prevent the immune system rejecting the donor kidney
questions.expected: To prevent the immune system rejecting the donor kidney
questions.memo: Donor tissue is recognised as 'foreign'. Drugs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus) suppress the response — but also raise infection risk.

questions.question: Which lifestyle factor PROTECTS kidneys?
options: Controlling blood pressure + blood sugar; staying well-hydrated; avoiding excess painkillers
questions.expected: Controlling blood pressure + blood sugar; staying well-hydrated; avoiding excess painkillers
questions.memo: NSAID overuse (ibuprofen, aspirin) damages kidneys. Stay hydrated, manage diabetes + BP, avoid alcohol excess.

questions.question: True or false: Untreated kidney failure can be FATAL.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Without dialysis or transplant, waste accumulation causes coma + death within days/weeks. Treatment is life-saving.

questions.question:
The table shows kidney transplant numbers in SA. What does the pattern suggest?

| Year  | Transplants |
|-------|-------------|
| 2014  | 235         |
| 2017  | 215         |
| 2020  | 198         |
options: Numbers are declining (donor shortage, limited capacity)
questions.expected: Numbers are declining (donor shortage, limited capacity)
questions.memo: SA has chronic kidney donor shortage. Public awareness + family discussion about organ donation is needed.

questions.question: How does HAEMODIALYSIS clean the blood?
options: Blood pumped past a semipermeable membrane; waste diffuses into dialysate, blood returned
Blood is replaced with new blood
questions.expected: Blood pumped past a semipermeable membrane; waste diffuses into dialysate, blood returned
questions.memo: Same diffusion principle as a kidney. Dialysate flows opposite direction (countercurrent) to maximise efficiency.

questions.question: PERITONEAL dialysis differs because:
options: Fluid is introduced into the abdomen; waste diffuses into it then drained
Done at home with no equipment
Blood is filtered with peritoneum membrane outside body
questions.expected: Fluid is introduced into the abdomen; waste diffuses into it then drained
questions.memo: Peritoneum (abdomen lining) acts as the filter. Can be done at home, multiple times a day.

questions.question: True or false: Dialysis fully REPLACES normal kidney function.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Dialysis cleans waste but doesn't make hormones (erythropoietin, calcitriol). Patients still need other treatments + restricted diet.

questions.question: Why are dialysis patients often given EPO injections?
options: Damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin → low red blood cells → injections compensate
questions.expected: Damaged kidneys make less erythropoietin → low red blood cells → injections compensate
questions.memo: Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell production. Kidney failure → low EPO → anaemia → fatigue.

questions.question: Kidney stones form when:
options: Crystals of calcium, oxalate or uric acid build up
questions.expected: Crystals of calcium, oxalate or uric acid build up
questions.memo: Dehydration + high oxalate diet + family history = risk. Pain is famously severe.

questions.question: True or false: Drinking plenty of water helps PREVENT kidney stones.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Dilute urine = crystals less likely to form. Simple cheap prevention. Most adults should drink ~2 L/day.

questions.question: A patient on dialysis is told to limit POTASSIUM in diet. Why?
options: Damaged kidneys can't remove excess K+, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms
questions.expected: Damaged kidneys can't remove excess K+, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms
questions.memo: High blood K+ (hyperkalemia) can stop the heart. Limit bananas, oranges, potatoes, beans.

questions.question: Why is ORGAN DONATION often a difficult choice for families?
options: Emotional, religious, cultural and practical considerations all play a role
There are too many organs available
questions.expected: Emotional, religious, cultural and practical considerations all play a role
questions.memo: Discussing donation in advance + registering as donor helps families decide. SA Organ Donor Foundation campaigns for awareness.

questions.question: Why is SA's BURDEN of kidney disease growing?
options: Rising rates of diabetes and hypertension, plus HIV-related kidney damage
questions.expected: Rising rates of diabetes and hypertension, plus HIV-related kidney damage
questions.memo: Three big drivers in SA. Plus access to dialysis is limited (often only public-sector patients meeting strict criteria).

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DIALYSIS access is a public-health and EQUITY issue in SA.
questions.expected: Dialysis is expensive with limited machine capacity, so not every patient who needs it can access treatment, raising hard ethical and equity questions.
questions.memo: Public-sector tiered access (age, co-conditions, employment). Private patients can pay but most cannot. A pressing ethical issue.
options: Dialysis is expensive with limited machine capacity, so not every patient who needs it can access treatment, raising hard ethical and equity questions.
Dialysis is cheap and widely available, so access is not really an equity issue in SA.
Dialysis is risky, so doctors simply choose not to offer it to most patients.
Everyone in SA can get dialysis free of charge, so the only issue is patient willingness.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why PREVENTION is better than dialysis for kidney health.
questions.expected: Dialysis is costly, time-consuming and limited, so preventing damage by managing blood pressure, blood sugar and lifestyle is far better for patients and the health system.
questions.memo: Prevention message resonates. Health clinics screen BP + glucose. Why early diagnosis saves lives and money.
options: Prevention is pointless because kidney damage cannot be avoided through lifestyle.
Dialysis fully cures kidney failure, so prevention offers no real advantage.
Dialysis is cheap and easy, so it is generally preferable to bothering with prevention.
Dialysis is costly, time-consuming and limited, so preventing damage by managing blood pressure, blood sugar and lifestyle is far better for patients and the health system.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SIGNING UP as an organ donor is important.
questions.expected: One donor can save several lives by donating organs, and registering plus discussing it with family makes donation more likely and easier for relatives.
questions.memo: One donor can save 7+ lives. SA Organ Donor Foundation (0800 22 66 11) coordinates. Many religions support donation.
options: One donor can save several lives by donating organs, and registering plus discussing it with family makes donation more likely and easier for relatives.
A donor can only ever help one recipient, so the impact of donating is quite small.
Organ donation is automatic at death, so there is no need to register or tell family.
Donating organs is discouraged because the body needs all its organs even after death.

LSC.G11.S3.POP.A1.title: Population growth and limiting factors
LSC.G11.S3.POP.A1.description: Birth/death rates; J/S curves; carrying capacity; density-dependent vs independent; sampling methods.
LSC.G11.S3.POP.A1.recovery_strategy: J-curve = unlimited, exponential. S-curve = approaches carrying capacity. Density-dependent: more crowded = more limiting. Density-independent: same effect regardless.

questions.question: A POPULATION is:
options: All members of one species living in an area
questions.expected: All members of one species living in an area
questions.memo: Population = same species, same place, same time. Many populations together = community.

questions.question: Population SIZE rises when:
options: Birth rate + immigration > death rate + emigration
Death rate is higher than birth rate
questions.expected: Birth rate + immigration > death rate + emigration
questions.memo: The 4 factors. Add the increases (born + arrived) → subtract the decreases (died + left).

questions.question: A J-curve (exponential) population growth happens when:
options: Resources are unlimited and growth accelerates rapidly
questions.expected: Resources are unlimited and growth accelerates rapidly
questions.memo: Looks like a J shape on a graph. Bacteria in fresh nutrient broth. Soon limits kick in → exponential growth never lasts forever.

questions.question: An S-curve (logistic) population growth happens when:
options: Growth slows and levels off at carrying capacity (K)
questions.expected: Growth slows and levels off at carrying capacity (K)
questions.memo: Realistic for most populations in nature. Growth slows as resources become limited; reaches plateau at K.

questions.question: CARRYING CAPACITY (K) is:
options: The maximum population an environment can support long-term
questions.expected: The maximum population an environment can support long-term
questions.memo: Determined by food, water, space, predation, disease. K varies between habitats and over time.

questions.question: Density-DEPENDENT limiting factors include:
options: Disease, predation, food competition — worse when population is denser
questions.expected: Disease, predation, food competition — worse when population is denser
questions.memo: Crowded → diseases spread, predators concentrate, food gets short. Density-dependent = self-regulating effect.

questions.question: Density-INDEPENDENT factors include:
options: Fire, drought, severe weather — same effect whatever the density
questions.expected: Fire, drought, severe weather — same effect whatever the density
questions.memo: A flood drowns animals regardless of how many there are. Density-independent = imposed from outside, no self-regulation.

questions.question:
On a population growth graph showing J-curve transitioning to S-curve, the CARRYING CAPACITY is the:
[Graph: population vs time, rising then plateau]
options: Horizontal line where the curve levels off
questions.expected: Horizontal line where the curve levels off
questions.memo: Plateau = the upper limit. The curve oscillates around it as births and deaths balance.

questions.question: Quadrat sampling is BEST suited for:
questions.expected: Plants and slow/stationary animals
questions.memo: Quadrat = fixed area square. Throw randomly, count. Best for stationary organisms or slow-moving ones (snails, insects).

questions.question: Mark-RECAPTURE sampling is used for:
questions.expected: Mobile animals (e.g. fish, birds)
questions.memo: Catch sample, mark them, release, catch again. Proportion marked → estimate total population (Lincoln index).

questions.question: If 100 fish are marked, then 50 caught later (5 marked), what's the population estimate?
questions.memo: Lincoln index: N = (first catch × second catch) / marked recaptures. (100 × 50) / 5 = 1000.

questions.question: True or false: A population growing on a J-curve will EVENTUALLY hit a limit.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Exponential growth can't last forever. Resources run out, disease spreads. Crash or transition to logistic.

questions.question: A FALLING population trend is shown when:
options: Deaths and emigration exceed births and immigration
questions.expected: Deaths and emigration exceed births and immigration
questions.memo: Decline = net loss. Many SA species (e.g. African penguin) show declining trends → conservation flag.

questions.question: Why might a population EXCEED carrying capacity briefly?
options: Reproduction continues for a while before resource limits kick in → crash often follows
questions.expected: Reproduction continues for a while before resource limits kick in → crash often follows
questions.memo: Boom-bust cycles common in nature. Overshoot followed by population crash (or starvation).

questions.question: True or false: HUMAN populations show J-curve growth globally.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Until recently, J-curve. Now growth is slowing in some regions. Forecasts suggest global stabilisation by 2100.

questions.question: A population pyramid shows:
options: Number of people at each age group, split by sex
Numbers of species in an area
questions.expected: Number of people at each age group, split by sex
questions.memo: Wide base = growing population (many young). Narrow base = stable/declining. SA has a broad-base + bulge in working ages.

questions.question: An African elephant herd at Kruger reaches carrying capacity. The most likely response is:
options: Lower birth rate, more starvation deaths, possible vegetation damage
questions.expected: Lower birth rate, more starvation deaths, possible vegetation damage
questions.memo: Real management challenge. Kruger has historically used culling, contraception, or translocation to manage elephant numbers.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why carrying capacity can CHANGE OVER TIME.
questions.expected: Carrying capacity changes because resource availability and disturbances like fire or alien invaders alter how many individuals an area can support, so K rises and falls with conditions.
questions.memo: Drought drops K. Alien clearing raises K for native species. Climate change is shifting K across the world.
options: Carrying capacity is fixed for each habitat and never changes once it is set.
Carrying capacity changes because resource availability and disturbances like fire or alien invaders alter how many individuals an area can support, so K rises and falls with conditions.
Carrying capacity only ever increases over time as populations adapt to their habitat.
Carrying capacity depends only on the number of predators, not on resources or disturbance.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why FIELD ecologists need SAMPLING methods rather than counting every individual.
questions.expected: Counting every individual is usually impractical, so ecologists use sampling to estimate population size or density reliably using statistics.
questions.memo: Imagine trying to count every fish in a dam. Sampling + statistics = standard scientific approach.
options: Counting every individual is the most accurate method, so ecologists always do it instead of sampling.
Sampling is used only when ecologists are lazy; a full count would always be better.
Sampling counts every individual but does so faster than counting by hand.
Counting every individual is usually impractical, so ecologists use sampling to estimate population size or density reliably using statistics.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why understanding CARRYING CAPACITY matters for SA conservation.
questions.expected: Knowing carrying capacity guides how many animals or plants a reserve can support, so SA conservationists can set reserve sizes and manage numbers, preventing overshoot and crashes.
questions.memo: Used by SANParks for stocking decisions, fence placement, culling/translocation. Vital for conservation planning.
options: Knowing carrying capacity guides how many animals or plants a reserve can support, so SA conservationists can set reserve sizes and manage numbers, preventing overshoot and crashes.
Carrying capacity is only useful for farming and has no role in SA conservation.
Conservationists ignore carrying capacity because protected populations can grow without limit.
Carrying capacity matters only for predators, so it does not affect reserve planning.

LSC.G11.S3.POP.A2.title: Community ecology and species interactions
LSC.G11.S3.POP.A2.description: Predation, competition, parasitism, mutualism, commensalism; niche; succession.
LSC.G11.S3.POP.A2.recovery_strategy: Mutualism = both benefit. Commensalism = one benefits, other unaffected. Parasitism = one benefits, other harmed. Predation = one eats other. Competition = same resource.

questions.question: Predation is when:
options: One species kills and eats another
questions.expected: One species kills and eats another
questions.memo: Lion + zebra. The predator benefits; the prey is killed. Predator-prey populations often cycle.

questions.question: Competition is when:
options: Two species or individuals need the same limited resource
questions.expected: Two species or individuals need the same limited resource
questions.memo: Same resource (food, water, shelter, mates). Intraspecific (within species) or interspecific (between species).

questions.question: PARASITISM is when:
options: One species (parasite) benefits while harming the other (host)
questions.expected: One species (parasite) benefits while harming the other (host)
questions.memo: Tapeworms, ticks, fleas, malaria. Usually parasites don't kill their host quickly — they want a long stay.

questions.question: MUTUALISM is when:
questions.expected: BOTH species benefit
questions.memo: Bee + flower (pollination + nectar). Mycorrhizae (fungus + plant roots). Win-win.

questions.question: COMMENSALISM is when:
options: One species benefits, the other is unaffected
questions.expected: One species benefits, the other is unaffected
questions.memo: Barnacles on a whale, birds nesting in a tree without harming it. Tricky to identify — often subtle effects on the host.

questions.question:
Match each interaction to the SA example:
1. Predation  2. Mutualism  3. Parasitism  4. Competition

A. Lion hunting zebra
B. Tick on cattle
C. Lions vs hyenas for a kill
D. Honeyguide bird leading honey badger to a hive
questions.memo: Lion-zebra = predation. Honeyguide-honey badger = mutualism (badger opens hive, both eat honey). Tick = parasite. Lions/hyenas = competition.

questions.question: An organism's NICHE is:
options: Its role and 'job' in the ecosystem (food, time of activity, etc.)
questions.expected: Its role and 'job' in the ecosystem (food, time of activity, etc.)
questions.memo: Niche = job description. Habitat = address. Two species can share a habitat but not an identical niche for long.

questions.question: The COMPETITIVE EXCLUSION principle says:
options: Two species can't share an identical niche for long — one will outcompete the other
questions.expected: Two species can't share an identical niche for long — one will outcompete the other
questions.memo: Strong rule. In practice, similar species partition resources (different times, food types, locations) to coexist.

questions.question: Predator and prey populations often:
options: Show cycles where each affects the other (lynx/hare cycles)
questions.expected: Show cycles where each affects the other (lynx/hare cycles)
questions.memo: Famous lynx/hare ecology data. More prey → more predators → fewer prey → fewer predators → more prey...

questions.question: Why are MYCORRHIZAE (fungus + root) examples of MUTUALISM?
options: Fungus gets sugars from the plant; plant gets minerals + water from the fungus
questions.expected: Fungus gets sugars from the plant; plant gets minerals + water from the fungus
questions.memo: Mycorrhizae found on ~80% of plant species. Both partners gain. Plants without them often struggle.

questions.question: SUCCESSION is:
options: The orderly change in community composition over time
questions.expected: The orderly change in community composition over time
questions.memo: Primary succession on bare rock; secondary on disturbed land. Ends at climax community (relatively stable).

questions.question: Secondary succession differs from primary because:
options: Starts with existing soil (after disturbance like fire or farming)
questions.expected: Starts with existing soil (after disturbance like fire or farming)
questions.memo: Existing soil + seed bank + nearby seed source → succession proceeds much faster than from bare rock.

questions.question: True or false: A CLIMAX community is permanent.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Climax is relatively stable but disturbance (fire, climate change) can reset succession. Climate is the master variable.

questions.question: In SA fynbos, FIRE causes:
options: Resetting of succession + germination of fire-stimulated seeds
Permanent destruction of all plant life
questions.expected: Resetting of succession + germination of fire-stimulated seeds
questions.memo: Fynbos is fire-adapted. Many species need fire to release seeds or resprout from underground storage. Old fynbos (>30y) loses diversity.

questions.question: The graph shows lion-zebra population over years. Lion peaks LAG behind zebra peaks. Why?

data.description: Two oscillating curves: zebra population rises and falls, lion population follows shifted by ~1 year

options: More prey → predators slowly reproduce → predators rise → prey drops → predators drop
questions.expected: More prey → predators slowly reproduce → predators rise → prey drops → predators drop
questions.memo: Classic predator-prey lag. Predators take time to respond to prey changes; the lag drives the cycle.

questions.question: Removing TOP PREDATORS often leads to:
options: Herbivore numbers rise → overgrazing → habitat damage (trophic cascade)
questions.expected: Herbivore numbers rise → overgrazing → habitat damage (trophic cascade)
questions.memo: Lions, wolves, wild dogs control herbivore numbers + behaviour. Yellowstone wolf reintroduction is a famous example.

questions.question: Why is a single species often a KEYSTONE in its ecosystem?
options: Its presence shapes the whole community — removing it causes major changes
questions.expected: Its presence shapes the whole community — removing it causes major changes
questions.memo: Examples: sea otters maintain kelp forests by eating sea urchins. African elephants shape savannas by knocking down trees.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DIVERSITY in a community often makes it more STABLE.
questions.expected: A diverse community has more species to fill ecological roles if one declines, making it more resistant to disturbance and better able to recover.
questions.memo: Diversity → redundancy → stability. Why monoculture farms are vulnerable to pest outbreaks.
options: More diversity makes a community unstable because the species constantly compete and wipe each other out.
Diversity has no effect on stability; a single-species community is just as stable as a diverse one.
A diverse community has more species to fill ecological roles if one declines, making it more resistant to disturbance and better able to recover.
Stability comes only from having large numbers of one species, not from having many different species.

questions.question: True or false: Plants of DIFFERENT species can compete with each other even without moving.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Plants compete for light (overshadow), water, nutrients (root systems). Allelopathy — some plants release chemicals to suppress neighbours.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the INTERACTION between aliens and natives causes problems in SA.
questions.expected: Alien invasive species can outcompete natives, prey on them, or spread disease, reducing native biodiversity and disrupting ecosystem services.
questions.memo: Black Wattle, Port Jackson use much more water than fynbos. Alien rats prey on seabird chicks. SA's Working for Water programme addresses this.
options: Alien species always die out quickly in SA, so they cause no real problems for native species.
Aliens and natives simply share resources peacefully, so biodiversity is unaffected.
Native species usually outcompete aliens, so it is the natives that cause the harm.
Alien invasive species can outcompete natives, prey on them, or spread disease, reducing native biodiversity and disrupting ecosystem services.

LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A1.title: Atmosphere — greenhouse effect, climate change and ozone
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A1.description: Greenhouse effect (natural + enhanced); main GHGs; climate consequences; ozone depletion.
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A1.recovery_strategy: Greenhouse = traps heat (CO2, CH4). Ozone depletion = upper atmosphere thinning (CFCs). They are DIFFERENT problems.

questions.question: The greenhouse effect is:
options: Atmospheric gases trapping heat that would otherwise escape to space
questions.expected: Atmospheric gases trapping heat that would otherwise escape to space
questions.memo: Natural process. Without it, Earth would be ~-18°C. The problem is the ENHANCED greenhouse effect from extra CO2.

questions.question: Which is a MAJOR greenhouse gas?
questions.expected: Carbon dioxide
questions.memo: CO2 ~76% of human GHG emissions. Methane (CH4) ~16%, N2O ~6%, F-gases ~2%.

questions.question: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) adds:
questions.expected: CO2 to the atmosphere
questions.memo: Combustion of carbon-based fuels releases CO2 that was locked away for millions of years. SA's coal-heavy power system is a major source.

questions.question: Methane (CH4) is a powerful GHG emitted by:
options: Cattle digestion, rice paddies, wetlands, fossil-fuel leaks
questions.expected: Cattle digestion, rice paddies, wetlands, fossil-fuel leaks
questions.memo: CH4 is ~28× more potent than CO2 over 100 years. Reducing methane is fast climate action.

questions.question: True or false: The greenhouse effect itself is NATURAL.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Natural greenhouse effect makes Earth liveable. The problem is the ENHANCED effect from extra human-emitted gases.

questions.question: Climate change in SA is expected to:
options: Make hot regions hotter and drier — water scarcity worse
questions.expected: Make hot regions hotter and drier — water scarcity worse
questions.memo: SA already shows warming trends. Western Cape drought (2015-18) showed climate vulnerability. Water security is a big concern.

questions.question: Sea-level rise is caused by:
options: Thermal expansion of water + melting ice sheets and glaciers
questions.expected: Thermal expansion of water + melting ice sheets and glaciers
questions.memo: Warming water expands. Melting Greenland + Antarctic ice raises sea level. Coastal SA cities will feel impacts (Cape Town, Durban).

questions.question: The OZONE LAYER is found in the:
questions.expected: Stratosphere — protects from UV radiation
questions.memo: Upper atmosphere ~20-30 km high. Absorbs harmful UV-B/C. Surface ozone (low altitude) is a pollutant.

questions.question: Ozone depletion was caused mainly by:
questions.expected: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) from fridges and aerosols
questions.memo: CFCs released → rise to stratosphere → chlorine destroys ozone. Montreal Protocol (1987) banned them — ozone layer slowly recovering.

questions.question: Effects of ozone-layer thinning include:
options: More UV reaching surface → skin cancer + crop damage
questions.expected: More UV reaching surface → skin cancer + crop damage
questions.memo: UV-B causes skin cancer, cataracts, immune effects, plankton damage. SA has high skin cancer rates partly due to UV intensity.

questions.question: True or false: The greenhouse effect and ozone depletion are the SAME problem.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Different problems, different chemicals, different effects. Greenhouse = warming (CO2, CH4). Ozone = UV reaching surface (CFCs).

questions.question: The graph shows atmospheric CO2 rising from 280 ppm (1850) to 420 ppm (today). What does this suggest?
options: Human activities (fossil fuels, deforestation) have raised atmospheric CO2 dramatically
questions.expected: Human activities (fossil fuels, deforestation) have raised atmospheric CO2 dramatically
questions.memo: Sharpest rise in geological record. Direct cause: industrial revolution + fossil fuel burning + land-use change.

questions.question: Ocean acidification is caused by:
options: CO2 dissolving in seawater, forming carbonic acid
questions.expected: CO2 dissolving in seawater, forming carbonic acid
questions.memo: Ocean has absorbed about 30% of human CO2 emissions. Lower pH → coral bleaching, shellfish difficulty, ecosystem disruption.

questions.question: Why has CAPE TOWN been singled out as climate-vulnerable?
options: Mediterranean climate dependent on winter rain — climate change disrupted this
questions.expected: Mediterranean climate dependent on winter rain — climate change disrupted this
questions.memo: 2015-18 drought brought 'Day Zero'. Average temperature up, rainfall trend down. Water restrictions saved the city.

questions.question: Renewable energy sources include:
questions.expected: Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal
questions.memo: Renewables don't add net CO2. SA's Renewable Energy IPP Programme has built wind + solar farms in Karoo and Cape areas.

questions.question: True or false: Trees PHOTOSYNTHESIS reduces atmospheric CO2.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Forests are carbon sinks. Loss of forests + replacement with farmland adds CO2. Reforestation is part of climate response.

questions.question: Why is the AMAZON RAINFOREST often called 'lungs of the planet'?
options: Releases large amounts of O2 and absorbs CO2 through photosynthesis
questions.expected: Releases large amounts of O2 and absorbs CO2 through photosynthesis
questions.memo: Huge area + dense vegetation = important global carbon sink. Deforestation reduces this capacity.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the GREENHOUSE EFFECT actually works.
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases let sunlight through but absorb the heat (infrared) radiated by Earth's surface, trapping it and warming the lower atmosphere.
questions.memo: Like a glass greenhouse. Without the natural effect, Earth would be frozen. Too much = warming.
options: Greenhouse gases block sunlight from reaching Earth, which cools the surface.
Greenhouse gases let sunlight through but absorb the heat (infrared) radiated by Earth's surface, trapping it and warming the lower atmosphere.
Greenhouse gases damage the ozone layer, and it is the resulting UV that heats the atmosphere.
Greenhouse gases reflect Earth's heat back into space, which is why the planet stays warm.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why GLOBAL action is needed for climate change.
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases mix throughout the global atmosphere, so emissions anywhere affect everyone, which is why international cooperation is needed to cut them.
questions.memo: Paris Agreement (2015). Each country sets targets (NDCs). SA has committed to specific reductions, including phasing out coal.
options: Each country's emissions stay over its own territory, so nations can solve climate change on their own.
Only the largest countries contribute to climate change, so global cooperation is unnecessary.
Greenhouse gases mix throughout the global atmosphere, so emissions anywhere affect everyone, which is why international cooperation is needed to cut them.
Climate change is purely local, so global agreements make no real difference.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why YOUNG PEOPLE are particularly concerned about climate change.
questions.expected: Young people will live with the worsening impacts throughout their lives, yet the decisions driving past emissions were made by earlier generations.
questions.memo: Climate justice issue. SA's young people are at the forefront of climate action — Greta Thunberg-style movements have grown locally.
options: Young people will live with the worsening impacts throughout their lives, yet the decisions driving past emissions were made by earlier generations.
Young people are more affected by climate change because their bodies are physically weaker than adults'.
Young people caused most of today's emissions, so they feel responsible for fixing the problem.
Climate change will mainly affect older generations, but young people worry on their behalf.

LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A2.title: Water, soil and alien invasive species
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A2.description: Water pollution; eutrophication; soil erosion + overgrazing; alien invasives (Black Wattle, water hyacinth).
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A2.recovery_strategy: Alien invasive = brought from outside, spreads aggressively. SA Working for Water clears them → saves water + restores indigenous vegetation.

questions.question: Eutrophication of water bodies is caused mainly by:
options: Excess nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) from fertilisers or sewage
questions.expected: Excess nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) from fertilisers or sewage
questions.memo: Nutrients → algal bloom → algae die → bacteria use up O2 decomposing them → fish die. Hartbeespoort Dam = SA example.

questions.question: Acid rain is caused mainly by:
options: Sulfur dioxide + nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels
questions.expected: Sulfur dioxide + nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels
questions.memo: Mpumalanga's coal-fired power stations are major SO2/NOx sources. Acid rain damages forests, lakes, buildings.

questions.question: OVERGRAZING by livestock causes:
options: Loss of plant cover → soil erosion, desertification, biodiversity loss
questions.expected: Loss of plant cover → soil erosion, desertification, biodiversity loss
questions.memo: Big problem in SA semi-arid areas. Combined with drought, can permanently degrade rangelands.

questions.question: Soil erosion is worst when:
options: Vegetation cover is removed and slopes are bare
questions.expected: Vegetation cover is removed and slopes are bare
questions.memo: Roots hold soil in place. Without roots, rain + wind strip topsoil. Centuries to form, decades to lose.

questions.question: Black Wattle in SA is:
options: An alien invasive tree from Australia, spreads aggressively
questions.expected: An alien invasive tree from Australia, spreads aggressively
questions.memo: Brought for tanning industry. Uses MUCH more water than fynbos. Now extensively cleared by Working for Water programme.

questions.question: Water hyacinth is an alien invasive in SA rivers and dams. It:
options: Forms thick floating mats blocking light + oxygen for aquatic life
questions.expected: Forms thick floating mats blocking light + oxygen for aquatic life
questions.memo: Hartbeespoort Dam famously affected. Biological control (weevils + moths) + manual removal used.

questions.question: Why are alien invasives often WORSE in their NEW environment than at home?
options: No natural predators, parasites or competitors in the new place
questions.expected: No natural predators, parasites or competitors in the new place
questions.memo: Ecological release. The pests + pathogens + competitors that controlled them at home are absent → unchecked spread.

questions.question: SA's Working for Water programme:
options: Clears alien invasive plants, restoring water flow and biodiversity, creating jobs
questions.expected: Clears alien invasive plants, restoring water flow and biodiversity, creating jobs
questions.memo: Win-win-win programme. Environmental + economic + social benefits. Model for sustainable development.

questions.question: True or false: Indigenous plants often use LESS water than alien invasives.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Fynbos = adapted to dry Cape summers. Black Wattle + Eucalyptus use 2-3× more water → less for rivers + people.

questions.question:
The table shows water flow reduction by alien plants. Which catchment has the biggest impact?

| Catchment    | Water reduction (%) |
|--------------|---------------------|
| Berg River   | 8%                  |
| Olifants     | 12%                 |
| Tugela       | 4%                  |
questions.expected: Olifants
questions.memo: 12% reduction = the largest. Why alien clearing in heavily affected catchments is a national water-security priority.

questions.question: Salinisation of soil happens when:
options: Irrigation evaporation leaves salts behind, making soil unfarmable
questions.expected: Irrigation evaporation leaves salts behind, making soil unfarmable
questions.memo: Big problem in irrigated dry regions. Solution: better drainage, less waste, drought-tolerant crops.

questions.question: Heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) in water from mining:
options: Bioaccumulate up the food chain, causing toxic effects
questions.expected: Bioaccumulate up the food chain, causing toxic effects
questions.memo: Bioaccumulation: concentration rises at each trophic level. Top predators (and humans) get highest doses. Mining + acid mine drainage = SA problem.

questions.question: Plastic in oceans:
options: Kills marine life (turtles, seabirds, fish) by entanglement or ingestion
questions.expected: Kills marine life (turtles, seabirds, fish) by entanglement or ingestion
questions.memo: Microplastics now in food chain + drinking water. Bans on single-use plastic + cleanup operations + recycling helping.

questions.question: True or false: Composting reduces waste AND adds to soil health.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Closes the nutrient cycle. Reduces landfill methane. Compost improves soil structure + water retention. Easy household action.

questions.question: Why are RIVERS often DOWNSTREAM of urban areas polluted?
options: Untreated sewage, industrial runoff and stormwater carry pollutants in
questions.expected: Untreated sewage, industrial runoff and stormwater carry pollutants in
questions.memo: SA municipal sewage treatment is patchy. Many WTW are failing → polluted rivers + costly downstream water treatment.

questions.question: Sustainable agriculture practices include:
options: Crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage, integrated pest management
questions.expected: Crop rotation, cover crops, conservation tillage, integrated pest management
questions.memo: Build soil + reduce inputs + protect biodiversity. Many SA farmers + agroecology projects piloting these methods.

questions.question: True or false: ALL alien species are invasive.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Many introduced species don't spread aggressively (e.g. crop plants like maize). Only some become invasive — usually fast-growing and prolific.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA invests in clearing ALIEN INVASIVE plants.
questions.expected: Alien plants use far more water than native vegetation, so clearing them restores river flow, supports biodiversity and provides jobs for unemployed people.
questions.memo: Working for Water = win-win-win programme. Environmental restoration + water security + poverty alleviation.
options: Alien plants are cleared mainly because they look untidy, not for any water or biodiversity reason.
Alien plants use far more water than native vegetation, so clearing them restores river flow, supports biodiversity and provides jobs for unemployed people.
Alien plants use less water than natives, so clearing them is really about creating jobs alone.
Clearing aliens harms biodiversity, but SA does it anyway to free up farmland.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SOIL EROSION is hard to REVERSE.
questions.expected: Building topsoil takes hundreds to thousands of years, so once it erodes the productive layer is essentially lost on human timescales.
questions.memo: Why prevention is so important. Practices like cover crops, terracing, no-till farming protect existing soil.
options: Eroded soil can be replaced within a season by adding fertiliser, so erosion is easy to reverse.
Soil erosion reverses naturally within a few years once farming stops.
Building topsoil takes hundreds to thousands of years, so once it erodes the productive layer is essentially lost on human timescales.
Erosion is reversible because rain quickly washes new soil back onto the land.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting WETLANDS matters for SA water security.
questions.expected: Wetlands filter pollutants and store water, releasing it slowly in dry periods, while supporting biodiversity and reducing flood risk, all key for SA water security.
questions.memo: SA has lost ~50% of its wetlands. Protection + rehabilitation = critical for clean water + climate resilience.
options: Wetlands waste water by letting it sit, so draining them would actually improve SA's water security.
Wetlands only matter for wildlife and have no effect on human water supply.
Wetlands add pollutants to water, so they must be protected to keep that pollution contained.
Wetlands filter pollutants and store water, releasing it slowly in dry periods, while supporting biodiversity and reducing flood risk, all key for SA water security.

LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A3.title: Biodiversity loss and South African conservation responses
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A3.description: Drivers of biodiversity loss; SA conservation responses (SANParks, CITES, Working for Water).
LSC.G11.S3.IMP.A3.recovery_strategy: SA conservation = government (SANParks, CapeNature), NGOs (WWF-SA), communities, private land. CITES regulates international trade.

questions.question: The biggest driver of biodiversity loss globally is:
questions.expected: Habitat loss (farming, development, infrastructure)
questions.memo: Habitat loss > climate change > overharvesting > invasive species > pollution. Habitat loss = biggest single driver.

questions.question: Rhino poaching in SA is driven by:
options: Demand for rhino horn in Asian markets (medicinal beliefs, status symbol)
questions.expected: Demand for rhino horn in Asian markets (medicinal beliefs, status symbol)
questions.memo: Horn = keratin (same as fingernails). Despite no medical evidence, demand drives poaching. SA has lost ~10,000 rhinos since 2010.

questions.question: Abalone (perlemoen) poaching is driven by:
options: High demand in Asian markets, especially for dried abalone
questions.expected: High demand in Asian markets, especially for dried abalone
questions.memo: Connected to criminal syndicates trading abalone for drugs. SA West Coast populations critically depleted.

questions.question: Habitat fragmentation occurs when:
options: Roads, fences, or development split habitat into smaller disconnected pieces
questions.expected: Roads, fences, or development split habitat into smaller disconnected pieces
questions.memo: Even if total habitat area is preserved, fragmentation isolates populations → genetic + ecological problems.

questions.question: SANParks manages:
options: A network of national parks including Kruger, Table Mountain, Addo, Tsitsikamma
questions.expected: A network of national parks including Kruger, Table Mountain, Addo, Tsitsikamma
questions.memo: SA's national park agency. Manages over 9 million hectares including some of Africa's most iconic parks.

questions.question: CITES is an international agreement that:
options: Regulates trade in endangered species across borders
questions.expected: Regulates trade in endangered species across borders
questions.memo: CITES Appendix I = no trade, II = controlled trade. SA participates. Used to protect rhino, elephant, cycads.

questions.question: An ENDEMIC species is found:
options: Only in a specific geographic area
questions.expected: Only in a specific geographic area
questions.memo: SA Cape Floral Kingdom = ~70% endemic plants. Many cycads endemic to single mountain valleys.

questions.question: Ecotourism can help conservation by:
options: Funding reserves + providing jobs that make biodiversity economically valuable
questions.expected: Funding reserves + providing jobs that make biodiversity economically valuable
questions.memo: When wildlife is worth more alive (tourism, lodges, jobs) than dead (poached), conservation strengthens. SA leader in this.

questions.question: True or false: SA private game reserves contribute to conservation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Hundreds of private reserves + sanctuaries supplement public parks. Some Big Five reserves now larger than parts of Kruger.

questions.question: The IUCN Red List categorises species by:
options: Risk of extinction (Critically Endangered to Least Concern)
questions.expected: Risk of extinction (Critically Endangered to Least Concern)
questions.memo: International standard. Categories: Extinct, Extinct in Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern.

questions.question: The Cape Floral Kingdom is GLOBALLY important because:
options: It is the smallest of six floral kingdoms but has the highest plant diversity per area + many endemic species
questions.expected: It is the smallest of six floral kingdoms but has the highest plant diversity per area + many endemic species
questions.memo: UNESCO World Heritage Site. ~9000 species in a small area, ~70% endemic. Major SA conservation priority.

questions.question: Climate change threatens SA biodiversity by:
options: Shifting climate envelopes — many species can't move fast enough or have nowhere to go
questions.expected: Shifting climate envelopes — many species can't move fast enough or have nowhere to go
questions.memo: Fynbos at risk of huge species loss under high-warming scenarios. Mountain endemics with nowhere higher to go.

questions.question: The graph shows SA's Red List threat trend (% of vertebrates threatened): 2000 = 14%, 2020 = 18%. What does this suggest?

data.description: % of SA vertebrates threatened by year: 2000 = 14%, 2010 = 16%, 2020 = 18%

options: Threat is rising over time — biodiversity is in decline
questions.expected: Threat is rising over time — biodiversity is in decline
questions.memo: Despite conservation efforts, threats outpace gains. Why intensified action is needed.

questions.question: True or false: Conservation only protects 'cute' animals (Big Five).
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: SA conservation protects whole ecosystems — plants, insects, fungi, microbes. Flagship species draw funding for broader protection.

questions.question: Wildlife corridors:
options: Link reserves so animals can move + populations stay connected
questions.expected: Link reserves so animals can move + populations stay connected
questions.memo: Greater Limpopo Transfrontier Park links SA, Mozambique, Zimbabwe. Corridors essential as climate shifts ranges.

questions.question: Why is COMMUNITY involvement essential for SA conservation success?
options: Communities living near reserves must benefit + participate, not be excluded
questions.expected: Communities living near reserves must benefit + participate, not be excluded
questions.memo: Top-down conservation often fails. SA's land reform + community conservancies + benefit-sharing are part of success.

questions.question: Why is the EBM (ecosystem-based management) approach used in SA?
options: Protects whole ecosystems and their processes, not just single species
questions.expected: Protects whole ecosystems and their processes, not just single species
questions.memo: Species don't exist in isolation. Protect food webs + processes + habitat — single-species focus often fails.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting BIODIVERSITY is important for HUMANS, not just animals.
questions.expected: Ecosystems provide services like clean water, pollination, climate regulation, medicines and food, so losing biodiversity weakens services that humans depend on.
questions.memo: Ecosystem services valuation. Pollinators alone worth billions per year globally. We're not separate from nature.
options: Biodiversity matters only for the animals themselves and has no real benefit for people.
Ecosystems provide services like clean water, pollination, climate regulation, medicines and food, so losing biodiversity weakens services that humans depend on.
Humans are separate from nature, so biodiversity loss affects only wild ecosystems.
Protecting biodiversity is purely an ethical choice with no practical benefit to people.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA is recognised as one of the world's MEGADIVERSE countries.
questions.expected: SA has many endemic species and diverse biomes in a small area, including the globally important Cape Floral Kingdom hotspot, giving it exceptional biodiversity.
questions.memo: 17 megadiverse countries hold ~70% of global biodiversity. SA on the list due to climate gradients + isolation + history.
options: SA is megadiverse simply because it is a very large country with lots of empty space.
SA earns the title because it has imported many species from around the world.
SA has many endemic species and diverse biomes in a small area, including the globally important Cape Floral Kingdom hotspot, giving it exceptional biodiversity.
SA is megadiverse only because of the big game animals in its famous reserves.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how a YOUNG SA citizen can contribute to conservation.
questions.expected: They can volunteer with conservation groups, choose sustainable products, avoid illegal wildlife products and cut their footprint, with individual actions adding up to community change.
questions.memo: Concrete actions: WWF-SA, BirdLife SA, alien clearing days, beach cleanups, reducing waste. Young people are powerful advocates.
options: An individual's actions are far too small to matter, so conservation should be left to the government.
Young people can only help by donating money, since direct action makes no difference.
Conservation is only for trained scientists, so ordinary citizens cannot contribute.
They can volunteer with conservation groups, choose sustainable products, avoid illegal wildlife products and cut their footprint, with individual actions adding up to community change.

LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A1.title: DNA structure and the genetic code
LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A1.description: Double helix; nucleotide; A-T G-C base pairing; Chargaff's rules; antiparallel strands.
LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A1.recovery_strategy: Double helix = two antiparallel strands. Backbone = sugar (deoxyribose) + phosphate. Bases inside: A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds).

questions.question: DNA has a:
questions.expected: Double-helix structure
questions.memo: Two strands wind around each other like a twisted ladder. Watson + Crick described this in 1953 using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data.

questions.question: A DNA NUCLEOTIDE is made of:
options: Sugar (deoxyribose), phosphate group, and one nitrogenous base
questions.expected: Sugar (deoxyribose), phosphate group, and one nitrogenous base
questions.memo: Universal monomer of DNA. Many nucleotides linked = a DNA strand.

questions.question: Which bases pair with each other in DNA?
options: A with T, G with C
A with G, T with C
A with C, T with G
questions.expected: A with T, G with C
questions.memo: Complementary base pairing. Adenine-Thymine (2 H-bonds). Guanine-Cytosine (3 H-bonds, stronger).

questions.question: What forms the BACKBONE of a DNA strand?
questions.expected: Alternating sugar and phosphate groups
questions.memo: Sugar-phosphate-sugar-phosphate chain. Bases stick out sideways and pair with bases on the other strand.

questions.question: The two strands of DNA are ANTIPARALLEL, meaning:
options: They run in opposite directions (one 5'→3', the other 3'→5')
They are parallel and same direction
questions.expected: They run in opposite directions (one 5'→3', the other 3'→5')
questions.memo: Strand orientation matters for replication and transcription. Polymerase enzymes only build 5'→3'.

questions.question: What holds the TWO STRANDS together in DNA?
questions.expected: Hydrogen bonds between base pairs
questions.memo: Many weak H-bonds = strong overall but can be unzipped easily for replication. G-C pair has 3 H-bonds, A-T pair has 2.

questions.question: Chargaff's rules state that in any DNA sample:
options: Amount of A = T, and G = C
questions.expected: Amount of A = T, and G = C
questions.memo: Critical clue for Watson + Crick. If A pairs only with T (and G with C), the amounts must match.

questions.question: A sample of DNA contains 30% A. What is the percentage of C?
questions.memo: Chargaff applied: A=30 → T=30. So G+C = 100-60 = 40%. G=C, so C=20%.

questions.question:
On the DNA diagram, which letter labels a hydrogen bond?
[Diagram: DNA double helix with sugar-phosphate backbone (A), base (B), H-bond (C), nucleotide (D)]
questions.expected: C (dotted lines between bases)
questions.memo: H-bonds usually drawn as dotted lines connecting the bases between the two strands.

questions.question:
Match each scientist to their contribution:
1. Watson + Crick  2. Rosalind Franklin  3. Chargaff

A. Base pairing rule (A=T, G=C)
B. Proposed double-helix model
C. X-ray diffraction images of DNA
questions.memo: Watson + Crick = double helix. Franklin = X-ray photo #51. Chargaff = base ratio rule. Franklin's images were crucial — she didn't get full credit during her lifetime.

questions.question: DNA stores genetic information by:
options: The sequence of bases (A, T, G, C) coding for amino acids
questions.expected: The sequence of bases (A, T, G, C) coding for amino acids
questions.memo: 4-letter alphabet (A,T,G,C). Triplets (codons) of 3 bases code for amino acids in proteins.

questions.question: True or false: DNA is found mainly in the cytoplasm.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: In eukaryotes, DNA is in the nucleus (also small amounts in mitochondria + chloroplasts). In prokaryotes, DNA is in the cytoplasm but they have no nucleus.

questions.question: Chromosomes are:
options: DNA tightly packed with histone proteins
questions.expected: DNA tightly packed with histone proteins
questions.memo: 2 m of DNA fits into each cell nucleus by wrapping around histones → forming chromatin → condensing into chromosomes for division.

questions.question: A GENE is:
options: A segment of DNA that codes for a protein
questions.expected: A segment of DNA that codes for a protein
questions.memo: Each gene = instructions for one protein. Humans have ~20,000 protein-coding genes. Variations in genes = differences between individuals.

questions.question: True or false: DNA molecules are IDENTICAL between unrelated humans.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: We share ~99.9% DNA, but the 0.1% differences are what make us individuals. DNA fingerprinting uses these differences.

questions.question: DNA fingerprinting is used in:
questions.expected: Forensic identification, paternity testing, conservation
questions.memo: Compare DNA patterns to identify individuals or relationships. SA forensic services + DNA database used in crime investigations.

questions.question: Why are DNA bases on the INSIDE of the double helix?
options: They are hydrophobic and shielded from water; pairing holds the strands together
They are too big to fit outside
questions.expected: They are hydrophobic and shielded from water; pairing holds the strands together
questions.memo: Hydrophilic sugar-phosphate backbone faces water; hydrophobic bases tucked inside. Structure follows chemistry.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the DOUBLE-STRANDED structure of DNA is BIOLOGICALLY USEFUL.
questions.expected: Two strands give a backup copy for repair if one is damaged, and each strand can act as a template for exact replication.
questions.memo: Beautiful design feature. Single-stranded RNA is less stable and lacks the built-in repair template.
options: Two strands give a backup copy for repair if one is damaged, and each strand can act as a template for exact replication.
The two strands carry completely different genetic information, doubling the amount stored.
The second strand is just structural padding and plays no role in repair or copying.
Two strands make DNA harder to copy, which is why replication is slow and error-prone.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DNA is described as a 'universal' molecule.
questions.expected: All known cellular life uses DNA as its genetic material with the same base-pairing rules, which points to a common ancestor for all life.
questions.memo: Same code from bacteria to humans. Strong evidence for common ancestry of all cellular life.
options: DNA is universal because the same physical molecule is shared and passed between all living things.
All known cellular life uses DNA as its genetic material with the same base-pairing rules, which points to a common ancestor for all life.
DNA is called universal because every organism has exactly the same DNA sequence.
DNA is universal only among animals; plants and bacteria use different genetic molecules.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the STRUCTURE of DNA fits its FUNCTION as the genetic material.
questions.expected: The sequence of bases stores information in coded form, and the double-stranded structure allows accurate replication and protection of that code.
questions.memo: Structure-function principle. The discovery of DNA's structure immediately revealed how genes could be copied.
options: DNA stores information in its sugar-phosphate backbone, while the bases simply hold the strands together.
DNA's single coiled shape is what lets it store and copy genetic information.
DNA's structure has little to do with its function; the information is stored chemically elsewhere in the cell.
The sequence of bases stores information in coded form, and the double-stranded structure allows accurate replication and protection of that code.

LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A2.title: DNA replication
LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A2.description: Semi-conservative replication; helicase, polymerase; importance of exact copying.
LSC.G12.S1.DNA.A2.recovery_strategy: Semi-conservative = each new molecule has 1 old + 1 new strand. Helicase unzips. Polymerase adds bases to match. Result: 2 identical DNA molecules.

questions.question: DNA replication is SEMI-CONSERVATIVE because:
options: Each new DNA molecule contains one old (parent) strand + one new strand
Only one new molecule is made
questions.expected: Each new DNA molecule contains one old (parent) strand + one new strand
questions.memo: Meselson + Stahl proved this in 1958 using density labelling. Critical for understanding inheritance.

questions.question: Which enzyme UNWINDS the DNA double helix during replication?
questions.expected: DNA helicase
questions.memo: Helicase 'unzips' by breaking H-bonds between bases. Polymerase comes next to add new bases.

questions.question: DNA POLYMERASE:
options: Adds new nucleotides to the growing strand using the old strand as template
questions.expected: Adds new nucleotides to the growing strand using the old strand as template
questions.memo: Reads template; adds matching complementary base. Has built-in proofreading to catch most errors.

questions.question: DNA replication produces:
options: Two identical DNA molecules from one
questions.expected: Two identical DNA molecules from one
questions.memo: Exact copies (under normal conditions). Each new cell after mitosis gets one identical molecule.

questions.question:
Order the steps of DNA replication:
(a) New nucleotides pair with templates
(b) Strands separate (helicase)
(c) Sugar-phosphate bonds form (polymerase)
(d) Two identical molecules produced
questions.expected: b → a → c → d
questions.memo: Unzip → bases pair → join with backbone → finish. Logical sequence.

questions.question: DNA replication happens during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.expected: S phase (synthesis) of interphase
questions.memo: Before mitosis or meiosis. By the time chromosomes appear, each consists of 2 sister chromatids = the 2 copies.

questions.question: True or false: DNA replication is ALWAYS perfect.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Polymerase has proofreading but small error rate (~1 in 10 billion bases). Uncorrected errors = mutations.

questions.question: Why does the body NEED DNA replication?
options: So new cells (from growth, repair, reproduction) have a complete copy of DNA
questions.expected: So new cells (from growth, repair, reproduction) have a complete copy of DNA
questions.memo: Without replication, daughter cells would have half the DNA. Body couldn't grow or heal.

questions.question: If the template strand reads 5'-A-T-C-G-3', the new strand will read:

data.calculation: Complementary: A-T, T-A, C-G, G-C, antiparallel direction

questions.memo: Complementary base pairing + antiparallel direction. A pairs with T, C pairs with G. New strand runs opposite direction.

questions.question: MUTATIONS often arise from:
options: Uncorrected errors during DNA replication, plus external mutagens
questions.expected: Uncorrected errors during DNA replication, plus external mutagens
questions.memo: Mutagens: UV light, tobacco smoke, X-rays, certain chemicals. They speed up errors or directly damage DNA.

questions.question: True or false: All cells in your body have the same DNA.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Same DNA inherited from one fertilised egg. Difference between liver/skin/muscle cells = different genes EXPRESSED, not different DNA.

questions.question: Cells with damaged DNA can:
options: Repair the damage, or undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death) if too severe
questions.expected: Repair the damage, or undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death) if too severe
questions.memo: Quality control. p53 protein triggers apoptosis. Failure → mutations accumulate → cancer risk.

questions.question: Why was the Meselson-Stahl experiment important?
options: It proved DNA replication is semi-conservative, supporting Watson and Crick's model
questions.expected: It proved DNA replication is semi-conservative, supporting Watson and Crick's model
questions.memo: Classic experimental design. Used heavy nitrogen (15N) to label parent DNA, then tracked density of daughter DNA.

questions.question: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) uses DNA replication to:
options: Make many copies of a DNA segment quickly in a test tube
questions.expected: Make many copies of a DNA segment quickly in a test tube
questions.memo: Cycle through temperatures to denature, anneal primer, extend. Doubling each cycle. SA forensic + medical labs use PCR daily.

questions.question: If one DNA molecule replicates 3 times, how many DNA molecules result?
questions.memo: Each round doubles. 1 → 2 → 4 → 8. Exponential — basis of PCR.

questions.question: True or false: Telomeres at chromosome ends shorten with each replication.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Telomere shortening linked to ageing + cellular senescence. Enzyme telomerase can rebuild them (active in stem cells + cancer cells).

questions.question: Why does the body INVEST so much in ACCURATE replication?
options: Errors accumulate over generations of cells → can cause cancer or birth defects
questions.expected: Errors accumulate over generations of cells → can cause cancer or birth defects
questions.memo: Mutation rate is balanced — low enough to prevent disease, high enough to allow evolutionary change.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SEMI-CONSERVATIVE replication is ELEGANT.
questions.expected: Each old strand acts as a template for a new strand through base pairing, giving two identical molecules that each keep a reference for future repair.
questions.memo: Beautiful self-templating system. Direct consequence of the double helix structure.
options: Each old strand acts as a template for a new strand through base pairing, giving two identical molecules that each keep a reference for future repair.
Both new molecules are made entirely from brand-new strands, with the old molecule discarded.
One new molecule keeps both old strands while the other is made of two new strands.
Replication scrambles the strands, so the two new molecules differ slightly from the original.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how DNA REPLICATION links GENERATIONS of cells.
questions.expected: Each cell division produces two daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent, which is how genetic information is faithfully passed on through growth, repair and reproduction.
questions.memo: Continuity of life at the molecular level. From zygote to adult, all cells trace back to one original DNA copy.
options: Daughter cells each get only half the parent's DNA, so information slowly fades over generations.
Each cell division produces two daughter cells with the same DNA as the parent, which is how genetic information is faithfully passed on through growth, repair and reproduction.
Replication changes the DNA each time, so daughter cells are genetically different from the parent.
Only reproductive cells pass on DNA; ordinary body cells do not copy their DNA when they divide.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DNA replication is essential for MITOSIS.
questions.expected: Mitosis splits a cell into two daughter cells that each need a full set of DNA, so DNA must replicate first, otherwise each daughter would receive only half.
questions.memo: Replication = preparation. Mitosis = distribution. Both must happen in the right order.
options: Mitosis copies the DNA itself, so a separate replication step is not really needed beforehand.
Replication happens after mitosis, once the two daughter cells already exist.
Mitosis splits a cell into two daughter cells that each need a full set of DNA, so DNA must replicate first, otherwise each daughter would receive only half.
Each daughter cell only needs half the DNA, so replication before mitosis is unnecessary.

LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A1.title: Transcription and translation
LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A1.description: RNA types; transcription (DNA → mRNA); translation (mRNA → protein); codon; one gene → one polypeptide.
LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A1.recovery_strategy: Transcription: DNA → mRNA (in nucleus). Translation: mRNA → protein (at ribosomes in cytoplasm). Codon = 3 mRNA bases = 1 amino acid.

questions.question: TRANSCRIPTION is:
