options: Making mRNA from a DNA template (in the nucleus)
questions.expected: Making mRNA from a DNA template (in the nucleus)
questions.memo: First step of protein synthesis. DNA stays in nucleus; mRNA carries the message out to ribosomes.

questions.question: TRANSLATION is:
options: Making protein from mRNA at the ribosome
questions.expected: Making protein from mRNA at the ribosome
questions.memo: Second step. mRNA codons are READ by tRNAs that bring matching amino acids. Ribosomes link them.

questions.question: A CODON is:
options: A triplet of 3 mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid
questions.expected: A triplet of 3 mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid
questions.memo: 4 bases × 3 positions = 64 possible codons → 20 amino acids (some codons are stop signals; many amino acids have multiple codons).

questions.question: RNA differs from DNA because RNA:
options: Has ribose sugar, uracil (U) instead of thymine, usually single-stranded
questions.expected: Has ribose sugar, uracil (U) instead of thymine, usually single-stranded
questions.memo: Key differences: sugar (ribose vs deoxyribose), base (U vs T), structure (single vs double strand).

questions.question: mRNA (messenger RNA) carries:
options: Genetic code from DNA to ribosome
questions.expected: Genetic code from DNA to ribosome
questions.memo: Made by transcription. Travels from nucleus → cytoplasm → ribosome. Once read, broken down.

questions.question: tRNA (transfer RNA) carries:
options: Amino acids to the ribosome, matching them to mRNA codons
questions.expected: Amino acids to the ribosome, matching them to mRNA codons
questions.memo: Each tRNA has an anticodon at one end (matches mRNA codon) and an amino acid at the other. Translates genetic code into protein.

questions.question: Where does TRANSLATION take place?
options: At ribosomes in the cytoplasm (or on rough ER)
questions.expected: At ribosomes in the cytoplasm (or on rough ER)
questions.memo: Free ribosomes make protein for use inside cell. Rough ER ribosomes make protein for secretion (with Golgi).

questions.question: If the DNA template reads 3'-T-A-C-A-A-A-3', the mRNA will be:
questions.memo: Complementary base pairing (T→A, A→U, C→G). Note T becomes U in RNA. Antiparallel direction.

questions.question: The mRNA codon AUG is special because:
options: It is the START codon — begins translation, codes for methionine
questions.expected: It is the START codon — begins translation, codes for methionine
questions.memo: AUG = 'start here, add methionine'. UAA, UAG, UGA = stop codons (translation halts).

questions.question:
Order the events of protein synthesis:
(a) tRNA brings amino acid to ribosome
(b) DNA transcribed to mRNA
(c) mRNA exits nucleus to ribosome
(d) Amino acids join into polypeptide
questions.expected: b → c → a → d
questions.memo: Transcription → transport → translation. Each step is logical and sequential.

questions.question:
On the labelled diagram of translation, which structure carries amino acids?
[Diagram: ribosome with mRNA, tRNAs labelled]
options: tRNA (transfer RNA, with amino acid attached)
questions.expected: tRNA (transfer RNA, with amino acid attached)
questions.memo: tRNAs shuttle in amino acids one by one. Anticodon end pairs with mRNA codon; amino acid end attached to the growing peptide chain.

questions.question: How many bases code for ONE amino acid?
questions.expected: 3 (one codon)
questions.memo: Triplet code. 3 bases = 1 codon = 1 amino acid. Universal across all life.

questions.question: True or false: The genetic code is the SAME in nearly all organisms.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Bacteria, plants, animals, fungi — same codon-amino acid table. Strong evidence for common ancestry. A few rare exceptions in mitochondria.

questions.question: After being made, a protein folds into:
options: A specific 3D shape determined by its amino acid sequence
questions.expected: A specific 3D shape determined by its amino acid sequence
questions.memo: Sequence → folding → shape → function. Protein folding diseases (Alzheimer's, Mad Cow) involve misfolded proteins.

questions.question: Why might TWO PEOPLE have different EYE COLOURS?
options: Different alleles of eye-colour genes → different proteins → different pigments
questions.expected: Different alleles of eye-colour genes → different proteins → different pigments
questions.memo: Variation at gene level → variation in protein → visible trait. The link from DNA to phenotype.

questions.question: Enzymes are PROTEINS, so they are made by:
questions.expected: Transcription + translation of their genes
questions.memo: Every enzyme = a protein = encoded by a gene. Defective gene → defective enzyme → disease (e.g. PKU).

questions.question: True or false: One gene can code for many different proteins.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Alternative splicing of mRNA + post-translational modification allow one gene to produce multiple proteins. Adds complexity beyond 'one gene = one protein'.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why PROTEIN SYNTHESIS is described as a 'two-step process'.
questions.expected: Transcription copies DNA into mRNA in the nucleus, then translation uses that mRNA at ribosomes to assemble amino acids into a protein.
questions.memo: Compartmentalisation in eukaryotes — DNA stays in nucleus, protein-making in cytoplasm. mRNA bridges them.
options: Transcription copies DNA into mRNA in the nucleus, then translation uses that mRNA at ribosomes to assemble amino acids into a protein.
DNA is first copied into a second DNA strand, which is then directly read by ribosomes to build the protein.
Ribosomes first read DNA into protein, then the protein is copied into mRNA for storage in the nucleus.
DNA leaves the nucleus, travels to the ribosome, and is translated straight into a protein in a single step.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a CHANGE in DNA can cause a CHANGE in PROTEIN function.
questions.expected: A DNA change can alter the codon sequence so a different amino acid is used, changing the protein's folded shape and so its function.
questions.memo: Direct link from gene to phenotype. Most mutations are neutral, but some (like sickle cell) have big effects.
options: A DNA change alters the size of the cell but leaves the protein's amino acid sequence completely unchanged.
A DNA change can alter the codon sequence so a different amino acid is used, changing the protein's folded shape and so its function.
A DNA change only affects how fast a protein is made, never which amino acids it contains.
A DNA change directly damages the finished protein without altering the gene or its coded amino acids.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why understanding the GENETIC CODE was a revolutionary scientific advance.
questions.expected: It explained how DNA's code is translated into specific proteins, linking genes to traits and underpinning modern genetics, medicine and biotechnology.
questions.memo: Cracking the code (1960s) opened biology to molecular precision. Today: PCR, GMOs, gene therapy, forensics, vaccines, all built on this foundation.
options: It proved that DNA has no role in determining traits, ending earlier ideas about genes.
It showed that proteins are inherited directly from parents rather than being built from DNA.
It explained how DNA's code is translated into specific proteins, linking genes to traits and underpinning modern genetics, medicine and biotechnology.
It allowed scientists to see chromosomes under a microscope for the first time, which is the basis of all biology today.

LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A2.title: Mutations and genetic conditions
LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A2.description: Point mutations; frameshift; genetic conditions (sickle cell, albinism, Down syndrome); mutagens.
LSC.G12.S1.PROT.A2.recovery_strategy: Point = one base. Frameshift = insertion/deletion that shifts the reading frame. Some mutations are neutral or beneficial.

questions.question: A MUTATION is:
options: A change in the DNA sequence
questions.expected: A change in the DNA sequence
questions.memo: Mutations are the raw material of evolution. Most are harmless or harmful; some are beneficial in particular environments.

questions.question: A POINT mutation involves:
options: A change in a SINGLE base (substitution)
questions.expected: A change in a SINGLE base (substitution)
questions.memo: Simplest mutation type. May change one amino acid, or have no effect (if codon redundant), or create a stop codon.

questions.question: A FRAMESHIFT mutation results from:
options: Insertion or deletion of a base, shifting the reading frame
questions.expected: Insertion or deletion of a base, shifting the reading frame
questions.memo: Reading frame = how codons are grouped. Shift = all codons downstream are wrong → usually a disastrous protein.

questions.question: SICKLE CELL anaemia is caused by:
options: A point mutation in the haemoglobin gene
questions.expected: A point mutation in the haemoglobin gene
questions.memo: A single base change → one amino acid swap → haemoglobin folds wrong → red cells deform into sickle shape under low O2.

questions.question: ALBINISM is caused by:
options: A mutation that disrupts melanin production
questions.expected: A mutation that disrupts melanin production
questions.memo: Recessive condition. Body can't make melanin (pigment in skin, hair, eyes). Higher sun-cancer risk → sun protection critical.

questions.question: DOWN SYNDROME is caused by:
options: Three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, from non-disjunction)
questions.expected: Three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, from non-disjunction)
questions.memo: Not a 'point' mutation — a whole-chromosome error. Risk rises with maternal age (less reliable meiosis).

questions.question: NON-DISJUNCTION is:
options: Failure of homologous chromosomes (or sister chromatids) to separate in meiosis
questions.expected: Failure of homologous chromosomes (or sister chromatids) to separate in meiosis
questions.memo: One gamete gets too many chromosomes; another gets too few. After fertilisation → trisomy or monosomy.

questions.question: Which is a MUTAGEN?
questions.expected: UV light
questions.memo: Mutagens = things that cause DNA damage. UV (sunlight, tanning beds), tobacco smoke, X-rays, asbestos, some chemicals.

questions.question: True or false: ALL mutations are HARMFUL.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most mutations are neutral. Some are harmful. A few are beneficial (e.g. lactose tolerance in adults, sickle-cell carrier's malaria resistance).

questions.question: MALARIA in SA + sickle-cell carriers: why is the SICKLE allele common in MALARIA areas?
options: Heterozygotes (one sickle, one normal) have partial malaria resistance
questions.expected: Heterozygotes (one sickle, one normal) have partial malaria resistance
questions.memo: Heterozygous advantage. Two sickle alleles = disease; two normal = vulnerable to malaria; one of each = best of both.

questions.question: True or false: SOMATIC mutations are passed on to children.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Somatic = body cells (not gametes). Skin cancer mutations don't pass to kids. Only germline mutations (in sperm/eggs) are inherited.

questions.question: Why does SMOKING increase CANCER risk?
options: Tobacco contains mutagens that damage DNA in lung cells
questions.expected: Tobacco contains mutagens that damage DNA in lung cells
questions.memo: Tobacco smoke has 70+ known carcinogens. They cause DNA mutations in lung cells → cells lose growth control → cancer.

questions.question: The DNA codon sequence changes from AUG-AAA to AUG-AGA. This is a:

data.description: One base changed in second codon

questions.expected: Substitution (point mutation)
questions.memo: Only one base swapped (A → G). Frame stays the same. New amino acid = arginine instead of lysine.

questions.question: Why do FRAMESHIFT mutations often cause SEVERE protein damage?
options: All codons after the insertion/deletion are read incorrectly
questions.expected: All codons after the insertion/deletion are read incorrectly
questions.memo: Imagine deleting one letter from a sentence: ABCDEFG reads correctly; ACDEFG shifts ALL letters down. Same for codons.

questions.question: Genetic counselling helps families:
options: Understand inheritance patterns + risk of passing on conditions
questions.expected: Understand inheritance patterns + risk of passing on conditions
questions.memo: Important for couples with family history of conditions like sickle cell, albinism, cystic fibrosis. Available in SA major centres.

questions.question: True or false: AGE at conception affects risk of non-disjunction.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Risk of trisomy 21 rises with maternal age. Why prenatal screening offered for older mothers.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why some MUTATIONS lead to TOTAL loss of protein function.
questions.expected: Some mutations create early STOP codons or disrupt the active site, so the protein is shortened or wrongly folded and cannot work.
questions.memo: Severe mutations → loss-of-function. Often disease-causing in essential genes.
options: Some mutations create early STOP codons or disrupt the active site, so the protein is shortened or wrongly folded and cannot work.
Some mutations simply make the protein larger, which always speeds up its normal function.
Some mutations change the DNA but cannot affect the protein, so function is always preserved.
Some mutations add extra amino acids that improve the protein's folding and boost its activity.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MUTATIONS are NECESSARY for EVOLUTION.
questions.expected: Mutations create new genetic variation in a population, and natural selection then acts on this variation, favouring traits that aid survival or reproduction.
questions.memo: No mutation = no new alleles = no evolution. Balance between mutation and selection drives biological diversity.
options: Mutations directly choose which traits will survive, replacing the need for natural selection.
Mutations always improve organisms, so every mutation is immediately favoured by evolution.
Mutations remove variation from a population so that selection can act on a uniform group.
Mutations create new genetic variation in a population, and natural selection then acts on this variation, favouring traits that aid survival or reproduction.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ALBINISM is a HEALTH concern in sunny areas like SA.
questions.expected: People with albinism lack melanin that protects against UV, so sunlight greatly raises their risk of skin cancer and eye damage; sun protection is essential.
questions.memo: Important SA public-health issue. People with albinism in some parts of southern Africa face health AND social stigma.
options: People with albinism produce extra melanin that reacts dangerously with sunlight, causing burns.
People with albinism lack melanin that protects against UV, so sunlight greatly raises their risk of skin cancer and eye damage; sun protection is essential.
Albinism only affects eye colour, so sunlight poses no real health risk to people with the condition.
People with albinism are immune to UV damage but must avoid sunlight for social reasons only.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why prenatal screening for DOWN SYNDROME is offered to many pregnant women.
questions.expected: Screening detects trisomy 21 early so parents can prepare and make informed decisions, and it is especially recommended because risk rises with the mother's age.
questions.memo: Ethical + medical consideration. Non-invasive prenatal testing now widely available in SA private sector.
options: Screening cures trisomy 21 before birth, so the baby is born without the condition.
Screening is offered only to young mothers, since older mothers have a much lower risk.
Screening detects trisomy 21 early so parents can prepare and make informed decisions, and it is especially recommended because risk rises with the mother's age.
Screening guarantees a healthy pregnancy and removes any need for further medical care.

LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A1.title: Meiosis — process and stages
LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A1.description: Meiosis I (homologues separate) and II (chromatids separate); crossing over; reduction division.
LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A1.recovery_strategy: Meiosis I = HOMOLOGUES separate (reduction). Meiosis II = SISTER CHROMATIDS separate (like mitosis). End: 4 genetically different haploid cells.

questions.question: Meiosis produces:
questions.expected: 4 haploid cells, each genetically different
questions.memo: Mitosis = 2 identical. Meiosis = 4 different. Cell goes through TWO divisions (I and II).

questions.question: Meiosis is a 'REDUCTION division' because:
questions.expected: Chromosome number halves (2n → n)
questions.memo: Diploid parent (2n) → haploid gametes (n). Restored to 2n at fertilisation.

questions.question: Meiosis happens in:
options: Sex organs (testes and ovaries) to make gametes
questions.expected: Sex organs (testes and ovaries) to make gametes
questions.memo: Only in gonads. Other cells use mitosis. Sperm + eggs are the gametes produced by meiosis.

questions.question: In Meiosis I, what separates?
questions.expected: Homologous chromosome pairs
questions.memo: Meiosis I = HOMOLOGUES separate. This is the 'reduction' step — chromosome number halves here.

questions.question: In Meiosis II, what separates?
questions.expected: Sister chromatids
questions.memo: Meiosis II = SISTER CHROMATIDS separate (just like in mitosis). Each cell already haploid; just splits into two more.

questions.question: CROSSING OVER happens during:
questions.expected: Prophase I of meiosis
questions.memo: Homologues pair up; exchange segments at chiasmata. Major source of genetic variation.

questions.question: Crossing over results in:
options: NEW combinations of alleles on chromosomes
questions.expected: NEW combinations of alleles on chromosomes
questions.memo: Mum's allele can end up on dad's chromosome and vice versa. Shuffles inheritance like a deck of cards.

questions.question: INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT means:
options: Different chromosome pairs separate independently → many possible combinations
Pairs always go to same pole
questions.expected: Different chromosome pairs separate independently → many possible combinations
questions.memo: 23 chromosome pairs in humans → 2^23 (8 million) possible gamete combinations from independent assortment alone.

questions.question: True or false: Meiosis I and Meiosis II together = TWO complete divisions.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: One cell → 2 cells after Meiosis I → 4 cells after Meiosis II. Two rounds of division but only one round of DNA replication beforehand.

questions.question:
Order the phases of meiosis:
(a) Prophase I
(b) Anaphase II
(c) Metaphase I
(d) Telophase II
questions.expected: a → c → b → d
questions.memo: Meiosis I phases (P→M→A→T) then Meiosis II phases (P→M→A→T). 8 phases total.

questions.question: If a HUMAN cell has 46 chromosomes (2n), how many in a GAMETE?
questions.expected: 23 (n, haploid)
questions.memo: Halving is the point of meiosis. Sperm + egg both have 23 chromosomes; fertilisation restores 46.

questions.question:
On the meiosis diagram, the cell with 4 visible chromosomes (was 4 originally) at PROPHASE I shows:
[Diagram: cell with homologous pairs lined up + crossing over]
options: Homologous chromosomes paired up with crossing over visible
questions.expected: Homologous chromosomes paired up with crossing over visible
questions.memo: Prophase I = pairing of homologues + crossing over. Only happens in meiosis, never mitosis.

questions.question: True or false: DNA is REPLICATED before BOTH meiotic divisions.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: DNA replicates ONCE (before Meiosis I). Two divisions follow without further replication = halving.

questions.question: Why is FERTILISATION the OPPOSITE of meiosis?
options: Two haploid gametes (n + n) combine → diploid zygote (2n)
questions.expected: Two haploid gametes (n + n) combine → diploid zygote (2n)
questions.memo: Meiosis halves; fertilisation restores. Balanced cycle. Without meiosis, chromosome number would double every generation.

questions.question: Identify the source of MOST genetic variation in sexual reproduction:
options: Crossing over + independent assortment + random fertilisation
questions.expected: Crossing over + independent assortment + random fertilisation
questions.memo: Three sources during meiosis + fertilisation. Mutations add new variation; meiosis shuffles existing variation.

questions.question: True or false: The 4 cells from meiosis are GENETICALLY identical.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: All 4 cells are genetically DIFFERENT due to crossing over + independent assortment. Mitosis gives identical; meiosis gives different.

questions.question: If a man and woman each have 2^23 possible gametes, how many possible offspring genotypes?
questions.expected: ~70 trillion (2^46)
questions.memo: Astronomical numbers. Why siblings (except identical twins) are never the same. Plus crossing over adds even more variation.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how MEIOSIS differs from MITOSIS.
questions.expected: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces 4 genetically different haploid cells to make gametes.
questions.memo: Two related but distinct processes. Mitosis = copy and divide. Meiosis = shuffle and halve.
options: Both mitosis and meiosis produce 4 identical diploid cells used to make gametes.
Mitosis produces 4 different haploid cells for growth, while meiosis produces 2 identical diploid cells for gametes.
Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair, while meiosis produces 4 genetically different haploid cells to make gametes.
Mitosis halves the chromosome number and meiosis keeps it the same, but both give identical cells.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MEIOSIS is essential for SEXUAL REPRODUCTION.
questions.expected: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores the diploid state without doubling it, and it also generates variation via crossing over and independent assortment.
questions.memo: Two key roles: prevent chromosome doubling AND generate variation. Both essential for sexual reproduction.
options: Meiosis keeps the chromosome number the same so fertilisation does not change it at all.
Meiosis doubles the chromosome number, which fertilisation then halves back to diploid.
Meiosis only copies chromosomes exactly, so it produces no genetic variation for offspring.
Meiosis halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores the diploid state without doubling it, and it also generates variation via crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how CROSSING OVER + INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT together create huge variation.
questions.expected: Crossing over shuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes, then independent assortment randomly sorts these mixed chromosomes into gametes, multiplying the variation.
questions.memo: Two shuffling steps + random fertilisation. The reason why each child is unique.
options: Crossing over shuffles alleles between homologous chromosomes, then independent assortment randomly sorts these mixed chromosomes into gametes, multiplying the variation.
Crossing over copies chromosomes exactly while independent assortment keeps every gamete genetically identical.
Crossing over only happens after fertilisation, and independent assortment occurs in body cells during mitosis.
Crossing over joins gametes together while independent assortment decides the sex of the offspring.

LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A2.title: Significance of meiosis and chromosomal abnormalities
LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A2.description: Meiosis generates variation; non-disjunction; Down syndrome; importance for evolution.
LSC.G12.S1.MEI.A2.recovery_strategy: Meiosis = variation (3 sources). Non-disjunction = chromosome stays with sibling → trisomy or monosomy.

questions.question: Why does MEIOSIS produce GENETIC VARIATION?
options: Crossing over + independent assortment shuffle alleles into new combinations
questions.expected: Crossing over + independent assortment shuffle alleles into new combinations
questions.memo: Two mechanisms during meiosis. Plus random fertilisation = three sources of variation.

questions.question: GENETIC VARIATION is important for evolution because:
options: Natural selection acts on variation → some individuals survive and pass on traits
questions.expected: Natural selection acts on variation → some individuals survive and pass on traits
questions.memo: No variation = no selection = no evolution. The raw material for adaptation.

questions.question: NON-DISJUNCTION causes:
options: Gametes with too many or too few chromosomes
questions.expected: Gametes with too many or too few chromosomes
questions.memo: Error during meiosis I or II. Resulting zygote has wrong chromosome number → various disorders.

questions.question: TRISOMY is when:
options: A cell has 3 copies of a chromosome instead of 2
questions.expected: A cell has 3 copies of a chromosome instead of 2
questions.memo: Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome (most common). Other trisomies (13, 18) usually fatal early in life.

questions.question: MONOSOMY is when:
options: A cell has 1 copy of a chromosome instead of 2
questions.expected: A cell has 1 copy of a chromosome instead of 2
questions.memo: Most monosomies are fatal. Turner syndrome (45,X) is the main viable case — affects females.

questions.question: Down syndrome features include:
options: Distinctive facial features + intellectual disability + heart issues
questions.expected: Distinctive facial features + intellectual disability + heart issues
questions.memo: Range of effects. Many people with Down syndrome lead full, productive lives with appropriate support.

questions.question: Risk of Down syndrome increases with:
questions.expected: Maternal age (older mothers)
questions.memo: Eggs are made before birth and held in arrested meiosis. Older eggs = more time for errors to accumulate.

questions.question: True or false: Down syndrome is INHERITED.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Usually not — it arises from a fresh meiosis error in the egg or sperm. Translocation Down syndrome (rare) can be inherited.

questions.question: Why are EGGS more prone to non-disjunction than SPERM?
options: Eggs are produced before birth and held in arrested meiosis for decades
questions.expected: Eggs are produced before birth and held in arrested meiosis for decades
questions.memo: Sperm regenerate fresh each ~70 days. Eggs sit waiting since fetus. More time = more error chance.

questions.question:
The graph shows Down syndrome risk vs maternal age. What pattern does it show?

| Mum's age | Risk per 1000 births |
|-----------|---------------------|
| 25        | 1                   |
| 30        | 1.3                 |
| 35        | 3                   |
| 40        | 16                  |
options: Risk rises steeply with age, especially after 35
questions.expected: Risk rises steeply with age, especially after 35
questions.memo: Non-linear rise. Many countries recommend prenatal screening for women over 35.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome (XXY):
options: Has an extra X chromosome → male with some development differences
questions.expected: Has an extra X chromosome → male with some development differences
questions.memo: 1 in ~600 males. Often diagnosed only at puberty. Hormone treatment can address some features.

questions.question: Turner syndrome (X0 / 45,X):
options: Female with one X missing → reduced fertility, shorter stature
questions.expected: Female with one X missing → reduced fertility, shorter stature
questions.memo: Only viable single-chromosome monosomy in humans. Hormone therapy + medical management help.

questions.question: True or false: Most non-disjunction events result in MISCARRIAGE.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Most chromosomal abnormalities are not compatible with development. ~50%+ of first-trimester miscarriages involve chromosomal errors.

questions.question: Why is MEIOSIS so IMPORTANT for biological diversity?
options: It produces genetically unique gametes, ensuring every offspring is different
questions.expected: It produces genetically unique gametes, ensuring every offspring is different
questions.memo: Why no two siblings (except identical twins) are alike. Provides the raw material for adaptation.

questions.question: Genetic testing on a fetus can identify Down syndrome by:
questions.expected: Counting chromosomes (karyotype) — 47 instead of 46
questions.memo: Karyotype = picture of chromosomes. Modern non-invasive prenatal tests use fetal DNA in maternal blood.

questions.question: True or false: People with Down syndrome can LIVE long fulfilling lives with support.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Average lifespan now ~60 years (was much shorter). Many lead productive lives. Inclusion + opportunity matter.

questions.question: Why does the BODY have so MANY CHECKS during MEIOSIS?
options: Errors create gametes that often produce non-viable or affected embryos
questions.expected: Errors create gametes that often produce non-viable or affected embryos
questions.memo: Checkpoints throughout meiosis catch most errors. Faulty cells often go through apoptosis.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MEIOSIS contributes more to genetic VARIATION than MUTATION alone.
questions.expected: Meiosis shuffles existing genetic variation every generation through crossing over and independent assortment, while mutation adds new variation only slowly.
questions.memo: Mutations = slow source of new alleles. Meiosis = fast shuffling of existing alleles. Both essential.
options: Meiosis creates brand-new alleles in every cell, while mutation only rearranges existing ones.
Meiosis shuffles existing genetic variation every generation through crossing over and independent assortment, while mutation adds new variation only slowly.
Meiosis removes variation each generation, so mutation alone is the faster source of diversity.
Meiosis and mutation both add new alleles at the same slow rate, so neither matters more.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why GENETIC COUNSELLING is helpful for families with chromosomal conditions.
questions.expected: Counsellors explain inheritance patterns and recurrence risks and support families in making their own informed decisions about pregnancy and care.
questions.memo: SA major centres offer genetic counselling. Provides knowledge + support without judgment.
options: Counsellors decide for families whether to continue a pregnancy and enforce that choice.
Counsellors guarantee that future children will be free of any chromosomal condition.
Counsellors only treat the affected person and do not involve the wider family.
Counsellors explain inheritance patterns and recurrence risks and support families in making their own informed decisions about pregnancy and care.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the VARIATION created by meiosis helps a POPULATION adapt to environmental change.
questions.expected: More variation means some individuals are likely to carry traits suited to new conditions, and natural selection can favour them, helping the population survive change.
questions.memo: Beneficial alleles already exist in the population due to meiotic shuffling. Selection just changes their frequency.
options: More variation means some individuals are likely to carry traits suited to new conditions, and natural selection can favour them, helping the population survive change.
Variation forces every individual to develop the same new trait at once, so the whole population changes together.
Variation causes the environment to change to suit the organisms, so no adaptation is needed.
Variation guarantees that all individuals survive any environmental change equally well.

LSC.G12.S2.VREP.A1.title: Reproduction in vertebrates — strategies
LSC.G12.S2.VREP.A1.description: External vs internal fertilisation; oviparity, ovoviviparity, viviparity; parental care; r vs K selection.
LSC.G12.S2.VREP.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.VREP.A1.recovery_strategy: External = fish/amphibians in water. Internal = reptiles/birds/mammals. Oviparous = lays eggs. Viviparous = live young. K-selection = few + much care. r-selection = many + little care.

questions.question: EXTERNAL fertilisation is typical of:
questions.expected: Most fish and amphibians (in water)
questions.memo: External = sperm + egg meet in water. Needs aquatic environment. Many gametes wasted → species produce huge numbers.

questions.question: INTERNAL fertilisation is typical of:
questions.expected: Reptiles, birds, mammals
questions.memo: Internal = sperm deposited inside female. Necessary on land where sperm can't swim freely. Fewer gametes needed.

questions.question: OVIPAROUS animals:
options: Lay eggs that develop outside the body
questions.expected: Lay eggs that develop outside the body
questions.memo: Birds, most reptiles, some fish + amphibians. Egg shell or membrane protects developing embryo.

questions.question: VIVIPAROUS animals:
options: Bear live young that developed internally
questions.expected: Bear live young that developed internally
questions.memo: Most mammals. Embryo nourished by mother through placenta. Higher investment per offspring.

questions.question: OVOVIVIPAROUS animals:
options: Keep eggs inside the body until hatching → live birth without placenta
questions.expected: Keep eggs inside the body until hatching → live birth without placenta
questions.memo: Intermediate strategy. Some sharks, snakes, lizards. Embryos nourished by egg yolk inside mother.

questions.question: r-SELECTED species typically:
options: Produce MANY offspring with LITTLE parental care
Have few offspring with much care
questions.expected: Produce MANY offspring with LITTLE parental care
questions.memo: Insects, fish, small mammals. High mortality of offspring → high numbers. 'Quantity over quality'.

questions.question: K-SELECTED species typically:
options: Produce FEW offspring with MUCH parental care
questions.expected: Produce FEW offspring with MUCH parental care
questions.memo: Elephants, humans, whales. Few offspring, long development, much investment per offspring. 'Quality over quantity'.

questions.question:
Match the animal to its reproductive strategy:
1. Frog  2. Snake  3. Lion  4. Crocodile

A. Oviparous + parental care
B. External fertilisation, oviparous
C. Viviparous, K-selected
D. Oviparous, internal fertilisation
questions.memo: Frog = external fertilisation in water. Snake = internal + lays eggs. Lion = viviparous K. Crocodile = lays eggs + guards nest.

questions.question: True or false: External fertilisation requires WATER.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Sperm need a watery medium to swim to the egg. That's why amphibians return to water to breed.

questions.question: Why do FISH typically lay HUGE numbers of eggs?
options: External fertilisation has high mortality — many eggs ensures some survive
questions.expected: External fertilisation has high mortality — many eggs ensures some survive
questions.memo: Salmon = thousands of eggs per spawn. Most don't survive. Bet hedging at extreme scale.

questions.question: Why do humans + elephants have ONE offspring at a time usually?
options: K-selected: high investment + long development → few offspring with high survival rate
questions.expected: K-selected: high investment + long development → few offspring with high survival rate
questions.memo: Long gestation + post-birth care → high cost per offspring. Population grows slowly but reliably.

questions.question: True or false: Birds always have INTERNAL fertilisation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Birds developed internal fertilisation as part of their reptilian heritage. Eggs are laid + incubated externally.

questions.question: PARENTAL CARE is typically GREATER in:
questions.expected: Mammals and birds (warm-blooded, longer-developing young)
questions.memo: Endothermic young = high energy cost = needs more care. K-selection associated.

questions.question: Why is the EGG SHELL an adaptation for life on LAND?
options: It prevents drying out + allows gas exchange + provides internal water for the embryo
questions.expected: It prevents drying out + allows gas exchange + provides internal water for the embryo
questions.memo: Amniotic egg = a 'private pond' for the embryo. Lets reptiles + birds reproduce on land without water.

questions.question: Why don't AMPHIBIANS reproduce in deserts?
options: They need water for external fertilisation + larval development
questions.expected: They need water for external fertilisation + larval development
questions.memo: Frogs return to water to breed. Tadpoles can't survive without water. Why amphibians decline with wetland loss.

questions.question: True or false: Reproductive STRATEGY is shaped by evolution.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Strategies (numbers, timing, care) are products of natural selection. Different strategies for different environments and lifestyles.

questions.question: Why is the SA cheetah's low birth rate a CONSERVATION concern?
options: Slow reproduction means populations recover slowly from declines
questions.expected: Slow reproduction means populations recover slowly from declines
questions.memo: Many SA wild cats (cheetah, wild dog, leopard) are K-strategists. Habitat loss + persecution can't be quickly reversed by reproduction.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why internal fertilisation enabled vertebrates to colonise LAND.
questions.expected: Internal fertilisation removes the need for water for sperm to reach the egg, and with amniotic eggs or live birth it freed vertebrates from water-dependent reproduction.
questions.memo: Key innovation enabling reptiles + birds + mammals to thrive far from water.
options: Internal fertilisation still needs water for sperm to swim, so it only worked near rivers and lakes.
Internal fertilisation removes the need for water for sperm to reach the egg, and with amniotic eggs or live birth it freed vertebrates from water-dependent reproduction.
Internal fertilisation made eggs dry out faster, forcing vertebrates to stay in water.
Internal fertilisation produced gills, which is what let vertebrates breathe on land.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how r-selected species cope with HIGH mortality.
questions.expected: They produce huge numbers of offspring with little parental care, so even though most die, enough survive to reproduce and maintain the population.
questions.memo: Math of survival: 0.1% of 10,000 = 10 survivors. Same survival numbers as 50% of 20. Quantity strategy.
options: They produce very few offspring but give each one intense care so none ever die.
They lower the death rate by stopping reproduction until conditions are perfectly safe.
They produce huge numbers of offspring with little parental care, so even though most die, enough survive to reproduce and maintain the population.
They survive high mortality by living much longer than other animals as individuals.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why VIVIPAROUS REPRODUCTION is EXPENSIVE.
questions.expected: The mother must nourish and protect each offspring internally at high energy and risk, so few are produced but each has a high chance of survival.
questions.memo: Trade-off across all biology: investment per offspring vs number of offspring.
options: The mother must nourish and protect each offspring internally at high energy and risk, so few are produced but each has a high chance of survival.
It is cheap because the mother carries many offspring at once with little energy cost.
It is expensive only because the eggs need large yolks before being laid externally.
The mother invests little in each offspring, producing many young with low survival.

LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A1.title: Human reproductive anatomy
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A1.description: Male and female reproductive structures; gamete production.
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A1.recovery_strategy: Sperm made in testes. Eggs released from ovaries. Fertilisation in fallopian tube. Implantation in uterus.

questions.question: Sperm cells are produced in the:
questions.expected: Testes (specifically seminiferous tubules)
questions.memo: Testes also make testosterone. Production continues throughout adult life — millions of sperm a day.

questions.question: Egg cells (ova) are produced in the:
questions.expected: Ovaries
questions.memo: Ova are made before birth + held in arrested meiosis. One matures + is released per cycle. Ovaries also make oestrogen + progesterone.

questions.question: After production, sperm pass through:
questions.expected: Testis → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra
questions.memo: Epididymis = sperm matures. Vas deferens = transport tube. Urethra = shared with urinary system.

questions.question: Seminal vesicles + prostate gland produce:
options: Seminal fluid that nourishes sperm and protects it from acidity
questions.expected: Seminal fluid that nourishes sperm and protects it from acidity
questions.memo: Seminal fluid contains sugars (energy), enzymes (clotting/dissolving), alkaline buffers (neutralise vaginal acid). With sperm = semen.

questions.question: Why are TESTES OUTSIDE the body (in the scrotum)?
options: Sperm production needs slightly LOWER temperature than core body temperature
questions.expected: Sperm production needs slightly LOWER temperature than core body temperature
questions.memo: Optimum ~35°C, not 37°C. Why high temperatures (saunas, tight underwear) can reduce fertility.

questions.question: Fallopian tubes function to:
options: Carry the egg from ovary to uterus + site of fertilisation
questions.expected: Carry the egg from ovary to uterus + site of fertilisation
questions.memo: Cilia + muscle waves move egg toward uterus. Sperm meet egg here. Implantation happens later in uterus.

questions.question:
On the labelled female reproductive system, which structure is the OVARY?
[Diagram: female reproductive anatomy front view]
options: A (small almond-shape either side of uterus)
questions.expected: A (small almond-shape either side of uterus)
questions.memo: Two ovaries, one each side. Connected to uterus by fallopian tubes.

questions.question: The uterus has three parts. Which is OUTERMOST?
questions.expected: Perimetrium (outer layer)
questions.memo: Perimetrium = outer cover. Myometrium = thick muscle. Endometrium = inner lining (where implantation happens, shed in menstruation).

questions.question: The CERVIX is:
options: The narrow lower opening of the uterus
questions.expected: The narrow lower opening of the uterus
questions.memo: Cervix connects uterus to vagina. Dilates during birth. Cervical cancer screening (pap smear) checks here.

questions.question: True or false: A woman is born with ALL the eggs she will ever have.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: ~1-2 million primary oocytes at birth. Most lost; ~400 mature + are released across a lifetime. Why eggs 'age'.

questions.question:
Match each structure to its function:
1. Testes  2. Ovaries  3. Fallopian tube  4. Uterus

A. Site of implantation + fetal development
B. Egg production + hormone production (female)
C. Sperm production + testosterone
D. Carries egg + site of fertilisation
questions.memo: Testes = sperm. Ovaries = eggs. Fallopian = fertilisation. Uterus = implantation + development.

questions.question: A SPERM cell is adapted for its job by having:
options: Long flagellum (tail), mitochondria-packed midpiece, head with enzymes
questions.expected: Long flagellum (tail), mitochondria-packed midpiece, head with enzymes
questions.memo: Designed for movement + penetration. Mitochondria for ATP. Acrosome enzymes to penetrate egg.

questions.question: An EGG cell is adapted by:
options: Large size with nutrient store + protective layers
questions.expected: Large size with nutrient store + protective layers
questions.memo: Egg = stationary; provides materials for early development. Sperm = motile; brings only DNA.

questions.question: True or false: One ejaculation contains MILLIONS of sperm.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: ~200-500 million per ejaculation. Most die en route. Only a few hundred reach the egg; only one fertilises.

questions.question: Why are MILLIONS of sperm needed for ONE fertilisation?
options: Most don't survive the journey; massive numbers maximise the chance of one reaching the egg
questions.expected: Most don't survive the journey; massive numbers maximise the chance of one reaching the egg
questions.memo: Vaginal acid + immune system + long journey kill most. Numbers are survival insurance.

questions.question: Which organ produces TESTOSTERONE?
questions.expected: Testes
questions.memo: Testes make testosterone (Leydig cells). Drives development of male features + sperm production.

questions.question: Which organs produce OESTROGEN and PROGESTERONE?
questions.expected: Ovaries
questions.memo: Ovaries make these female hormones. Drive menstrual cycle + sexual development. Adrenal also makes small amounts.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why FERTILISATION normally happens in the FALLOPIAN TUBE.
questions.expected: The egg released from the ovary enters the fallopian tube, and sperm travel up through the uterus to meet it there.
questions.memo: Ectopic pregnancy (implantation in tube) is a medical emergency — tube can rupture.
options: The egg is fertilised inside the ovary before it is released into the tube.
Fertilisation happens in the uterus, where the egg waits for sperm to arrive.
The egg released from the ovary enters the fallopian tube, and sperm travel up through the uterus to meet it there.
Sperm fertilise the egg in the vagina, and the zygote then moves up to the tube.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the SCROTUM is OUTSIDE the body cavity.
questions.expected: Sperm production needs a temperature slightly cooler than the body, and the scrotum's external position keeps the testes at this lower temperature.
questions.memo: Beautiful evolutionary solution. Cremaster muscle pulls testes closer to body in cold and lets them hang lower in heat.
options: Sperm production needs a temperature slightly cooler than the body, and the scrotum's external position keeps the testes at this lower temperature.
Sperm production needs heat higher than the body, so the scrotum hangs outside to trap extra warmth.
The scrotum is outside only to make room for the bladder inside the body cavity.
The external position protects sperm from light, which would otherwise damage them.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the FEMALE reproductive system has fallopian tubes connected to BOTH ovaries.
questions.expected: Each fallopian tube collects eggs from the ovary on its side, so if one is blocked the other can still allow fertilisation, giving a backup.
questions.memo: Bilateral anatomy = redundancy. Surgical removal of one (some cancers) doesn't end fertility.
options: Both tubes connect to a single ovary, so losing one tube ends fertility completely.
The two tubes share one egg between them, splitting it before fertilisation.
Each fallopian tube collects eggs from the ovary on its side, so if one is blocked the other can still allow fertilisation, giving a backup.
Having two tubes lets a woman release two eggs every month from the same ovary.

LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A2.title: Menstrual cycle, fertilisation and pregnancy
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A2.description: Cycle phases; FSH, LH, oestrogen, progesterone; fertilisation; implantation; pregnancy; birth.
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A2.recovery_strategy: 28-day cycle: Day 1 = menstruation; ~Day 14 = ovulation; Day 28 = end. FSH grows follicle, LH triggers ovulation.

questions.question: The menstrual cycle typically lasts:
questions.expected: About 28 days (range 21-35)
questions.memo: Average 28 days; varies between women + cycles. Day 1 = first day of menstruation.

questions.question: Ovulation typically happens around:
questions.expected: Day 14 (mid-cycle)
questions.memo: Mid-cycle for the typical 28-day cycle. Timing varies between women + cycles. Critical for fertility awareness.

questions.question: FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone) is released by the:
options: Pituitary gland; stimulates follicle growth in ovaries
questions.expected: Pituitary gland; stimulates follicle growth in ovaries
questions.memo: FSH from pituitary → follicle grows → follicle makes oestrogen. Negative feedback then lowers FSH.

questions.question: LH (Luteinising Hormone) triggers:
questions.expected: Ovulation (egg release from follicle)
questions.memo: Surge of LH at ~Day 12-13 → ovulation ~Day 14. Ovulation predictor tests detect this LH surge.

questions.question: Oestrogen is made by:
options: The growing follicle in the ovary
questions.expected: The growing follicle in the ovary
questions.memo: Oestrogen → uterine lining (endometrium) thickens. Peaks just before ovulation, triggering the LH surge.

questions.question: After ovulation, the follicle becomes the:
questions.expected: Corpus luteum (makes progesterone)
questions.memo: Empty follicle reorganises → corpus luteum. Releases progesterone for ~14 days. If no pregnancy → degenerates → period.

questions.question: Progesterone's main role is to:
options: Maintain the endometrium for possible implantation
questions.expected: Maintain the endometrium for possible implantation
questions.memo: Progesterone = 'pro-gestation'. Keeps the uterine lining ready. Drops if no pregnancy → menstruation.

questions.question: If no fertilisation, the endometrium:
options: Sheds as menstruation when progesterone falls
questions.expected: Sheds as menstruation when progesterone falls
questions.memo: Falling progesterone → blood vessels constrict → lining breaks down → menstrual bleeding for 3-7 days.

questions.question:
Order the steps of fertilisation:
(a) Sperm penetrates egg's outer layer
(b) Sperm + egg nuclei fuse
(c) Sperm enters fallopian tube
(d) Zygote forms with full chromosome number
questions.expected: c → a → b → d
questions.memo: Travel → penetration → fusion → diploid zygote. Then mitosis starts → embryo.

questions.question: After fertilisation, the embryo IMPLANTS in the:
questions.expected: Endometrium of the uterus
questions.memo: Implantation ~Day 7 after fertilisation. Placenta develops to support the embryo. Ectopic implantation in tube = emergency.

questions.question: The PLACENTA's function is to:
options: Exchange O2, nutrients, waste between mother and fetus
questions.expected: Exchange O2, nutrients, waste between mother and fetus
questions.memo: Disc-shaped organ. Fetal + maternal blood separated but very close → diffusion exchange. Also makes hormones.

questions.question: True or false: Maternal and fetal blood MIX freely in the placenta.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: They stay separate (just very close). Prevents immune rejection + blood-type incompatibility issues.

questions.question: Pregnancy in humans lasts:
options: About 40 weeks (9 months) from last menstrual period
questions.expected: About 40 weeks (9 months) from last menstrual period
questions.memo: Divided into 3 trimesters. Each has different developmental milestones. Babies before 37 weeks = premature.

questions.question: BIRTH (labour) is triggered partly by:
options: Oxytocin from the pituitary, causing uterine contractions
questions.expected: Oxytocin from the pituitary, causing uterine contractions
questions.memo: Positive feedback: contractions → more oxytocin → stronger contractions → baby pushed out. Then breastfeeding stimulates oxytocin for milk release.

questions.question: BREASTFEEDING is supported by hormones:
questions.expected: Prolactin (milk production) + oxytocin (milk release)
questions.memo: Prolactin = factory. Oxytocin = trigger for release. Suckling stimulates both.

questions.question: Why is the FIRST trimester especially important for fetal development?
options: Organs form during these weeks; harmful exposures (alcohol, drugs, infections) can cause severe defects
questions.expected: Organs form during these weeks; harmful exposures (alcohol, drugs, infections) can cause severe defects
questions.memo: Organogenesis (weeks 3-8) = most vulnerable period. Why prenatal alcohol use causes Fetal Alcohol Syndrome.

questions.question: True or false: A pregnant woman should AVOID alcohol entirely.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: No safe level. Crosses placenta → can cause Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder. SA has highest FASD rates globally.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the MENSTRUAL CYCLE is hormonally regulated.
questions.expected: Hormones from the pituitary and ovary coordinate egg development, ovulation and endometrium preparation, timing them to maximise the chance of fertilisation and implantation.
questions.memo: Beautifully synchronised system involving pituitary, ovary, uterus, brain. Disruption (stress, illness, low body fat) can stop cycles.
options: The cycle runs purely on a fixed internal clock with no hormones involved.
Hormones from the pituitary and ovary coordinate egg development, ovulation and endometrium preparation, timing them to maximise the chance of fertilisation and implantation.
Hormones only act after pregnancy begins and play no role before fertilisation.
The cycle is controlled by nerves from the spinal cord rather than by hormones.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why PRENATAL CARE matters for both mother and baby.
questions.expected: Regular check-ups detect problems early, while good nutrition, advice and screening reduce risks of complications, premature birth and birth defects for mother and baby.
questions.memo: SA antenatal clinics provide HIV testing + treatment + nutrition + folic acid. Free at public clinics.
options: Regular check-ups detect problems early, while good nutrition, advice and screening reduce risks of complications, premature birth and birth defects for mother and baby.
Prenatal care matters only for the baby, since the mother's health is unaffected by pregnancy.
Prenatal care is needed only in the final week to plan the delivery itself.
Prenatal care cures any birth defects before the baby is born, so problems never occur.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the human PREGNANCY is so LONG compared to many other mammals.
questions.expected: Humans have large brains and complex bodies needing extended development, so the long gestation produces relatively well-developed babies but usually only one at a time.
questions.memo: Trade-off: longer development = more capable baby but slower reproduction = K-strategy.
options: Humans take longer because their babies are born more helpless than any other mammal's.
Human pregnancy is long only because the mother stores extra food for the baby.
Humans have large brains and complex bodies needing extended development, so the long gestation produces relatively well-developed babies but usually only one at a time.
Human pregnancy is long because humans always produce large litters at once.

LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A3.title: Contraception and STIs
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A3.description: Contraceptive methods; common STIs; SA epidemiology; prevention.
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A3.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.HREP.A3.recovery_strategy: Condom = pregnancy + STI. Pill = pregnancy only. HIV = virus, ARV treatment + U=U. Many STIs are bacterial (curable).

questions.question: BARRIER methods of contraception include:
questions.expected: Condoms and diaphragms
questions.memo: Physically block sperm from reaching egg. Condoms also block STIs.

questions.question: HORMONAL contraceptives work by:
questions.expected: Preventing ovulation (using oestrogen and/or progestin)
questions.memo: Pill, patch, injection, implant. Tricks the body into 'thinking it's already pregnant' → no ovulation.

questions.question: An IUD (intrauterine device):
options: Sits in the uterus, preventing implantation or fertilisation
questions.expected: Sits in the uterus, preventing implantation or fertilisation
questions.memo: Copper IUD = creates hostile environment for sperm. Hormonal IUD = also thins endometrium. 5-10 years of use.

questions.question: STERILISATION (vasectomy or tubal ligation):
options: Permanent surgical method blocking sperm or eggs
questions.expected: Permanent surgical method blocking sperm or eggs
questions.memo: Considered permanent (though sometimes reversible). Vasectomy = cut vas deferens. Tubal ligation = cut/block fallopian tubes.

questions.question: NATURAL family planning relies on:
options: Avoiding sex during fertile days based on cycle tracking
questions.expected: Avoiding sex during fertile days based on cycle tracking
questions.memo: Requires regular cycles + careful tracking. Higher failure rate than hormonal methods. Cultural + religious choice for some.

questions.question: Which contraceptive method ALSO protects against STIs?
questions.expected: Male and female condoms
questions.memo: Only barrier methods block both pregnancy AND STIs. Other methods are pregnancy-only.

questions.question: HIV stands for:
questions.expected: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
questions.memo: Virus that attacks CD4+ T-cells → weakens immune system → AIDS if untreated. Major SA public health issue.

questions.question: HIV transmission DOES occur via:
options: Unprotected sex, sharing needles, mother-to-baby in pregnancy/birth/breastfeeding
questions.expected: Unprotected sex, sharing needles, mother-to-baby in pregnancy/birth/breastfeeding
questions.memo: Body fluids: blood, semen, vaginal fluid, breast milk. NOT saliva/tears/sweat. NOT casual contact.

questions.question: ARV (antiretroviral) therapy:
options: Suppresses HIV replication, lowering viral load to undetectable levels
questions.expected: Suppresses HIV replication, lowering viral load to undetectable levels
questions.memo: U=U: Undetectable = Untransmittable. People on effective ARVs can't transmit HIV. Free at SA public clinics.

questions.question: Mother-to-child HIV transmission can be prevented by:
options: Pregnant mothers taking ARVs to suppress viral load
questions.expected: Pregnant mothers taking ARVs to suppress viral load
questions.memo: PMTCT programmes in SA reduced mother-to-child HIV transmission from ~30% to <2%. Major public-health success.

questions.question: Gonorrhoea is caused by:
questions.expected: A bacterium (Neisseria gonorrhoeae)
questions.memo: STI → treated with antibiotics. Now showing antibiotic resistance globally. Untreated → infertility.

questions.question: Syphilis is caused by:
questions.expected: A bacterium (Treponema pallidum)
questions.memo: STI → progresses through stages → can be fatal untreated. Treated with penicillin. Easy to test for.

questions.question: HPV (human papillomavirus):
options: Causes warts; some types linked to CERVICAL CANCER; preventable by vaccine
questions.expected: Causes warts; some types linked to CERVICAL CANCER; preventable by vaccine
questions.memo: HPV vaccine offered in SA to Grade 5 girls. Cervical screening (pap smear) catches early changes.

questions.question: True or false: STIs are ALWAYS symptomatic.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Many STIs are asymptomatic. People can spread them without knowing. Regular testing recommended for sexually active people.

questions.question: Which STIs are typically BACTERIAL (curable with antibiotics)?
questions.expected: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia
questions.memo: Bacterial STIs are curable. Viral STIs (HIV, HSV, HPV) are managed but not eliminated.

questions.question: The graph shows SA HIV prevalence by age in women: peaks at 40% in age 30-34. What does this suggest?
options: Higher rates in working-age women; targeted prevention needed for younger ages
questions.expected: Higher rates in working-age women; targeted prevention needed for younger ages
questions.memo: Peak in 30s reflects long-term accumulation. New infections often in 15-24 age group → targeted youth campaigns critical.

questions.question: Why is COMPREHENSIVE sex education important?
options: Reduces unwanted pregnancies + STIs + supports healthy relationships
questions.expected: Reduces unwanted pregnancies + STIs + supports healthy relationships
questions.memo: Evidence shows good sex ed reduces both STIs and pregnancies. Knowledge + access to services = better outcomes.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why CONDOMS are still recommended even for couples using other contraception.
questions.expected: Methods like the pill or IUD do not protect against STIs, so condoms add this protection, especially with new or multiple partners.
questions.memo: Dual protection messaging. Free condoms widely distributed in SA clinics + public spaces.
options: Other methods like the pill or IUD prevent STIs as well, so condoms are just a backup for pregnancy.
Condoms are only useful for couples who use no other contraception at all.
Condoms protect against pregnancy but not against STIs, unlike the pill.
Methods like the pill or IUD do not protect against STIs, so condoms add this protection, especially with new or multiple partners.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why SA's HIV/AIDS programme is a global success story.
questions.expected: Free ARV treatment, PMTCT programmes and condom distribution have sharply cut HIV deaths and mother-to-child transmission, so many on ARVs reach normal life expectancy.
questions.memo: From devastating epidemic to managed chronic illness. SA has the world's largest HIV treatment programme.
options: It succeeded by banning HIV-positive people from public life rather than treating them.
Free ARV treatment, PMTCT programmes and condom distribution have sharply cut HIV deaths and mother-to-child transmission, so many on ARVs reach normal life expectancy.
It succeeded because a vaccine eradicated HIV entirely from the population.
It is a success only because HIV naturally disappeared without any treatment programme.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why HPV VACCINATION is offered to young SA girls.
questions.expected: HPV causes most cervical cancers, so vaccinating girls before sexual activity prevents infection and greatly reduces their cervical cancer risk later in life.
questions.memo: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in SA women. HPV vaccine + screening = effective prevention combo.
options: HPV causes most cervical cancers, so vaccinating girls before sexual activity prevents infection and greatly reduces their cervical cancer risk later in life.
The HPV vaccine cures cervical cancer after it has already developed in adult women.
HPV vaccination is given to protect girls against pregnancy rather than against cancer.
HPV only causes mild infections, so the vaccine is offered mainly to prevent skin warts.

LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A1.title: Central nervous system — brain and spinal cord
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A1.description: Brain parts; spinal cord; meninges; CSF; functions of each region.
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A1.recovery_strategy: Cerebrum = thinking. Cerebellum = balance/coordination. Medulla = heartbeat/breathing. Hypothalamus = temperature/water/hormones.

questions.question: The CENTRAL nervous system consists of:
questions.expected: Brain + spinal cord
questions.memo: CNS = central processing. PNS (peripheral) = all nerves outside CNS, connecting it to the body.

questions.question: The CEREBRUM is responsible for:
options: Thinking, voluntary movement, sensory perception, memory
questions.expected: Thinking, voluntary movement, sensory perception, memory
questions.memo: Largest brain region. Highly folded surface = more area for processing. Divided into lobes with different roles.

questions.question: The CEREBELLUM is responsible for:
questions.expected: Balance + coordination of voluntary movements
questions.memo: Small brain at back of head. Damage = clumsy, uncoordinated movements (ataxia). Crucial for skilled actions.

questions.question: The MEDULLA OBLONGATA controls:
options: Vital involuntary functions like heartbeat, breathing, swallowing
questions.expected: Vital involuntary functions like heartbeat, breathing, swallowing
questions.memo: At the base of the brain. Damage often fatal. Boxing, head injuries can affect medulla.

questions.question: The HYPOTHALAMUS controls:
options: Body temperature, water balance, hunger, link to endocrine system
questions.expected: Body temperature, water balance, hunger, link to endocrine system
questions.memo: Small but mighty. Maintains homeostasis. Links nervous system to endocrine system via pituitary.

questions.question: The SPINAL CORD function is to:
options: Carry signals between brain and body; control reflexes
questions.expected: Carry signals between brain and body; control reflexes
questions.memo: Information highway. Reflexes happen here without involving the brain → faster response.

questions.question: MENINGES are:
options: Three protective membranes around brain + spinal cord
questions.expected: Three protective membranes around brain + spinal cord
questions.memo: Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater. Inflammation = meningitis (often serious infection).

questions.question: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF):
options: Cushions brain + spinal cord; supplies nutrients; removes waste
questions.expected: Cushions brain + spinal cord; supplies nutrients; removes waste
questions.memo: Clear fluid in ventricles + around the CNS. Tested via lumbar puncture for meningitis or other conditions.

questions.question:
Match each brain part to its function:
1. Cerebrum  2. Cerebellum  3. Medulla  4. Hypothalamus

A. Body temperature, water
B. Balance + coordination
C. Thinking + voluntary movement
D. Heartbeat + breathing
questions.memo: Cerebrum=thinking. Cerebellum=balance. Medulla=vital reflexes. Hypothalamus=homeostasis.

questions.question:
On the labelled brain diagram, which structure is the cerebellum?
[Diagram: brain side view with cerebrum, cerebellum, brain stem, hypothalamus labelled]
options: The wrinkled rounded structure at the back-bottom
The largest folded mass at the top
The narrow stalk at the base
questions.expected: The wrinkled rounded structure at the back-bottom
questions.memo: Cerebellum = 'little brain'. Tucked behind brainstem. Coordination centre.

questions.question: True or false: The left half of the brain controls the LEFT side of the body.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Crossover. Left brain controls RIGHT body, right brain controls LEFT body. Why a stroke on left side of brain often paralyses right side.

questions.question: Which part of the cerebrum mainly controls VISION?
questions.expected: Occipital lobe (back)
questions.memo: Each lobe specialised: frontal=planning/movement, parietal=touch/space, temporal=hearing/memory, occipital=vision.

questions.question: True or false: Brain cells (neurons) can divide and replace themselves freely like skin cells.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Most neurons can't divide once mature. Some new neurons form in certain regions (hippocampus). Why brain injury is hard to repair.

questions.question: A patient has trouble with BALANCE + coordination. Likely affected area:
questions.expected: Cerebellum
questions.memo: Cerebellum damage = ataxia (uncoordinated movement). Can result from stroke, alcohol abuse, brain injury.

questions.question: STROKES happen when:
options: Blood flow to part of brain is interrupted (blockage or bleed) → brain cells die
questions.expected: Blood flow to part of brain is interrupted (blockage or bleed) → brain cells die
questions.memo: Brain cells die within minutes without O2. Why fast treatment matters. SA FAST campaign teaches stroke recognition.

questions.question: Why is the SKULL important for the brain?
options: Bony case protects soft brain tissue
questions.expected: Bony case protects soft brain tissue
questions.memo: Plus the meninges + CSF inside. Layered protection. Helmets save lives — rugby, cycling, construction.

questions.question: Why is the BRAIN highly FOLDED on its surface?
options: Folds pack more surface area into a small skull = more processing power
questions.expected: Folds pack more surface area into a small skull = more processing power
questions.memo: Gyri (folds) + sulci (grooves). About 2/3 of cortex hidden in folds. Same principle as villi, alveoli.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why a HEAD INJURY can be so serious.
questions.expected: The brain controls all body functions and is fragile, and because most neurons cannot regenerate, damage to brain tissue is often permanent.
questions.memo: Why helmets matter. SA has high rates of head injuries from road accidents + assault.
options: Head injuries are serious only because the skull bleeds heavily, not because of the brain itself.
The brain easily regrows damaged tissue, so head injuries usually heal completely within weeks.
The brain controls all body functions and is fragile, and because most neurons cannot regenerate, damage to brain tissue is often permanent.
Head injuries are minor since other organs can take over the brain's functions.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the SPINAL CORD reflexes don't go through the BRAIN.
questions.expected: Reflexes bypass the brain by going directly through the spinal cord, giving very fast responses that protect the body from harm, such as pulling a hand off a hot stove.
questions.memo: Speed matters. Brain involvement would add hundreds of milliseconds.
options: Reflexes bypass the brain by going directly through the spinal cord, giving very fast responses that protect the body from harm, such as pulling a hand off a hot stove.
Reflexes go through the brain first, which is why they are the body's slowest responses.
Reflexes skip the spinal cord and travel straight from muscle to muscle without nerves.
Reflexes avoid the spinal cord so the brain has full conscious control over them.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the HYPOTHALAMUS is described as the body's 'master regulator'.
questions.expected: It monitors and adjusts temperature, water balance, hunger and more, and it links the nervous system to the endocrine system through the pituitary gland.
questions.memo: Small but central. Damage = wide-ranging homeostatic failures.
options: It controls only body temperature and has no link to any other body system.
It pumps blood around the body and so regulates every other organ directly.
It stores memories and reasoning, which makes it the body's master regulator.
It monitors and adjusts temperature, water balance, hunger and more, and it links the nervous system to the endocrine system through the pituitary gland.

LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A2.title: Neurons, reflex arc and nervous disorders
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A2.description: Neuron structure; sensory, motor, relay; synapse; reflex arc; disorders.
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.NRV.A2.recovery_strategy: Reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay) → motor neuron → effector → response. Bypasses brain.

questions.question: A NEURON is:
options: A specialised cell that transmits electrical impulses
questions.expected: A specialised cell that transmits electrical impulses
questions.memo: Building block of the nervous system. ~86 billion in human brain. Long projections (axons) for communication.

questions.question: The parts of a neuron include:
questions.expected: Dendrites (receive), cell body, axon (sends signals)
questions.memo: Dendrites = signal input. Cell body = processing. Axon = signal output. Direction: dendrite → cell body → axon.

questions.question: MYELIN sheath:
options: Fatty insulation around axon, speeds up signal
questions.expected: Fatty insulation around axon, speeds up signal
questions.memo: Like insulation on electric wire. Allows signals to jump between gaps (saltatory conduction). MS damages myelin.

questions.question: SENSORY neurons carry signals:
questions.expected: From receptors to CNS
questions.memo: 'Afferent' = inward to CNS. Sensory (in) → relay → motor (out).

questions.question: MOTOR neurons carry signals:
options: From CNS to effectors (muscles or glands)
questions.expected: From CNS to effectors (muscles or glands)
questions.memo: 'Efferent' = outward from CNS. Causes the action that responds to a stimulus.

questions.question: RELAY (interneuron) neurons:
options: Connect sensory + motor neurons in spinal cord / brain
questions.expected: Connect sensory + motor neurons in spinal cord / brain
questions.memo: Bridge between sensory + motor in CNS. Essential for reflexes + complex processing.

questions.question:
Order a typical reflex arc:
(a) Receptor detects stimulus
(b) Effector responds
(c) Relay neuron in spinal cord
(d) Sensory neuron carries signal
(e) Motor neuron carries signal
questions.expected: a → d → c → e → b
questions.memo: Stimulus → receptor → sensory → relay → motor → effector → response. Critical for survival.

questions.question: A SYNAPSE is:
questions.expected: The junction between two neurons
questions.memo: Tiny gap between neurons. Signals cross via neurotransmitters (chemicals). Where many drugs + diseases act.

questions.question: Across a synapse, signals are transmitted by:
options: Neurotransmitter chemicals released into the synaptic gap
questions.expected: Neurotransmitter chemicals released into the synaptic gap
questions.memo: Examples: dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine. Drugs (caffeine, nicotine, antidepressants) affect this.

questions.question: PARKINSON'S disease is caused by:
options: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain
questions.expected: Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain
questions.memo: Causes shaking, slow movement, stiffness. Treatment: dopamine replacement (L-DOPA). No cure yet.

questions.question: ALZHEIMER'S disease causes:
questions.expected: Progressive memory loss + cognitive decline
questions.memo: Most common cause of dementia. Linked to abnormal protein buildup. Risk rises with age. Some genetic + lifestyle factors.

questions.question: MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS (MS) damages:
questions.expected: Myelin sheath of neurons
questions.memo: Autoimmune disease — immune system attacks myelin → signals slow → various neurological symptoms.

questions.question: True or false: Reflex actions are FASTER than voluntary actions.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Reflexes bypass brain → ~30 ms response. Voluntary actions involve brain processing → ~200+ ms.

questions.question: Touching a HOT object triggers a reflex that:
options: Withdraws the hand before pain is consciously felt
questions.expected: Withdraws the hand before pain is consciously felt
questions.memo: Withdrawal reflex. Pain signals reach brain afterward. Saves tissue from further damage.

questions.question:
On the reflex arc diagram, which arrow shows the path from RELAY to MOTOR neuron?
[Diagram: reflex arc with receptor, sensory, relay, motor, effector]
options: The arrow inside the spinal cord between two interneurons connecting to outgoing fibre
questions.expected: The arrow inside the spinal cord between two interneurons connecting to outgoing fibre
questions.memo: Relay synapses with motor neuron in spinal cord grey matter. Then motor sends signal out to effector.

questions.question: Why are NEURAL pathways HARD to REPAIR after injury?
options: Most neurons can't divide or regenerate effectively
questions.expected: Most neurons can't divide or regenerate effectively
questions.memo: Why spinal cord injuries often cause permanent paralysis. Active research area: stem cells, neural grafts.

questions.question: DRUGS like CAFFEINE work by:
options: Affecting neurotransmitters and receptors in the brain
questions.expected: Affecting neurotransmitters and receptors in the brain
questions.memo: Caffeine blocks adenosine (sleep signal) → feel awake. Many drugs (legal + illegal) work at synapses.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why the REFLEX ARC is a SURVIVAL adaptation.
questions.expected: Reflexes respond to danger before the brain processes it consciously, so the fast response can prevent injury or even save life.
questions.memo: Classic examples: hand off hot stove, blinking, knee-jerk. Universal in vertebrates.
options: Reflexes respond to danger before the brain processes it consciously, so the fast response can prevent injury or even save life.
Reflexes work slowly and deliberately so the brain has time to plan the safest response.
Reflexes are learned habits that take years to develop and offer no survival benefit.
Reflexes wait for the brain's conscious decision, which is why they protect the body so well.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how an electrical signal CROSSES a synapse.
questions.expected: At the axon end, vesicles release neurotransmitters into the synaptic gap, which bind to receptors on the next neuron and trigger a new electrical signal.
questions.memo: Chemical messenger system. Modular design — different transmitters for different functions.
options: The electrical signal jumps directly across the synaptic gap as a spark to the next neuron.
The two neurons are fused, so the electrical current simply flows through without any gap.
At the axon end, vesicles release neurotransmitters into the synaptic gap, which bind to receptors on the next neuron and trigger a new electrical signal.
Neurotransmitters block the next neuron, stopping the signal from continuing past the synapse.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why CHRONIC DISEASES like Alzheimer's are MAJOR challenges for SA's healthcare system.
questions.expected: Long-term care for cognitive decline is expensive and ongoing, and with SA's ageing population and limited resources, planning for these conditions is increasingly urgent.
questions.memo: Demographic shift = more elderly people = rising chronic disease burden. Family + community + state systems need to adapt.
options: They are minor challenges because cognitive decline needs only short-term, cheap treatment.
Long-term care for cognitive decline is expensive and ongoing, and with SA's ageing population and limited resources, planning for these conditions is increasingly urgent.
They affect only the elderly individual and place no burden on families or the state.
They are easily solved because chronic diseases like Alzheimer's can be fully cured.

LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A1.title: The eye — structure, vision and defects
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A1.description: Eye anatomy; image formation; accommodation; myopia; hypermetropia; cataracts.
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A1.recovery_strategy: Rods = low-light, B&W. Cones = colour. Myopia = eyeball too long → CONCAVE lens. Hypermetropia = too short → CONVEX lens.

questions.question: The CORNEA:
options: Clear front layer that bends light entering the eye
questions.expected: Clear front layer that bends light entering the eye
questions.memo: Provides most of the eye's focusing power. Laser surgery (LASIK) reshapes the cornea.

questions.question: The IRIS:
options: Coloured ring that controls pupil size
questions.expected: Coloured ring that controls pupil size
