questions.memo: Muscles in iris adjust pupil size for light level + close vision. Eye colour = iris pigmentation.

questions.question: The PUPIL is:
options: The dark opening in the iris that lets light through
questions.expected: The dark opening in the iris that lets light through
questions.memo: Looks black because light enters but doesn't reflect out. Pupil dilates (gets bigger) in dim light.

questions.question: The LENS:
options: Focuses light on the retina; changes shape for near or far vision (accommodation)
questions.expected: Focuses light on the retina; changes shape for near or far vision (accommodation)
questions.memo: Lens fine-tunes focus. Cataracts = clouding of lens → blurred vision. Surgery replaces with artificial lens.

questions.question: The RETINA contains:
questions.expected: Light-detecting cells (rods + cones)
questions.memo: Inner back surface of eye. Photoreceptors here send signals to brain via optic nerve.

questions.question: RODS detect:
questions.expected: Low-light + movement, black-and-white
questions.memo: More rods (~120 million) than cones. Why we see in dim light but not in colour.

questions.question: CONES detect:
questions.expected: Colour, especially in bright light
questions.memo: ~6 million cones. Three types: red, green, blue. Their combined signals give all colours.

questions.question:
On the labelled eye diagram, which structure is the LENS?
[Diagram: eye cross-section]
questions.expected: Transparent disc-like structure behind iris
questions.memo: Lens sits just behind iris. Changes shape via ciliary muscles for focus.

questions.question: MYOPIA (short-sightedness) means:
options: Can't see far objects clearly; eyeball too long → focus too short
questions.expected: Can't see far objects clearly; eyeball too long → focus too short
questions.memo: Image forms in front of retina. Corrected with CONCAVE lens (spreads light apart).

questions.question: HYPERMETROPIA (long-sightedness) means:
options: Can't see close objects clearly; eyeball too short → focus too long
questions.expected: Can't see close objects clearly; eyeball too short → focus too long
questions.memo: Image forms behind retina. Corrected with CONVEX lens (bends light closer together).

questions.question: Myopia is corrected with:
questions.expected: Concave lens
questions.memo: Concave = thinner in middle. Diverges light → image forms further back → on retina.

questions.question: CATARACTS are:
options: Clouding of the lens, causing blurred vision
questions.expected: Clouding of the lens, causing blurred vision
questions.memo: Common in older age + UV-exposed populations. SA initiatives provide cataract surgery — major cause of preventable blindness.

questions.question: ACCOMMODATION is:
options: Lens changing shape to focus on near or far objects
questions.expected: Lens changing shape to focus on near or far objects
questions.memo: Ciliary muscles pull on lens via suspensory ligaments. Near: lens thicker; far: lens flatter.

questions.question: Why does the LENS become STIFFER with age (presbyopia)?
options: Lens loses elasticity → can't change shape easily → reading glasses needed
questions.expected: Lens loses elasticity → can't change shape easily → reading glasses needed
questions.memo: Common after ~45. Why people start holding things further to read. Reading glasses = convex lens for close work.

questions.question: ASTIGMATISM is:
options: Uneven cornea/lens shape → blurred vision in some directions
questions.expected: Uneven cornea/lens shape → blurred vision in some directions
questions.memo: Often present from birth. Corrected with special cylindrical lenses in glasses.

questions.question: True or false: COLOUR blindness is more common in MALES.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: X-linked recessive condition. Males (XY) only need one bad copy. Females (XX) need two. ~8% of males vs ~0.5% of females.

questions.question: Why is the PUPIL larger in DIM light?
options: More light can enter → better vision in low light
questions.expected: More light can enter → better vision in low light
questions.memo: Reflex regulated by iris muscles. Same reason: cats' pupils slit in bright sun, round in dark.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how an IMAGE is FORMED on the retina.
questions.expected: Light is focused by the cornea and lens onto the retina, where rods and cones convert it into electrical signals carried by the optic nerve to the brain.
questions.memo: The brain processes images right-side up + filters them. Image on retina is actually inverted.
options: The retina focuses light onto the cornea, which then sends the image straight to the brain.
Light is focused by the cornea and lens onto the retina, where rods and cones convert it into electrical signals carried by the optic nerve to the brain.
Photoreceptors bend the incoming light and pass it unchanged through the optic nerve as light.
The pupil records the image directly and the lens stores it without involving the retina.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why prevention of CATARACTS matters in SA.
questions.expected: Cataracts are a leading cause of treatable blindness, and with limited eye-care access many South Africans stay blind despite a simple curative surgery.
questions.memo: SA government + Brien Holden + private sector initiatives provide free cataract surgery. Major impact on quality of life.
options: Cataracts are contagious, so preventing them stops eye infections spreading between South Africans.
Cataracts are a leading cause of treatable blindness, and with limited eye-care access many South Africans stay blind despite a simple curative surgery.
Cataracts only affect the very elderly, so prevention mainly matters for retirement planning in SA.
Cataracts cause permanent incurable blindness, so prevention is the only thing that can ever help.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why protecting EYES from UV LIGHT (sunglasses, hats) matters.
questions.expected: UV light over time damages the lens and retina, raising cataract and macular degeneration risk, so sunglasses and hats preserve vision for longer.
questions.memo: SA has high UV. Worth investing in good sunglasses, especially for kids whose eyes are more vulnerable.
options: UV light only causes temporary glare, so sunglasses are about comfort rather than protecting vision.
UV light tans the iris harmlessly, so hats and sunglasses are merely a fashion choice in sunny SA.
UV light over time damages the lens and retina, raising cataract and macular degeneration risk, so sunglasses and hats preserve vision for longer.
UV light strengthens the lens with exposure, so limiting sun actually weakens the eyes over time.

LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A2.title: The ear — hearing and balance
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A2.description: Ear anatomy; sound transmission; ossicles; cochlea; semicircular canals; deafness.
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.SENS.A2.recovery_strategy: Sound: pinna catches → eardrum vibrates → hammer/anvil/stirrup amplify → oval window → cochlea (sound) or semicircular canals (balance).

questions.question: The PINNA is:
options: The visible outer ear that catches sound
questions.expected: The visible outer ear that catches sound
questions.memo: Funnels sound waves into the ear canal. Shape varies by species (rabbits + bats have huge ones for sensitive hearing).

questions.question: The EARDRUM (tympanum):
options: Vibrates when sound waves hit it
questions.expected: Vibrates when sound waves hit it
questions.memo: Thin membrane at end of ear canal. Vibrations passed to middle-ear bones.

questions.question: The THREE ossicles (bones in middle ear) are:
questions.expected: Hammer (malleus), anvil (incus), stirrup (stapes)
questions.memo: Three smallest bones in the body. Amplify and transmit vibration from eardrum to inner ear.

questions.question: The COCHLEA is responsible for:
options: Detecting sound (converting vibrations to nerve signals)
questions.expected: Detecting sound (converting vibrations to nerve signals)
questions.memo: Spiral-shaped fluid-filled organ. Hair cells inside detect vibrations + send signals via auditory nerve to brain.

questions.question: SEMICIRCULAR canals control:
options: Balance and detection of head position/movement
questions.expected: Balance and detection of head position/movement
questions.memo: Three loops at right angles, filled with fluid. Hair cells detect fluid movement when head turns.

questions.question:
Order the path of sound through the ear:
(a) Eardrum vibrates
(b) Cochlea sends nerve signal
(c) Pinna catches sound
(d) Ossicles amplify vibration
(e) Oval window receives vibration
questions.expected: c → a → d → e → b
questions.memo: Outer (pinna + canal + eardrum) → middle (ossicles) → inner (oval window → cochlea → nerve).

questions.question: EUSTACHIAN tube connects:
options: Middle ear to back of throat — equalises pressure
questions.expected: Middle ear to back of throat — equalises pressure
questions.memo: Why ears 'pop' on planes or when diving. Blocked tube = ear pain + hearing changes.

questions.question:
On the labelled ear diagram, which is the cochlea?
[Diagram: ear cross-section]
options: Spiral snail-like structure in inner ear
questions.expected: Spiral snail-like structure in inner ear
questions.memo: Cochlea = Latin for 'snail'. Curled up to fit in skull. Sound = the part of inner ear for hearing.

questions.question: True or false: The ear is responsible for BOTH hearing and balance.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Cochlea = hearing. Semicircular canals = balance. Both in inner ear, both use hair cells in fluid.

questions.question: DEAFNESS can be caused by:
options: Damage to eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, hair cells, or auditory nerve
questions.expected: Damage to eardrum, ossicles, cochlea, hair cells, or auditory nerve
questions.memo: Many possible sites. Common: noise damage to hair cells, age-related loss, genetic deafness, infection.

questions.question: Loud NOISE exposure can damage:
options: Hair cells in the cochlea (permanent loss)
questions.expected: Hair cells in the cochlea (permanent loss)
questions.memo: Loud music + machinery + concerts damage hair cells. Won't grow back. Use hearing protection. SA mining = major risk industry.

questions.question: A COCHLEAR IMPLANT:
options: Bypasses damaged hair cells, directly stimulating the auditory nerve
questions.expected: Bypasses damaged hair cells, directly stimulating the auditory nerve
questions.memo: For people with profound deafness. Different from hearing aids (which amplify). SA implants available in major centres.

questions.question: Why does the brain interpret different vibration FREQUENCIES as different PITCHES?
options: Different parts of cochlea respond to different frequencies → mapped to pitches
questions.expected: Different parts of cochlea respond to different frequencies → mapped to pitches
questions.memo: Tonotopic organisation. Why hearing tests check different frequencies. Bass to treble = different cochlear locations.

questions.question: Why does the OVAL WINDOW have a smaller area than the eardrum?
options: To amplify pressure as vibrations transfer from air to fluid
questions.expected: To amplify pressure as vibrations transfer from air to fluid
questions.memo: Smaller area = greater pressure for same force. Critical because moving fluid (cochlea) needs more force than moving air.

questions.question: DIZZINESS often involves problems with:
options: Semicircular canals or related balance pathways
questions.expected: Semicircular canals or related balance pathways
questions.memo: Motion sickness = mismatched signals (e.g. eyes say still, balance says moving). Vertigo = problems with inner ear or brain pathways.

questions.question: Why are HEARING AIDS important for ELDERLY people?
options: Improve communication + social engagement + cognitive health
questions.expected: Improve communication + social engagement + cognitive health
questions.memo: Hearing loss linked to social isolation + faster cognitive decline. Hearing aids = significant quality-of-life improvement.

questions.question: Why is INFANT hearing screening important?
options: Early intervention dramatically improves language + cognitive development
questions.expected: Early intervention dramatically improves language + cognitive development
questions.memo: Critical period for language. SA newborn hearing screening rolling out in major centres + private hospitals.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the EAR converts SOUND WAVES into NERVE signals.
questions.expected: Sound vibrates the eardrum and ossicles, passing the vibration to cochlear fluid where hair cells bend and trigger nerve signals to the brain.
questions.memo: Mechanical → fluid → electrical chain. Each link essential. Damage anywhere = hearing loss.
options: Sound vibrates the eardrum and ossicles, passing the vibration to cochlear fluid where hair cells bend and trigger nerve signals to the brain.
Sound waves travel straight down the optic nerve, where the cochlea converts them directly into vision-like signals.
Sound is detected by the eardrum alone, which sends electrical signals to the brain without any cochlea involvement.
Sound vibrates the pinna, which generates nerve impulses directly without moving any fluid or hair cells.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MINING-RELATED hearing loss is a major SA occupational health issue.
questions.expected: Loud machinery and blasting in mines damage cochlear hair cells over time, so many SA miners suffer noise-induced hearing loss and need workplace hearing protection.
questions.memo: Compensation Fund covers occupational hearing loss claims. Prevention > treatment.
options: Mining hearing loss is caused by dust blocking the ear canal, so cleaning ears regularly prevents it.
Loud machinery and blasting in mines damage cochlear hair cells over time, so many SA miners suffer noise-induced hearing loss and need workplace hearing protection.
Mining hearing loss only affects miners after retirement, so it is a social rather than occupational health issue.
Hearing loss in mines comes from cold underground temperatures freezing the eardrum during shifts.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why YOUNG PEOPLE should limit LISTENING to loud music with EARPHONES.
questions.expected: Loud earphone music damages cochlear hair cells that do not regenerate, so the harm accumulates and can cause permanent hearing loss later in life.
questions.memo: Sub-clinical damage early → noticeable problems later. WHO recommends 60% volume + 60 min/day max.
options: Earphone music only causes temporary ringing that always fully heals, so volume limits are unnecessary.
Loud earphones bruise the eardrum, which grows back thicker, improving hearing over time.
Hearing damage from earphones only happens to older adults, so young people are not at risk.
Loud earphone music damages cochlear hair cells that do not regenerate, so the harm accumulates and can cause permanent hearing loss later in life.

LSC.G12.S2.END.A1.title: Endocrine system — major glands and hormones
LSC.G12.S2.END.A1.description: Glands; major hormones; target effects; negative feedback.
LSC.G12.S2.END.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.END.A1.recovery_strategy: Pituitary = master gland. Thyroid = thyroxine. Pancreas = insulin/glucagon. Adrenals = adrenaline/cortisol. Negative feedback keeps levels stable.

questions.question: The endocrine system uses:
options: Hormones released into the blood to regulate body functions
questions.expected: Hormones released into the blood to regulate body functions
questions.memo: Slower than nervous system but longer-lasting effects. Hormones target specific cells via receptors.

questions.question: The PITUITARY GLAND is called the:
options: 'Master gland' because it controls many other glands
questions.expected: 'Master gland' because it controls many other glands
questions.memo: Small but powerful. Controlled by hypothalamus. Releases hormones that direct thyroid, adrenals, gonads.

questions.question: THYROID gland produces:
questions.expected: Thyroxine (T3 + T4) — controls metabolic rate
questions.memo: Located in front of neck. Needs iodine. Underactive = sluggish + weight gain. Overactive = jittery + weight loss.

questions.question: PANCREAS produces:
options: Insulin (lowers blood sugar) + glucagon (raises blood sugar)
questions.expected: Insulin (lowers blood sugar) + glucagon (raises blood sugar)
questions.memo: Pancreas has dual role: digestive enzymes (exocrine) + hormones (endocrine). Islets of Langerhans make the hormones.

questions.question: ADRENAL glands produce:
questions.expected: Adrenaline + cortisol
questions.memo: On top of each kidney. Adrenaline = quick stress response (fight or flight). Cortisol = longer-term stress + metabolism.

questions.question: Ovaries produce:
questions.expected: Oestrogen + progesterone
questions.memo: Female sex hormones. Drive female sexual development + menstrual cycle.

questions.question: Testes produce:
questions.expected: Testosterone
questions.memo: Male sex hormone. Drives male sexual development + sperm production.

questions.question: HYPOTHALAMUS connects:
options: Nervous system to endocrine system (via pituitary)
questions.expected: Nervous system to endocrine system (via pituitary)
questions.memo: Hypothalamus monitors body + tells pituitary what to do. Pituitary then commands other endocrine glands.

questions.question:
Match each gland to its hormone:
1. Thyroid  2. Pancreas  3. Adrenal  4. Ovary

A. Cortisol
B. Thyroxine
C. Oestrogen
D. Insulin
questions.memo: Thyroid=thyroxine. Pancreas=insulin. Adrenal=cortisol. Ovary=oestrogen.

questions.question:
On the labelled body diagram, which gland is the pituitary?
[Diagram: body with endocrine glands labelled]
options: The small pea-shape at base of brain
questions.expected: The small pea-shape at base of brain
questions.memo: Pituitary sits in a bony pocket at base of brain. Connected to hypothalamus directly above.

questions.question: NEGATIVE feedback in hormones means:
options: Rising hormone level triggers a response that decreases further release
questions.expected: Rising hormone level triggers a response that decreases further release
questions.memo: Like a thermostat. Keeps levels stable. Most hormone systems use this. Critical for homeostasis.

questions.question: Adrenaline causes:
options: Faster heart rate, dilated pupils, energy released — 'fight or flight'
questions.expected: Faster heart rate, dilated pupils, energy released — 'fight or flight'
questions.memo: Acts in seconds. Quick stress response. Why hearts race in scary situations.

questions.question: Cortisol effects include:
options: Raises blood sugar, suppresses immune system, longer-term stress response
questions.expected: Raises blood sugar, suppresses immune system, longer-term stress response
questions.memo: Slow stress response. Chronic high cortisol = obesity, immune suppression, depression risk.

questions.question: True or false: Hormones can affect any cell in the body.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Only cells with the right receptor respond. Why testosterone affects muscle/voice but not eyes.

questions.question: ENDOCRINE differs from EXOCRINE because:
options: Endocrine = into blood. Exocrine = into ducts (saliva, sweat).
questions.expected: Endocrine = into blood. Exocrine = into ducts (saliva, sweat).
questions.memo: Pancreas does both! Endocrine = insulin into blood. Exocrine = enzymes into gut via duct.

questions.question: Why is HORMONAL action SLOWER than nervous system action?
options: Hormones travel via bloodstream — takes longer than electrical signals
questions.expected: Hormones travel via bloodstream — takes longer than electrical signals
questions.memo: Nervous = milliseconds. Hormonal = seconds to hours to days. Different time scales for different functions.

questions.question: Why does the body have BOTH nervous AND endocrine systems?
options: Different speed + duration requirements — fast short responses + slow long-term regulation
questions.expected: Different speed + duration requirements — fast short responses + slow long-term regulation
questions.memo: Complementary systems. Nervous = quick + brief. Endocrine = slow + sustained. Coordinated via hypothalamus.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how NEGATIVE FEEDBACK keeps thyroxine levels STABLE.
questions.expected: When thyroxine rises it inhibits the pituitary from releasing TSH, so less TSH means the thyroid makes less thyroxine, bringing levels back down.
questions.memo: Self-regulating loop. Same pattern for other hormone axes. Disruption = disease.
options: When thyroxine rises it tells the pituitary to release even more TSH, raising thyroxine further still.
When thyroxine rises it inhibits the pituitary from releasing TSH, so less TSH means the thyroid makes less thyroxine, bringing levels back down.
Thyroxine levels are kept stable by the kidney filtering excess hormone out of the blood.
When thyroxine falls the thyroid shuts down completely, so levels are controlled by switching off, not feedback.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ADRENALINE is sometimes called the 'fight or flight' hormone.
questions.expected: It prepares the body for sudden action by raising heart rate, releasing energy and dilating pupils, helping a person fight a threat or flee from it.
questions.memo: Ancient survival response. Still active in modern stress (exams, deadlines, traffic).
options: It slows the heart and relaxes the body so a person can rest and recover from a threat.
It is released only during sleep, preparing the body to wake up calmly the next morning.
It prepares the body for sudden action by raising heart rate, releasing energy and dilating pupils, helping a person fight a threat or flee from it.
It is called 'fight or flight' because it controls long-term growth and the decision to stay or move home.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the HYPOTHALAMUS + PITUITARY connect NERVOUS + ENDOCRINE systems.
questions.expected: The hypothalamus senses body state and signals the pituitary, which releases hormones controlling other glands, linking the nervous and endocrine systems.
questions.memo: Central integration point. Damage = wide-ranging hormonal + neural problems.
options: The hypothalamus senses body state and signals the pituitary, which releases hormones controlling other glands, linking the nervous and endocrine systems.
The hypothalamus and pituitary are both purely nervous organs that send only nerve impulses, never hormones.
The pituitary detects nerve signals and produces movement, while the hypothalamus stores hormones for later use.
They keep the nervous and endocrine systems completely separate so hormones never affect the brain.

LSC.G12.S2.END.A2.title: Diabetes and hormone disorders
LSC.G12.S2.END.A2.description: Type 1 vs Type 2 diabetes; symptoms; insulin therapy; SA prevalence; other endocrine disorders.
LSC.G12.S2.END.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.END.A2.recovery_strategy: T1 = autoimmune, no insulin. T2 = insulin resistance, often middle-aged + lifestyle. Both need management.

questions.question: DIABETES is characterised by:
questions.expected: High blood sugar levels (hyperglycaemia)
questions.memo: Body can't regulate glucose. Either no insulin (T1) or insulin doesn't work well (T2).

questions.question: TYPE 1 diabetes:
options: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells; no insulin produced
questions.expected: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells; no insulin produced
questions.memo: Usually starts in childhood/youth. Requires insulin injections for life. Not caused by lifestyle.

questions.question: TYPE 2 diabetes:
options: Body resists insulin's effects; often linked to obesity + lifestyle
questions.expected: Body resists insulin's effects; often linked to obesity + lifestyle
questions.memo: Most common type (90%+). Often manageable with diet + exercise + meds. Strong link to obesity.

questions.question: Diabetes SYMPTOMS include:
options: Frequent thirst, urination, fatigue, blurred vision
questions.expected: Frequent thirst, urination, fatigue, blurred vision
questions.memo: 'Three Ps': polyuria (urination), polydipsia (thirst), polyphagia (hunger). + Weight loss in T1, weight gain often in T2.

questions.question: Why is GLUCOSE in URINE a sign of diabetes?
options: Blood sugar is so high that kidney filtration can't reabsorb it all
questions.expected: Blood sugar is so high that kidney filtration can't reabsorb it all
questions.memo: Renal threshold for glucose ~10 mmol/L. Above this, glucose 'spills' into urine. Classic diagnostic sign.

questions.question: T1 diabetes is treated with:
questions.expected: Insulin injections + careful diet management
questions.memo: Without insulin, T1 patients would die. Modern pumps + continuous monitors improve management.

questions.question: T2 diabetes is managed by:
options: Lifestyle (diet, exercise, weight loss) + medication if needed
questions.expected: Lifestyle (diet, exercise, weight loss) + medication if needed
questions.memo: First line = lifestyle. Then oral meds (metformin). Some need insulin eventually. Can sometimes reverse with major lifestyle change.

questions.question: Untreated diabetes can lead to:
options: Heart disease, kidney failure, blindness, nerve damage, amputations
questions.expected: Heart disease, kidney failure, blindness, nerve damage, amputations
questions.memo: Chronic high sugar damages blood vessels everywhere. SA kidney failure cases largely diabetes-related.

questions.question:
The table shows SA diabetes prevalence over time. Pattern?

| Year  | Adults with diabetes |
|-------|--------------------|
| 2000  | 3.8%               |
| 2010  | 5.5%               |
| 2020  | 8.0%               |
options: Rising sharply — linked to urbanisation + diet changes
questions.expected: Rising sharply — linked to urbanisation + diet changes
questions.memo: More than doubled in 20 years. T2 diabetes major SA health concern. Why sugar tax + screening matter.

questions.question: True or false: GOITRE is caused by iodine deficiency affecting the thyroid.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Thyroid swells trying to compensate. Why SA salt is iodised. Goitre largely eliminated by iodisation programmes.

questions.question: GIGANTISM is caused by:
options: Excess growth hormone (GH) from pituitary during childhood
questions.expected: Excess growth hormone (GH) from pituitary during childhood
questions.memo: Usually due to pituitary tumour. After bone growth stops in adults, excess GH → acromegaly (enlarged hands, jaw).

questions.question: DWARFISM (pituitary) is caused by:
questions.expected: Insufficient growth hormone during childhood
questions.memo: Pituitary dwarfism. Can be treated with synthetic GH if caught early. Not to be confused with genetic forms.

questions.question: ADDISON'S disease is:
questions.expected: Adrenal glands underactive → low cortisol
questions.memo: Causes fatigue, weight loss, low BP, darker skin. Requires lifelong cortisol replacement. JFK had Addison's.

questions.question: True or false: STRESS can affect HORMONE balance + health.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Chronic stress → high cortisol → many effects: weight gain, immune suppression, mood disorders. Why managing stress matters.

questions.question: PREVENTING T2 diabetes involves:
options: Healthy diet + regular exercise + maintaining healthy weight
questions.expected: Healthy diet + regular exercise + maintaining healthy weight
questions.memo: Powerful intervention. Even modest weight loss + exercise can prevent or delay T2 onset.

questions.question: Why is INSULIN essential to LIFE for T1 diabetics?
options: Without insulin, body cells can't take in glucose → starvation despite high blood sugar
questions.expected: Without insulin, body cells can't take in glucose → starvation despite high blood sugar
questions.memo: Cells starve while blood is full of sugar. Before insulin discovery, T1 was a death sentence. Banting + Best 1921.

questions.question: Why does diabetes increase risk of FOOT amputation?
options: Nerve damage + poor circulation + slow wound healing → infections that don't heal
questions.expected: Nerve damage + poor circulation + slow wound healing → infections that don't heal
questions.memo: Small foot injuries unnoticed → infected → can't heal → amputation. Daily foot checks + good shoes = prevention.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why T2 DIABETES is a major SA PUBLIC HEALTH problem.
questions.expected: Rising obesity and urbanisation are driving T2 diabetes rates up in SA, and its serious complications strain the health system and reduce quality of life for millions.
questions.memo: SA among the top 10 globally for T2 in workers. Costs the country billions.
options: Type 2 diabetes is purely genetic and rare in SA, so it is a minor concern compared to infectious disease.
Type 2 diabetes is caused only by eating sugar and is easily cured, so it places little burden on SA.
Rising obesity and urbanisation are driving T2 diabetes rates up in SA, and its serious complications strain the health system and reduce quality of life for millions.
Type 2 diabetes mainly affects children, so it is chiefly a schooling rather than a public-health issue.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DIABETES SCREENING at clinics matters.
questions.expected: Many people have undiagnosed diabetes with no obvious symptoms, so early detection allows lifestyle changes and treatment that prevent serious complications.
questions.memo: SA clinics offer finger-prick screening. Worth doing for adults at risk.
options: Screening matters only for people who already feel very ill, since healthy people cannot have diabetes.
Many people have undiagnosed diabetes with no obvious symptoms, so early detection allows lifestyle changes and treatment that prevent serious complications.
Screening is mainly useful to confirm a cure, because once diagnosed diabetes usually resolves on its own.
Clinic screening matters because diabetes is infectious, so testing stops it spreading to other patients.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MANAGING diabetes well requires more than just MEDICATION.
questions.expected: Diet, exercise and weight management directly affect blood sugar and complication risk, so medication alone cannot fully control diabetes without these lifestyle elements.
questions.memo: Integrated approach = best outcomes. Medication adherence + lifestyle = synergy.
options: Medication fully controls diabetes by itself, so diet and exercise make no real difference to outcomes.
Diet, exercise and weight management directly affect blood sugar and complication risk, so medication alone cannot fully control diabetes without these lifestyle elements.
Once on medication a patient can eat anything, because the tablets cancel out the effect of food entirely.
Lifestyle changes replace the need for medication, so good diabetics never require any drugs at all.

LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A1.title: Thermoregulation and osmoregulation
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A1.description: Skin response; kidney + ADH; feedback loops.
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A1.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A1.recovery_strategy: Hot: sweat + vasodilation. Cold: shiver + vasoconstriction. Dry: ADH high → small concentrated urine.

questions.question: HOMEOSTASIS is:
options: Maintaining a stable internal environment despite external changes
questions.expected: Maintaining a stable internal environment despite external changes
questions.memo: Temperature, water, glucose, pH all kept within narrow ranges. Critical for cell function. Many feedback loops involved.

questions.question: Normal human body temperature is about:
questions.memo: 37 ± 0.5°C is normal. Above 38 = fever. Above 41 = dangerous (heatstroke). Below 35 = hypothermia.

questions.question: When body temperature RISES, body responds by:
questions.expected: Sweating + vasodilation (more blood to skin)
questions.memo: Sweat evaporates → cools. Vasodilation brings warm blood to skin → loses heat to air.

questions.question: When body temperature FALLS, body responds by:
questions.expected: Shivering + vasoconstriction (less blood to skin)
questions.memo: Shiver = muscle contractions generate heat. Vasoconstriction keeps blood in core → less heat lost from skin.

questions.question: The skin role in thermoregulation is to:
options: Lose/conserve heat via sweating, vasodilation/constriction, and hairs
questions.expected: Lose/conserve heat via sweating, vasodilation/constriction, and hairs
questions.memo: Skin is the body's heat exchanger. Hairs raise (goosebumps) trap air in cold. Sweat cools via evaporation.

questions.question: OSMOREGULATION is:
questions.expected: Maintaining water balance + solute concentration
questions.memo: Critical for cells. Done mainly via kidney + ADH hormone. Why drinking water + sodium matter.

questions.question: ADH (anti-diuretic hormone) released when:
options: Body is dehydrated → makes urine more concentrated
questions.expected: Body is dehydrated → makes urine more concentrated
questions.memo: Hypothalamus detects high blood concentration → ADH from pituitary → kidney reabsorbs more water → less urine.

questions.question: If you drink lots of water, what happens?
options: ADH decreases → kidneys reabsorb less water → urine more dilute + larger
questions.expected: ADH decreases → kidneys reabsorb less water → urine more dilute + larger
questions.memo: Negative feedback in action. Hypothalamus senses dilute blood → less ADH needed.

questions.question: True or false: Sweating COOLS the body by evaporation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Evaporation absorbs heat from skin. Why sweating in humid weather is less cooling (sweat doesn't evaporate well).

questions.question: VASOCONSTRICTION is:
options: Blood vessels narrowing → less blood flow to area
questions.expected: Blood vessels narrowing → less blood flow to area
questions.memo: Cold + stress trigger this. Why hands + feet get cold first in winter. Conserves core heat.

questions.question: VASODILATION is:
options: Blood vessels widening → more blood flow
questions.expected: Blood vessels widening → more blood flow
questions.memo: Heat + exercise trigger this. Face flushes red. Helps lose heat through skin.

questions.question: HEATSTROKE happens when:
options: Body's cooling mechanisms fail → core temperature dangerously high
questions.expected: Body's cooling mechanisms fail → core temperature dangerously high
questions.memo: Medical emergency. Symptoms: confusion, very hot dry skin, collapse. Common in SA summer for athletes + elderly.

questions.question: HYPOTHERMIA is:
questions.expected: Body temperature drops dangerously low
questions.memo: Severe cold exposure. Body shivers + reduces blood to extremities. Below 32°C = serious. Drakensberg + winter risks.

questions.question: FEVER is caused by:
options: Brain raising the body's 'thermostat' to fight infection
questions.expected: Brain raising the body's 'thermostat' to fight infection
questions.memo: Pyrogens from immune cells reset hypothalamic set point. Higher temperature inhibits pathogens + speeds immune response.

questions.question: Why is OSMOREGULATION especially important for cells?
options: Cells can swell + burst or shrink + die if water balance is wrong
questions.expected: Cells can swell + burst or shrink + die if water balance is wrong
questions.memo: Osmotic pressure damages cells. Why drinking too much pure water can cause cell swelling. Salt matters too.

questions.question: True or false: NEGATIVE FEEDBACK is the main mechanism in homeostasis.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Sensor → change detected → response → return to set point. Used for temperature, water, glucose, hormones, etc.

questions.question: Why does the BODY have so MANY OVERLAPPING control systems for homeostasis?
options: Multiple backup mechanisms ensure stability even if one fails
questions.expected: Multiple backup mechanisms ensure stability even if one fails
questions.memo: Body has fast (nervous) + slow (hormonal) + behavioural responses. Redundancy = robustness.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the BODY responds to a COLD day.
questions.expected: The body shivers to generate heat and constricts skin blood vessels to reduce heat loss, and hairs may stand up to trap a layer of warm air.
questions.memo: Multiple parallel responses to one stimulus. Behavioural responses too: putting on jumper, moving.
options: The body sweats heavily and widens skin blood vessels to release stored heat on a cold day.
The body shivers to generate heat and constricts skin blood vessels to reduce heat loss, and hairs may stand up to trap a layer of warm air.
The body lowers its set-point so it feels comfortable matching the cold air around it.
The body does nothing internally and relies only on putting on a jumper to stay warm.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the KIDNEY adjusts urine VOLUME to body water needs.
questions.expected: When dehydrated more ADH is released, making the collecting duct more water-permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and small, concentrated urine is produced.
questions.memo: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors → ADH → kidney. Beautiful 3-step regulation.
options: When dehydrated the kidney makes less ADH, so more dilute urine is produced to save the body water.
When dehydrated the kidney stops filtering blood entirely, so no urine is made until water is drunk.
When dehydrated more ADH is released, making the collecting duct more water-permeable, so more water is reabsorbed and small, concentrated urine is produced.
Urine volume is fixed and unaffected by hydration, since the bladder alone decides how much to release.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why HEATSTROKE is a special concern in SA's HOT regions.
questions.expected: In SA's hot regions high temperatures, intense sun and humidity overwhelm the body's cooling, and outdoor workers, athletes and the elderly are especially vulnerable, needing hydration and shade.
questions.memo: Risk rising with climate change. Public-health campaigns increasingly important.
options: Heatstroke only happens indoors, so SA's hot regions are actually safer than air-conditioned cities.
Heatstroke is caused by drinking too much water, so people in hot SA regions should limit fluids.
Heatstroke affects everyone equally, so no group needs special hydration or shade in hot regions.
In SA's hot regions high temperatures, intense sun and humidity overwhelm the body's cooling, and outdoor workers, athletes and the elderly are especially vulnerable, needing hydration and shade.

LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A2.title: Glucose regulation
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A2.description: Insulin + glucagon; negative feedback loop; link to diabetes.
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A2.strand: S2 — Life Processes in Plants and Animals
LSC.G12.S2.HOM.A2.recovery_strategy: Insulin LOWERS glucose. Glucagon RAISES glucose. Glycogen stored in liver + muscle. Feedback keeps blood sugar steady.

questions.question: Normal blood glucose is about:
questions.expected: 4-7 mmol/L (fasting)
questions.memo: Tight range. Above 11 = diabetes. Below 3 = hypoglycaemia = dangerous.

questions.question: When blood glucose is HIGH:
options: Pancreas releases INSULIN → cells take in glucose → liver stores it as glycogen
questions.expected: Pancreas releases INSULIN → cells take in glucose → liver stores it as glycogen
questions.memo: Beta cells of islets detect high blood sugar. Insulin pushes glucose into cells + storage. Lowers blood sugar.

questions.question: When blood glucose is LOW:
options: Pancreas releases GLUCAGON → liver breaks down glycogen to release glucose
questions.expected: Pancreas releases GLUCAGON → liver breaks down glycogen to release glucose
questions.memo: Alpha cells of islets detect low blood sugar. Glucagon = sugar-raising hormone. Insulin's opposite.

questions.question: Insulin LOWERS blood glucose by:
options: Helping cells take up glucose + telling liver to store glucose as glycogen
questions.expected: Helping cells take up glucose + telling liver to store glucose as glycogen
questions.memo: Most cells need insulin to take in glucose. Brain doesn't (it can use glucose without insulin). Liver stores excess.

questions.question: Glucagon RAISES blood glucose by:
options: Triggering liver to break down glycogen to glucose
questions.expected: Triggering liver to break down glycogen to glucose
questions.memo: Released between meals + during fasting. Keeps brain supplied with glucose.

questions.question: GLYCOGEN is mainly stored in:
questions.expected: Liver + muscles
questions.memo: Liver stores ~100g (for blood sugar). Muscles store ~400g (for own use only — they can't release it).

questions.question: BOTH insulin and glucagon are made in the:
questions.expected: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)
questions.memo: Different cells of the same gland. Beta = insulin. Alpha = glucagon. Coordinated opposites.

questions.question: Which is an example of NEGATIVE FEEDBACK in glucose regulation?
options: High glucose → insulin released → glucose returns to normal
questions.expected: High glucose → insulin released → glucose returns to normal
questions.memo: Classic negative feedback. Same loop for low glucose with glucagon. Keeps blood sugar in narrow band.

questions.question: The graph shows blood glucose vs time after a sugary drink. What's the typical response?

data.description: Blood glucose: baseline 5 mmol/L. After drink rises to 9 mmol/L, peaks at 30 min, then falls back to 5 mmol/L by 2 hours.

options: Rises after drink, then falls back due to insulin
questions.expected: Rises after drink, then falls back due to insulin
questions.memo: Normal glucose tolerance. Diabetics show much higher peaks + slow recovery. Test used in diagnosis.

questions.question: True or false: T2 DIABETICS produce no insulin at all.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: T2 = insulin resistance + reduced insulin production. T1 = NO insulin produced (autoimmune). Different mechanisms.

questions.question: When you EXERCISE, glucose use:
options: Rises sharply → liver releases more glucose + muscles burn glycogen
questions.expected: Rises sharply → liver releases more glucose + muscles burn glycogen
questions.memo: Sustained exercise depletes glycogen. Why athletes 'hit the wall' = glycogen runs out, fatigue hits.

questions.question: HYPOGLYCAEMIA in diabetics happens when:
options: Too much insulin / too little food → blood sugar dangerously low
questions.expected: Too much insulin / too little food → blood sugar dangerously low
questions.memo: Trembling, sweating, confusion, can become unconscious. Treat with quick sugar (sweet drink, sweets).

questions.question: Why is the LIVER central to GLUCOSE regulation?
options: It stores glycogen + releases glucose + responds to both insulin + glucagon
questions.expected: It stores glycogen + releases glucose + responds to both insulin + glucagon
questions.memo: Liver = glucose buffer. Smooths out meal-to-meal glucose changes. Why liver disease affects blood sugar.

questions.question:
On the glucose regulation diagram, which arrow shows the response to HIGH blood sugar?
[Diagram: glucose homeostasis showing pancreas, liver, blood sugar level]
options: Pancreas releases insulin → cells absorb / liver stores
questions.expected: Pancreas releases insulin → cells absorb / liver stores
questions.memo: Insulin pathway for high blood sugar. Glucagon for low. Coordinated opposites.

questions.question: Why does the BRAIN need a STEADY supply of glucose?
options: Brain doesn't store glycogen + can't use fat as quickly → relies on blood glucose
questions.expected: Brain doesn't store glycogen + can't use fat as quickly → relies on blood glucose
questions.memo: Brain uses ~20% of glucose despite being 2% of body weight. Low blood sugar = quick mental impairment.

questions.question: True or false: GLUCOSE HOMEOSTASIS involves BOTH the nervous system + endocrine system.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Stress + emotions (nervous) trigger adrenaline → raises sugar. Pancreas hormones (endocrine) tune it. Both interact.

questions.question: Why does INSULIN RESISTANCE develop in T2 DIABETES?
options: Long-term high insulin causes cells to become less responsive
questions.expected: Long-term high insulin causes cells to become less responsive
questions.memo: Sustained pressure on cells → receptors downregulate. Why catching pre-diabetes early matters.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how the BODY keeps blood sugar STEADY between meals.
questions.expected: When blood sugar falls between meals the pancreas releases glucagon, which triggers the liver to break glycogen down into glucose and release it into the blood.
questions.memo: Mirror image of insulin response. Why we can fast for hours without crashing.
options: When blood sugar falls between meals the pancreas releases glucagon, which triggers the liver to break glycogen down into glucose and release it into the blood.
When blood sugar falls the pancreas releases more insulin, telling the liver to store glucose as glycogen.
Between meals the kidney makes new glucose from urine and pumps it back into the blood.
Blood sugar stays steady because the stomach keeps digesting food continuously, even when empty.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DIABETES is essentially a homeostasis FAILURE.
questions.expected: Diabetes is a homeostasis failure: normally insulin and glucagon hold blood sugar in a narrow range, but in T1 there is no insulin and in T2 insulin does not work, so blood sugar swings dangerously.
questions.memo: Beautiful framing: diabetes = homeostasis breaking. Treatment = restoring control externally.
options: Diabetes is a homeostasis failure: normally insulin and glucagon hold blood sugar in a narrow range, but in T1 there is no insulin and in T2 insulin does not work, so blood sugar swings dangerously.
Diabetes is caused by eating too little sugar, so blood sugar simply stays too low all the time.
Diabetes is a failure of the lungs to oxygenate blood, which indirectly raises blood sugar levels.
Diabetes only means the body cannot store fat, and it has nothing to do with controlling blood sugar.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why TYPE 1 DIABETES patients must carefully BALANCE insulin + food.
questions.expected: Too much insulin or too little food drops blood sugar dangerously low (hypoglycaemia), while too little insulin keeps it high and causes long-term damage, so the two must be balanced.
questions.memo: Tightrope walk. Modern continuous glucose monitors + smart insulin pumps make it easier.
options: Insulin and food never interact, so a Type 1 patient can take any insulin dose with any meal safely.
More insulin always means better control, so patients should take the largest dose they can regardless of food.
Too much insulin or too little food drops blood sugar dangerously low (hypoglycaemia), while too little insulin keeps it high and causes long-term damage, so the two must be balanced.
Type 1 patients only need to balance food, since insulin has no effect on how much they should eat.

LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A1.title: Darwinism and evidence for evolution
LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A1.description: Natural selection (variation, struggle, survival of fittest, inheritance). 5 evidence types.
LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A1.recovery_strategy: Variation + struggle + selection + inheritance over generations. Evidence: fossils, biogeography, anatomy, embryology, DNA.

questions.question: EVOLUTION is BEST defined as:
options: Change in inherited traits in a population over generations
questions.expected: Change in inherited traits in a population over generations
questions.memo: Populations evolve, not individuals. Over generations, not lifetimes.

questions.question: Charles Darwin proposed that the mechanism of evolution is:
questions.expected: Natural selection
questions.memo: Co-developed with Alfred Russel Wallace. 'On the Origin of Species' 1859. Foundation of modern biology.

questions.question: Natural selection has FOUR key elements:
options: Variation, struggle for existence, survival of fittest, inheritance
questions.expected: Variation, struggle for existence, survival of fittest, inheritance
questions.memo: Memorise these four. They're the engine of Darwinian evolution.

questions.question: 'Survival of the fittest' means:
options: Those best ADAPTED to their environment survive + reproduce
questions.expected: Those best ADAPTED to their environment survive + reproduce
questions.memo: Fitness = reproductive success, not strength. A small fast mouse is fitter than a strong slow mouse in many environments.

questions.question: Lamarck's idea (acquired characteristics) was:
options: WRONG: traits gained in life can't be passed to offspring
questions.expected: WRONG: traits gained in life can't be passed to offspring
questions.memo: Giraffes don't have long necks because ancestors stretched. Long necks evolved because long-necked individuals had more offspring.

questions.question: FOSSIL evidence shows evolution by:
options: Recording species over geological time + transitional forms
questions.expected: Recording species over geological time + transitional forms
questions.memo: Tiktaalik = fish-tetrapod transition. Archaeopteryx = dinosaur-bird transition. Powerful evidence of evolution.

questions.question: BIOGEOGRAPHY evidence shows:
options: Related species often found near each other → suggests shared ancestry + spread
questions.expected: Related species often found near each other → suggests shared ancestry + spread
questions.memo: Darwin's finches in Galapagos. SA endemic species. Australia's marsupials. All make sense via shared ancestry + isolation.

questions.question: COMPARATIVE ANATOMY evidence includes:
questions.expected: Homologous structures (same origin, different functions)
questions.memo: Whale flippers, bat wings, human arms — same underlying bone structure (forelimb), different uses. Common ancestry.

questions.question: EMBRYOLOGY evidence shows:
options: Early embryos of vertebrates look similar → shared ancestry
questions.expected: Early embryos of vertebrates look similar → shared ancestry
questions.memo: Fish, frog, chicken, human embryos all show gill slits, tails. Suggests shared developmental program.

questions.question: MOLECULAR (DNA) evidence shows:
options: Closely related species have similar DNA sequences
questions.expected: Closely related species have similar DNA sequences
questions.memo: Humans share ~98% DNA with chimps, ~95% with mice, ~50% with bananas. Strong evidence of common ancestry.

questions.question:
Match evidence type to example:
1. Fossil  2. Biogeography  3. Anatomy  4. Molecular

A. Tiktaalik (fish-tetrapod)
B. SA Cape fynbos endemics
C. Whale flippers vs human arms
D. ~98% human-chimp DNA similarity
questions.memo: Each evidence type with classic example. Each independently supports evolution. Together = overwhelming case.

questions.question: True or false: All EVIDENCE TYPES point to the SAME conclusions about evolution.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Convergence of evidence. Independent lines (fossils, DNA, anatomy, etc.) lead to same evolutionary tree.

questions.question: ARTIFICIAL SELECTION (breeding dogs, crops) shows:
options: Humans can select traits → analogous to natural selection over generations
questions.expected: Humans can select traits → analogous to natural selection over generations
questions.memo: All dog breeds from wolves. All maize from teosinte. Powerful evidence that selection works.

questions.question: Why are HUMAN APPENDIX + WISDOM TEETH called VESTIGIAL?
options: Reduced features inherited from ancestors who needed them more
questions.expected: Reduced features inherited from ancestors who needed them more
questions.memo: Appendix = cellulose digestion in herbivore ancestors. Wisdom teeth = larger jaw in ancestors. Evidence of evolutionary history.

questions.question: True or false: Individuals EVOLVE.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Common misconception. Individuals develop + age. POPULATIONS evolve through changes in gene frequencies over generations.

questions.question: Natural selection requires:
options: Heritable variation in traits affecting reproduction
questions.expected: Heritable variation in traits affecting reproduction
questions.memo: Three requirements: variation must exist, must be heritable, must affect reproductive success. If any missing = no selection.

questions.question: Why is EVOLUTION considered SCIENCE not opinion?
options: Testable predictions + repeatedly confirmed by independent evidence types
questions.expected: Testable predictions + repeatedly confirmed by independent evidence types
questions.memo: Predictions about transitional fossils, DNA similarities, biogeography, embryology — all confirmed. Falsifiable + tested.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why VARIATION is essential for natural selection.
questions.expected: Selection can only act when individuals differ in traits affecting survival and reproduction; without variation all individuals share the same fate and no selection can occur.
questions.memo: First requirement of evolution. Why mutation + meiosis are so important.
options: Selection can only act when individuals differ in traits affecting survival and reproduction; without variation all individuals share the same fate and no selection can occur.
Variation is unimportant because natural selection creates the new traits it needs as the environment changes.
Variation only matters for artificial selection by breeders, not for natural selection in the wild.
Selection works best when all individuals are identical, since it can then act on the whole population equally.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why MOLECULAR evidence is so POWERFUL.
questions.expected: DNA sequences give a detailed record of evolutionary relationships across all life that can be quantitatively compared and produce trees consistent with other evidence.
questions.memo: Mathematical + reproducible + universal. Changed evolutionary biology since 1960s.
options: Molecular evidence is powerful because DNA can be altered to make any two species look related on demand.
Molecular evidence is weak because DNA changes randomly and cannot be compared between species.
DNA sequences give a detailed record of evolutionary relationships across all life that can be quantitatively compared and produce trees consistent with other evidence.
Molecular evidence only works for closely related species and tells us nothing about distant relationships.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why DARWIN'S theory was REVOLUTIONARY in 1859.
questions.expected: It offered a natural mechanism, selection, explaining life's diversity without supernatural intervention, and implied humans are part of nature, sharing ancestry with other species.
questions.memo: Massive intellectual shift. Slowly accepted by scientific community + then society. Foundation of modern biology.
options: It was revolutionary because it proved that life never changes and species are fixed forever.
It offered a natural mechanism, selection, explaining life's diversity without supernatural intervention, and implied humans are part of nature, sharing ancestry with other species.
It was revolutionary because it showed humans were created separately and are unrelated to any other species.
It mattered mainly because it described how individual animals choose to evolve during their lifetimes.

LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A2.title: Speciation and modern examples
LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A2.description: Allopatric vs sympatric speciation; modern selection examples; SA examples.
LSC.G12.S4.DAR.A2.recovery_strategy: Allopatric = geographic separation. Sympatric = same place but split. Resistance to antibiotics/pesticides = real-time natural selection.

questions.question: SPECIATION is:
questions.expected: Formation of a new species
questions.memo: End result of evolution. Usually slow, but can be fast under strong selection. Increases biodiversity.

questions.question: ALLOPATRIC speciation happens when:
options: Populations are GEOGRAPHICALLY separated → evolve differently
questions.expected: Populations are GEOGRAPHICALLY separated → evolve differently
questions.memo: Most common mode of speciation. Mountains, oceans, rivers split populations → different selection pressures → new species.

questions.question: SYMPATRIC speciation:
options: Species splits in the SAME geographic area (e.g. polyploidy in plants)
questions.expected: Species splits in the SAME geographic area (e.g. polyploidy in plants)
questions.memo: Rarer in animals. Common in plants via polyploidy (genome doubling → instant species). Some sympatric cichlid fish too.

questions.question: Antibiotic-RESISTANT bacteria evolved because:
options: Antibiotics killed susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survived + reproduced
questions.expected: Antibiotics killed susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survived + reproduced
questions.memo: Real-time evolution. Selection pressure = antibiotic. Why MDR-TB + MRSA are growing problems. SA major concern.

questions.question: PESTICIDE-resistant insects evolved similarly because:
options: Pesticides killed susceptible insects; resistant ones survived + multiplied
questions.expected: Pesticides killed susceptible insects; resistant ones survived + multiplied
questions.memo: Same mechanism. SA agriculture battles resistant pests, especially fall armyworm in maize.

questions.question: PEPPERED MOTH example shows:
options: Industrial pollution darkened trees → dark moths better camouflaged → more dark moths
questions.expected: Industrial pollution darkened trees → dark moths better camouflaged → more dark moths
questions.memo: Classic example of natural selection in action. Reversed when pollution decreased. Decades of evidence.

questions.question: GALAPAGOS finches are famous because:
options: Different beaks evolved for different diets on different islands — allopatric speciation
questions.expected: Different beaks evolved for different diets on different islands — allopatric speciation
questions.memo: Darwin's classic example. Each island offered different food sources → different beak shapes evolved.

questions.question: African CICHLID fish:
options: ~1000 species evolved in African Great Lakes from common ancestors
questions.expected: ~1000 species evolved in African Great Lakes from common ancestors
questions.memo: One of the fastest known adaptive radiations. Each lake has unique cichlid species adapted to different niches.

questions.question: True or false: Evolution requires MILLIONS of years.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Strong selection can produce change in years (resistance) or decades (peppered moths). Major speciation usually takes longer but not always millions.

questions.question: GENETIC DRIFT is:
options: Random changes in allele frequency, especially in small populations
questions.expected: Random changes in allele frequency, especially in small populations
questions.memo: Important alongside selection. Founder effect + bottleneck = strong drift effects. Affects evolution of small + isolated populations.

questions.question: ADAPTIVE RADIATION is:
options: Single species rapidly diversifies into many new species filling different niches
questions.expected: Single species rapidly diversifies into many new species filling different niches
questions.memo: Like Darwin's finches or cichlids. Often happens after mass extinctions or colonising new environments.

questions.question: True or false: HUMANS are STILL EVOLVING.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Examples: lactose tolerance evolved with dairying. High-altitude adaptation in Tibetans. Even modern medicine doesn't stop evolution.

questions.question: SA's CAPE FLORAL KINGDOM contains many endemic species because:
options: Isolation + diverse microclimates + fire = adaptive radiation of plants
questions.expected: Isolation + diverse microclimates + fire = adaptive radiation of plants
questions.memo: 9000+ species, mostly endemic. Classic example of adaptive radiation + speciation in plants.

questions.question:
The table shows antibiotic resistance rates in SA over time. Pattern?

| Year | MRSA prevalence |
|------|----------------|
| 2000 | 10%            |
| 2010 | 25%            |
| 2020 | 35%            |
options: Rising — selection from antibiotic use driving resistance
questions.expected: Rising — selection from antibiotic use driving resistance
questions.memo: Methicillin-resistant Staph aureus. Real-time natural selection. Why antibiotic stewardship matters globally.

questions.question: REPRODUCTIVE ISOLATION is:
options: When populations can no longer interbreed and produce fertile offspring
questions.expected: When populations can no longer interbreed and produce fertile offspring
questions.memo: Cornerstone of biological species concept. Once isolated, populations evolve independently.

questions.question: Why are CAGED RATS in cities sometimes RESISTANT to rat poison?
options: Natural selection: poison killed susceptible rats; resistant ones bred
questions.expected: Natural selection: poison killed susceptible rats; resistant ones bred
questions.memo: Warfarin-resistant rats common in many cities. Same principle as antibiotic resistance, pesticide resistance.

questions.question: Why does SA's HIGH RATE of antibiotic resistance matter GLOBALLY?
options: Resistant bacteria spread internationally via travel + trade
questions.expected: Resistant bacteria spread internationally via travel + trade
questions.memo: Modern travel + global commerce mean local resistance becomes global problem. SA's MDR-TB has spread internationally.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how ALLOPATRIC SPECIATION happens.
questions.expected: A population is geographically split by a barrier, and the two groups face different selection pressures and mutations until they become reproductively incompatible.
questions.memo: Most common mode of speciation. Underlies SA's high biodiversity given its diverse biomes.
options: A single population stays in one place but suddenly splits into two species through a chance mutation in one individual.
Two separate species merge in the same area and interbreed until they become one new species.
A population is geographically split by a barrier, and the two groups face different selection pressures and mutations until they become reproductively incompatible.
Animals choose to mate only with those that look like them, splitting the population without any geographic barrier.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE in SA is a major public health issue.
questions.expected: Resistant bacteria make infections harder and more expensive to treat, and combined with SA's HIV/TB burden this threatens to undo decades of medical progress.
questions.memo: Why antibiotic stewardship campaigns + new drug development matter. SA on frontline.
options: Resistance is a minor lab curiosity, so it has little effect on real patients or SA's health system.
Resistant bacteria make infections harder and more expensive to treat, and combined with SA's HIV/TB burden this threatens to undo decades of medical progress.
Antibiotic resistance happens because patients become immune to antibiotics, so doctors simply change the patient's diet.
Resistance only develops in countries that overuse antibiotics, so SA with its disease burden is not affected.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why STUDYING natural selection in ACTION today helps understand EVOLUTION over deep time.
questions.expected: Modern examples like antibiotic resistance and peppered moths show the same selection that shaped life for billions of years, confirming the mechanism and how small changes accumulate.
questions.memo: Past + present = same process. Why evolution is robust science not just historical.
options: Modern examples like antibiotic resistance and peppered moths show the same selection that shaped life for billions of years, confirming the mechanism and how small changes accumulate.
Selection today is a completely different process from past evolution, so modern examples cannot inform deep-time history.
Evolution can never be observed, so studying selection today tells us nothing about the past.
Modern examples prove evolution is too fast to have happened slowly over deep time, contradicting the fossil record.

LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A1.title: Hominin lineage — australopithecines to Homo
LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A1.description: Major hominin species; bipedalism, brain size, tool use trends.
LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A1.recovery_strategy: Australopithecines → Homo habilis → H. erectus → H. sapiens. We share a common ancestor with chimps, not descended from them.

questions.question: HOMININS are:
options: Humans + extinct relatives + ancestors after split from chimps
questions.expected: Humans + extinct relatives + ancestors after split from chimps
questions.memo: Includes Homo sapiens + extinct species like Australopithecus, Homo erectus, Neanderthals.

questions.question: BIPEDALISM is:
questions.expected: Walking on two legs
questions.memo: Key hominin trait. Evolved long before large brains. Frees hands for tool use, carrying.

questions.question: AUSTRALOPITHECUS species were:
options: Early hominins, bipedal, small brains, ~4-2 Mya
questions.expected: Early hominins, bipedal, small brains, ~4-2 Mya
questions.memo: First hominins. Combination of human + ape features. Mostly East + South African.

questions.question: LUCY is a famous example of:
questions.expected: Australopithecus afarensis (3.2 Mya, Ethiopia)
questions.memo: Iconic find. 40% of skeleton preserved. Clearly bipedal but small-brained.

questions.question: MRS PLES (Sterkfontein, SA) is:
questions.expected: Australopithecus africanus
questions.memo: Found by Robert Broom 1947. Cradle of Humankind. ~2.5 Mya. SA's famous hominin fossil.

questions.question: HOMO HABILIS is known as:
questions.expected: 'Handy man' — first stone tools, ~2.5-1.5 Mya
questions.memo: First Homo species. Stone tools (Oldowan). Slightly bigger brain than Australopithecus.

questions.question: HOMO ERECTUS is known for:
options: First hominin to leave Africa, ~1.8 Mya, control of fire, hand axes
questions.expected: First hominin to leave Africa, ~1.8 Mya, control of fire, hand axes
questions.memo: Sophisticated tools (Acheulian hand axes). Fire control. Migrated across Asia + Europe.

questions.question: NEANDERTHALS:
options: Robust Homo species lived in Europe + Asia, extinct ~40 kya
questions.expected: Robust Homo species lived in Europe + Asia, extinct ~40 kya
questions.memo: Brain size similar to Homo sapiens. Interbred with us — modern non-African humans have ~2% Neanderthal DNA.

questions.question: HOMO SAPIENS:
options: Modern humans, evolved in Africa ~300 kya
questions.expected: Modern humans, evolved in Africa ~300 kya
questions.memo: Our species. Out-of-Africa expansion ~70 kya. Reached every continent. Only surviving hominin.

questions.question:
Order hominins from EARLIEST to LATEST:
(a) Homo sapiens
(b) Australopithecus afarensis
(c) Homo erectus
(d) Homo habilis
questions.expected: b → d → c → a
questions.memo: Lucy (4 Mya) → handy man (2.5 Mya) → erectus (1.8 Mya) → sapiens (300 kya).

questions.question: BRAIN SIZE trend in hominin evolution shows:
options: Gradual increase, from ~400 cc (Australopithecus) to ~1400 cc (modern humans)
questions.expected: Gradual increase, from ~400 cc (Australopithecus) to ~1400 cc (modern humans)
questions.memo: Roughly tripled. Largest jumps in genus Homo. Why human bipeds with big brains are unusual.

questions.question: True or false: Humans evolved FROM CHIMPANZEES.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Common misconception. Humans + chimps share a COMMON ANCESTOR ~6 Mya. Both lineages have evolved since then.

questions.question: BIPEDALISM is advantageous because:
options: Frees hands for tools + carrying + signalling + better long-distance walking
questions.expected: Frees hands for tools + carrying + signalling + better long-distance walking
questions.memo: Multi-purpose advantage. Why bipedalism is the SIGNATURE hominin trait, evolved before large brains.

questions.question: TOOL USE in hominins shows progression from:
options: Simple Oldowan stones → Acheulean hand axes → more refined stone tools → composite tools
questions.expected: Simple Oldowan stones → Acheulean hand axes → more refined stone tools → composite tools
questions.memo: Million+ years of progression. Each step required more cognition + dexterity.

questions.question: FIRE USE was a major innovation because:
options: Provided warmth, cooking + protection from predators + enabled different foods
questions.expected: Provided warmth, cooking + protection from predators + enabled different foods
questions.memo: Cooking unlocked more nutrition + softened foods → smaller jaws + teeth evolved. Major dietary + social impact.

questions.question: Why is AFRICA central to human evolution?
options: Most early hominin fossils + DNA evidence place origins in Africa
questions.expected: Most early hominin fossils + DNA evidence place origins in Africa
questions.memo: Cradle of humanity. From Lucy in Ethiopia to SA's Sterkfontein + Naledi. African origin = consensus view.

questions.question: Many human traits are linked to:
options: Big brains + tool use + social cooperation + language
questions.expected: Big brains + tool use + social cooperation + language
questions.memo: Our 'package' of adaptations. None alone makes us human; together they do. Why we became dominant species.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why BIPEDALISM is considered the FIRST major human trait.
questions.expected: Bipedalism evolved millions of years before large brains, freeing the hands and enabling new food gathering, tool use and travel that shaped later human evolution.
questions.memo: Lucy walked upright 3 Mya but had small brain. Bipedalism was the gateway adaptation.
options: Bipedalism evolved after large brains, so walking upright was simply a result of being intelligent.
Bipedalism and large brains evolved together at exactly the same time as a single linked change.
Bipedalism evolved millions of years before large brains, freeing the hands and enabling new food gathering, tool use and travel that shaped later human evolution.
Bipedalism mainly evolved to help early humans swim, and only later affected life on land.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences why FOSSIL EVIDENCE for human evolution is INCOMPLETE.
questions.expected: Fossilisation is rare and many bones are lost to erosion or damage, yet despite the gaps the existing fossils consistently support the evolutionary pattern.
questions.memo: Gaps don't refute evolution — they reflect taphonomy. New finds (like Naledi) keep filling in.
options: The fossil record is incomplete because evolution did not really happen, so there are no transitional forms to find.
The gaps in the fossil record prove humans appeared suddenly without any evolutionary ancestors.
Fossils are incomplete because scientists hide bones that contradict evolution.
Fossilisation is rare and many bones are lost to erosion or damage, yet despite the gaps the existing fossils consistently support the evolutionary pattern.

questions.question: Explain in two sentences how MULTIPLE EVIDENCE TYPES converge on HUMAN EVOLUTION.
questions.expected: Fossils show transitional forms, DNA confirms relationships with other primates, and anatomy and embryology show shared origins, all independently pointing to humans evolving from earlier hominins.
questions.memo: Convergent evidence = strongest form of scientific support.
options: Only fossils support human evolution, while DNA and anatomy actually point to separate human creation.
Fossils show transitional forms, DNA confirms relationships with other primates, and anatomy and embryology show shared origins, all independently pointing to humans evolving from earlier hominins.
Each line of evidence gives a different answer, so the evidence for human evolution actually conflicts.
Human evolution rests on a single DNA study, with no support from fossils or anatomy.

LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A2.title: South African fossils and Out-of-Africa
LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A2.description: Mrs Ples, Karabo, Naledi; Cradle of Humankind; Out-of-Africa theory; SA contributions.
LSC.G12.S4.HUM.A2.recovery_strategy: Mrs Ples = A. africanus. Karabo = A. sediba. Naledi = Homo naledi. Out-of-Africa: H. sapiens evolved in Africa ~300 kya, then spread globally.

questions.question: The CRADLE OF HUMANKIND is:
options: A UNESCO site near Johannesburg with major hominin fossil discoveries
questions.expected: A UNESCO site near Johannesburg with major hominin fossil discoveries
questions.memo: Includes Sterkfontein, Malapa, Rising Star, more. Some of world's most important hominin fossil sites.

questions.question: MRS PLES was found at:
questions.expected: Sterkfontein cave (SA)
questions.memo: Robert Broom 1947. Major SA discovery. Skull of Australopithecus africanus ~2.5 Mya.

questions.question: KARABO is:
options: Australopithecus sediba — Malapa cave SA, ~2 Mya
questions.expected: Australopithecus sediba — Malapa cave SA, ~2 Mya
questions.memo: Found 2008 by Lee Berger's son Matthew. Mix of australopith + Homo features. Possible transition.

questions.question: HOMO NALEDI was found at:
questions.expected: Rising Star cave system, SA (announced 2015)
questions.memo: Led by Lee Berger. Hundreds of fossils. Mosaic features. Age debated — possibly only ~250 kya, surprisingly recent.

questions.question: OUT-OF-AFRICA theory says:
options: Modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa, then spread globally ~70 kya
questions.expected: Modern Homo sapiens evolved in Africa, then spread globally ~70 kya
questions.memo: Now well-supported by DNA + fossil evidence. Africa is the cradle, with everyone outside Africa descended from these migrants.

questions.question: GENETIC evidence supports out-of-Africa because:
options: African populations have most genetic diversity → reflects oldest origin
questions.expected: African populations have most genetic diversity → reflects oldest origin
questions.memo: Subsequent migrations were small subsets of African diversity = founder effects on each continent.

questions.question: True or false: SA has globally important HOMININ fossil sites.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Cradle of Humankind alone has ~40% of world's known hominin fossils. SA scientists central to discoveries.

questions.question: Robert Broom discovered:
questions.expected: Many australopith fossils at Sterkfontein
questions.memo: Scottish-born SA physician + palaeontologist. Made Sterkfontein into a major hominin site. Mrs Ples + many others.

questions.question: Lee Berger is famous for:
questions.expected: Discovering Australopithecus sediba + Homo naledi
questions.memo: Modern SA palaeoanthropologist. Used new methods (citizen scientists, social media announcement, open access).

questions.question: Phillip Tobias contributed:
options: Major work on Sterkfontein australopiths + brain evolution
questions.expected: Major work on Sterkfontein australopiths + brain evolution
questions.memo: Wits University professor. International authority on hominin brain evolution. Highly respected globally.

questions.question: Why is the Cradle of Humankind a UNESCO WORLD HERITAGE site?
options: Globally unique density + diversity of hominin fossils
questions.expected: Globally unique density + diversity of hominin fossils
questions.memo: Declared 1999. Recognises scientific + cultural significance for understanding human origins.

questions.question: When did MODERN HUMANS leave Africa?
questions.expected: ~70 thousand years ago (last major wave)
questions.memo: Earlier waves too, but the dominant out-of-Africa migration was ~70 kya. Reached every continent except Antarctica.

questions.question: True or false: SA Indigenous KHOI-SAN people have especially DEEP genetic ROOTS.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Khoi-San carry some of oldest genetic lineages on Earth. Direct evidence of Africa as cradle. Globally significant heritage.

questions.question: FOSSIL DATING uses methods like:
questions.expected: Radiocarbon (younger), uranium-lead (older), stratigraphy
questions.memo: Different methods for different time scales. Multiple methods used together for reliability.

questions.question: Why are NEW DISCOVERIES like NALEDI exciting?
options: They reveal new hominin diversity + sometimes overturn previous assumptions
questions.expected: They reveal new hominin diversity + sometimes overturn previous assumptions
questions.memo: Naledi's possibly recent age (~250 kya) was surprising for a primitive species. May have co-existed with H. sapiens.

questions.question: TheJacovec Cavern at Sterkfontein contains some of:
options: The OLDEST known southern Africa hominin fossils
questions.expected: The OLDEST known southern Africa hominin fossils
